title: Sharing Local MCP Tools Between Machines with MCPWire
description:
A teammate’s agent needs to use a tool that already works on your machine, but running it on theirs means installing the server, configuring credentials, and reproducing access to the systems behind it. If the tool depends on a local database, an internal network, or a browser session, copying its configuration may not be enough.

I built MCPWire to share that existing execution environment through MCP, while keeping the server process and its configured credentials on the host. The guest runs a small bridge that looks like a local stdio MCP server to their client, and requests travel across a Noise-encrypted peer connection to your machine.

The interesting part is where execution and authority end up, because keeping a credential on your laptop still lets someone else exercise some of its permissions through an allowed tool. The architecture has to make that delegation explicit.

Two bridges around an existing server

MCPWire has two commands, share on the host and join on the guest, with the existing MCP server running as a child process on the host side. The client and server continue exchanging newline-delimited JSON-RPC through standard input and output.

On the guest, join connects the client’s stdin and stdout to the peer socket, while diagnostic messages go to stderr so they do not corrupt the protocol stream. It accepts one host connection per join process.

On the host, share inspects the traffic before forwarding it to the child process, rejecting disallowed tool calls and filtering the tool descriptors returned to the guest. The implementation is small enough to follow in join.ts and share.ts, without introducing a separate application protocol around MCP.

Each connected peer gets its own MCP child process, so two guests do not send their initialization messages into the same server process or share its in-memory session state. They can still reach the same files, database, and external services, and starting a separate process does not create an operating-system sandbox.

Discovery and the session ticket

When the host starts sharing, it generates 32 random bytes and encodes them as a wire:// ticket, which both sides use as the discovery topic in Hyperswarm. The host announces on that topic, and the guest looks for a host using the same value.

The default discovery network is the public Hyperswarm DHT, with HyperDHT handling connection establishment and attempting UDP hole punching across NATs. MCPWire does not operate its own relay service, but the connection still depends on networking infrastructure and the behavior of the networks at both ends.

That means a restrictive firewall or NAT configuration can prevent a connection, even when both developers have internet access and the ticket is correct. A peer connection reduces the infrastructure you need to deploy, while giving up the predictable reachability you might get from a publicly accessible hosted endpoint.

The ticket identifies the discovery topic, and the Noise connection supplies encryption; the ticket itself is neither an encryption key nor an identity certificate for your teammate. MCPWire does not bind it to a named user, so it must be handled as an access credential and delivered through a trusted channel.

A ticket remains reusable while its host session is running, and starting a new host session generates a new one, rather than maintaining a permanent address for that server. Custom DHT bootstrap nodes are configurable through MCPWIRE_BOOTSTRAP, as shown in the network setup code.

Following a tool call through the host

Suppose you expose a filesystem server with read_file and list_directory allowed, and the guest asks their agent to inspect a file in the shared directory. The agent first discovers the server’s tools, then sends a tools/call request through its local MCP client.

When the server returns its tool descriptors, MCPWire filters the list using the host’s policy, so the guest sees the tools selected for that session. When an actual call arrives, MCPWire checks the requested tool name again before writing the request to the server’s stdin.

Both checks matter, because hiding write_file from the advertised list does not stop a client from sending a request with that name anyway. The execution check is what prevents a disallowed call from reaching the child process.

The policy implementation gives an explicit deny precedence over an allow, and an omitted allowlist permits every tool that has not been denied. An empty allowlist permits no tools.

With --confirm, an allowed call also requires approval in the host terminal, where the operator can reject it, approve it once, or approve that tool for the rest of the session. That last choice is shared session policy, so it should not be interpreted as approval limited to one guest connection.

The boundary of a tool permission

Allowing read_file controls which operation can be requested, but the filesystem server still decides which paths are valid and which files its process can read. Similarly, allowing a SQL tool says nothing about whether the submitted query can modify data, unless the server or database enforces that restriction.

The current policy checks tool names, without validating their arguments, filtering MCP resources or prompts, or restricting the child process’s access to the host. Credentials with limited permissions and a narrowly configured server remain necessary, even when the session exposes only one tool.

This also explains the difference between keeping credentials local and keeping data local, because a tool can use a local credential to retrieve information that it then returns to the guest. MCPWire avoids requiring the guest to configure that credential, but the permitted responses still cross the connection and enter the guest’s MCP client.

Optional --redact-secrets processing scans outbound messages for recognized patterns before sending them, replacing matches with [REDACTED_BY_MCPWIRE]. Pattern matching can miss a private value or change legitimate output, so it adds a check on responses without establishing that everything leaving the machine is safe.

Session limits and failure semantics

The host can set a time limit with --ttl and a forwarded tool-call budget with --max-calls, with the call counter shared across the session’s peers. Neither limit is enabled by default, and redaction and manual approval also require explicit flags.

On a peer disconnect, the host requests termination of that peer’s child process, but terminating a process cannot reverse an operation already committed to a database or external service. A tool that completed a write just before the connection failed may leave the guest without its response.

MCPWire does not automatically replay calls after a disconnect, because resending a request could execute that write a second time while making the failure look recovered. The application needs an operation identifier, a way to inspect the result, or another recovery mechanism before a retry can be considered safe.

The optional session recorder stores local events and response metadata, including timing and success or error status, rather than full response bodies. Its records also include the ticket, server command, and unredacted argument previews, so a recording can itself contain sensitive information even when response redaction is enabled.

A small filesystem example

For a first test, use a dedicated directory with disposable data, then expose only the read and directory-listing tools for a session lasting 30 minutes. The CLI requires Node.js 18 or newer, while the pinned filesystem server below requires Node.js 24 or newer on the host.

mkdir -p "$HOME/mcpwire-demo"
printf 'Hello from the host.\n' > "$HOME/mcpwire-demo/hello.txt"

npx -y @mcpwire/cli share \
  --name shared-files \
  --allow "read_file,list_directory" \
  --redact-secrets \
  --ttl 30m \
  -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem@2.0.1 \
  "$HOME/mcpwire-demo"

The host prints a client configuration containing its session ticket, which the guest adds to a client that supports stdio MCP servers. A configuration using the mcpServers convention has this shape, with the placeholder replaced by the full ticket from the host:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "shared-files": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y",
        "@mcpwire/cli",
        "join",
        "wire://PASTE_THE_FULL_TICKET_FROM_THE_HOST"
      ]
    }
  }
}

Give the guest the absolute path to hello.txt on the host, then ask their agent to read it and check that the returned text matches the file. A useful second check is a direct write_file request, which should be rejected by MCPWire even though the underlying filesystem server implements it.

Where this architecture fits

For temporary collaboration, this arrangement lets a teammate use an existing local environment without reproducing its dependencies or moving the server to a hosted service. For a persistent team endpoint, requirements such as named-user authentication, centralized policy, and reliable reachability may justify a different deployment model.

The design keeps execution on the host and puts selected controls in front of it, while leaving argument validation, data permissions, and recovery from ambiguous execution to the systems that own those decisions. A remote agent can only be constrained as precisely as those underlying boundaries allow.

title: Building the Interface That Vanishes: From Subvocal to Dichoptic VR
description:
Building the Interface That Vanishes: From Subvocal to Dichoptic VR

From subvocal whispers to dichoptic VR, the interface vanishes.

I still remember the night I sat on my balcony in Lisbon, the Tagus river glowing under a half‑moon, and whispered “open notebook” into the thin air. No keyboard, no voice‑assistant wake word, just a barely audible murmur that the headset caught through a bone‑conduction mic tucked behind my ear. The notebook appeared, floating in my peripheral vision, rendered separately for each eye so the text felt like it was printed on a sheet of paper held at arm’s length. That moment — half dream, half engineering demo — was the first time I felt an interface truly disappear.

Why the old stack felt heavy

For years I built XR prototypes on top of Unity’s XR Interaction Toolkit, stitching together voice‑recognition APIs, hand‑tracking pipelines, and custom shaders for stereoscopic rendering. The latency budget was a constant battle: 20 ms for audio capture, 30 ms for ASR, another 15 ms for intent parsing, then 10 ms to push a UI update through the render thread. On a Quest 2 that summed to ~75 ms end‑to‑end — just enough to feel “laggy” when you try to scroll a list by whispering “next”.

The dichoptic approach changes the math. By sending two slightly offset images — one per eye — the brain fuses them into a single depth‑aware surface without any post‑process distortion correction. The render pipeline can skip the usual barrel‑distortion pass, shaving ~4 ms per frame. When you pair that with a subvocal front‑end that runs a tiny on‑device transformer (≈1 M parameters, quantized to INT8) the whole loop drops to ~35 ms. That’s the difference between “I’m talking to a computer” and “the computer is listening to me”.

The subvocal front‑end — a tiny model that lives on the headset 

# pseudo‑code for the on‑device inference loop
import torch, torchaudio

model = torch.jit.load("subvocal_int8.pt")   # 1 M params, INT8
mic   = torchaudio.io.StreamReader("bone_conduction")

def infer():
    chunk = mic.read(160)                     # 10 ms @ 16 kHz
    feat  = torchaudio.compliance.kaldi.fbank(chunk, num_mel_bins=40)
    logits = model(feat.unsqueeze(0))
    return decode(logits)                     # greedy CTC decode

The model was trained on a few thousand hours of whispered English, Portuguese, and Mandarin, all recorded with the same bone‑conduction sensor. Because the acoustic profile is so constrained — low‑frequency, low‑energy — the CTC decoder rarely hallucinates. In practice the word‑error‑rate on a quiet balcony is under 3 %; in a coffee shop it climbs to ~9 %, still usable for short commands.

Dichoptic rendering — two eyes, one surface

The dichoptic shader is deliberately simple:

// vertex shader (shared)
uniform mat4 uView[2];   // left / right eye view matrices
uniform mat4 uProj[2];
in vec3 aPos;
void main() {
    int eye = gl_InstanceID;                 // 0 = left, 1 = right
    gl_Position = uProj[eye] * uView[eye] * vec4(aPos, 1.0);
}

Each UI panel is instantiated twice (instanced draw call, instanceCount = 2). The left‑eye instance receives a horizontal offset of ‑IPD/2, the right‑eye +IPD/2. No post‑process, no lens‑distortion mesh. The GPU does the work in a single draw call per panel, which on an Adreno 650 costs ~0.3 ms.

Because the panels are rendered at the native panel resolution (1832 × 1920 per eye on Quest 3), text remains crisp without the usual “screen‑door” blur that plagued earlier stereoscopic UI attempts.

A personal turning point

Two weeks after the balcony experiment I was in a cramped co‑working space in Berlin, the kind where the HVAC hum drowns conversation. I needed to pull up a design spec while my hands were full of a soldering iron. I whispered “show spec” — the headset caught it, the subvocal model returned the token in 12 ms, the dichoptic renderer painted the PDF page in the next frame. I didn’t have to glance at a controller, didn’t have to say “Hey Assistant”. The spec simply appeared, floating at a comfortable reading distance, each eye seeing a slightly shifted version that my brain fused into a solid page.

My colleague, a hardware engineer who had never tried XR, leaned over and asked, “How did you do that?” I handed her the headset. She whispered “open terminal”. The terminal spawned, cursor blinking, ready for git status. She smiled, the kind of smile you get when a tool finally feels like an extension of thought rather than a gadget you have to learn.

Trade‑offs we accepted

Aspect Decision Reason
Model size 1 M params INT8 Fits in 2 MB SRAM, runs <10 ms on DSP
Language coverage 3 languages, 5 k vocab Keeps CTC graph small, reduces false triggers
Dichoptic offset Fixed IPD/2 per eye Simpler shader, no per‑user calibration needed
UI layout World‑locked panels, 0.5 m distance Avoids vergence‑accommodation conflict
Power budget <1.2 W average Keeps headset thermals under 38 °C

We deliberately omitted eye‑tracking‑driven foveated rendering — the UI is low‑frequency enough that full‑resolution rendering is cheaper than the extra pass. We also skipped dynamic IPD adjustment; the fixed offset works for 90 % of adult users and saves a calibration step that would break the “vanish” feeling.

What’s next

The current stack runs on Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2 and the newer XR2+ Gen 1. Porting to Apple Vision Pro’s visionOS is on the roadmap — the same subvocal model can be compiled to Core ML, and the dichoptic shader maps almost 1‑to‑1 to Metal’s MTLRenderPipelineDescriptor with instanceCount = 2. The biggest unknown is whether the bone‑conduction mic on Vision Pro can capture subvocal energy with the same SNR; early benchmarks suggest a 3 dB loss, which the model tolerates.

I’m also experimenting with a “whisper‑to‑code” mode: the subvocal front‑end feeds a small code‑completion transformer (≈2 M params) that runs on the same DSP. Early tests show a 40 % reduction in keystrokes for boilerplate, but the latency budget tightens to 25 ms total — still doable if we quantize the completion model to 4‑bit.

Closing thought

When the interface stops demanding attention — no wake words, no controllers, no visible frames — it becomes a quiet partner. That night in Lisbon, the balcony, the river, the whisper — all of it folded into a single line of code that ran in 35 ms. The technology didn’t shout; it listened. And that, for me, is the moment the interface truly vanished.

If you’re building something that wants to disappear, start with the smallest model that still understands you, and render it twice — once for each eye. The rest is just engineering.

title: Reading an ER Diagram for API Review
description:
Quick answer: The ER diagram draws the entities and their foreign keys, and the node state reflects the reconciliation status, so a reviewer can see the missing, drift, matched, and extra tables at a glance and trace the relationships behind an API operation. It is a visual map of the same four-layer reconciliation rather than a separate model.

Why the diagram helps the review

A table of statuses and diffs is accurate but slow to read, especially when the model has many relationships. The diagram shows the entities and how they connect, and the node state carries the comparison, so the eye can move from the changed table to its neighbors rather than cross-reference a list.

This keeps the review focused on the structure and the blast radius rather than on assembling the relationships by hand.

What the diagram shows

Element How it appears
Entity A node carrying the table
Foreign key A link between nodes
Link table A node connecting two entities
Node state Color or state reflecting the table status
Impact The connected operations and tables

Because the node state reflects the reconciliation, a matched table and a drift table are distinguishable without opening the field list, and an inferred link table stays visually separate from an observed one.

How to read it during a review

  1. Scan the node states and find the missing and drift tables first.
  2. Follow the links to the related tables and the foreign keys.
  3. Open the field diffs on a drift node.
  4. Trace the impacted operations from the table.
  5. Confirm the inferred link tables and the open questions.

The bidirectional analysis works through the same map. Starting from an operation, the reviewer follows the tables it touches, and starting from a table, the connected operations are visible, which keeps the blast radius in one place.

Take a review of a change to the orders service. On the diagram, the reviewer first sees the orders node marked drift and a new preferences node marked missing, while the customers and products nodes stay matched and drop out of the work. Following the links, the drift on orders leads to a foreign key that the new preferences node also references, so the reviewer sees the dependency before reading a field list. The inferred link table between orders and products sits in a separate visual state, and the open question on its cardinality is attached. The same map then traces the impacted operations from orders, so the reviewer confirms which requests need a check. Doing this from a flat table would require following the keys and operations by hand, and the visual keeps the whole blast radius in one view.

Honest reading

The diagram is a view of the reconciliation, not a runtime result. A node that looks matched says the model and the live table agree, and it does not prove the behavior is correct, and an inferred node stays a proposal until confirmed. Treat the visual as a guide to where the evidence is rather than a verdict on its own.

When the business logic is ambiguous, the open question is attached rather than hidden behind a clean-looking node. The generated SQL behind the diagram is still never executed by the modeling package.

Powerduck keeps the ER diagram and the node states in the desktop so the review reads the structure and the comparison together.

Frequently asked questions

Does the node state match the table status? Yes. The node reflects missing, drift, matched, or extra, so the comparison is visible on the diagram.

Can I see impact from the diagram? Yes. The bidirectional analysis connects tables to operations and back through the same map.

Is a matched node a verified behavior? No. It says the model and table agree, and runtime behavior still needs tests.

The bottom line

The ER diagram is a visual map of the reconciliation, showing entities, keys, and link tables with node states that carry the table status. Start with the missing and drift nodes, follow the relationships, and trace the impacted operations rather than reading a flat list. Keep it as a guide to the evidence, since a matched node does not prove runtime behavior and an inferred node stays a proposal. The diagram makes the structure readable, not automatic. Read more in the API data model guide.

title: Creating Durable Background Job Queues for Game Renewal Reminders
description:
The short answer

For a game renewal notice, the queue is not the system of record. Store the reminder intent and its business deadline in durable state, enqueue a small wake-up job, and make the worker re-check that state before sending. The retry path should preserve the deadline, count attempts, quarantine poison messages, and expose enough history for an operator to recover a missed notice.

The useful unit is therefore a recoverable reminder, not a delayed message. A queue can wake a worker; it cannot decide whether a renewal is still eligible after a subscription change, a clock correction, or an outage.

In a Node.js service, I would keep the event-loop work small and push delivery to workers, but I would make the same storage and recovery rules apply no matter which queue implementation sits behind the interface. The deadline is a business fact. The delivery timestamp is an attempt. Mixing those two is how a harmless retry becomes a late, duplicate message.

The first design mistake is easy to make: treating the delayed message as the reminder itself. The message is only a pointer to work. Creating a background job queue around that distinction gives the worker somewhere durable to look when the original timing assumption no longer holds.

What is the bill actually made of?

Start with retention, because that is usually the dominant term in a reminder system that appears inexpensive at first. The rough retained footprint is:

reminder_storage = (active_reminders + attempts + audit_events) * average_record_bytes
monthly_cost_driver = reminder_storage * retention_months

The change that moves this term is not shaving milliseconds from enqueue latency. It is choosing what remains after a reminder is sent, canceled, or permanently failed. A compact active record might contain an identifier, user reference, due time, business deadline, status, attempt count, and a version. Delivery attempts can be kept for a bounded operational window; the message body, rendered templates, and transient worker logs do not need indefinite retention in the same store.

For an illustrative workload of 1,000,000 reminders, retaining one active row and five small attempt records per reminder produces six records per reminder before indexes and audit metadata are counted. That is a planning example, not a benchmark. It shows why the retention policy deserves a number: keeping every payload forever multiplies the dominant term even when the send path is quiet.

There is a cost to deleting history. If a player says a renewal notice arrived twice, a short attempt record may be enough to reconstruct the decision, while a long-lived compliance or support requirement may demand more. I would retain immutable decision events longer than delivery payloads, and I would state the deletion boundary in the runbook. The thing deliberately stopped is full message history; the thing preserved is evidence of the state transition and attempt outcome.

That boundary matters.

Data Keep while active After terminal state Recovery value
Reminder intent and deadline Yes Until support or policy window ends Rebuilds the work item
Delivery payload Yes, or a reproducible reference Short bounded window Explains what was sent
Attempt outcome Yes Longer bounded window Separates retryable from permanent failure
Worker logs Operational window Aggregated or expired Diagnoses an incident

A queue that stores every detail forever is not automatically more durable. It is often just harder to operate and harder to delete correctly.

What practices make creating a background job queue for reminders reliable?

The game scenario has two times: when the service may send and the business deadline after which sending is useless or wrong. Suppose a renewal offer should be announced at 09:00, but the player has until 23:59 to renew. A worker that wakes at 09:07 can still send. A worker recovering at 00:04 cannot fix that by retrying harder.

Persist both values, plus a cancellation or eligibility version. On wake-up, the worker reads the current record, checks the deadline and version, and claims an attempt with a conditional update. That last step matters when two workers receive the same message or when a visibility timeout expires while the first worker is still calling a provider.

def handle_wakeup(message, clock, reminders, sender):
    reminder = reminders.read(message.reminder_id)
    if reminder is None or reminder.status in {"canceled", "sent", "expired"}:
        return "discard"

    now = clock.now()
    if now >= reminder.business_deadline:
        reminders.expire_if_version(reminder.id, reminder.version, now)
        return "expired"

    claimed = reminders.claim_attempt(
        reminder.id,
        expected_version=reminder.version,
        lease_until=now + 60,
    )
    if not claimed:
        return "already_claimed"

    try:
        sender.send(reminder.recipient, reminder.template_ref)
    except RetryableDeliveryError:
        reminders.schedule_retry(reminder.id, now)
        raise
    except PermanentDeliveryError:
        reminders.mark_failed(reminder.id, now)
        return "failed"

    reminders.mark_sent(reminder.id, now)
    return "sent"

The code is deliberately boring. It does not trust the queue timestamp, and it does not mark a reminder sent before delivery succeeds. In production, the sender boundary also needs an idempotency key derived from the reminder and attempt policy; otherwise a timeout after remote acceptance can produce a duplicate on retry. Exactly-once behavior is not a property to assume from a queue. It is a business effect that must be designed and measured.

What fails first during recovery?

A useful failure inventory is more specific than “the queue may fail.”

  • A worker crashes after claiming an item: the lease expires, and a recovery scan or redelivery makes it eligible again.
  • The delivery call times out after acceptance: the next attempt uses the same idempotency identity and records the result conservatively.
  • The reminder is canceled while waiting: the worker re-reads state and discards the stale wake-up.
  • A malformed payload keeps failing: the message moves to a dead-letter queue after a bounded receive count, where an operator can inspect it without blocking healthy work.
  • The queue is unavailable: the durable reminder table remains the source for a reconciliation job that finds due, unclaimed records.

A dead-letter queue is a quarantine, not a repair mechanism. Its useful fields are the original identifier, failure reason, receive count, first-seen time, and the business deadline. An operator can then decide whether to fix data, replay before the deadline, or mark the reminder expired. The decision should be visible in the audit trail.

The reconciliation job deserves the same idempotency rules as the normal worker. It should select a bounded batch, claim rows conditionally, and emit wake-ups; it should not send directly while holding a database scan open. This keeps recovery work observable and prevents a large backlog from turning one restart into a delivery storm.

There is a real boundary here. A durable table plus a queue improves recovery, but it adds two state machines, reconciliation work, and operational ownership. A tiny game with no deadline-sensitive messaging may reasonably use one scheduled process and accept coarser recovery. A high-volume service may need partitioning and separate workers, which increases testing and deployment complexity. The queue is the wrong tool if the team cannot operate the source-of-truth table and its repair path.

A practical operating contract

Before choosing a queue, write down the contract in terms an on-call engineer can test:

  1. A reminder must never be sent after its business deadline.
  2. A retry may repeat a delivery attempt, but the user-visible effect must be deduplicated where the channel supports it.
  3. Cancellation and subscription changes win over stale queued work.
  4. Every terminal result has an auditable reason.
  5. A bounded outage can be repaired from durable reminder state without hand-editing messages.

For Node.js, expose this contract through a small adapter with operations such as enqueue, acknowledge, retry, and quarantine. Keep provider-specific settings behind that adapter. Test the state machine with time injected as a dependency: advance the clock across the deadline, interrupt after claim, deliver a duplicate wake-up, and replay a quarantined message. The tests should assert state transitions and user-visible sends, not only that a promise resolved.

The trade-off is deliberate: stronger recovery costs more state, more observability, and more code paths to test. It is justified when missing a game renewal deadline matters more than keeping the scheduler minimal. It is not a universal argument for adding a queue to every reminder feature.

Operational dashboards should show age of the oldest due reminder, deadline misses, retry counts, lease expirations, quarantine depth, and reconciliation lag. Queue depth alone is a poor signal: 10,000 future reminders may be healthy, while 20 overdue reminders may be an incident. Alert on the business deadline and recovery lag, not on an arbitrary pile of waiting messages.

The decision rule is straightforward. Use a queue for wake-up and load distribution; use durable application state for truth; use leases, conditional writes, and idempotency for recovery; use bounded retention for cost and deletion control. The exact queue can change. Those boundaries should not.

Further reading

  • AWS, “Amazon SQS dead-letter queues”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • Node.js, “Event loop, timers, and nextTick()”: https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/event-loop-timers-and-nexttick
  • RFC 9110, “HTTP Semantics”: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • PostgreSQL documentation, “Explicit Locking”: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html

title: Introducing Geist Serif
description:
Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens.

Today, we're adding a new member to the family: Geist Serif.

Geist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices.

Same system, new voice

At Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu.

A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines. It's our homage to the artists behind Rolling Stone and Harper's Bazaar.

From the beginning, each Geist family has read from a chapter of type history: the Swiss design movement, early terminal and DOS computing, and now editorial print.

Display first

Geist Serif began as a set of sketches by Evil Rabbit, which Andrés Briganti then expanded. The first letters already showed an expressive serif, in the spirit of typefaces like Victor Serif and Stanley.

When Mark Davis took over the drawings, we made the first release a display face for headlines, posters, and other large sizes, while work on the full family continued. Print has always struggled to hold fine hairlines and sharp serifs, but today's displays can handle a high level of detail. We wanted the new face to take full advantage of modern screens, so we thinned every downstroke by 50% and tightened the sidebearings to push the contrast as far as it would go.

Each serif has a wedge on one side and a curve on the other, so the proportions are classical and look beautiful in print, but the construction is new and optimized for digital devices.

From the first prototype to today

The first prototype of Geist Serif was shared on April 1, 2026. Here's the same word, Geist, in that prototype, compared with the display drawing shipping today.

Geist grew teeth

The goal was to honor our original intent and keep the serif closely tied to the sans, even when the letters sit on top of each other. Geist Serif’s stems match Geist Sans, and the two share widths and postures.

The saw-toothed serifs and high contrast give Geist an editorial voice. One phrase kept coming up as each character was drawn: “Geist grew teeth.”

Four families, one x-height

Geist Serif uses the same cap height and x-height as Geist Sans, so you can drop it into any Geist layout without moving a line. Mix Sans, Mono, Pixel, and Serif in the same sentence and every word looks the same size.

Metric

Geist Sans

Geist Serif

UPM

1000

1000

Cap height

710

710

x-height

530

530

Ascender

710

750

Descender

-150

-200

Four variants, one axis

Like Geist Pixel, Geist Serif has a variable axis that swaps the shape of every dot in the font, including those on i and j and in punctuation. The axis is called Element Shape (ELSH), and it gives you four variants: Regular with round dots (the default), Square, Triangle (a nod to the Vercel logo), and Heart.

Each variant also ships as its own static file. If you use the variable font, pick a variant with font-variation-settings:

Crafted by hand

In July the font had 227 glyphs. It now has 894 and covers 352 Latin-script languages, and we worked through more than 52,000 kerning pairs to get the spacing right. Some of the details are tiny. The eye of the g, for example, is tilted exactly 7°.

Specs at a glance

Geist Serif ships with:

  • 1 weight (Regular)

  • 4 variants (Regular, Square, Triangle, Heart)

  • 894 glyphs

  • 5 stylistic sets (ss01 to ss05)

  • 352 supported languages

Getting started

Geist Serif ships in the same package as the rest of the family:

Exports and CSS variables:

  • GeistSerif (variable, all shapes): --font-geist-serif

  • GeistSerifRegular: --font-geist-serif-regular

  • GeistSerifSquare: --font-geist-serif-square

  • GeistSerifTriangle: --font-geist-serif-triangle

  • GeistSerifHeart: --font-geist-serif-heart

Each one has its own entry point, so you only ship the font file you use. For example, in layout.tsx with GeistSerifRegular:

You can also download the font files, test every stylistic set, and inspect each glyph at vercel.com/font.

What’s next

Regular is the first style we’re releasing, and the rest of the family is already in progress. We’re testing future versions while building this one, so this release is just the start.

Weights from Thin to Black

The variable font will range from Thin (100) to Black (900). In this week’s proofs, the g in Black is the letter we can’t stop looking at.

Toward a text face

To explore a text version, we built a foundry tool that measures strokes, including where they meet, and thickens the display outlines. It edits the outlines directly, so we can set real words and see which strokes need more weight.

Italics, built rule by rule

We’re also developing an italic generated entirely in Python. We slanted existing italics back upright and compared them with their romans. With the angle removed, the remaining differences show up clearly, and we turned them into rules we can test and revise. This italic won’t be the final version, but breaking glyphs in code helps us find the limits faster.

More scripts and Google Fonts

Cyrillic support is planned to match Geist Sans and Geist Mono, and Geist Serif will come to Google Fonts after launch.

One family

With Geist Sans, Geist Mono, Geist Pixel, and now Geist Serif, the family runs from UI text and code to expressive display type, and all four feel at home together.

Download Geist Serif and start building.

Thank you to everyone who made Geist Serif possible.

None of this would have been possible without an incredible group of people behind the scenes.

Huge thanks to Andrés Briganti for starting this journey with me and drawing the first version that everything else grew from, and to Mark Davis for carrying it across the finish line with obsessive craft, from the expanded glyph set and variable axis to every last kerning pair. Thanks also to Patrick McDonald and Marijana Pavlinić for the poster designs, to Luis Gutierrez Rico for the motion and incredible magic, to Christopher Kindl for shipping the package and rebuilding the landing page down to the smallest details, and to Zahra Jabini for the coordination and technical support that brought it all together. This was a true team effort, and I’m grateful to have built it with all of you.

title: Testing an A2A JSON-RPC Error Inside a 200
description:
Quick answer: An A2A call can return HTTP 200 while the body carries a JSON-RPC error. The transport succeeded, but the method did not, and a test that only checks the status will treat the failure as a pass. Read the payload, distinguish a JSON-RPC result from an error, and assert the protocol-level outcome rather than the HTTP code alone.

Why the two layers can disagree

A2A runs over JSON-RPC, and the HTTP layer is only the carrier. The server can accept the request, return a healthy 200, and still report inside the body that the method was rejected, a parameter was invalid, or the task could not be created. There is no rule that forces a protocol error to surface as an HTTP error code.

That means a green status is ambiguous until you open the body.

Two outcomes in one response

Layer What you read A 200 can show
HTTP Status code 200, transport accepted
JSON-RPC result or error Either a method result or an error

A 200 with a result is a full success. A 200 with an error is a transport success and a method failure, and the two have to be read together.

Say a caller sends a task creation request with a missing required field. The server accepts the HTTP message and returns 200, because the transport itself worked, but the JSON-RPC body carries an error naming the invalid parameter. A test that reads only the status records a pass, while the method was rejected and no task exists. When the same request is sent with the field complete, the body carries a result with the task reference, and the two cases are distinguishable only inside the payload. The test should assert a result for the valid case and the specific error code for the invalid one rather than treating both as success.

How to test it honestly

Build the request in the Debug surface with the generated body and the A2A-Version header, then assert at the right layer.

  1. Send the request and confirm the HTTP status.
  2. Open the body and check whether it carries a result or an error.
  3. If it is an error, read the error code and message.
  4. Assert the protocol outcome rather than treating 200 as a pass.
  5. Keep the transport and protocol findings separate in the report.

A test that stops at the status line misses exactly this failure, and it can report a suite as green while methods are being rejected. The assertion has to look inside the payload to be meaningful.

Where this fits the broader pattern

This is the same boundary that keeps a 200 response from being trusted when a field assertion fails. A transport-level success says the message arrived and was accepted at the wire, and it says nothing about whether the method behaved. Treat the two as separate questions, and verify the contract at the layer where it actually lives.

When the error is intermittent, such as a task that is rejected only under certain inputs, keep the request and the full body in the report so the failure is reproducible rather than reduced to a single status label.

Powerduck keeps the JSON-RPC layer visible in the Debug surface rather than collapsing it into the HTTP status, so the error does not hide behind a 200.

Frequently asked questions

Is a 200 always a successful A2A call? No. The body can carry a JSON-RPC error even at 200, so read the payload and check for result or error.

What should the assertion target? The protocol-level result inside the body, not just the HTTP status code.

Why does the server return 200 with an error? Because HTTP is the transport and JSON-RPC carries its own method outcome, which is not required to map to an HTTP error.

The bottom line

Never let an HTTP 200 stand in for a method-level pass. A2A can return a healthy transport status while the JSON-RPC body reports an error, and the honest test reads both layers and asserts the protocol result. Build the request with the version header, open the body, and keep the two findings separate. Treating the carrier as the contract is how rejected methods get reported as green. Continue in the A2A guide.

title: Routing Middleware now supports Python
description:
You can now write routing middleware in Python for FastAPI, Flask, Django, and other Python frameworks. It runs before requests reach your app, and can rewrite, redirect, or answer them.

To set it up, point the proxy entrypoint in vercel.toml at your proxy:

Your middleware is an ASGI or WSGI app that runs separately from your main app, with only the packages in the vercel.proxy dependency group of your pyproject.toml. Add the packages your middleware imports to that group:

The vercel-proxy package provides utilities for writing routing middleware on Vercel, including a Proxy app that routes requests by path:

title: dxsrc’s Global RSS Feed Is Now a Paid Feature
description:
TL;DR: Access to dxsrc’s main feed—which features some exclusive content—now requires becoming a dxsrc supporter.

Over the years, dxsrc has become one of the leading sources of frontend development news and tools. dxsrc’s growing archives provide unique access to the history of the wider field of web development.

Providing this service for free is not sustainable, however. Book sales pay for some of the work, but so far, few people acknowledge dxsrc’s value by supporting the project on Open Collective.

Starting today, the global RSS feed (with the 250 newest articles and videos) is a paid feature.

You can secure access by a monthly or yearly contribution.

If you don’t like to support dxsrc, you can still follow dxsrc’s individual topic feeds as well as dxsrc’s social media accounts on Mastodon and Bluesky. These are less convenient and reliable but still workable options to stay up-to-date.

Also, if you want to support dxsrc in a different manner and so that the main feed may be made free again, consider buying dxsrc’s books or contributing to the project on Open Collective. You’re not alone: We do the same for the projects we use and like. Thank you.

title: Browser Object Upload Control Plane With Presigned PUT and Private Signed Downloads
description:
The operational constraint is not how quickly an application can mint a URL. It is whether the signing path, browser policy, object namespace, and cleanup process still behave predictably when uploads surge and clients retry.

Short answer: keep the bucket private, let the application authorize a narrowly scoped upload and return a short-lived presigned PUT URL, send the file from the browser directly to object storage, and issue a separate short-lived signed download URL only after the application has verified the object record.

Treat signing as a control plane with an SLO. Treat file bytes as a data plane that should never cross the Node.js or Express process. This pattern fits a React client and an Express authorization route even though the implementation below uses Go to make the protocol boundaries explicit: the browser receives a URL, a method, required headers, an object identifier, and an expiry. It doesn't receive storage credentials.

What should a React, Node.js, and Express browser upload contract contain?

A direct-to-storage design has four steps. First, React asks the application for upload authorization using the user's normal session. Second, Express applies application policy: identity, object size, media type, quota, and destination prefix. Third, the browser performs the presigned PUT against the returned storage URL. Last, the application records completion only after it has evidence that the expected object exists. A successful authorization response is not proof of a completed upload.

Keep the contract boring. A useful response contains object_key, upload_url, method, required_headers, and expires_at. The method should be fixed to PUT, while the required headers should be copied exactly into the browser request. The application should generate the object key; accepting an arbitrary bucket key from a client turns a storage primitive into a namespace-policy bypass.

The browser flow is straightforward: request authorization, perform a PUT fetch using the returned URL, headers, and file body, then notify the application using the opaque object identifier. That last notification is a hint, not an attestation. Don't mark durable business state complete merely because React says the PUT returned success.

One detail causes disproportionate confusion. The upload request is cross-origin, so the browser may send a CORS preflight before PUT. The documented browser behavior uses an OPTIONS request carrying the intended method and headers; the storage origin must answer with policy that permits the web origin, PUT, and every non-safelisted request header. CORS is browser enforcement, not upload authentication, and making the bucket public does not repair a bad preflight policy.

Build the signing path as a small control plane

The authorization handler should depend on a signer interface, not on a vendor SDK throughout the application. This makes policy testable and keeps a future storage migration from leaking into route handlers. It also makes the operational boundary visible: the signer creates capability URLs, while a metadata store owns application state.

package upload

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

type PutGrant struct {
    ObjectKey      string            `json:"object_key"`
    UploadURL      string            `json:"upload_url"`
    Method         string            `json:"method"`
    RequiredHeader map[string]string `json:"required_headers"`
    ExpiresAt      time.Time         `json:"expires_at"`
}

type Signer interface {
    SignPut(context.Context, string, string, int64, time.Duration) (PutGrant, error)
    SignGet(context.Context, string, time.Duration) (string, error)
}

type Policy interface {
    AuthorizeUpload(context.Context, string, string, int64) (string, error)
}

type Handler struct {
    Signer Signer
    Policy Policy
    TTL    time.Duration
}

type authorizeRequest struct {
    ContentType string `json:"content_type"`
    Size        int64  `json:"size"`
}

func (h Handler) AuthorizeUpload(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    userID, _ := r.Context().Value("user_id").(string)
    if userID == "" {
        http.Error(w, "unauthorized", http.StatusUnauthorized)
        return
    }

    var in authorizeRequest
    dec := json.NewDecoder(http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, 4096))
    dec.DisallowUnknownFields()
    if err := dec.Decode(&in); err != nil || in.Size <= 0 || in.ContentType == "" {
        http.Error(w, "invalid upload request", http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }

    objectKey, err := h.Policy.AuthorizeUpload(r.Context(), userID, in.ContentType, in.Size)
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "upload rejected", http.StatusForbidden)
        return
    }

    grant, err := h.Signer.SignPut(r.Context(), objectKey, in.ContentType, in.Size, h.TTL)
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "authorization unavailable", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
        return
    }

    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(grant)
}

The example deliberately leaves signature generation behind Signer. Presigned URL formats, canonicalization rules, and SDK calls are provider-specific; the application-facing behavior does not need to be. In an Express service, the route should enforce the same sequence before calling its chosen signing library. React should remain unaware of which library created the URL.

Expiry needs a capacity-planning answer rather than a fashionable default. Set it long enough for an authorized client to begin the transfer under the slowest network condition you support, but short enough to limit reuse. The correct value depends on file-size limits, connection distribution, retry policy, and the storage service's signature semantics. I'm not sure a universal number exists; a load test with throttled clients and expired grants would resolve it for a specific system.

Capacity, SLOs, and failure modes

Moving bytes away from Express removes application bandwidth from the hot path, but it does not make capacity free. Authorization requests still hit identity, quota, policy, signing, and metadata dependencies. If 20,000 clients reconnect after a frontend release, they can create a signing spike even when only a fraction completes an upload. Capacity plans therefore need separate rates for grants issued, PUTs started, PUTs completed, completion checks, and signed downloads. Those numbers won't be equal.

Define an SLO for the control plane, such as the proportion of valid authorization requests completed within the chosen latency target, then instrument policy rejections separately from dependency failures. Useful dimensions include requested byte range, content-type class, tenant, grant age at first use, and completion lag. Avoid placing full signed URLs in logs: query strings may carry capability material, and high-cardinality object keys make poor metric labels.

A browser-visible failure commonly appears as a generic CORS message even when the useful distinction is elsewhere. Start with the browser network panel: did an OPTIONS preflight occur, did its response allow the exact origin and PUT method, and did it allow the headers React intends to send? Then compare the actual PUT method and headers with the grant contract. A changed Content-Type can turn an apparently identical request into a rejected signed request under schemes that bind headers. The symptom might be a 403, but randomly widening CORS or making the bucket public is the wrong response.

Run that diagnosis in a fixed order because two requests are involved and changing several controls at once destroys the evidence. Consider a React build served from app.example.test that asks Express for a grant containing PUT plus a required Content-Type. In the browser network panel, first inspect OPTIONS: its requested method must be PUT, its requested-header list must include the header the client will send, and the response must permit the exact application origin rather than a similar preview hostname. Only after that exchange is accepted should the actual PUT become the focus. Compare its method and headers byte for byte with the grant contract, then repeat with one deliberate mismatch and confirm rejection. Finally, repeat from a disallowed origin and confirm that the browser does not expose the cross-origin response. This sequence — preflight, exact upload, deliberate mismatch, hostile origin — separates browser policy from signature policy without relying on a vague console message, and it leaves a compact regression case that can run whenever origins or upload headers change.

Measure both.

Retries need policy too. A client may retry the same PUT only if the signing scheme and application state permit it; otherwise it requests a new grant for the same pending object. Use idempotency at the authorization boundary so a lost JSON response does not allocate an unbounded series of keys. The completion transition should also be idempotent.

Short version: retries are state transitions, not a loop around fetch.

This is where private uploads accumulate trash. Clients close laptops, mobile radios disappear, and tabs get killed after authorization. Object lifecycle policies can expire abandoned temporary objects; a scheduled reconciler is the alternative when the storage layer cannot express the required rule. Keep the temporary prefix separate from committed objects so cleanup policy cannot erase valid data.

Verify the deployment and make rollback dull

Test the whole browser boundary in a staging origin. Unit tests for the signer are necessary but cannot prove that preflight policy, signed headers, DNS, browser behavior, and storage responses agree. The verification matrix should include the allowed origin, a disallowed origin, maximum and over-limit sizes, allowed and rejected media types, an expired grant, a modified required header, a duplicate completion call, and a private download attempted without application authorization.

Use a small Go client in CI to verify the grant contract outside the browser, while retaining one real-browser test for CORS. This client intentionally sends only the headers returned by the control plane.

package uploadtest

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
)

type Grant struct {
    UploadURL      string
    Method         string
    RequiredHeader map[string]string
}

func Put(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, grant Grant, body []byte) error {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, grant.Method, grant.UploadURL, bytes.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    for name, value := range grant.RequiredHeader {
        req.Header.Set(name, value)
    }

    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return fmt.Errorf("upload status %d", resp.StatusCode)
    }
    return nil
}

Roll out behind a server-side capability flag, because the application controls whether it issues a direct-upload grant. During the first stage, compare authorization counts, starts, verified completions, abandoned objects, and p95 completion lag with the previous path. Rollback means stop issuing new grants and return clients to the old upload path; already issued grants should be allowed to expire naturally, while reconciliation continues. Don't delete the temporary prefix during rollback.

The key alert is not raw PUT error rate alone. Alert on a sustained fall in verified-completion ratio, control-plane SLO burn, or growth in unreconciled temporary bytes. A storage service can report successful PUTs while the application never commits the corresponding records, which is an integrity failure even though transport dashboards look healthy.

Buy, build, or keep uploads on the application tier?

The direct pattern is not suitable for every workload. Stick with application-proxied uploads when the server must inspect or transform every byte synchronously before accepting it, when clients cannot use the storage endpoint, or when upload volume is too small to justify a second-origin CORS and reconciliation runbook. For very large or interruption-prone files, a resumable or multipart protocol may be the better design, but it adds session state and cleanup work that this single-PUT example intentionally does not model.

Choice On-call surface Lock-in pressure Capacity consequence Prefer when
Application-proxied PUT One public origin, plus bandwidth and timeout tuning Lower storage-protocol exposure App instances carry every byte Mandatory inline inspection or low volume
Direct presigned PUT CORS, signing, verification, and cleanup Signature and lifecycle behavior need adapters Control plane scales separately from file bytes Private objects and meaningful upload traffic
Managed upload component Provider-specific callbacks and limits Usually higher More transfer mechanics are outsourced The team accepts the boundary to reduce protocol ownership
Self-hosted resumable gateway Upgrades and session recovery Lower commercial dependency, higher operational ownership Gateway and state store need explicit headroom Resume behavior is required and the team can own it

The catch is operational ownership. Direct upload replaces one obvious bottleneck with several quieter consistency boundaries. A team without time to test CORS, reconcile abandoned objects, rotate signing credentials, and rehearse rollback should not pretend the browser-to-storage path is maintenance-free. Managed services reduce some implementation work, while self-hosting offers more control; neither choice cancels on-call load, it moves it.

Private download is a separate authorization decision. The browser asks the application for access to a committed object, the application checks current identity and policy, and only then does the signer return a short-lived GET URL. Do not reuse an upload grant, expose a permanent public URL, or assume that possession of an object key proves authorization. If download policy needs immediate revocation, signed URL lifetime becomes part of the revocation budget; the exact trade-off depends on the storage system's guarantees.

A sound design can be summarized without a product recommendation: private namespace, narrow grants, exact CORS policy, explicit completion verification, lifecycle cleanup, measured control-plane capacity, and a rehearsed fallback.

That's the runbook.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html

title: Customer File Retention: Object Storage Links and Presigned URL 403 Signature Mismatch
description:
Short answer: keep the export private, preserve one canonical object key, and debug the signed request as a tuple of method, path, query, credentials, and time before changing CORS or making the object public. For a customer download, a 403 is usually useful evidence: the storage service did not accept the request that arrived.

This matters in a B2B SaaS product because an export link is part of the customer workflow, while the file often has a retention and deletion policy behind it. A link that works in a developer browser but fails for a customer after a queue delay is an availability problem. A link that exposes a deleted export is a policy problem. Treat both as one design.

The incident lesson: verify the signed request, not the URL

I would bound the first investigation to one export record and one failed request. Capture the object key as stored, a non-reversible key hash, the signing method, the signing scope, the issuer timestamp, the requested lifetime, the storage request ID, and the final request path. Do not log the complete presigned URL: its query string is temporary authorization.

The invariant is narrow: the bytes used to sign the bucket, key, method, query parameters, and validity window must describe the bytes in the request that reaches object storage. A 403 signature mismatch is the expected result when an intermediate layer decodes and rebuilds a path, changes a space representation, appends a query parameter after signing, or sends HEAD where GET was signed. The URL can look perfectly plausible.

Three quick checks usually separate the branches. First, compare the exact path before signing with the path at the storage boundary. Second, compare the signing service's clock with a trusted time source and leave useful lifetime after the message is delivered, rather than expiring the link while it sits in a notification queue. Third, verify the key and signing credential selected for this tenant and environment. Wrong key encoding and the wrong credential can produce the same opaque status code.

For example, a report named renewals + churn.csv can cross four representations: the database value, the signer input, the encoded URL path, and the proxy's access-log path. If one layer treats + as a space, the object may exist and the user's permissions may be correct, yet the signature is being checked against different bytes. Record each representation in a redacted diagnostic event, then compare them in order. That is slower than swapping a policy setting, but it leaves a testable explanation and a regression case.

Don't start by changing ACLs.

Measure it.

What makes a presigned download URL return 403 after a signature mismatch?

Make the application own a canonical key string and pass it through the same boundary for metadata checks and signing. Do not use a browser-decoded path as the database value. Do not normalize the signed URL after the signer returns it. The example below is deliberately a small policy layer; the provider SDK or HTTP client remains behind it, and the storage provider's documented signer is responsible for the actual signature.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

var errInvalidLink = errors.New("invalid download link policy")

// DownloadPolicy contains inputs that must remain stable across verification and signing.
type DownloadPolicy struct {
    Method      string
    ObjectKey   string
    IssuedAt    time.Time
    Lifetime    time.Duration
    MaxLifetime time.Duration
}

func (p DownloadPolicy) Validate(now time.Time) error {
    if p.Method != http.MethodGet || p.ObjectKey == "" {
        return errInvalidLink
    }
    if p.IssuedAt.IsZero() || p.Lifetime <= 0 || p.Lifetime > p.MaxLifetime {
        return errInvalidLink
    }
    if now.Before(p.IssuedAt) || now.After(p.IssuedAt.Add(p.Lifetime)) {
        return errInvalidLink
    }
    return nil
}

func keyFingerprint(key string) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(key))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])[:16]
}

func prepareDownload(p DownloadPolicy, now time.Time) (string, error) {
    if err := p.Validate(now); err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    // The signer must receive this exact key; do not decode or rebuild it later.
    return fmt.Sprintf("method=%s key-fingerprint=%s expires=%s",
        p.Method, keyFingerprint(p.ObjectKey), p.IssuedAt.Add(p.Lifetime).UTC().Format(time.RFC3339),
    ), nil
}

func main() {
    now := time.Now().UTC()
    policy := DownloadPolicy{
        Method:      http.MethodGet,
        ObjectKey:   "accounts/42/exports/2026-08/report.csv",
        IssuedAt:    now,
        Lifetime:    15 * time.Minute,
        MaxLifetime: 30 * time.Minute,
    }
    description, err := prepareDownload(policy, now)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(description)
}

This does not prove that the object exists or that a provider accepts the request. It establishes the inputs your service can observe and test. In a Node.js implementation, apply the same rule around the official signer: store the key once, avoid string concatenation around encoded paths, and test the final method and URL without rewriting them in a middleware layer. Your mileage may vary with a proxy that canonicalizes paths; its access log and the storage request log are the two records that resolve that uncertainty.

Which failure mode is actually consuming the download SLO?

A useful runbook classifies failures before assigning an owner:

Observation First hypothesis Evidence to collect
403 with a signature-mismatch message Signed bytes differ from received bytes Canonical method, path, query, key fingerprint, request ID
403 after a long queue or email delay Validity window has ended Issued-at time, expiry, trusted server time, delivery delay
403 only for names containing spaces or non-ASCII text Encoding changed at a boundary Stored key bytes, encoded path before and after the proxy
Browser reports a CORS block while a server client gets a response Browser policy, not necessarily storage authorization Browser network details and the CORS response headers
403 for one tenant or environment Credential, scope, bucket, or key selection Redacted identity, tenant mapping, region or scope, object metadata

CORS deserves its own branch. It controls whether browser JavaScript may read a cross-origin response; it does not repair a bad signature. MDN's CORS reference is useful here because the browser console can obscure the difference between a policy failure and a response that storage already rejected. Test the URL with a controlled server-side client as well as in the browser, and keep the original storage status and request ID.

The operational target is an SLO for link issuance and a separate SLO for completed downloads. Count presign latency, metadata-check latency, and failed issuance separately from object transfer time. Capacity planning should model peak exports, retry amplification, notification delay, and the number of customers who click near expiry. Averages are poor protection against a month-end batch.

Buy, wrap, or operate the storage contract?

The decision is about ownership, not the existence of a presigned URL. A direct provider integration gives the platform team the provider's contract and tooling; an internal wrapper gives product services a stable interface but leaves the platform team responsible for translating semantics; a self-hosted gateway gives maximum control and puts clocks, credentials, capacity, and the SLO on your pager.

Approach Good fit Trade-off
Direct provider API The organization has committed to one provider and its signing contract Product or platform code absorbs provider-specific migration work
Internal storage adapter Several products need one application-facing contract The adapter becomes a platform product with compatibility and test obligations
Self-hosted gateway Policy requires control over credentials and the request path The team owns scaling, patching, signing correctness, and incident response
Managed abstraction The team values a single HTTP contract across supported backends Provider coverage, retention semantics, and export features may not match the requirement

The catch is that a managed abstraction is unsuitable when you need provider-specific features, immutable retention guarantees, public non-expiring assets, or a backend outside its supported set. The direct option is the better fit when those requirements are contractual. The same caution applies to an internal gateway: it is not automatically simpler just because the product teams see fewer SDK calls.

There is no universal expiry value.

Retention changes the decision. Use unique export keys when regeneration must not replace evidence, record deletion eligibility separately from link expiry, and make deletion idempotent. A presigned URL expiring does not delete the object. Conversely, deleting an object does not make every already-delivered URL disappear from a customer's inbox; your authorization and retention model must account for that gap.

Make the fix repeatable

Add a test corpus containing spaces, plus signs, Unicode, nested prefixes, and empty or deleted records. Generate a link, preserve it byte-for-byte, and exercise the exact signed method through the same proxy path used in production. Add a clock-skew test with a controlled issuer clock. Redact query credentials in logs while retaining a request ID and key fingerprint.

During an incident, change one boundary at a time. Compare the stored key to the signer input, the signer output to the client input, and the client request to the storage log. That sequence keeps a 403 from becoming a permission broadening exercise.

References

  • MDN, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • AWS S3 pricing page, for the general distinction between storage, requests, and transfer cost: https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/

title: Fintech Tenant Isolation: Node.js/Postgres State for Browser Uploads to Object Storage
description:
Short answer: put report bytes directly into object storage with a short-lived signed upload URL, but let Node.js and Postgres decide which tenant owns the object and when a signed download URL may be issued.

That rule is useful for a fintech SaaS because the dangerous failure is not a slow upload. It is a valid object becoming visible to the wrong tenant, or a database row claiming that a report exists when the object never finished uploading. The application should therefore treat a signed URL as a temporary capability, not as a document record and not as proof of authorization.

The browser can move the bytes. It cannot choose the tenant boundary.

How can tenant isolation protect Node.js browser uploads, signed URLs, Postgres, and object storage?

The bounded scenario is a customer generating a monthly report while the browser tab is backgrounded. The API has created a pending record and returned a signed upload URL. The tab disappears before the completion request. A different failure has the opposite order: the object transfer succeeds, then the API process loses the response before it records completion. Neither case is unusual enough to justify pretending that object storage and Postgres share a transaction.

I model the document as pending, ready, or rejected, and keep the object key unique per revision. The create operation authenticates the caller, writes the tenant ID, document ID, revision ID, content type, and key in one database transaction, and only then signs the upload. The completion operation checks the object and performs a conditional pending to ready transition. A retry that finds ready can be idempotent; a completion for a different tenant must look exactly like a missing document to the caller.

The invariant is concrete: every downloadable report has one ready row for the requesting tenant and one matching object. A prefix listing cannot establish that relationship. It belongs in reconciliation, where it can find abandoned objects without becoming the authorization database.

One short sentence matters here.

Do not use a customer filename as the storage key. Store quarterly-report.pdf as display metadata in Postgres and use an opaque key containing generated IDs. Otherwise two tenants can collide through a careless overwrite, and a download path that accepts a filename becomes an access-control problem disguised as a routing problem.

Governance: tenant identity is application data

The request path has four distinct decisions. Node.js authenticates the session and validates the requested content type and size policy. Postgres records ownership and reserves a key. The storage adapter signs a narrowly scoped upload URL. The browser sends the bytes to storage and later calls a completion endpoint. For a download, Node.js first selects a ready row by both tenant_id and document_id, then asks the adapter for a short-lived signed download URL.

The URL must not carry the platform credential. The browser receives only the capability for the one object and operation it needs, while the credential used to create that capability stays on the server. A signed URL can be copied during its lifetime, so expiry, object-key secrecy, tenant checks, and audit records still matter.

The storage interface should be small enough to test without a live provider. Here is the state transition I would put behind the Node.js route layer; the Go example keeps the important database predicate visible and leaves URL syntax to the adapter.

package reports

import (
    "context"
    "database/sql"
    "errors"
)

var ErrDocumentNotReady = errors.New("document is not ready")

type ObjectStore interface {
    Head(ctx context.Context, bucket, key string) error
    SignPut(ctx context.Context, bucket, key, contentType string) (string, error)
    SignGet(ctx context.Context, bucket, key string) (string, error)
}

type Service struct {
    DB     *sql.DB
    Store  ObjectStore
    Bucket string
}

func (s Service) Complete(ctx context.Context, tenantID, documentID string) error {
    var key string
    err := s.DB.QueryRowContext(ctx, `
        SELECT object_key
        FROM report_documents
        WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND id = $2 AND status = 'pending'`,
        tenantID, documentID).Scan(&key)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    if err := s.Store.Head(ctx, s.Bucket, key); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    result, err := s.DB.ExecContext(ctx, `
        UPDATE report_documents
        SET status = 'ready', completed_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
        WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND id = $2 AND status = 'pending'`,
        tenantID, documentID)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    changed, err := result.RowsAffected()
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if changed != 1 {
        return ErrDocumentNotReady
    }
    return nil
}

func (s Service) Download(ctx context.Context, tenantID, documentID string) (string, error) {
    var key string
    err := s.DB.QueryRowContext(ctx, `
        SELECT object_key
        FROM report_documents
        WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND id = $2 AND status = 'ready'`,
        tenantID, documentID).Scan(&key)
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    return s.Store.SignGet(ctx, s.Bucket, key)
}

The read query is the important line, not the URL helper. The tenant predicate must be present in every read, completion, replacement, and deletion query. Row-level security can add a second barrier, but it should reinforce an explicit service-level authorization rule rather than replace it. Test the negative case: the same document ID under tenant A must never produce a signed download for tenant B.

Code path: make failed transfers visible in Postgres

A pending row is not an error by itself. It is evidence that the workflow has not reached its durable point. Give it a creation time, expected size, checksum when available, and an expiry policy. A cleanup worker can mark an old row rejected and remove its object if one exists; a reconciliation worker can also find objects with no corresponding row. The exact age threshold depends on maximum report size, browser retry behavior, and the service objective for abandoned storage, so I would measure those inputs before choosing it.

Completion should verify more than existence when the application has a reliable expected size or checksum. Content type is useful for product behavior, but it is not an identity check. If the provider supports conditional writes or checksum validation, use those capabilities in the adapter; otherwise, keep the check and the state transition observable so a later reconciliation pass can detect disagreement.

Replacement deserves its own rule. Do not overwrite a ready key while a customer can still download it. Allocate a new revision key, upload it as pending, validate it, and change the current revision in a database transaction. This makes rollback a row change and gives incident response an audit trail.

The operational signals are straightforward: pending rows by age, completion latency, object-check failures, cross-tenant authorization denials, signed-link issuance, and reconciliation backlog. Set an SLO for the time from successful storage transfer to ready; alert on a sustained breach, not on every browser that closes a tab. Capacity planning should include the largest concurrent report set, database write rate, signing request rate, and cleanup throughput.

Reliability signals for interrupted transfers

The choice is a boundary decision, not a URL-format decision. I would compare the options this way:

Design Tenant-isolation control Operational trade-off Choose it when
Direct provider integration Your adapter owns credentials, key policy, and signing behavior More provider-specific code to maintain One provider's controls, regions, or compliance evidence are mandatory
Common storage abstraction The application keeps one authorization and state model while the adapter varies The abstraction may hide provider-specific features The platform team values a small migration surface and can accept the abstraction's limits
Self-hosted object storage The team controls placement, network, and access policy Durability, upgrades, recovery, and capacity become on-call responsibilities Data placement requires it and the team has permanent operating capacity

The common abstraction is not a security boundary on its own. Postgres still owns tenant membership, the application still owns signed-link issuance, and reconciliation still owns the gap between two systems. A direct integration is not automatically safer either; it can be safer when a required provider control is unavailable behind the abstraction.

The catch is that this pattern is unsuitable for an immutable archive unless the selected storage system and retention policy provide the required immutability guarantee. It is also a poor fit for files that must be public forever, because short-lived signed links intentionally provide temporary access. Choose a design with explicit retention, replication, and legal-hold semantics when those are the actual requirement. Don't stretch a private-report upload flow into an archive platform.

Rollout: a storage boundary by on-call ownership

Use browser-to-storage transfer for large private reports, but keep the control plane in Postgres: tenant ownership, revisions, display metadata, status, expiry, and audit events. Sign uploads only after reserving an opaque key. Mark a row ready only after an object check. Sign downloads only after a tenant-scoped ready-row query. Reconcile both directions and measure the lag.

This design does not remove failure; it gives failure a state, a query predicate, and an operator action. That is the useful property. Your mileage may vary on checksum enforcement and retention windows because those depend on the storage API and the report policy, but tenant identity should not vary between them.

References

  • AWS S3: Using presigned URLs
  • MDN: Using XMLHttpRequest, including upload progress events
