title: My First Contribution to Zerocode: Building a Configurable Delay Executor,I Fixed the Code, But Who's Going to Fix My Sleep Schedule? 💀
description:
Writing

My First Contribution to Zerocode: Building a Configurable Delay Executor
Introduction
My open-source journey with Zerocode became a practical learning experience when I started working on Issue #810 — Configurable Delay Executor.

Instead of simply writing a delay using Thread.sleep(), the challenge was to understand how Zerocode handles API execution internally and integrate a dedicated delay executor into its existing architecture.

I spent approximately 6–7 hours understanding the codebase, implementing the feature, debugging integration points, writing tests, and verifying the final implementation.
The Problem
The requirement was to introduce a configurable delay mechanism that could be used directly inside Zerocode test scenarios.

A test scenario should be able to request a delay in milliseconds without requiring an external API.

For example:
{
"name": "wait_for_100_ms",
"url": "util://DelayExecutor",
"operation": "DELAY",
"request": 100,
"assertions": {
"status": "Success",
"delayMillis": 100
}
}
The challenge was not just waiting for a specified duration. The delay operation needed to work with Zerocode's existing execution flow, dependency injection, API routing, and scenario runner.
What I Implemented

  1. Dedicated Delay Executor I created a DelayExecutor interface and its implementation, DelayExecutorImpl.

The executor accepts a delay value in milliseconds, validates it, executes the delay, and returns a structured JSON response.

  1. API Routing Integration I introduced a dedicated DELAY_CALL API type and configured the URL:

util://DelayExecutor

This ensures that delay requests are recognized as delay operations instead of being incorrectly routed through the generic Java API execution path.

  1. Dependency Injection with Guice I integrated the new executor into Zerocode's Guice dependency injection configuration.

This allowed the scenario execution layer to access the delay executor through the framework's existing dependency injection mechanism.

  1. Scenario Runner Integration I updated ZeroCodeMultiStepsScenarioRunnerImpl to recognize DELAY_CALL and delegate execution to the API executor.

This made the new functionality available directly inside test scenarios.

  1. Validation and Interruption Handling I implemented handling for:
  2. Null and empty delay values.
  3. Invalid numeric values.
  4. Negative delay values.
  5. Thread interruption during execution. When interrupted, the implementation restores the thread's interrupt status before reporting the failure.
  6. Testing and Documentation I added unit tests, API routing tests, and an integration scenario.

I also updated the README with usage instructions and an example of the new executor.
Testing Results
The targeted Maven test execution completed successfully:

  • 19 tests executed.
  • 0 failures.
  • 0 errors.
  • 1 skipped.
  • Build: SUCCESS. The tests covered delay execution, zero delay, invalid inputs, negative values, interruption handling, API routing, and scenario-level integration. What I Learned This contribution helped me understand several important concepts in real-world Java development:
  • Understanding an existing codebase: How to trace execution across interfaces, implementations, API routing, and scenario runners.
  • Dependency Injection: How Guice connects components without tightly coupling their implementations.
  • Framework Architecture: Why adding a feature requires integration across multiple layers rather than writing an isolated method.
  • Exception Handling: How to handle invalid inputs and thread interruption correctly.
  • Unit and Integration Testing: Why testing individual methods is not enough when a feature must work across an entire execution pipeline.
  • Open-Source Workflow: How to investigate an issue, work on a fork and feature branch, create commits, push changes, and submit a pull request. Contribution Status I submitted my implementation through:

Pull Request #814 — [Issue #810] Add configurable delay executor

Repository: https://github.com/authorjapps/zerocode

Pull Request: https://github.com/authorjapps/zerocode/pull/814

The pull request is currently open and awaiting review.
Final Thoughts
This contribution was a reminder that real software development involves much more than writing code.

Understanding an unfamiliar codebase, identifying the correct integration points, handling edge cases, writing meaningful tests, and verifying the implementation are all part of the engineering process.

My goal with open source is to keep learning how production-level projects are structured while contributing useful, tested improvements to the developer community.

title: Best Claude Code Plugins 2026: 11 Tested, 4 Worth Keeping
description:
Originally published on Build to Launch. This is the condensed version.

I wrote the original article. An AI assistant condensed it, and I checked this version before I published it.

Have you installed a Claude Code plugin and then wondered why your sessions got slower, or why something ran that you never asked for?

That was my starting point. I build and ship with Claude Code every day. When the official marketplace grew to 101 plugins (as of March 2026), I stopped guessing and tested them on real work. Content plugins went on my actual writing system. Business plugins got my actual positioning questions. Coding plugins went into a real feature build for an app I maintain.

Eleven plugins in total. Below are the parts that matter most if you are deciding what to install this week.

What a Claude Code plugin is

"Plugin" gets used for four different things, and they cost you in four different ways. A plugin can bundle any of these:

  • Skills. What most people mean by "using a plugin." You trigger one with a slash command like /brand-voice:enforce-voice or /marketing:seo-audit. It runs once and stops. Cost: per use.
  • Hooks. They attach to events (session start, file write, commit) and fire every time without you asking. Cost: every session they are active.
  • Commands. The management layer: /plugin install, /plugin disable, /plugin marketplace add. Free.
  • MCP servers. Connections to databases, APIs and file systems. They ship inside plugins so often that people treat the two as the same thing. Cost: per query. (I wrote up the MCP servers I use daily separately.)

One install can give you a skill, a hook and an MCP config at once. Three behaviors, three cost levels. When a session feels heavy, this is the first place I look.

One more source of confusion: the plugin system lives in Claude Code only. Claude on the web has MCPs and built-in tools, with no terminal, no hooks and no slash-command plugins. Claude Desktop has MCP-based extensions. If you read about a Claude Code plugin and cannot find it in the web app, that is why.

/plugin install security-guidance@claude-plugins-official
/plugin marketplace add owner/repo
/plugin install brand-voice@knowledge-work-plugins

Three levels of trust

Level 1: Anthropic's official marketplace. claude-plugins-official is built in. As of March 2026 it held 101 plugins: 33 built by Anthropic and 68 from partners such as GitHub, Playwright, Supabase, Figma, Vercel, Linear, Sentry and Stripe. Two more Anthropic marketplaces need a manual add: life-sciences (17 plugins) and knowledge-work-plugins (14 role-based plugins, including Sales, Marketing and Brand Voice).

A side note on labels: claude.com/plugins tags 11 plugins as Cowork-only. I installed Brand Voice, Marketing, Sales, Productivity and Cowork Plugin Management directly in Claude Code. They work there.

Level 2: community marketplaces. Any GitHub repo, added with /plugin marketplace add owner/repo. No verification. Also, a repo that advertises "1,916 skills" does not hold 1,916 things you can /plugin install. Some entries are full plugin packages and some are loose skill files.

Level 3: discovery sites. Indexes that scan GitHub for plugin.json. Useful for search, and they are not a source of trust.

Anthropic's own docs put it plainly: "Plugins and marketplaces are highly trusted components that can execute arbitrary code on your machine. Only install from sources you trust."

The results I can share here

Each plugin got three questions. Where does it work? Where does it break? Does it earn a place in the stack?

First, something that went wrong before any test ran. The knowledge-work-plugins marketplace failed schema validation when I tried to install from it. I had to fix the files in a local copy before I could test Brand Voice, Marketing, Sales or Productivity at all. An official Anthropic marketplace that would not install was not the start I expected.

Brand Voice: KEEP

Three skills: discover your brand materials, generate guidelines, enforce them while you write. On my content-engine folder it:

  • found 15 brand documents spread across subdirectories
  • found 34 Gumroad products I had never checked for consistency
  • wrote a 963-line guidelines file that loads in later sessions

It breaks if you write for several channels in different voices. Left on globally, it pulls everything toward one guideline set. The one-time discovery pays back on every article after, so it stays.

explanatory-output-style: CONDITIONAL KEEP

This one is a hook, so it shapes every response. When I asked Claude to explain the plugin marketplace, the answer scored 9/10 for clarity from me: layered explanation, component walkthroughs, ASCII flow diagrams. For tutorials and docs, that is the structure you want.

A quick coding question also gets a structured lesson. So does a content edit. And every exchange pays the token cost. I turn it on for teaching work and leave it off the rest of the time.

Marketing: KEEP

Six skills covering SEO audit, drafting, brand review, competitive research, campaign planning and email sequences. I ran four of them over about 1 hour 40 minutes:

  • SEO audit (30 min): 25 keyword opportunities, 7 competitors benchmarked, a 90-day plan.
  • Drafting (45 min): three SEO-driven drafts of about 2,900, 4,100 and 3,600 words with Brand Voice applied. They still needed editing, and they were real working drafts.
  • Brand review (25 min): 4 high-priority issues, including missing personal intros, uncited revenue claims and gaps in affiliate disclosure. Compliance score 85/100.

I enable it for content planning sessions and disable it for short social posts.

Sales: SKIP (for creators and builders)

I ran /competitive-intelligence on Build to Launch. In 2 minutes it produced an HTML battlecard with tabs, a comparison matrix, a dark theme and talk tracks. It looked finished.

Then I read the data. It said I had 2,000 subscribers. I have 5,000+. It compared me to The Rundown AI (2M subscribers) and DeepLearning.AI (7M learners), a different league entirely.

Marketing has a competitive-brief skill, so I asked both the same question. Marketing took about 45 minutes and came back with 3 comparable competitors, a "stuck-in-the-middle builder" positioning gap, 10+ content gaps and 7 actions. Grounded in my real tier. Sales is built for people with CRM pipelines and regular customer calls. If that is not you, most of it sits unused.

Productivity: SKIP if you already have a system

/start gives you task breakdowns, priority ranking and file-based memory across sessions. The design is thoughtful. If you already run Notion, Linear or a well-kept markdown file, it adds a second layer that manages the same information. I confirmed it works and moved on.

What is in the full guide

Those are 5 of the 11. The full guide on Build to Launch continues with:

  • the coding plugin results, including feature-dev cutting 4 database tables before a line of code was written
  • the stack I keep, with always-on vs session-based toggle logic for content, coding and UI work
  • a 9-question scorecard to run before you install anything
  • every breakage I hit and what I would do instead

If you are new to Claude Code, How to Onboard to Claude Without the Learning Curve covers the setup this post assumes. The Claude Code Hub indexes every guide I have on Claude tools.

FAQ

Do Claude Code plugins work in Claude Desktop or on claude.ai? No. The plugin system (skills, hooks, slash commands, marketplaces) is Claude Code only. Desktop and web support MCP connections.

Are the "Cowork" plugins limited to Cowork? The site labels them that way. I installed five of them from knowledge-work-plugins and ran them in Claude Code.

Are community plugins safe? Community marketplaces have no verification, and plugins can run arbitrary code on your machine. Start with the official marketplace and read what a plugin bundles before you install it.

Why does my session feel slower after installing plugins? Check for hooks. A hook runs on every session or every response, so its cost adds up even when you never call it. A skill costs you only when you use it.

Where do plugins live? In ~/.claude/plugins/. Install once globally and they work across projects.

Which plugin earned a permanent place in your setup, and which one did you uninstall after a day? Tell me in the comments. I am collecting candidates for the next round of tests.

More of my tests on real work are on my blog, Build to Launch.

— Jenny

title: Neuropixels のニュースと、分子構造ビューアの入力デバイス問題
description:
Neuropixels のニュースと、分子構造ビューアの入力デバイス問題

Neuropixels の話を聞くたびに、僕は学生時代の夜を思い出す。脳の細胞外記録の話だ。数千の電極を一度に刺して、スパイクを拾う。あのニュースを読んだとき、僕の頭に浮かんだのは「計測デバイスの解像度が上がると、必ずその先の入力側が詰まる」という、地味だけれど逃げられない法則だった。

三年前、僕は小さな研究室で分子構造ビューアのフロントエンドを触っていた。タンパク質のリガンド結合部位を眺めながら、ドッキングの座標を手で合わせる。マウスでぐりぐり回して、ホイールでズームして、また戻す。正直、楽しかった。でも午前二時を過ぎると、手首が痛くなって、指の動きが雑になる。回転のたびに意図しない軸に吸い込まれて、さっきの角度に戻れない。あの「戻れなさ」が、いちばん堪えた。

Neuropixels は、計測の側の解像度を一気に押し上げた。じゃあ、それを操作する側は？ 僕らはまだ、指一本で 3D の回転をやっている。ここに、静かな非対称がある。

僕が使っていたビューアは、いわゆる Web ベースの分子構造ビューアだった。特徴はシンプルで、ブラウザで動くこと、そして入力デバイスを選ばないことだった。特別なハードは要らない。マウスでも、トラックパッドでも、ペンでも、動く。ありがたい。でもその「何でも動く」は、同時に「何も最適化されていない」ということでもあった。

だから僕は、地味な実験を始めた。入力のレイテンシを測る。回転の開始から画面が動くまでの時間。マウス、トラックパッド、そして手元にあった安いペンタブレット。結果は、まあ予想どおりで、トラックパッドがいちばん遅く、ペンが意外に健闘した。でも差は数十ミリ秒の世界で、体感では「指の疲れ」のほうがずっと効いてきた。

ここで気づいた。分子構造ビューアのボトルネックは、レンダリングでも、通信でもない。入力の連続性だ。回転は、単発のクリックではなく、連続したドラッグの積分でできている。だから、途中で手が止まると、角度の連続性が壊れる。壊れた角度からまた探し直す。この往復が、地味に時間を食う。

Neuropixels の設計者たちは、たぶんこの手のことをよく知っている。電極の数を増やせば、データの帯域と、後段の解析の設計が問われる。同じように、ビューアの解像度を上げれば、入力の解像度と連続性が問われる。レンダリングのパイプラインを組むように、入力のパイプラインも組まないといけない。

僕が試した小さな改善は、たとえば、ドラッグ中の感度を速度に応じて変えること。ゆっくり動かせば細かく、速く動かせば大きく回る。これは新しい発明ではなくて、ただの慣性とゲインの調整だ。でも、これだけで「戻れなさ」はかなり減った。あとは、回転の軸をロックするキーを一つ用意する。修飾キーを押している間だけ、単一軸に固定する。これも地味だけど、構造を見るときの思考の流れを切らない。

技術的な話を少しだけ。Web で 3D を回すとき、多くのビューアは requestAnimationFrame のループで状態を更新する。ポインタのイベントは、そのループとは別のタイミングで飛んでくる。だから、イベントをそのまま反映すると、フレームとフレームの間で取りこぼしが出る。対策は単純で、イベントをバッファに貯めて、フレームごとにまとめて適用する。これで、見た目のカクつきと、入力の取りこぼしの両方が減る。

ベンチマークというほどのものではないけれど、手元のノート PC で、回転の 1 フレームあたりの処理を測ったことがある。バッファリングを入れる前は、フレーム時間のばらつきが大きくて、ときどき 30ms を超えていた。入れた後は、平均はほぼ変わらないのに、ばらつきが縮んだ。体感は、平均よりばらつきに効く。これは Neuropixels の解析でも同じだろう。平均のスパイクレートより、ばらつきのほうが解析を難しくする。

僕は、このビューアを「すごいツール」として紹介したいわけじゃない。むしろ、地味な道具として紹介したい。ブラウザで動いて、特別なハードを要求しない。入力デバイスを選ばない。だからこそ、自分の手に合う入力に、自分で寄せていける。マウスの感度をいじる。ペンを試す。キーボードショートカットを覚える。その積み重ねが、深夜の作業を、少しだけ人間的なものにする。

Neuropixels のニュースは、計測の話だった。でも、その裏にはいつも、操作する人間がいる。分子構造ビューアも同じだ。構造を見るのは、機械じゃなくて、僕らだ。だから、入力のデバイス問題は、ずっと地味で、ずっと大事だ。

もし君も、深夜に構造を回しながら「戻れない」と感じたことがあるなら、一度、入力の側から見直してみてほしい。感度、軸のロック、イベントのバッファリング。小さな調整が、思考の連続性を守る。そのビューアは、ここにある。

title: Vercel Connect adds webhook triggers for more providers
description:
Vercel Connect now supports webhook triggers for Resend, X, Twilio, Notion, and Telegram.

Connect receives webhook events, such as Telegram bot messages or emails received by your Resend domain, and forwards them to an endpoint in your Vercel project. It verifies incoming requests and handles provider heartbeats and verification challenges for you.

To get started:

  1. Open Vercel Connect in the dashboard. Enable triggers when creating a connector for your provider or in an existing connector’s settings. Connect registers webhooks automatically for Resend and Telegram.

  2. For Twilio, Notion, and X, use the webhook URL from Connect and follow its instructions to complete setup in the provider’s settings.

  3. Add a trigger destination to choose the project and endpoint that should receive events.

You can turn triggers on or off later in the connector’s settings.

In the connector’s Observability tab, select Live to watch incoming trigger events.

These connectors join existing trigger support for Slack, Discord, Microsoft Teams, GitHub, and Linear.

Learn more in the Connect triggers documentation.

title: Fitting Gentoo in redb
description:
portage-cli is a Rust reimplementation of Gentoo's Portage tools; Like Portage, it reads the package repository from the file system: ~132k files plus some more if you are using git as backend:

What Files Share of files Size Avg per file
Ebuilds (cat/pkg/*.ebuild) 33,788 25.5% 56.5 MiB 1.7 KiB
md5-cache (metadata/md5-cache/) 33,788 25.5% 64.7 MiB 2.0 KiB
Package metadata.xml 19,460 14.7% 9.5 MiB 0.5 KiB
files/ (patches, configs, init scripts) 18,375 13.9% 26.0 MiB 1.5 KiB
Manifest 18,220 13.8% 28.1 MiB 1.6 KiB
metadata/glsa/ (security advisories) 3,855 2.9% 9.6 MiB 2.6 KiB
profiles/ 3,414 2.6% 2.9 MiB 0.9 KiB
licenses/ 645 0.5% 4.9 MiB 7.7 KiB
metadata/ other (news, DTDs, QA checks, …) 279 0.2% 2.0 MiB 7.3 KiB
eclass/ 255 0.2% 2.3 MiB 9.4 KiB
Category metadata.xml 174 0.1% 0.2 MiB 1.2 KiB
Top-level files, .github/, scripts/ 8 <0.1% <0.1 MiB —
Total 132,261 100% 207 MiB 1.6 KiB

That is a lot of small files to sync, store and stat.

Since on file systems like ext4 it does have a large impact, I tried to see how different would be if the repository is a single redb database instead, filled straight from git, with no checkout at all.

TL;DR

It works:

  • Sync is much faster: one day behind, 0.54 s against 0.83–0.97 s for git, and 8.28 s for emerge-webrsync. There is no worktree to update.
  • About a quarter of the space on a plain filesystem: 174 MiB against 593 MiB of checkout files plus a 96 MiB .git. NOTE: btrfs with zstd provides similar gains if tuned properly.
  • Reads are faster, but not dramatically: em -p @world is about 10% faster cold and the same warm.

The idea

A git repository is already a database of objects. A sync only needs the new commit's objects and a diff of two trees. A checkout is something you write out afterwards for tools that want files.

So the database holds:

  • the git objects (blobs and trees, zstd-compressed when that saves space), keyed by object id;
  • a paths index from repository path to object;
  • derived tables: the md5 of every ebuild and eclass, the package list, and what symlinks point to.

A sync speaks git protocol v2 directly, thanks to gix:

  1. ask for a thin pack against the stored commit;
  2. complete it with base objects already in the database, all in memory;
  3. check the tip's signature;
  4. diff the old and new root trees;
  5. apply everything in one write transaction.

There is no .git directory, no worktree and no temporary files. The tree is always exactly one signed commit: the old one or the new one, never a mix.

As long we do not need the actual files materialized we can at least spare space.

The main work

All the codebase had to avoid doing direct file system access and that required a bit of refactor here and there, zero cost abstraction is a Rust promise and it held well:

  • TreeSource reads bytes by repository-relative path: read, list, kind. FsTree is the file system checkout and RedbTree is the database. The parsers for profiles, layout.conf, categories, Manifests and USE descriptions are shared and no longer care where the bytes come from.
  • EntrySource produces valid metadata entries, and each backend answers it in its own way:
    • A fs checkout needs mtimes, a gap index and md5 re-digests, because files may change under you.
    • A redb tree is always a commit, so its answer is a merge of two ordered tables.
  • A build gets one real directory: FILESDIR, EBUILD and the Manifest need a package directory on disk. For redb that is a copy of just that package directory, kept per tree. Ebuild text, eclasses and profiles are read through the tree.

Masters, overlays and alias repositories sit above storage, so they mix freely. An overlay on disk can use a redb ::gentoo as its master, and inherit reads eclasses through the master's tree without copying anything.

This split was worth doing even if redb experiment goes nowhere. On the default path it costs nothing measurable:

em -p @world, warm, 15 runs master branch (no redb)
851 ± 10 ms 855 ± 9 ms

Results

All runs were on one machine (Ampere-1a, 128 cores), pinned to one NUMA node, with the checkout and the database at the same commit. That last detail matters, as you'll see later.

Sync: the clear win

Behind git fetch + reset --hard redb sync Wire pack
1 day 0.83–0.97 s 0.54 s 106 KB
7 days 1.46–1.48 s 1.25–1.26 s 1.81 MB
12 days 1.96–1.98 s 1.41 s 3.83 MB

Over GitHub, 12 days behind, it was 2.7–2.9 s against 3.5–5.3 s for git. For comparison, emerge-webrsync takes 8.28 s for the 1-day case and downloads 50 MB.

About 40% of the 1-day redb sync is compact(). It keeps the file near its import size; without it, 14 daily syncs grow the file from 143 to 178 MiB.

Size: it depends on your filesystem

checkout files .git (depth 1) redb tree + md5-cache
Plain filesystem (ext4, 4 KiB blocks) 593 MiB 96 MiB 143 + 31 MiB
btrfs with compress=zstd:3 112 MiB not measured 173 MiB

On an uncompressed filesystem, every small file costs at least a block, and redb is about a quarter of the size. On btrfs with zstd, most of the tree's files are stored inline in metadata. Then the checkout's files are smaller than the database, which is already zstd-compressed, and the saving is only the .git directory.

Reading metadata: parallelism matters more than the container

Reading the whole md5-cache:

Threads directory redb
1 318–350 ms 335–336 ms
8 61–76 ms 66–74 ms
12 46–57 ms 38–40 ms
32 33 ms 20–21 ms

Most of the gain is parallelism, and a directory read gets that too. In em itself:

checkout redb
Valid entries for ::gentoo 70 ms 55 ms
em -p @world, warm 934 ± 41 ms 920 ± 40 ms
em -p @world, cold page cache 1.32–1.42 s, 124 MiB read 1.19–1.25 s, 119 MiB read
em search -S, warm 62 ms 76 ms (every entry is decompressed)

The two backends give the same @world plan and the same search output. Cold, redb is about 10% faster with about the same bytes read; warm, they are equal.

A slow path lingering

Running with no metadata cache at all exposed something unrelated to storage. Ebuilds without a valid cache entry were checked and sourced one at a time, on every backend. Moving that onto the worker pool em regen already uses made the process snappier:

Case before after
Overlay without md5-cache, 3,909 ebuilds, cold 12.75 s 1.50 s
redb, no cache database, 33,977 ebuilds, cold 73.1 s 7.64 s

So far

Sync is where a database pays. One thin pack and one transaction beat git fetch plus reset --hard at every delta, and leave no worktree to repair. Since the tree is always one verified commit, its metadata needs no freshness checks.

The tree and the metadata cache live different lives. They ended up as two files. The cache can lag behind the tree, run ahead of it, or be missing. Each backend says which entries it lacks, and shared code fills them.

A build needs one real directory, not a checkout. My first attempt copied eclass/ and the repository's identity files and opened the copy as the repository. It was a shortcut, and it hid profiles/thirdpartymirrors. Tracing a real build showed that only the package directory has to exist on disk.

Measure on matching inputs. One early cold-cache figure (99 against 124 MiB read) came from a build that still read profiles and eclasses from the checkout. A redb tree from a different commit than the checkout made an overlay's cache look stale on every run. Re-measured on one commit, it is 119 against 124 MiB. Several wrong turns were beliefs that a trace, a profile or the reference tool then corrected.

redb's readers and writer exclude each other. In its default mode both lock the file when they open it, so a running em keeps a sync from starting, and the other way round. Now the second one fails at once with an error naming the first.

Independent reviews find what the author stops seeing. Reviews of the branch found:

  • pruning old package copies could delete one another em was still building from;
  • a locked or corrupt database silently fell back to a stale checkout next to it;
  • a remote that hadn't moved skipped the signature check against the current keyring;
  • symlinks read as their target's name instead of its contents;
  • em clean treated a database-stored repository's distfiles as unreferenced.

Each of these became a regression test.

Try it (experimental)

The redb backend lives on the tree-source branch, behind cargo features, and the database format may still change.

cargo install --git https://github.com/lu-zero/portage-cli --branch tree-source portage-cli --features redb,sync-gix

Then set the sync type in repos.conf:

[gentoo]
location = /var/db/repos/gentoo
sync-type = git-redb
sync-uri = https://github.com/gentoo-mirror/gentoo.git

em sync imports the checkout's current commit from its git objects, or fetches the tip if there is no checkout. Later syncs fetch thin packs into the database.

What's still open

This first experiment is far from being a complete redb backend:

  • the db layout is naive
  • the compression can be tweaked
  • the db vacuum/housekeeping strategy can be better
  • the whole sync db-updates can be batched/streamed so the resident set can be reduced.

The design notes and the full measurements are in the repository: tree-storage.md and tree-storage-experiment.md.

title: Rune Is a Rust UI Framework Written for Agents, Not You
description:
The top comment on the Rune thread did not argue. It posted a table.

nicoburns, who maintains Dioxus Native, opened with one line: "maybe skip this vibe coded project."

Then he listed eight Rust GUI frameworks by crates.io downloads. egui at 30.3 million. Iced at 3.2 million. Slint at 2.4 million. GPUI at 447k.

Rune was not on the list.

The thread hit 177 points and 130 comments in a day. That ratio is the whole story.

People did not show up to praise it. They showed up to argue about what counts as a real framework.

I read the whole thing twice. The part that stuck with me was not the download numbers. It was a reply further down.

So it's a UI framework by agents, for agents?

That is not a joke. It is close to a literal description of the repo.

What Rune actually ships

Rune is a Rust UI framework from Anomaly, the team behind OpenCode. It has its own renderer, its own text stack, its own layout, and its own spring animation system. macOS, Windows, Linux and web from one wgpu backend.

The stack list is unusually specific:

  • wgpu for the GPU layer
  • Taffy for flex, grid and block layout
  • Parley, HarfRust, skrifa and fontique for text
  • AccessKit for accessibility
  • one instanced SDF quad pass plus a glyph atlas for most drawing

The goal in their own PLAN.md is "SwiftUI-on-iOS at 120 Hz." Springs are analytic tracks with duration and bounce. The render thread owns the presented tree and retargets with velocity instead of re-rendering views on the main thread.

That last part matters more than it sounds. Most Rust UI frameworks animate by rebuilding the view. Rune animates on the render thread and lets app code state a target.

The example code is another matter. Here is the toggle from the README:

let switch = el().key("switch").role("switch").label("Lights")
    .checked(s.on).focusable(true).size(38.0, 22.0).radius(11.0)
    .fill(if s.on { tok::accent(0, true) } else { t.control_off })
    .motion(motion::SNAPPY)
    .on_press(|s: &mut State| s.on = !s.on)
    .child(knob);

A commenter on HN put it better than I can: "egads man! It literally hurts my brain trying to parse it." He said he'd rather have Perl 5 line noise.

I don't hate it as much as he does. But I did have to read the absolute() line three times before I understood the knob was being positioned by hand.

The Electron comparison is the easy one

Electron bundles Chromium and Node into every app. You get a mature UI stack and you pay for it in RAM. That trade is old news.

The interesting number comes from Cap, the screen recorder. It moved from Tauri to GPUI in 0.6.1. On an M4 Max, release builds, four runs each:

Build CPU Memory
Tauri 76.6% 3,724 MiB
GPUI 17.5% 440 MiB

That is not a small delta. Cap's own report notes the win came partly from a redesigned path, where video frames stay on the GPU on macOS. Still, the direction is clear.

Discord's CTO announced on November 4 that the new desktop client uses GPUI. Discord is one of the biggest Electron apps on the planet. When that team moves, people notice.

Rune is aiming at the same target from a different angle. The flagship test in the plan is recreating OpenCode Desktop in Rune.

Which is a strange thing to put in a roadmap.

The GPUI section is the most honest part

Here's a question people always ask: why not just use GPUI? Zed built it, it works, it's fast.

Rune's plan answers that with a list of specific failures. Their team rebuilt the same small surfaces three times in ten days.

A pill went GPUI, then hand-written Metal, then a SwiftUI helper process. The reasons they give:

  • no backdrop or glass, because GPUI draws one forward pass into one layer
  • the Metal pill dropped 85 frames on finish until it got its own display-link thread
  • window and focus behavior wrong for HUDs and launchers
  • text looked thin, and unseen glyphs stalled the first frame by about 13 ms
  • no springs, so every app hand-rolled them
  • upstream frozen at 0.2.2

Their verdict: don't fork GPUI. Start fresh and lift the good parts under Apache-2.0. Rope, sum_tree, BoundsTree, the line cache, the macOS IME code.

I believe the list. It reads like someone who got burned, not someone writing marketing.

And then a reply on HN quoted Dax from Zed: "we just couldn't get gpui to look good enough." I can't verify that beyond the comment. But it fits the mood of the thread.

The part nobody else is doing

Rune's real bet is not the renderer. It's who writes the code.

From the README: "We don't take pull requests. Have your agent open an issue describing the bug or idea, and our agents usually turn it around fast."

Every app can run headless. An agent can render to PNG, dump the element tree, and drive scripted input. The accessibility tree and the agent inspector tree are the same tree.

That is genuinely new. I have not seen another UI framework ship that as a first-class feature.

And this is where the thread turned. One comment: "why are we giving more accessibility to agents than to like disabled human users?" Another asked if it was a framework by agents, for agents.

I don't think that's unfair.

The name is a mess

There is rune.build, a Go IDE that open sourced under GPLv3 two months ago. There is rune-rs, an embeddable dynamic language for Rust.

There is RuneScape. There is a viking game.

On the Reddit thread for the Go IDE, someone wrote "oh wait it's another Rune." Another person: "calling your C IDE Make."

I went looking for reactions to the UI framework and landed in a thread about a text editor written in Go. Two projects, one word, zero overlap. That's an afternoon gone.

The search results are just as bad. Half of my queries returned the language, the IDE, or RuneScape lore videos.

Who this is actually for

Rune is pre-release. The install line is a git rev of the dev branch. There is no crate on crates.io you should trust yet.

The docs are written for agents. A commenter called the README "more of a DONTREADME." He wasn't wrong. I read it and came out knowing less about building an app than I did going in.

If you are building a product this quarter, do not use this. Use egui, use Iced, use Tauri, use Qt. Something with a version number and users.

And if you're on Windows with no GPU fallback, ask what happens. The thread asked that and never got a clean answer.

Rune is for Anomaly, and for people who want to watch a bet get made in public.

One more thing the thread kept circling. There is no live demo on the site.

For a framework whose pitch is feel, that is a strange gap. Someone replied to that point with just: "And no live examples..."

That's the thing I'd fix first. Before tests, before docs, before the crate. Put the toggle on a page and let people click it.

The line I keep coming back to

Someone sat down and wrote documentation for a UI framework and decided the reader would be a model. Not a person learning layout. Not a contributor.

A process that renders PNGs and checks its own work.

But I keep thinking about the headless thing. An agent that can see its own output is a small idea with a long tail. Every framework will want that in two years.

I don't know if this is the future or a very expensive way to avoid writing docs for humans. But it's the first time in a while that a framework made me stop and ask who software is actually for.

title: pd.to_numeric(errors="coerce") Hid a $22.6M Bug in My Test Billing Feed
description:
Whenever a nightly CSV import starts failing on dirty strings, somebody eventually opens a pull request with this one-liner:

python 

df["amount"] = pd.to_numeric(df["amount_raw"], errors="coerce").fillna(0.0)

I get why people write it. When you have 500,000 payment events waiting to load and row 41,209 contains "$1,299.00" instead of "1299.00", letting float() blow up the whole job at 3:00 AM feels worse than coercing bad strings to NaN.

Except errors="coerce" doesn't just skip broken rows. Paired with .fillna(0.0), it turns formatted enterprise invoices into zero-dollar charges without logging a single warning. And if the same CSV feed also contains webhook retries or legacy cent-denominated rows (4900 instead of 49.00), your script finishes with exit code 0 and hands finance a completely made-up number.

I put together a 500,000-row benchmark (github.com/endlessfountain/silent-data-quarantine
) to see how badly a standard pandas script drifts on realistic payment noise, and how fast we can quarantine bad rows with reason codes instead of dropping or guessing values.

Where the numbers actually go wrong

If your CSV comes from a single clean Postgres table, you rarely see this. It shows up as soon as you merge exports from two or three sources: checkout webhooks, manual finance uploads, and older API versions.

Four things usually slip into the same column set. Manual enterprise exports show up with currency formatting like "$1,299.00" or commas, which to_numeric wipes out to NaN. Timed-out webhooks get delivered two or three times with the exact same event_id. Legacy mobile or v1 billing endpoints send integer cents (4900) next to v2 decimal dollars (49.00), and both parse cleanly as floats. Finally, missing timestamps often arrive as 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z because an upstream serializer defaulted null to zero, quietly wrecking monthly cohort queries even though pd.to_datetime() accepts the string.

Running the naive script against 500,000 rows

In generate_corrupt_feed.py, I generated 485,000 clean USD subscription charges ($19, $49, $99, and $299) adding up to an exact ground truth of $26,870,210.00, then mixed in 15,000 dirty rows across those four failure modes:

5,000 formatted enterprise charges like "$1,299.00" ($9,525,000.00 total)
5,000 duplicate event_id retries
3,000 rows recorded in USD_CENTS (4900, 9900)
2,000 rows stamped 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z

Running the usual coercion script (naive_pipeline.py) takes 2.48 seconds:

python 

df = pd.read_csv(csv_path, dtype=str)
df["amount"] = pd.to_numeric(df["amount_raw"], errors="coerce").fillna(0.0)
df["ts"] = pd.to_datetime(df["created_at"], errors="coerce", utc=True)
naive_total = round(float(df["amount"].sum()), 2)

Here is what it prints on Python 3.11:

json 

{
  "pipeline": "naive_pandas_coerce",
  "exit_status": "SUCCESS (0 errors raised!)",
  "rows_counted": 500000,
  "reported_revenue_usd": 49472490.0,
  "true_clean_revenue_usd": 26870210.0,
  "silent_dollar_error_usd": 22602280.0,
  "dropped_enterprise_invoices_usd": 9525000.0,
  "elapsed_ms": 2483.4,
  "memory_delta_mb": 55.4
}

What caught me off guard wasn't just the size of the error, it was that two huge bugs partially masked each other's tracks. The script threw away $9.52M of enterprise revenue by zeroing out "$1,299.00", yet still came out $22.6M above reality because the 3,000 USD_CENTS rows got summed at 100x face value alongside 5,000 duplicate webhook IDs. If you only spot-checked row counts (500,000 in == 500,000 out), everything looked healthy.

Splitting clean and dirty rows without iterrows()

The tempting fix is validating row by row with Pydantic or df.iterrows(). On 500,000 rows, Python-level row loops drag runtime from ~2 seconds out to 30+ seconds.

We can keep the check under five seconds (including writing CSVs back to disk) by building a vectorized reasons Series in pandas. Instead of failing the whole file or filling NaN with zero, every rule appends a tag to rows that fail it:

python 

MIN_VALID_TS = "2020-01-01T00:00:00Z"
MAX_SINGLE_CHARGE_USD = 10_000.00
def quarantine_dataframe(df: pd.DataFrame) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame, dict]:
    reasons = pd.Series("", index=df.index, dtype="object")
    bad_unit = df["currency_unit"] != "USD"
    reasons = reasons.where(~bad_unit, reasons + "UNIT_NOT_USD;")
    parsed_amount = pd.to_numeric(df["amount_raw"], errors="coerce")
    bad_number = (
        parsed_amount.isna()
        | (parsed_amount <= 0)
        | (parsed_amount > MAX_SINGLE_CHARGE_USD)
    )
    reasons = reasons.where(~bad_number, reasons + "UNPARSED_OR_OUT_OF_RANGE_AMOUNT;")
    parsed_ts = pd.to_datetime(df["created_at"], errors="coerce", utc=True)
    bad_ts = parsed_ts.isna() | (parsed_ts < pd.Timestamp(MIN_VALID_TS))
    reasons = reasons.where(~bad_ts, reasons + "INVALID_OR_EPOCH_TIMESTAMP;")
    dupe_id = df.duplicated(subset=["event_id"], keep="first")
    reasons = reasons.where(~dupe_id, reasons + "DUPLICATE_WEBHOOK_ID;")
    is_quarantined = reasons != ""
    clean_df = df.loc[~is_quarantined].copy()
    clean_df["amount_usd"] = parsed_amount.loc[~is_quarantined].astype(float)
    quarantine_df = df.loc[is_quarantined].copy()
    quarantine_df["quarantine_reason"] = reasons.loc[is_quarantined].str.rstrip(";")
    return clean_df, quarantine_df, {
        "total_input_rows": int(len(df)),
        "clean_rows_accepted": int(len(clean_df)),
        "quarantined_rows_rejected": int(len(quarantine_df)),
        "verified_clean_revenue_usd": round(float(clean_df["amount_usd"].sum()), 2),
        "quarantine_breakdown": quarantine_df["quarantine_reason"].value_counts().to_dict(),
    }

Notice why reasons concatenates strings rather than stopping at the first failed if check. When a single broken webhook row has both USD_CENTS and a 1970 timestamp, its quarantine_reason comes out as UNIT_NOT_USD;INVALID_OR_EPOCH_TIMESTAMP. Whoever fixes the upstream exporter sees every problem on that row in one pass instead of playing whack-a-mole across two re-runs.

Meanwhile, the 485,000 valid charges don't wait on manual cleanup. They land straight in clean_events.csv, and the 5,000 "$1,299.00" enterprise invoices sit safely in quarantined_events.csv where you can strip currency symbols and replay them without losing a cent.

Measured output and where pandas hits a wall

Running python quarantine_gate.py processes all 500,000 rows and writes both output files:

Metric Naive errors="coerce" Quarantine Gate
Reported USD total $49,472,490.00 $26,870,210.00
Error vs. ground truth +$22,602,280.00 $0.00
Enterprise invoices lost to $0 $9,525,000.00 $0 (5,000 rows quarantined)
Wall time 2.48 s (read only) 4.58 s (read + check + write 2 CSVs)
Process RAM delta 55.4 MB 138.6 MB

I also added a small regression test in test_quarantine.py with five synthetic rows covering all four failure types. Anytime someone touches the ingestion logic later, python -m unittest test_quarantine.py runs in 0.09s and fails immediately if .fillna(0) creeps back in.

One honest caveat before you copy this into a tiny container: look at that 138.6 MB memory jump. Reading columns as dtype=str in pandas and building string masks allocates eager copies in RAM. For hourly batches up to a million rows on a normal worker, 4.5 seconds and 139 MB is completely fine. Once single files grow past 5 million rows, or if your API runs inside a tight 512MB container with multiple requests arriving at once, eager pandas DataFrames will OOM-kill your worker. At that point you are much better off expressing these exact filter masks in Polars (scan_csv / scan_parquet) or DuckDB.

title: Preparing for Re:Invent 2026
description:
It's one of those times again! There is one big conference hosted by AWS that I always look forward to. Yep, I'm talking about AWS Re:Invent.

Every year, I'm excited to see what new services, tools, and announcements AWS has in store.

Out of curiosity, I did some research and discovered that the conference started back in 2012. That took me back to 2018, when I was just getting started with cloud computing. Fast forward to today, 14 years since the first one, and the conference is still going strong.

I attended for the first time last year, and it was an incredible experience!

Being surrounded by thousands of people, all sharing the same excitement, ambition, and curiosity about technology, was something else. I have to admit, I felt a little overwhelmed at first, but in the best possible way.

There was so much to see, learn, and explore. After experiencing it firsthand, I learned that attending is one thing, but preparing for it beforehand is another.

So, if you are planning to attend AWS Re:Invent for the first time, or even if you've been before, I'd love to share a few things I learned from my experience to help you prepare and make the most of your time there.

Along with all the excitement about attending sessions, workshops, and exploring what's new, I have one more thing on my agenda.

I am excited about something I've been planning for a while. I have one mission: run a 5K.

It's happening on Wednesday at 6 AM. Yes, you read that right. I'm swapping my usual conference morning routine for a 5K race!

I'm pretty excited, and it's definitely one of the things I'm looking forward to most.

I went ahead and created a training plan, of course, using ChatGPT. I set an ambitious goal: run a 5K in 30 minutes. I even wanted to run every day. Sounds ambitious, but I thought it was possible!

My training plan included easy runs, tempo runs to improve speed, and long runs to build endurance. I ended up running three times a week, adding strength training and taking only one rest day per week.

A month went by, and I felt great. I'd run during my lunch break or in the evening. I kept tracking my time and pace. Always looking for ways to improve.

But then I started noticing something wasn't quite right. My body was getting tired, and I was not giving it enough time to recover. I was pushing myself too hard and had not accounted for how much recovery my body actually needed.

I started reflecting on what I was doing wrong. My body was telling me something, and I needed to listen.

I stopped running completely for two weeks. Instead, I started doing yoga and gentle stretching. I also stopped lifting weights for a while. I wanted to be gentle to my body. I also spent time in the sauna and hot tub to relax and unwind.

Looking back, I realized I had overlooked a few things. I was not warming up before my runs or cooling down afterward. I was not stretching either. I had been so focused on running faster, and I forgot about taking care of my body along the way.

As of today, I feel that taking a step back was the right decision.

Now, I'm planning my training again, this time with a more balanced approach and the time I have left before race day.

My new plan includes two running days, one strength training day, two swimming days, and two rest days each week. I want to focus on quality rather than simply doing more.

There are a few things I am paying more attention to this time.

  • Warm up before running. A dynamic warm-up is important to prepare my muscles and joints before hitting the run.
  • Paying attention to my running form. Engage my core, maintain a comfortable stride, and be mindful of how my feet land. I also want to improve my balance and lower body strength because running involves repeatedly supporting my body on one leg at a time.
  • Make strength training count. Focus on strengthening my lower body and improving stability and balance.
  • Add swimming. It's a great way to get more low-impact, full-body exercise while giving my legs a break from running.
  • Fuel my body properly. Make sure I'm eating enough, especially getting enough carbohydrates and protein to support my training.
  • Get enough sleep. Recovery doesn't happen only at the gym or on the running trail. I had a great run, as always, after getting good sleep last night, so a good night's sleep matters too.
  • Stay hydrated. Drink enough water and consider electrolytes(coconut water) when needed, especially after longer or sweatier workouts.

If you've made it this far, I hope you've found something useful in my little training journey.

But most importantly, don't forget to listen to your body. It's easy to get caught up in chasing a goal and forget that recovery or rest is just as important as training.

And if you are running the 5K at AWS Re:Invent, I'll see you at the starting line. Come say hi!

See ya!

title: Google Just Bought a Stalled Wyoming Data Centre Site — and Is Spending $17 Billion on It
description:
Google has taken over an unfinished data centre project in southeastern Wyoming from Crusoe, and will invest $17 billion to develop the campus — its first data centre in the state. Crusoe confirmed the sale on November 6, a day after Google announced the investment. The deal closes a troubled chapter for a project that was meant to become one of the largest data centre campuses in America.

First, one clarification: $17 billion is Google's long-term investment in the campus, not the price it paid Crusoe. The sale price was not disclosed. The two numbers describe different things.

What changed hands

Crusoe, a Denver-based data centre developer recently valued at $30.9 billion, sold Google an unfinished project near Terry Ranch Road in Laramie County, in southeastern Wyoming. Crusoe said it has completed its involvement in the pre-development phase — site selection, government approvals and power strategy — and Google is taking over development.

Crusoe had originally announced the project last year with Tallgrass, a Blackstone-backed infrastructure company, planning to eventually scale it to 10 gigawatts. Google had been the target customer, but reportedly raised concerns about cost and construction timelines under Crusoe's management. In the end, Google did not become the customer. It bought the site instead.

Bloomberg first reported the sale back in June. The setback did not stop Crusoe from raising a $3.9 billion funding round in September, and the two companies are still working together: Crusoe is developing another Google data centre campus near Amarillo, Texas.

The $17 billion commitment

Google announced the investment on November 5, describing a long-term $17 billion commitment to build its first Wyoming data centre. Its partners are Tallgrass Energy, Black Hills Energy, American Electric Power and Related Digital. Google says it will pay for all the power it uses and for infrastructure needs directly caused by its growth, and forecasts hundreds of millions of dollars in property taxes for Laramie County and School District 1.

The scale is hard to overstate: $17 billion going into a single campus in a state with fewer than 600,000 people. The reason is simple — AI needs power, land and cooling, and Wyoming has all three.

Why Crusoe stepped aside

The deal shows how hard it has become for independent developers to deliver massive projects on time and on budget. Securing equipment, lining up power and managing construction at gigawatt scale is a different job from developing the site — and when the customer is Google, the tolerance for delays is short.

Crusoe CEO Chase Lochmiller said the company has more than 6 gigawatts of contracted capacity and over 40 gigawatts in its development pipeline. The Wyoming sale does not end Crusoe's business; it ends one project that had outgrown its original developer.

Powering the campus

Google's first announced power development is a planned 702-megawatt fuel-cell project using natural gas with carbon capture and storage, contracted with American Electric Power and using Bloom Energy fuel cells, with capture at Tallgrass's nearby Eastern Wyoming Sequestration Hub. Black Hills Energy described a broader 2.7-gigawatt resource mix, and the facility will use air cooling to reduce local water demands.

Those are planned systems and studies, not operating equipment — construction was planned to start in 2026, with full operation expected by the end of 2028. But the shape is clear: a hybrid of fuel cells, grid power and natural-gas turbines, with a longer-term carbon-capture roadmap.

For Wyoming, the deal is a landmark: a first Google data centre, billions in investment, and a new anchor for the state's energy economy. For the rest of the industry, the message is simpler. When a project this big stalls, the hyperscalers do not wait. They buy the site and finish it themselves.

Read the full story on Rohan Tech Official: Google Buys Crusoe's Wyoming Data Centre Site and Invests $17 Billion in the State

title: One SQL predicate, eleven implementations: unifying them and what our differential harness caught
description:
This is a story about paying down the most expensive kind of technical debt in a query engine — duplicated semantics — and the testing harness that made it safe. It comes from building MoteDB, an embedded multimodal database in Rust for robotics workloads, but the pattern applies to any engine that grew fast.

The bug that kept coming back

Through four rounds of pre-release bug hunting on v0.17, we kept landing on the same shape of bug:

The same SQL predicate, evaluated by different code paths, returned different answers.

WHERE emb = '[1.0, 2.0]' matched rows on one path and not another. DELETE filtered differently than SELECT for the identical WHERE. A JOIN with the predicate as its condition disagreed with the comma-join form of the same query. Every fix was correct; every fix was also whack-a-mole, because the root cause wasn't any single bug. It was this:

SQL comparison semantics lived in 11 separate implementations.

The interpreter had its own eval_binary_op. The fast per-row evaluators (two of them). The compiled WHERE path with hand-rolled arms per operator. The vectorized scan leaves. The JOIN predicate pushdown. The aggregate pre-filter. Plus two inline closures. They each made their own decisions about NULL handling, type coercion, and what happens when types are incomparable. Eleven implementations, eleven opinions.

Step 0: lock the present before changing it

The instinct is to immediately write the One True Implementation. We did the opposite first: characteristic tests that lock what every path currently does, before touching anything.

A 38-row matrix of type pairs × 8 operators, with the equality route and the ordering route asserted separately. Plus a dozen engine-level probes asserting NULL and three-valued logic behavior per path.

This mattered for two reasons:

  1. When we unified semantics and intentionally changed behavior (more below), the characteristic tests told us exactly which changes were deliberate. Every behavior change was a conscious verdict, not an accident that slipped through review.
  2. It produced the inventory. You can't unify what you haven't enumerated.

Step 1: one semantics layer

Everything now routes through a single module. The core is deliberately small — a three-valued result, one comparison function, and a coercion pair built on Cow so the common case allocates nothing:

pub enum Cmp3 { True, False, Unknown }

pub fn compare(a: &Value, b: &Value, op: OrdOp) -> Cmp3 {
    if matches!(a, Value::Null) || matches!(b, Value::Null) {
        return Cmp3::Unknown;
    }
    if !needs_coercion(a, b) {
        return match a.partial_cmp(b) {
            Some(ord) => Cmp3::from_bool(op.matches_ordering(ord)),
            None => Cmp3::Unknown,   // incomparable types
        };
    }
    let (a2, b2) = coerce_pair(a, b); // Bool↔numeric, bracketed-vector text, …
    match a2.partial_cmp(&b2) {
        Some(ord) => Cmp3::from_bool(op.matches_ordering(ord)),
        None => Cmp3::Unknown,
    }
}

Eleven call sites became eleven thin adapters. The subtle decisions got made once:

  • =/<> route through equality; <..>= route through ordering — because in SQL they are different questions when types are incomparable.
  • Incomparable types in an ordering comparison return Unknown, which filters as "no match" — the standard three-valued behavior.

Step 2: the differential harness (the fun part)

Characteristic tests lock one path at a time. What we needed was a machine that asks all paths the same question and demands the same answer.

So: a differential harness that generates random predicates — mixed types, NULLs, boundary values, bracketed vector literals, ISO timestamps — and runs each one through nine execution paths:

  1. SELECT … WHERE p (fast path)
  2. DELETE … WHERE p (on a copy, comparing affected row sets)
  3. UPDATE … WHERE p (same)
  4. INNER JOIN with p as the condition, left-to-right
  5. …and with the table order flipped
  6. Comma-join with p in WHERE
  7. Subquery IN (SELECT … WHERE p)
  8. Aggregate with p in WHERE
  9. GROUP BY … HAVING p

Any path disagreeing with any other fails the run, printing the seed, the predicate, and all nine answers. Seeded, so a failure reproduces with one environment variable.

Day one, it caught seven pre-existing divergences. All of them present in the released 0.17. My two favorites:

A path evaluated NOT (flag IN (0,1)) and returned every row. The IN branch used a bare == for membership. A NULL in the list matched a NULL value (bare equality says yes; SQL three-valued logic says UNKNOWN, which NOT keeps as UNKNOWN, which filters nothing through). Classic two-valued leak in one path while ten others had it right.

The harness filed a bug report against itself. Our UPDATE probe marked affected rows with SET a = a + 1000, then compared row sets. First run flagged disagreement everywhere. Diagnosis: rows with a = NULL stayed put — NULL + 1000 is NULL — so the "affected set" wasn't what the probe computed. The engine was right; our probe was wrong. (The fix was a sentinel constant instead of arithmetic.) If you build a differential harness, budget for it to catch your own test bugs first. That's it working.

Step 3: the verdict that overruled our own locked expectations

Here's the part that changed how I think about characteristic tests.

One divergence survived initial triage as "genuinely different": hash-set normalization for IN lists was parsing pure-numeric text like '7' as a microsecond timestamp. That's the timestamp parser's first-try bleeding into an unrelated normalization step. And our Step-0 characteristic tests had locked this in as current behavior — we'd documented the quirk as intentional.

The differential forced the question: the equality route doesn't parse '7' as a timestamp, the hash route does, the same predicate disagrees across paths, and one of them is clearly an accident. The verdict: pure-numeric text no longer normalizes as timestamps — and we amended the characteristic tests we'd written six weeks earlier.

The lesson I took: characteristic tests are for knowing what you do today. Differential tests are for discovering what's true. When they disagree, trust the differential.

Step 4: a ratchet, so it stays fixed

Unification decays if new code can quietly add a bare partial_cmp back. So the CI now counts raw value-comparison sites in src/sql (with an allowlist annotation for the legitimate ones inside the semantics layer itself) and compares against a ceiling number stored in a separate file:

check_sql_cmp: ok — violations 50 / ceiling 50

The rule is simple: the number can only go down. Lower the ceiling when you retire sites; raising it requires editing a file whose diff is conspicuous in review. It's the same ratchet pattern as coverage or lint baselines, applied to semantic concentration.

What this means if you're building an engine

  • Semantics that live in N places are not N implementations — they are N diverging timelines of the same spec. Budget for the unification before the divergence budget runs you.
  • Lock current behavior with characteristic tests before unifying, so every behavior change is a deliberate verdict.
  • Then build the differential. Same input, every path, demand agreement. It will catch your test tooling's bugs too; that's a feature.
  • Ratchet the count so the debt can't silently regrow.

The product, briefly

If you're curious what the engine is for: MoteDB is an embedded, MIT-licensed, single-process database in Rust for robotics and embodied-AI workloads — VECTOR columns with DiskANN indexes, time-series with continuous views, BM25 full text (CJK tokenization built in), BLOB, ACID, Arrow interop, and single-file snapshot export for fleet distribution. cargo add motedb, pip install motedb-python, or npm install motedb. There's a 10-minute runnable notebook in the repo's examples/ directory.

The 0.18 release this work shipped in also added CREATE CONTINUOUS VIEW, ALTER TABLE DROP/RENAME COLUMN, multi-process shared read-only mode, and EXPLAIN that records real execution decision points instead of a heuristic guess. Ten good first issues are up if you'd like to poke around a storage engine with the safety net on.

Thanks for reading. I'm happy to go deeper on the harness design or the coercion rules in the comments.

title: How to design client reports people actually read
description:
Business owners and agency leads often spend hours compiling monthly performance reports, client analytics, and project summaries. Yet when those reports are delivered, clients often skim past them, get confused by cluttered numbers, or ignore them completely.

The issue is rarely a lack of data. Most reports fail because they present raw figures without context, rely on confusing chart types, or break apart when someone tries to export or print them for an executive meeting.

When I build custom React dashboards & reports, my main focus is making complex information clear and immediately useful. Designing an effective report requires focusing on narrative structure, thoughtful chart selection, and practical export capabilities.

Lead with the summary and highlight what changed

Most stakeholders have about two minutes to understand what happened during the previous month or quarter. If the top of your report is a crowded grid of sixteen disconnected metric cards, your reader will not know where to focus.

Every report should open with a concise executive summary. Highlight three or four key performance indicators (KPIs), which are measurable values that show how effectively a business is achieving its core goals. Place these figures right at the top alongside clear comparisons to the previous period.

Raw numbers rarely tell the whole story on their own. Seeing that a website had 20,000 visitors does not help a client unless they know whether that figure represents growth or a drop. Showing delta indicators, such as absolute differences and percentage changes, provides immediate context so clients do not have to do mental math.

  • Show current totals alongside percentage changes from the previous billing cycle or quarter.
  • Group high-level business outcomes above granular operational metrics.
  • Include a brief written takeaway explaining the primary factor behind notable changes.

Choose the right chart and skip visual novelties

Data visualization is meant to make comparisons intuitive, but decorative charts often obscure the truth. Multi-layered donut charts, complex radar graphs, and 3D bar layouts look sophisticated on a design canvas, but they are difficult to read in practice.

Standard chart types remain the most reliable choice for business reporting. A simple horizontal or vertical bar chart makes comparing categories straightforward. A clean line chart is the clearest way to display continuous trends over time.

If a clean table can convey the information more clearly than a chart, use a table. When you do use charts, avoid plotting too many competing data series on a single axis. If three lines intersect repeatedly across twelve months, separating them into smaller individual charts makes the underlying pattern obvious.

Use color for meaning rather than decoration

Clients scan reports rather than reading them word for word. They look for headings, callout boxes, and color cues to locate the information that affects their decisions.

Color should always serve a functional purpose instead of acting as background decoration. When every chart in a report uses a different bright hue from a palette, none of the data stands out. It creates visual noise that slows down comprehension.

A neutral palette of grays and muted tones works best for grids, labels, and supporting axes. Save strong accent colors exclusively for items that require immediate attention, such as positive milestones, negative performance drops, or missed targets. Consistent color rules across all pages help readers interpret findings without checking the legend repeatedly.

Build print-friendly layouts and reliable PDF exports

Even in fully digital workflows, many executives still print monthly reports or download PDFs to read on a tablet or share in board meetings. If a dashboard is designed solely for wide desktop screens, exporting or printing it often results in cut-off graphs, broken tables, and wasted paper.

When developing reports in React, accounting for print styles from the start prevents major headaches later. CSS print style sheets allow you to hide interactive elements like date pickers, dropdown filters, and site navigation that serve no purpose on paper.

You can also use CSS page-break rules to keep charts and tables intact across pages. Ensuring your layouts adapt neatly to standard letter and A4 page dimensions makes your web-based reporting tools feel like finished, high-grade publications.

Practical takeaways for better client reports

Designing client reports that people actually read does not require heavy animations or overwhelming data dumps. It requires respecting the reader's time by giving them clear answers quickly.

By focusing on what changed, using dependable chart types, applying purposeful color, and ensuring clean print outputs, you transform raw data into a reliable decision-making tool that clients appreciate.

  • Lead with three or four primary metrics and clearly display the change from the prior period.
  • Rely on familiar bar charts, line graphs, and clear tables rather than complex visual widgets.
  • Keep backgrounds and supporting elements neutral so alert colors carry real weight.
  • Test print previews early to ensure exported PDFs look polished and legible offline.

Want help with this? See my React dashboards & reports service, or send me your site for a free review.

title: Testing Async and SSE Flows as a Scenario
description:
Quick answer: Test an asynchronous or SSE flow as an ordered scenario: start the long-running job, connect to the event stream, assert on the events as they arrive, and confirm the final completion state instead of polling one fixed response. SSE is modeled with a text/event-stream media type and an item schema describing one event, and the scenario engine can follow the real streaming system.

Why a single request does not fit async work

A long-running task does not return its result in one immediate response. It starts, emits progress over time, and completes later, often through an event stream. A single request that checks only the initial 202 or 200 cannot tell you whether the job finished or emitted the right events.

A scenario follows that lifecycle in order.

  • A first step starts the job and extracts a job or stream reference.
  • A later step connects to the SSE stream.
  • Assertions check the streamed events and the final state.

How SSE is modeled

Server-sent events are represented with a text/event-stream media type and an OpenAPI 3.2 item schema that describes a single event. That keeps the streaming operation a normal path item rather than forcing it into a plain REST shape, and the protocol is preserved when editing rather than silently converted.

Stage What the scenario does
Start job Send the request and extract the job or stream reference
Open stream Connect to the event endpoint and read events as they arrive
Assert events Check event types, order, and payload fields
Confirm completion Assert the terminal event or final state is reached

Assert across the streamed events

Streaming assertions differ from a one-shot check because the evidence arrives as a sequence of events.

  1. Assert the start step returns the expected accepted status and reference.
  2. Assert the stream opens and begins emitting events.
  3. Check the event types and order, since progress usually follows a defined sequence.
  4. Assert the payload fields on the events that matter.
  5. Confirm the terminal event marks the job complete.

Asserting the order and the terminal event matters, because a stream that emits progress but never reaches completion is a real defect even when every intermediate event looks fine. The engine runs the connected requests in the main process with streamed progress and a cancel action, so a hung stream can be stopped.

When a 200 hides a problem

An SSE or async step can return a healthy status while the event payload carries an error or an unexpected shape, just as a 200 can mask a contract break elsewhere. Assert the event fields against the item schema rather than trusting the connection status alone. If the expected events do not arrive, the result is inconclusive or a failure, not a pass based on silence.

Multi-protocol support is a supporting capability here. It lets the scenario follow the real system across SSE and other protocols, but it should not be treated as the headline. Scenarios stay outside the OpenAPI document with no x-scenarios keys and run against real connected requests rather than mocks.

Powerduck keeps the streaming steps and event assertions in the ordered run, so you can see the exact event where an async flow breaks.

Frequently asked questions

How is SSE represented in the spec? With a text/event-stream media type and an item schema describing one event. The operation stays a normal path item and is not converted into REST.

Can a single request verify a long-running job? No. It only sees the initial response. A scenario starts the job, follows the event stream, and confirms the terminal state across ordered steps.

What if the stream never completes? A missing terminal event is a failure even when intermediate events look correct. Assert completion so an unfinished job is caught.

The bottom line

Async and SSE work calls for an ordered scenario that starts the job, follows the event stream, asserts on the events, and confirms completion. Model the stream with the event media type and item schema, check event order and the terminal state, and do not let a healthy connection status hide a bad event payload or a job that never finishes. The scenario follows the real streaming system, which is what makes it more trustworthy than polling a single fixed response. Read more in the API scenario testing guide.

Feature

The AI.AGG function is generally available (GA). You can use this function to semantically aggregate unstructured input data based on natural language instructions.

Feature

BigQuery generative AI functions now support the gemini-4-argon model. This model is generally available.

Cloud Asset Inventory

Feature

The following resource types are publicly available through the ExportAssets, ListAssets, BatchGetAssetsHistory, QueryAssets, Feed, and Search (SearchAllResources, SearchAllIamPolicies) APIs.

  • Cloud Service Mesh: networkservices.googleapis.com/AgentGateway

Cloud Billing

Feature

Spend cap budgets are now generally available for a limited set of services

For eligible services, you can configure a spend cap budget to automatically pause usage when your estimated spend exceeds the budget amount you set. You can manage spend cap budgets in the Budgets page in the Google Cloud console and using the Cloud Billing Budget API.

Spend caps are a cost control mechanism. A spend cap is enforced when usage costs exceed your budget target amount. When enforced, any new request to the eligible services, within the specified project, are paused and no further usage costs are accrued until the spend cap is lifted. You can manually lift an enforced spend cap, or wait until the start of the next month when the spend cap is automatically lifted.

Spend caps use gross, estimated costs to trigger the alerts and caps, enforcing a cap much faster than the actual costs are processed and appear on billing reports. Even though faster than reports, the enforcement of spend caps isn't instant and any cost overages are billed as normal.

More information about spend cap budgets

For managing spend cap budgets in the Google Cloud console, see:

  • How spend cap budgets work to help you control spend
  • Limitations of spend cap budgets
  • Configure a spend cap budget
  • Lift an enforced spend cap

For managing spend cap budgets using the Cloud Billing Budget API, see:

  • Lift an enforced spend cap
  • Cloud Billing Budget API REST reference

Private Service Connect lets you connect to your instance from multiple Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks across different groups, projects, or organizations, and supports automatic endpoint and DNS record provisioning. When you configure private IP for an instance, you can still choose to use private services access or both connectivity options.

For more information, see Private IP configuration options and Configure Private Service Connect.

When you configure private IP for an instance, you can still choose to use private services access or both connectivity options.

Cluster Toolkit

Cluster Toolkit v1.106.0 is available. This release adds support for flexible managed instance groups on static compute nodes, multiple network interfaces (multi-NIC) for Google Cloud Managed Lustre instances, and parallelism controls for Terraform to accelerate cluster deployment and teardown.

This release also introduces the cloud-build community module to build container images with Cloud Build.

Additionally, this release adds preflight checks for storage profiles when you submit jobs and cleans up gateways when you cancel jobs.

This update also scopes the --main-only flag in the gcluster job logs command to the main Pod and its default container.

For more information, see the release announcement on GitHub.

Compute Engine

Generally available: You can query regional views of global Compute Engine project and OS image resources by using the regional read-only projectViews and imageViews endpoints. Querying regional views isolates your control-plane read requests to a specific region, helping your workloads stay available during global API disruptions. For more information, see Use regional views for resilient control-plane reads and Access global resources regionally for high availability.

Dataform

Gemini
