title: 5 Reasons Your AWS Bill Keeps Growing (Even When Nobody Uses Your App)
description:
You built a small side project on AWS. Traffic is basically zero. Yet every month the bill creeps up, and the line items look like error codes: USE1-NatGateway-Hours, USE1-PublicIPv4:InUseAddress...

If that sounds familiar, you're not bad at AWS. Most surprise bills come from the same five causes, and each one takes only a few minutes to check.

Note: Prices below are AWS list prices for US East (N. Virginia), checked in November 2026. Other regions can cost more, and AWS updates prices over time. Always confirm on the official pricing pages (links at the end).

  1. Resources that charge just for existing

Many AWS services bill by the hour, not by how much you use them. If the resource exists, the meter is running.

The classic example is the NAT Gateway:

$0.045 per hour, which is about $32.85 a month, even with zero traffic
Plus $0.045 per GB of data it processes

Lots of beginner tutorials create a NAT Gateway so private subnets can reach the internet. The tutorial ends, the gateway stays.

Other usual suspects:

Public IPv4 addresses. Since February 1, 2024, every public IPv4 address costs $0.005 per hour (about $3.60 a month), whether it's attached to something or not.
EBS volumes from instances you stopped or terminated. The disk can outlive the server.
Load balancers with no traffic.
RDS databases left running 24/7 for a test you finished weeks ago.

Quick check: find unattached EBS volumes and unused Elastic IPs in your current region:

bash
aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available \
--query "Volumes[].[VolumeId,Size]" --output text

aws ec2 describe-addresses \
--query "Addresses[?AssociationId==null].[PublicIp,AllocationId]" --output text

If anything shows up that you don't need, delete it. Stopping isn't always enough.

  1. Resources hiding in another region

The AWS console only shows resources in the region you currently have selected.

So if a tutorial had you build in N. Virginia (us-east-1) but you normally work in Oregon (us-west-2), those first resources seem to vanish. They haven't. They're still running, and still billing.

Quick check (console): open Resource Groups & Tag Editor → Tag Editor, set Regions to All regions and Resource types to All supported resource types, then search. Anything you don't recognize deserves a closer look.

Quick check (CLI): list EC2 instances in every region:

bash
for r in $(aws ec2 describe-regions --query "Regions[].RegionName" --output text); do
echo "== $r"
aws ec2 describe-instances --region "$r" \
--query "Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,State.Name]" --output text
done

  1. Data transfer and logs that add up quietly

Data transfer out: sending data from AWS to the internet costs money. You get 100 GB per month free, but that allowance is shared across all regions combined, not per region. Serving images or video straight from an EC2 instance can burn through it quickly.

CloudWatch Logs: ingesting logs costs $0.50 per GB, plus about $0.03 per GB per month to store them. Two things make this sneaky:

Verbose debug logging you turned on "just for today" and never turned off.
Log groups keep data forever by default.

Quick fix: set a retention period on your log groups:

bash
aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name "/aws/lambda/my-app" --retention-in-days 14

  1. Assuming "Free Tier" means "free"

AWS overhauled its Free Tier on July 15, 2025, and a lot of tutorials still describe the old model.

If your account was created on or after July 15, 2025, you chose one of two plans at sign-up:

Free plan: starts with $100 in credits (up to $100 more for completing onboarding activities). It's designed so you aren't charged. It ends after 6 months or when your credits run out, whichever comes first, and the account is closed unless you upgrade.
Paid plan: same credits, but once they're used up, normal charges apply automatically.

If your account was created before July 15, 2025, you're on the legacy Free Tier: 12-month trials with usage limits per service. Go over a limit, and you pay.

Either way, "free" has conditions. Check which model applies to you before you trust a tutorial's "this costs nothing" claim.

  1. Leaked access keys

This is the scary one.

Security researchers have planted AWS access keys in public GitHub repos to see what happens. In those experiments, attackers found and started using the keys within 1 to 2 minutes. A common move is to launch the largest instances they can, often for cryptocurrency mining.

These bills don't stop at tens of dollars.

Quick checks:

Search your repos (including old commits) for AKIA, the prefix of AWS access key IDs.
In IAM, deactivate any access keys you don't actively use.
Never create access keys for your root user, and turn on MFA for it.
The root problem: no automatic spending cap

All five causes share one thing. Unless you're on the new Free plan, AWS has no built-in spending cap that shuts everything down for you. It's not like a prepaid phone plan. If you don't notice, the charges keep coming.

So the first priority is a system that tells you early:

AWS Budgets: create a monthly cost budget with an email alert at 80% of an amount you're comfortable with. Budgets that only send notifications are free.
Cost Anomaly Detection: it learns your normal spending and alerts you when something looks off, at no additional cost. It's on by default for accounts that enabled Cost Explorer after March 2023, but check that the alerts go to an inbox you actually read.

One catch: budget data updates up to three times a day, typically 8 to 12 hours apart. An alert is a smoke detector, not a sprinkler. It tells you early; it doesn't put out the fire.

Wrapping up

Most surprise AWS bills aren't mysterious. They're idle resources, forgotten regions, chatty logs, Free Tier assumptions, or leaked keys. Spend 30 minutes setting up alerts and sweeping all regions, then 10 minutes a month reviewing your bill, and you'll catch almost all of it.

If you'd like the whole thing as a step-by-step setup, I put together a short PDF guide: a 30-minute action plan, copy-paste CLI commands, and a 10-minute monthly checklist. It's $9 on Gumroad: Stop AWS Bill Shock. Everything in this article works without it, though.

Sources (checked November 2026)

Amazon VPC pricing (NAT Gateway, public IPv4)
AWS News Blog: Public IPv4 address charge
AWS Global Network FAQs (100 GB free data transfer out)
Amazon CloudWatch pricing
AWS News Blog: Free Tier update, July 2025
AWS Budgets pricing
AWS Budgets user guide (update frequency)
Orca Security: 2023 Honeypotting in the Cloud Report
Comparitech: AWS credentials on GitHub abused within 1 minute

title: October 20, 2026
description:
Agent Platform Workbench

Change

M154 Release

Change

Installed latest packages from upstream dependencies.

Fixed

Fixed dataset and table search in the BigQuery panel, which sometimes failed to return results. Root cause is due to Datacatalog API being sunsetted in favor of Dataplex API.

Apigee X

Announcement

On October 20th, 2026, we began maintenance updates of Apigee instances configured for maintenance windows.

If you set a preferred window for maintenance for your instance, and your instance version is below 1-18-0-apigee-6, your instance will be updated to 1-18-0-apigee-6 within the next seven to 21 days. A notification containing the expected date of upgrade will be sent within the next two business days.

Note: Instances that meet either of the following two criteria will not be updated:
  • Your instance has a DNS misconfiguration, as described in Known Issue 445936920.
  • Your instance uses an Apigee Java Library that has been removed, as described in Apigee release notes dated October 16, 2025.

For more information on participating in scheduled maintenance windows, see Maintenance overview and Manage Apigee instance maintenance windows.

Cloud Workstations

Feature

Cloud Workstations supports automatic failover for boost configurations in Preview. When you enable automatic failover, Cloud Workstations automatically provisions a workstation VM using the boost configuration if Compute Engine lacks capacity for the default machine type during startup.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Antigravity Enterprise Gateway support

Antigravity Enterprise Gateway lets organizations route model inference requests from the Antigravity app, Antigravity CLI, and Antigravity for IDEs through a centralized enterprise gateway before forwarding them to Google Cloud. This deployment enables organizations to inspect and audit model traffic, enforce custom security and network egress policies, and authenticate developers through a gateway API key without requiring individual Google Account sign-in.

Requests routed through Antigravity Enterprise Gateway use a centralized Google Cloud service account and are billed on a pay-as-you-go (PAYG) consumption basis through the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. This deployment model doesn't use your Gemini Enterprise seat-based subscription quotas (such as included Standard or Plus monthly allowances). You can't use a gateway and sign in with a Google Account at the same time. If you want to use your included subscription quota instead, disable the enterprise gateway and sign in with your Google Account.

This feature is generally available (GA).

For more information, see:

  • Deploy Antigravity Enterprise Gateway
  • Connect Antigravity to an Enterprise Gateway.

Breaking

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 2.5 Pro discontinued in Canada and Japan

Gemini 2.5 Pro has been discontinued for in-country Gemini Enterprise app deployments in Canada and Japan. Agents and chat sessions in these regions that previously used Gemini 2.5 Pro automatically switch to in-country Gemini 3.5 Flash.

Gemini 2.5 Pro remains available in the global, us, and eu regions.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise and Manage web app features.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Fixed

A security issue in GKE fleet management that could have allowed unauthorized configuration changes to clusters registered to a fleet has been resolved. The fixes are rolled out to all regions, and no action is required.

Fixed

This is an update to the release note regarding the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver issue published on October 2, 2026.

This issue has been resolved. You can upgrade your cluster control plane to the following versions to fix the issue for ubuntu_containerd and older cos_containerd node pools:

Managed Service for Apache Airflow

Feature

Upgrade rollbacks are available in Managed Airflow (Gen 3). You can roll back an environment upgrade if you encounter degraded performance, Airflow bugs, or compatibility issues with your DAGs, plugins, or dependencies.

This feature is gradually rolling out over several releases. In this release, it's available in the following regions: africa-south1, asia-northeast2, asia-south2, australia-southeast2, europe-north2, europe-southwest1, europe-west10, europe-west12, europe-west8, me-central1, me-central2, me-west1, northamerica-northeast2, northamerica-south1, southamerica-west1, us-south1, asia-east1, asia-northeast3, asia-southeast2, europe-central2, europe-west4, europe-west6, europe-west9, northamerica-northeast1, southamerica-east1, us-east5, us-west3, us-west4, asia-east2, asia-southeast3.

Improved Airflow worker health checks to detect task queue connection issues more quickly.

Change

New Airflow builds are available in Managed Airflow (Gen 3):

  • composer-3-airflow-3.3.1-build.5
  • composer-3-airflow-3.2.2-build.9
  • composer-3-airflow-2.11.1-build.22 (default)

New images are available in Managed Airflow (Gen 2):

  • composer-2.17.16-airflow-2.11.1 (default)

Spanner

Feature

Spanner supports approximate aggregate functions for both GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL dialects. These functions produce statistical estimates of distinct counts, allowing you to compute results faster and save resources on large datasets compared to exact aggregation.

For more information, see approximate aggregate functions (GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL), HyperLogLog++ functions, and Sketches.

title: How Rillet ships 3× faster with AI agents on Vercel
description:
Rillet on Vercel

  • Tripled shipping rate in three months with eve agents deployed on Vercel

  • Two-person team closed 800+ Linear tickets in its first 4 months

  • Builder access via Enterprise Managed Users, SSO, and Directory Sync

  • Ships customer-requested changes to production in as little as two hours

  • Gives every builder access to models through AI Gateway

Rillet is an AI-native enterprise resource planning (ERP) platform. Their AI agents do accounting work inside a real-time general ledger, with human approval and a full audit trail. Rillet serves more than 600 customers working toward a zero-day close, reducing the time needed to close their books at month-end.

A product that helps customers close their books in near real time needs a team that can respond quickly to their requests. Anthony Liang heads Rillet’s two-person frontend team, formed only a few months ago, and leads the push to put agents to work across internal workflows, from shipping customer fixes to reviewing code.

The team builds agents with eve and runs them on Vercel, using Vercel Connect to give them access to Slack and Linear, while AI Gateway routes their model requests.

Standardizing every internal agent on eve

Anthony had been building AI applications since the GPT-3.5 era and had evaluated nearly every agent framework on the market, from the major model providers' SDKs to the open-source ecosystem. Each gave him primitives for the model loop but left him to decide where instructions lived, how tools registered, and how an agent reached Slack and GitHub.

Anthony could make those choices for his own agents, but he wanted conventions everyone at Rillet could follow, including people who had never touched TypeScript.

An agent is a directory

Anthony chose eve, Vercel's open-source agent framework for building, running, and scaling agents that keeps instructions, tools, and skills together in one directory.

People who know what an agent should do can shape its behavior through markdown instructions and skills without writing code, while its tools live in TypeScript files whose names become the API. Once an agent is ready, it can move from a laptop to Vercel without changing how it behaves. Rillet manages all of these deployments in one company-controlled Vercel organization.

Rillet uses Vercel Connect to give its agents access to Slack and Linear through reusable connections the team can attach to the projects that need them. Connect supplies short-lived tokens at runtime and handles refresh through its SDK, keeping long-lived provider secrets out of each application and giving builders fewer credentials to maintain. If a runtime token leaks, its expiration limits how long it can be used.

Anthony's team built a Slack bot that picks up tickets and opens PRs, while others run agents for incident analysis and Linear board management. Shared conventions make that work easier to reuse, and agent building has spread beyond engineering.

Running customer requests through agents, end to end

Before, when a customer would ask for a change, and the request would scatter across a Linear ticket, a Slack thread, and a catch-up conversation with an engineer. By the time anyone had the full context, the fastest part of the job was writing the code.

The person closest to the customer ships the fix

Rillet's customer success team now opens a Chrome extension alongside the Rillet app, highlights what the customer is seeing, and describes the change. The extension's eve agent captures the context and, if the change is safe and well-scoped, hands it to a coding agent that writes the spec, makes the change, and opens a pull request assigned to Anthony. Agents also spin up a browser in a sandbox to test the change and attach screenshots as proof, while Anthony reviews the pull request and merges it. If he requests changes, the agent resumes its session and addresses them.

Rillet's CEO recently posted that the company shipped more in the past few weeks than in the entire first half of 2026, on top of tripling its shipping rate over the prior three months. Rillet’s CPA team ships customer requests through its in-house agent, Nebula, within two hours of the ask. As one of their customers put it, Rillet has "completely ruined my expectations" for how quickly software vendors should make changes.

Using AI Gateway to give every builder every model

As more people at Rillet started building agents, connecting directly to Anthropic and OpenAI meant configuring access to each model provider separately. AI Gateway routes model requests to both through one integration, so builders can add an agent without setting up separate provider connections.

The model is a string

In eve, builders choose the model by setting a string in the agent’s configuration:

Agents deployed on Vercel authenticate to AI Gateway automatically. Builders can try different models for a task by changing the model string, without changing the integration. Usage breakdowns show Anthony which models the team uses and what they cost, helping him track spending and choose models as more people build autonomous agents.

Managing builder access through Enterprise Managed Users

As more people are building agents, Rillet also needs to manage their access to Vercel. With Enterprise Managed Users, builders sign in through Google Workspace single sign-on using company-managed accounts rather than personal ones. Directory Sync adds and removes their access based on assignments in Rillet’s identity provider, so account administration follows the company’s directory.

Rillet set up Enterprise Managed Users on its own and moved builders from personal to company-managed accounts in one transition, bringing their Vercel sign-in and account access under Rillet’s identity provider.

What's next

Anthony is building what Rillet thinks of as its agent factory, so bigger features can follow the same pipeline as small fixes. One agent writes PRDs and technical specs, while another connects to Rillet's Linear boards, Miro diagrams, and knowledge base to give other agents the context they need. With subagents and delegation built into eve, Anthony can add these specialized agents as directories within the same framework.

For a company whose mission is collapsing month-long processes into zero days, building agents in eve and running them on Vercel brings that same focus on speed to its internal tooling.

About Rillet: Rillet is the AI-native ERP built for the era of agentic finance. By combining a real-time general ledger, continuous close architecture, and AI agents in one system, Rillet enables humans and agents to run finance together with full context, controls, and auditability.

title: Zero Trust Between Services, Not Just Users: A Practical Pattern for Multi-Cloud Estates
description:
Most zero-trust conversations start with people: single sign-on, MFA, device posture, and conditional access for engineers and employees. That work matters. It is also only half the traffic in a modern estate.

The other half never touches a browser. A checkout service calls an inventory service. A reporting job reads from a database in another cloud. An inference endpoint receives requests from an application running somewhere else entirely. Those service-to-service calls are usually trusted because of where they come from — a VPC, a subnet, a VPN tunnel, a private range that was considered safe when it was drawn.

That assumption is the problem zero trust was meant to remove. If network location is the credential, then anything that reaches that network segment inherits the trust, including a compromised workload, a misconfigured job, and a test service that was never meant to run in production.

1. Give every workload an identity that is not an IP address

The first step is separating identity from location.

A workload identity should answer three questions on every call: which service is calling, in which environment, and with what proof that the identity was issued recently to that exact workload?

Patterns that hold up in practice:

  • Short-lived credentials over static keys. A token or certificate that expires in minutes limits the damage from a leak in a way a long-lived API key copied into configuration never can. Rotation stops being a calendar event when issuance is automatic.
  • Identity bound to the workload, not the host. Containers move, instances are replaced, and jobs run once and disappear. Tying trust to a machine name or an address breaks in exactly the environments where automation is working correctly.
  • Separate identities per environment. Production, staging, and development should not share a service identity, even when they share code. Environment confusion is a common incident pattern; distinct identities make it a policy denial instead of a data incident.
  • No shared service accounts across teams. When five services authenticate as the same generic account, logs can show what happened but not who did it. Per-service identity is what makes an authorization policy, and an audit trail, meaningful.

Cloud platforms across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle all offer workload identity mechanisms, but they do not automatically compose across clouds. In a multi-cloud estate, the design work is choosing one consistent identity model for cross-cloud calls instead of letting each cloud's defaults create a different trust story at every boundary.

2. Authorize the call, not just the connection

A firewall rule that allows one subnet to reach another on a port answers a connectivity question. It does not answer an authorization question.

Zero trust between services means each call is evaluated against policy: is this caller allowed to perform this action on this resource, in this environment, right now?

That evaluation does not need to be slow or centralised for every request, but it does need to be explicit:

  • Default deny between services. A new service should reach nothing until its outbound and inbound relationships are declared. The declaration is documentation that enforces itself.
  • Policy at the resource, not only at the perimeter. If a database accepts connections from the whole application tier, the tier is the perimeter. Narrow the rule to the named services that actually read and write that store.
  • Distinguish read, write, and admin paths. Many flat designs grant a reporting job the same path as the transactional service that owns the data. Separate policies for read-only consumers make least privilege practical instead of theoretical.
  • Make policy reviewable as code. A policy expressed in versioned configuration can be reviewed in a pull request, tested in staging, and rolled back. A policy that lives only as portal clicks cannot.

A useful test is to pick an internal service at random and ask: which named services are allowed to call it, and where is that written down in a form that would still be true after the team changes? If the answer is a diagram from last year, the policy does not really exist yet.

3. Encrypt and authenticate in transit, even on private paths

Private connectivity reduces exposure. It does not remove the need to authenticate the ends of a conversation.

Mutual TLS, signed tokens, or an equivalent authenticated transport should be the normal path for service-to-service traffic, including traffic that never leaves a private network. That provides two things a private route alone cannot: proof that the other end is the intended service, and protection if a route, tunnel, or segment is misconfigured later.

The operational lesson from teams that have rolled this out is to automate certificate and credential issuance from the start. Manual certificate handling is where service identity projects stall — not because the cryptography is hard, but because expiry becomes an outage pattern. Issuance, renewal, and revocation belong in the platform, with alerts on failed renewal long before expiry.

Start with the highest-value paths if a full rollout is unrealistic: calls that carry customer data, calls that cross a cloud or account boundary, and administrative interfaces. Then expand. A partial rollout with clear coverage is better than a mandate that every team quietly routes around.

4. Log the decision, not just the traffic

Traditional flow logs show that bytes moved between addresses. Zero-trust systems should also record the identity decision: which workload identity called which service, whether policy allowed it, and which policy version was in effect.

That record changes troubleshooting as much as it changes security:

  • A denied call from a legitimate service usually means a missing policy after a deployment, visible immediately instead of discovered as a silent failure.
  • An allowed call from an unexpected identity is a signal worth alerting on, even if the data accessed was ordinary.
  • Repeated denials from the same workload often reveal a stale configuration or a retired service that was never decommissioned.

Treat denials as telemetry, review them weekly during a rollout, and tune policy from evidence. A zero-trust deployment that generates denials nobody reads trains teams to request broad permissions to make the noise stop — which recreates the flat network, one exception at a time.

5. Roll it out without rebuilding everything at once

The estates that succeed rarely start with a flag day. They start with inventory and observation:

  1. List the real service-to-service flows from flow logs and application dependencies, not from architecture diagrams alone.
  2. Issue identities to workloads in observe mode, logging which identity would have called what, before enforcing denial.
  3. Enforce default-deny first on new services, where there is no legacy behaviour to break.
  4. Move the highest-risk existing paths — cross-cloud, cross-environment, and data-store access — to authenticated, policy-checked calls.
  5. Retire the broad network rules those paths relied on. This last step is the actual security gain, and it is the step most often skipped, leaving the new controls layered on top of the old trust instead of replacing it.

That sequencing also clarifies where help is useful. Designing identity, policy, and private connectivity consistently across several clouds is the combined problem CloudVerg works on for US businesses — private cloud and AI connectivity with VergShield covering zero-trust security alongside the wider platform set (VergMesh, VergForge, VergMind, and VergRail): https://cloudverg.com

Whether the work is handled internally or with outside support, the measure of success is the same: a network location on its own should no longer be enough for one service to reach another.

A short checklist

For each important service-to-service path:

  • [ ] Caller and callee each have a distinct workload identity, separate per environment
  • [ ] Credentials are short-lived and issued automatically; no shared static keys remain on the path
  • [ ] Policy names which services may call which resources, with read, write, and admin separated
  • [ ] Default is deny; new services start with no access until relationships are declared
  • [ ] Transport is authenticated and encrypted, including on private routes
  • [ ] Allowed and denied calls are logged with identity and policy outcome, and denials are reviewed
  • [ ] Broad subnet-to-subnet rules retired once identity-based policy is enforced

Zero trust for users changed how people sign in. Zero trust between services changes something more fundamental: it replaces inherited trust in a network diagram with explicit, checkable permission for every conversation that matters. In a multi-cloud estate, that is the difference between a segmentation story and segmentation that actually holds.

title: Password Generator: Why Math.random() Passwords Get Cracked (and What to Use Instead)
description:
Password Generator: Why Math.random() Passwords Get Cracked (and What to Use Instead)

Two years ago I shipped a password reset flow where the temporary password came from Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 14). Twelve characters, mixed letters and digits. It looked random. Our pen tester asked for two consecutive reset emails, pasted both tokens into a script, and reconstructed the generator's internal state in under a minute. Every "random" password our server could produce was now a short list for him.

That day taught me the difference between unpredictable-looking and unpredictable. I have rewritten that generator three times since, for three different employers, and the bug keeps coming back in code review because Math.random() is one line long and looks completely innocent. Here is how I generate passwords now, in Python, in Node, and when I am too lazy to write code at all.

Why Math.random() fails at this

Math.random() is a pseudorandom number generator, not a secure one. V8 (Chrome and Node.js) uses an algorithm called xorshift128+ that keeps 128 bits of internal state. The state evolves deterministically from one call to the next, so a few consecutive outputs are enough to solve for it offline. This is not a theoretical concern; the technique is well documented and the tools to do it are public. The MDN page for Math.random() says it outright: it should not be used for anything security-related.

The fix is always the same idea: read randomness from the operating system's CSPRNG instead of a PRNG with recoverable state.

Method 1: Python's secrets module (Python 3.11.1)

Python makes this almost boring. The secrets module was added exactly for this job, and secrets.choice() picks a character uniformly.

# Python 3.11.1
import math
import secrets
import string

ALPHABET = string.ascii_letters + string.digits  # 62 symbols

def gen_password(length: int = 16) -> str:
    return "".join(secrets.choice(ALPHABET) for _ in range(length))

for _ in range(3):
    print(gen_password(16))

print("entropy:", round(16 * math.log2(len(ALPHABET)), 1), "bits")

Output from my machine:

p65Q27UkKzPhpNwe
qUPeJyfHVhF5333I
Br13QDK4tsv2zeYl
entropy: 95.3 bits

Ninety-five bits is well beyond brute-force reach. The secrets documentation recommends the same pattern for tokens, reset links, and anything else an attacker might guess.

Method 2: Node.js crypto.randomInt (Node 22.13.1)

In Node, reach for node:crypto. I use crypto.randomInt() per character. It performs rejection sampling internally, so every index is equally likely, which matters more than most people think (see pitfall 2).

// Node 22.13.1 (CommonJS)
const crypto = require("node:crypto");
const ALPHABET = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789";

function genPassword(length = 16) {
  return Array.from({ length }, () =>
    ALPHABET[crypto.randomInt(ALPHABET.length)]
  ).join("");
}

for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) console.log(genPassword(16));

Output:

qC3nGqZj5HZOwvkw
PCh5EqjcXuVvUokb
9eLoGcWlrzZX3nKB

In the browser the equivalent is crypto.getRandomValues(), which fills a typed array from the same class of OS entropy. Never reach for Math.random() as a fallback there either.

Method 3: when I just need one password, right now

Half the time I am not building a flow. I am setting up a database user or rotating an API credential, and I want one strong password in the next five seconds. Writing a script for that is overhead, and pasting something from a code snippet on the internet is how the modulo-bias bug from pitfall 1 survives into 2026. This is where I open a free online password generator, set length and character sets, and copy the result. This browser-based tool generates everything locally in JavaScript, so the password never leaves my machine, which is the whole point of a password generator in the first place. If you are auditing your own habits, the password generator is also a fast way to compare what a real 20-character password looks like against whatever your old script produced.

Three pitfalls that quietly weaken "random" passwords

1. Modulo bias when mapping bytes to characters. A common shortcut is charset[randomBytes(1)[0] % charset.length]. With 62 characters, 256 % 62 = 8, so the first 8 symbols get hit 5 times per 256 bytes while the rest get 4. I measured it with 620,000 single bytes in Python 3.11.1: index 0 landed 1.957% of the time versus 1.613% expected. That is roughly 21% more likely than its neighbors, on every single character of every password. secrets.choice() and crypto.randomInt() both avoid this; hand-rolled % does not.

2. Slicing Base64 strings. crypto.randomBytes(12).toString("base64") gives 16 characters of 96-bit entropy, which sounds great until you look at it:

+KQcdtawbjaxhglg   <- full string
+KQcdtawbj         <- slice(0, 10): about 60 bits left

Cutting to 10 characters throws away a third of the entropy you paid for. The full string also carries + and /, which break URLs and some CSV imports, and a 12-byte input always ends in exactly one = pad. If someone pastes os.urandom(12) output around, they probably shipped padding and bias together.

3. Requiring "complexity rules" on a strong generator. Forcing a digit, a symbol, and an uppercase letter into a 12-character password shrinks the effective search space and trains users to predict where the symbol sits (usually the end). A uniform 16-character alphanumeric password at 95.3 bits beats a rule-mangled 12-character one at roughly 71 bits. Length beats punctuation.

Summary

Method Entropy (16 chars) Best for
Python secrets.choice() ~95 bits Server-side token generation
Node crypto.randomInt() ~95 bits Node services, unbiased per-char picks
Math.random() tricks Recoverable state Nothing. Stop.

The pattern is simple: OS entropy in, uniform selection, no truncation games. Everything else is decoration.

More free browser-based utilities at utilvy.com.

title: Move an installed Windows app to a new PC, even from a dead PC's drive
description:
Reinstalling software on a new PC usually means hunting down installers, license files and settings. Sometimes the installer doesn't exist anymore, the vendor is gone, or the old PC won't boot. That's what WinAppMigrator is for: it works backward from what's installed and packs the app into one installer you run on the other machine.

What it does

  • Pick an app on this PC, or on a drive pulled out of a dead one. Connect the old disk and choose Connected drive.
  • See what goes in before you build: how big the installer can be, whether it fits, and what leaving a folder out would break.
  • Choose to migrate the license too. Tick License and activation data and its license files, values and stores go along. Anything that looks tied to the old machine is flagged. It never decrypts license data or bypasses activation, so a hardware-locked license may still need reactivating.
  • Runtimes ride along. The Visual C++ and .NET 6–10 runtimes the app needs are downloaded at build time and embedded, so the new PC doesn't need internet for them.
  • One installer, hash-checked. On the new PC it lists every service, task, shortcut, file type and firewall rule it will set up before it changes anything, rolls back if the install fails, and uninstalls from Settings like any other app.

How it finds what an app owns

  • Install records first: MSI, Inno Setup and NSIS logs, App Paths. Reading Inno logs by their blocks and length prefixes took Git for Windows from 0 resolved paths to 9,220 files.
  • Then exact names only: folders and registry keys must match the product's whole name or Vendor\Product, never a substring. On one test PC that took VS Code from 175,182 files to about 68,900.
  • Near matches (a folder with a close name, a hidden entry from the same publisher) are offered unticked, each with the reason.

Tested on real apps

Every push moves 7-Zip, PuTTY, Eclipse Mosquitto, windows_exporter and Git LFS from one CI runner to fresh Windows Server 2022, Server 2025 and Windows 11 on Arm runners, then makes Windows use what was restored: an archive made and unpacked, a COM class activated, a file type opened, a shortcut started, and a service answering a real client.

Limits

  • Microsoft Store apps aren't listed.
  • The app's own updater may not know it moved.
  • Desktop Windows 10/11 and a real pulled disk haven't been run on CI yet, so try an installer before you rely on it.
  • Reading a failing drive can finish it off. Image it first.

Get it

Portable and signed, MIT licensed, written in Rust with egui. Windows 10 and 11, x64.

👉 https://github.com/RandyNorthrup/WinAppMigrator

If it saves you a reinstall, a ⭐ on the repo helps other people find it.

title: Catch the Risk Before the First Dose - Building an AI Drug Safety Reviewer That Remembers
description:
💡 In one line: I built TrialSleuth AI, an agent that reviews a new drug before its first human trial and remembers every past drug result, so it gets smarter with each one.

🚀 Try the live demo · 💻 See the code

🧪 The first dose is the scariest moment

Every new medicine eventually reaches a day when it is given to a human for the first time. By then it has passed lab tests and animal studies. Yet people in early trials still sometimes get hurt.

When you read about those cases afterwards, many of them look predictable:

What went wrong Was it known before?
A similar molecule damaged the liver ✅ Yes, in an earlier drug of the same class
A chemical feature affected heart rhythm ✅ Yes, a well-known warning sign
A common medicine pushed drug levels 2.5× higher ✅ Yes, seen in a past trial
Six volunteers were dosed on the same morning ✅ Yes, a lesson learned the hard way

The knowledge existed. It was just scattered across old reports, papers and people's memories.

So I asked myself: what if a tool could remember every past drug result and check each new drug against all of it before anyone takes the first dose?

📋 What TrialSleuth does

A pharma team describes their drug the way they would in a planning meeting:

  • 🧬 What it is: composition and chemical features
  • 💊 How much: the dose and how it goes up
  • 👥 Who gets it: which patients are allowed in
  • 🗓️ How: the trial design
  • 🔗 With what: which other medicines are allowed
  • 🔬 What we know: lab results so far

TrialSleuth then gives back a clear review:

  1. An overall risk level (High, Medium or Low)
  2. Risks by body system (liver, heart, kidneys…), each with the evidence it used
  3. Suggested changes: lower the starting dose, exclude a patient group, ban an interacting medicine, dose one person first
  4. Tests to run before anyone is dosed
  5. Limits of the review: what memory can't tell us

👉 Click to see a sample TrialSleuth report

Risk level: High - changes needed before human dosing

System Risk Why (IDs)
Liver 2–3× higher exposure in Child-Pugh B patients; interaction with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors HB-02, HB-03, PC-101, PC-102
Heart Possible hERG block and QT prolongation (aniline + basic amine core) PC-702, HB-05
Whole group Six people dosed on the same morning PC-801

Suggested changes

  1. Exclude Child-Pugh B patients until liver data exists (HB-02)
  2. Ban strong CYP3A4 inhibitors with a 14-day washout (PC-102)
  3. Dose one sentinel participant first and wait before the rest (PC-801)
  4. Run a hERG assay and add ECG monitoring (PC-702)

This is an example of the report format. It flags known risks; it never declares a drug safe.


⚠️ The rule I never broke: TrialSleuth never says a drug is "safe" or "will work". No software can promise that. Its job is to make sure known risks are designed out before human dosing, so experts start from a better plan.

🤖 Why not just ask ChatGPT?

A normal AI chatbot only knows what you paste into the chat, and forgets it when the chat ends. Ask it to review a drug and you get:

"Monitor liver function. Watch for drug interactions."

That sounds sensible, but it's generic. It isn't linked to any real past case, and it never learns.

A real safety expert works differently. They remember what went wrong before, and what fixed it. That's exactly what agent memory gives an AI. If the idea is new to you, Vectorize has a great explainer: What is agent memory?

🧠 Giving the agent a memory with Hindsight

I built the memory layer on Hindsight, an open-source agent memory system by Vectorize. I used Hindsight Cloud with its Python client, and the Hindsight docs got me from zero to a working memory quickly.

The agent uses four simple operations:

Operation What TrialSleuth does with it
🏦 Create bank One memory bank, drug-safety-memory, told to keep IDs, doses and percentages exact
💾 Retain Saves body knowledge, past drug outcomes (with the fix that worked), and a summary of every review
🔎 Recall For each new drug, pulls back the relevant body facts, similar past drugs and earlier reviews
🪞 Reflect A "What have you learned?" button that sums up lessons across all memory

vectorize-io / hindsight

Hindsight: Agent Memory That Learns

Documentation • Integrations • Cookbook • Benchmarks • Paper • Hindsight Cloud



What is Hindsight?

Hindsight™ is an agent memory system built to create smarter agents that learn over time. Most agent memory systems focus on recalling conversation history. Hindsight is focused on making agents that learn, not just remember.

hindsight-learning-demo.mp4

It eliminates the shortcomings of alternative techniques such as RAG and knowledge graph and delivers state-of-the-art performance on long term memory tasks.

🆕 Introducing Hindsight Models: decision, rerank and embedding models built for agent memory. Open weights on Hugging Face, or hosted on Hindsight Inference. Read the post →

Contents

  • Memory Performance & Accuracy
  • Quick Start — server · clients · platforms · embedded
  • Adding Hindsight to Your Agent — LLM Wrapper · integrations · coding agents · MCP
  • Core Concepts — memory types · retain / recall / reflect · observations · mental models & knowledge…
View on GitHub

Every memory has an ID, like HB-02 for a body fact or PC-102 for a past drug. The language model (Groq, running openai/gpt-oss-120b) must cite the ID for every claim. That makes each point traceable, and the app shows exactly what was recalled in a side panel, so reviewers can check the evidence themselves.

✨ The moment it clicked

Our demo drug is a made-up cancer medicine called HLV-772. Its plan hides a few quiet problems: patients with weak livers are allowed in, six people are dosed on the same day, and no other medicines are banned.

  • 😶 Memory OFF: a generic answer with no evidence.
  • 🧠 Memory ON: it flagged a liver risk, citing HB-02 (weak livers can mean 2–3× more drug in the blood) and PC-102 (a similar drug where certain common medicines raised levels 2.5×). It suggested banning those medicines before the first dose, which is exactly the fix that worked last time.

Then I taught it one new result: a sister drug that affected heart rhythm in animal tests (PC-702). I ran the same review again and a brand-new ❤️ Heart row appeared, citing PC-702 and asking for ECG monitoring and heart tests before dosing.

🌱 One new result, saved once, and every future review gets better. That learning loop is the whole point.

🛠️ What I learned building it

1. Better memory beats more memory.
At first I sent everything recalled to the model. The prompt grew with every saved review until the model refused it. Recalling a tighter set of the most relevant records fixed the errors and made the reports sharper.

2. Show the evidence.
The side panel of recalled memories became the most convincing part of the app. People trust a review more when they can see what it's based on.

3. Honest framing is a feature.
"Here are the known risks and how to reduce them" is more useful, and far more responsible, than a confident yes or no.

🔭 What's next

Right now the memory holds a small, curated set of example records. A real version would be filled from a company's own trial history, published safety data and regulator reports, with access controls and expert sign-off on every review. I'd also love reviewers to mark which suggestions they accepted, so the agent learns which advice actually helps.

🔗 Links

  • 🚀 Live demo: trialsleuthai.streamlit.app
  • 💻 Source code: github.com/Sohapatel-26/trialsleuth-production
  • 🧠 Hindsight on GitHub: github.com/vectorize-io/hindsight
  • 📚 Hindsight docs: hindsight.vectorize.io
  • 📖 What is agent memory? vectorize.io/what-is-agent-memory

If you're building AI agents that should get better with experience instead of starting from zero every time, give agent memory a try. I'd love to hear what you build! 🙌

title: November 05, 2026
description:
Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

Scheduled maintenance of Management/Control Plane for the Apigee Edge for Public Cloud on November 6, 2026.

Scheduled maintenance of Management/Control Plane for the Apigee Edge for Public Cloud production will take place on Friday, November 6, 2026, from 9:00 PM PT to 10:00 PM PT (Saturday, November 7, 2026, from 5:00 AM UTC to 6:00 AM UTC). This maintenance follows the monthly maintenance window schedule documented in the Apigee Edge release notes archive.

During the scheduled maintenance window, the following services will be temporarily unavailable, and attempts to access them will return a 4xx status code:

  • Management Services UI
  • Management Services APIs
  • Monetization Management APIs
  • New proxy deployments
  • DevPortal Service
  • Microgateway Services
  • Edge Query (Analytics Stats APIs)

Runtime API calls to deployed API proxies are unaffected. While access to analytics queries may be temporarily unavailable during the maintenance window, all analytics and metrics data from this period will be available once maintenance ends.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.14.10

On November 5, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.14.10.

title: Browser Direct Uploads to Private Object Storage — Node.js, Express, and React
description:
Short answer: use a private bucket, let your Node.js/Express server issue one presigned PUT URL per receipt, and return a short-lived presigned download URL only after authorization. This keeps the original file available for audit while making tenant isolation an application decision, not a browser setting.

The decision table

Option Pick it when Tenant-isolation shape Watch for
Amazon S3 You need the deepest IAM, lifecycle, and compliance catalogue IAM policies, account boundaries, and bucket policy More policy surface to operate
Cloudflare R2 Egress economics and S3 compatibility matter API tokens plus bucket/key conventions Check which S3 features your workflow actually uses
Google Cloud Storage Your platform already lives in Google Cloud IAM and project-level controls Cross-cloud portability takes deliberate work
Infrai storage You want a self-describing HTTP surface across backend capabilities Your API enforces tenant prefixes and download authorization No public ACLs or self-service CORS rules; private access is the contract

The least complex option is usually the one your team already secures well. A receipt upload is not a file-hosting feature. It is an audit write with an identity attached.

How should a browser direct upload to object storage use presigned URLs?

Think of the request path as a small diagram in words: React sends file bytes to storage; Express never proxies those bytes, but it decides the bucket and object key; the database records tenant_id, user_id, MIME type, and the immutable business receipt ID. A later download starts with an authenticated tenant check, then Express mints a temporary URL.

Use a key that makes accidental cross-tenant reads difficult, such as tenant/{tenantId}/receipts/{receiptId}/original.pdf. Do not accept a complete key from the browser. Derive it from a server-side receipt record.

The following example keeps the storage calls small. It uses the documented bucket lookup and presign routes, and the browser performs the direct PUT.

import express from "express";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

const apiBase = process.env.STORAGE_API_BASE;
if (!apiBase) throw new Error("STORAGE_API_BASE is required");
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function storage(path: string, init: RequestInit = {}) {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${apiBase}${path}`, {
      ...init,
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        ...(init.headers ?? {})
      }
    });
    if (response.status !== 429) {
      if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Storage request failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
      return response.json();
    }
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "1");
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, Math.min(retryAfter * 1000, 8000)));
  }
  throw new Error("Storage rate limit persisted after retries");
}

app.post("/receipts/presign", async (req, res) => {
  const { tenantId, receiptId, mimeType } = req.body as { tenantId: string; receiptId: string; mimeType: string };
  // In production, derive tenantId and receiptId from the authenticated session and DB.
  const bucket = "receipts-private";
  const key = `tenant/${encodeURIComponent(tenantId)}/receipts/${encodeURIComponent(receiptId)}/original`;

  await storage(`/storage/bucket/get/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}`, { method: "GET" });
  const signed = await storage(`/storage/object/presign/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}/${encodeURIComponent(key)}`, {
    method: "POST",
    body: JSON.stringify({ content_type: mimeType })
  });
  res.json({ key, uploadUrl: signed.url });
});

app.listen(3000);

On the React side, upload the File to the returned URL with an explicit PUT and the same content type used when signing:

export async function uploadReceipt(file: File, tenantId: string, receiptId: string) {
  const presign = await fetch("/receipts/presign", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ tenantId, receiptId, mimeType: file.type })
  });
  if (!presign.ok) throw new Error(`Presign failed: ${presign.status}`);
  const { uploadUrl } = await presign.json() as { uploadUrl: string };
  const put = await fetch(uploadUrl, { method: "PUT", headers: { "Content-Type": file.type }, body: file });
  if (!put.ok) throw new Error(`Upload failed: ${put.status}`);
}

I keep the database write next to the presign transaction, then mark the receipt complete only after an upload confirmation or a server-side head check. That ordering matters: a URL being issued is not evidence that bytes arrived. In a real logistics queue, the sequence looks like this: the clerk opens a receipt page, the API authenticates the session and checks the tenant, a row is created with an object key and an expected MIME type, and only then does the API sign the PUT. The browser reports the result, a worker or callback verifies the object headers, and the row moves from pending to stored. If the tab closes after the PUT but before the confirmation, a reconciliation job can list the tenant prefix and compare it with pending rows. That is why the prefix is an index hint, not your authorization layer. The database remains the place where ownership, status, and retention decisions live; storage holds the bytes and enough headers to verify that the expected object exists.

Keep it boring.

Pick this when the storage boundary is private by design

Private-only access is a feature for receipts. There is no public or public-read ACL, so public_url is always null. Your download handler should check the caller's tenant and receipt permissions, call the presign operation for that exact key, and send the temporary URL back. Never store that URL as the canonical audit reference; store the object key and the database record instead.

Infrai's useful distinction here is a self-describing API: discovery exposes request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so wiring a new capability means reading one endpoint instead of adopting another SDK. Infrai also offers one key and one bill for storage plus other backend capabilities; a small team can keep one integration boundary instead of maintaining separate key rotation and invoice plumbing for every service. Those points reduce integration friction; they do not remove your authorization work.

The catch: browser CORS and audit guarantees have hard edges

Custom browser CORS can be a blocker. Although the bucket model has a cors_rules field, there is no exposed route for self-service CORS management, so a frontend that needs unusual origins or headers may fit S3 or GCS better.

There is also no object versioning or object lock (WORM). An accidental overwrite cannot be recovered from storage alone. For financial-grade immutability, add an external retention or archival system. There is no If-Match conditional write either; strict concurrent updates need a queue or a database lock.

Lifecycle expiration starts at one day, not an hour, and multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule. Server-side metadata search is limited: listing filters by prefix, so keep searchable attributes in your database. Cross-region replication and bulk cross-cloud migration are not included, and the supported vendor set covers R2, S3, OSS, and COS rather than GCS or B2.

For an audit trail, record the presign request ID, the object key, the authenticated principal, and the final head result. Keep those events append-only in the application log, with a retention period that matches your policy. A nightly reconciliation can flag rows that remain pending, objects whose headers do not match the recorded MIME type, and prefixes that have no corresponding receipt. This catches abandoned browser tabs and duplicate submissions without making the storage service responsible for business state. It also gives reviewers a concrete chain from tenant authorization to original bytes, which is the useful evidence during a dispute.

Stick with S3 when you need its mature policy ecosystem, object lock, or broad replication tooling. Choose R2 when its edge distribution model is the main requirement. Choose GCS when Google IAM and regional controls are non-negotiable. Your mileage may vary if compliance auditors require provider-specific evidence.

A practical ship checklist

Create or verify the private bucket once during deployment. Generate keys only from authenticated tenant and receipt identifiers. Persist MIME type and ownership in your database. Limit URL lifetime, log the receipt ID and request ID, and reject a download before signing when the tenant check fails.

Test the failure paths, too: a second tenant must receive no URL, a mismatched content type must be rejected by your application, and a retry after HTTP 429 must wait rather than spin. Small checks. Big audit payoff.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html

title: 10 Things Even AI Can't Do in Frontend Development (At Least Not on Its Own)
description:
AI can build a React component, generate a landing page, write CSS, connect an API, and even create an entire frontend from a short description.

A few years ago, getting that much code generated automatically would have sounded unrealistic. Today, it's part of a normal development workflow.

But here's something worth remembering: generating a working interface and building a good user experience are two very different things.

An AI-generated page might look impressive in a screenshot. Open it, resize the browser, navigate with a keyboard, test it on a slower connection, or use it with real content. That's usually when the missing details start to appear.

I've been thinking about this from a frontend developer's perspective. AI is becoming a useful part of the job, but there are still areas where generated code needs human judgment, experience, and a proper review process.

Here are ten of them.

1. Understand What the User Actually Needs

AI is very good at following instructions. The problem is that users don't always know how to describe what they need.

A product owner might ask for a dashboard with five charts, three filters, and a sidebar. AI can generate that layout without much trouble.

But does the dashboard actually help anyone make a decision?

Maybe users only need two important metrics. Maybe the filters are unnecessary. Maybe the information should be organized around tasks rather than categories.

These are product decisions, not coding problems.

A frontend developer needs to understand the reason behind a feature before deciding how to implement it. That includes business goals, user behavior, accessibility needs, and the context in which the interface will be used.

AI can suggest solutions based on the information it receives. It cannot reliably discover missing requirements or know which assumptions are wrong without additional evidence.

The difference: AI can implement a requested feature. Understanding whether that feature should exist in the first place requires product thinking.

2. Create a Distinctive Design, Not Just Another Familiar Interface

There is a reason so many AI-generated dashboards and landing pages look similar.

The same gradients, rounded cards, purple buttons, oversized headings, and familiar layouts appear again and again.

These patterns aren't necessarily bad. In fact, many are perfectly reasonable design choices. The problem starts when every product ends up looking like a variation of the same template.

A good interface needs more than visual consistency. It needs an identity.

A developer working with a designer considers questions that are difficult to reduce to a prompt:

  • What should users notice first?
  • Which elements deserve visual emphasis?
  • Does the design communicate the personality of the product?
  • Is the layout appropriate for the audience?
  • Does the interface feel different for a meaningful reason?

A 2026 study comparing AI-generated and human-created interface prototypes found that participants could evaluate generated interfaces positively on practical usability dimensions, while the more experience-oriented dimensions, such as originality and innovation, were less convincing. It's one study, not a universal verdict, but it illustrates an important distinction.

Read the study: Usable but Conventional — An Empirical Study on the UX of AI-Generated Interface Prototypes.

AI can give you a good starting point. Turning that starting point into a recognizable product experience takes design direction.

3. Make Animations Feel Natural

Animations are easy to underestimate.

A button changes color. A modal appears. A card moves into place. Technically, everything works.

But good motion design is not simply about making elements move. It communicates relationships, provides feedback, and helps users understand changes in the interface.

AI-generated code often starts with generic transitions. That is fine for a prototype, but applying the same duration and easing curve to every interaction can make an application feel mechanical.

Consider the difference between a quick button response and a page transition. They shouldn't necessarily have the same timing or visual weight.

Performance is another part of the problem. Animating layout-heavy properties such as width, height, or position can cause additional layout work. Sometimes a transform-based animation is a better choice.

There is also a simple accessibility detail that should not be forgotten:

.card {
  transition: transform 220ms ease;
}

.card:hover {
  transform: translateY(-4px);
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .card {
    transition: none;
  }

  .card:hover {
    transform: none;
  }
}

The prefers-reduced-motion media query lets the interface respect users who have enabled reduced motion in their operating system.

The goal isn't to remove every animation. It's to make sure that unnecessary movement doesn't get in the way.

The difference: AI can generate transitions. Deciding how motion should communicate an interaction, remain performant, and respect user preferences takes more than generating CSS.

Reference: MDN — prefers-reduced-motion.

4. Personalize an Experience Without Making It Feel Intrusive

Personalization is one of the most interesting areas of modern frontend development.

An application can recommend content, remember preferences, adapt its interface, and respond to previous interactions.

AI can help implement these features, but there is a subtle problem: more personalization does not automatically mean a better experience.

Imagine a fitness application that recommends a difficult workout because the user hasn't exercised recently.

That recommendation might be based on real activity data. But perhaps the user is recovering from an injury, travelling, or simply taking a planned break.

The application has information, but it doesn't necessarily have enough context to make a useful decision.

Personalization should have a clear purpose. It should solve a problem rather than demonstrate how much information an application has collected.

Good implementations also give users control over their preferences and explain why certain recommendations appear.

For example, a recommendation such as:

"You saved a similar article last week. Here are three related resources."

Feels more relevant than a random recommendation with no explanation.

Developers need to decide what data is appropriate, which recommendations are useful, and when personalization becomes uncomfortable.

The difference: AI can recognize patterns. Deciding whether those patterns should influence someone's experience requires context and judgment.

5. Understand Localization Beyond Translation

Translating an interface is not the same as localizing it.

AI can translate a collection of interface strings into multiple languages very quickly. However, a technically correct translation can still sound unnatural or communicate the wrong meaning.

Idioms, humor, cultural references, tone, and local expectations are difficult to handle with literal translations.

The same problem applies to visual design.

A layout designed for a left-to-right language may need adjustments for Arabic or Hebrew. Dates, currencies, address formats, number formatting, and even familiar symbols can differ between markets.

For example, an interface should not assume that every language uses the same text direction.

<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">
  <body>
    <main>
      <h1>مرحباً بك</h1>
      <button>متابعة</button>
    </main>
  </body>
</html>

CSS logical properties also make layouts easier to adapt:

.card {
  padding-inline: 1.25rem;
  margin-inline-start: 1rem;
  border-inline-start: 3px solid #6366f1;
}

Instead of hardcoding left and right, logical properties work with the document's writing direction.

The W3C explains that localization involves adapting an application to the language, cultural, and other requirements of a target market. It goes well beyond translating text.

W3C — Localization vs. Internationalization.

The difference: AI can translate strings. Making a product feel native to another audience requires cultural understanding and real local feedback.

6. Build Accessibility Into the Experience

This is one of the most important points on the list.

A frontend can look perfect and still be difficult to use for someone navigating with a keyboard or screen reader.

AI-generated interfaces sometimes contain buttons without meaningful labels, poor color contrast, confusing heading structures, missing alternative text, or controls that are difficult to operate without a mouse.

The issue is that accessibility is not always visible.

A screenshot cannot tell you whether a screen reader announces a button correctly or whether a keyboard user can reach every important interaction.

Consider this example:

<div class="button" onclick="submitForm()">
  Submit
</div>

It may look like a button, but it does not provide the native keyboard and accessibility behavior of an actual button.

A better implementation is straightforward:

<button type="submit">
  Submit
</button>

Native HTML elements already provide important semantics and interaction behavior.

For more complex interfaces, developers also need to manage focus, labels, keyboard navigation, error messages, and dynamic content.

The WCAG 2.2 guidelines organize accessibility around four principles:

  • Perceivable: Users must be able to perceive the information.
  • Operable: Users must be able to interact with the interface.
  • Understandable: Content and behavior should be understandable.
  • Robust: Content should work with current and future assistive technologies.

Recent research continues to identify accessibility issues in AI-generated interfaces. A 2026 IEEE study of AI-generated UI components reported problems including missing labels, incorrect ARIA usage, focus issues, and keyboard navigation failures.

Read the IEEE study.

Automated accessibility tools are useful, but they are not a replacement for manual testing with keyboards and assistive technologies.

The difference: AI can help write accessible markup. Making sure the whole experience is accessible requires testing with real interaction methods and users.

7. Make Responsive Design Work Beyond a Screenshot

A layout that looks good at 1440 pixels is not automatically responsive.

Real users have different devices, browser settings, text sizes, orientations, input methods, and screen dimensions.

A navigation bar that works on a desktop may become unusable on a narrow screen. A heading may overflow when translated. A card may look fine with short sample text but break when real content arrives.

AI can generate media queries, flexible grids, and responsive components. But it doesn't automatically prove that the result works across the situations your users encounter.

For example, this is a reasonable starting point:

.product-grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns:
    repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 16rem), 1fr));
  gap: 1.25rem;
}

The layout adapts to the available space without requiring a separate breakpoint for every device.

But responsive design is not just about screen width.

Consider:

  • Does the interface still work with larger text?
  • Are buttons comfortable to use on touchscreens?
  • Does the navigation support keyboard interaction?
  • Does the layout handle long translations?
  • What happens in landscape orientation?

These details need to be tested.

MDN's Responsive Design guide covers the platform features used to build layouts that adapt to different environments.

The difference: AI can write responsive CSS. Verifying the experience across real devices, content, and interaction methods is a separate job.

8. Optimize Performance Based on Real Users

AI can suggest code optimizations, lazy loading, code splitting, caching, and image compression.

However, performance is not something you can judge by looking at the source code alone.

A page can load quickly on a developer's laptop and feel painfully slow on an older phone or a poor network connection.

The actual experience depends on many things:

  • Device capabilities.
  • Network conditions.
  • JavaScript execution.
  • Third-party scripts.
  • Image and font loading.
  • Layout and rendering work.
  • User interactions.

That's why modern frontend performance uses real-world measurements.

Google's Core Web Vitals provide three important signals:

Metric What it measures Good target
LCP Loading performance 2.5 seconds or less
INP Interaction responsiveness Less than 200 ms
CLS Visual stability Less than 0.1

These targets are useful, but hitting them in a local test doesn't guarantee that every user has the same experience.

You need both controlled testing during development and field data from actual users.

Google — Core Web Vitals

The difference: AI can suggest performance improvements. Knowing which improvement matters requires profiling, measurement, and an understanding of the application's real usage.

9. Debug Problems That Only Exist in Production

A bug report that says "the page sometimes freezes" is not very helpful.

What browser was being used? Which device? What happened immediately before the freeze? Was the network slow? Did a third-party script fail? Was the user working with unusual data?

These questions matter.

AI can analyze logs, explain stack traces, and suggest possible fixes. That's genuinely useful. But it can only reason from the information available to it.

Production problems are often difficult because several things happen together.

For example, a race condition might only appear when a user quickly changes filters while a previous API request is still running.

A basic implementation might look like this:

async function searchProducts(query) {
  const response = await fetch(
    `/api/products?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`
  );

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error("Failed to load products");
  }

  return response.json();
}

The function is reasonable, but it doesn't handle the situation where users trigger multiple searches quickly and responses return in a different order.

A more complete implementation might use AbortController to cancel outdated requests:

let controller;

async function searchProducts(query) {
  controller?.abort();
  controller = new AbortController();

  try {
    const response = await fetch(
      `/api/products?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`,
      { signal: controller.signal }
    );

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error("Failed to load products");
    }

    return await response.json();
  } catch (error) {
    if (error.name === "AbortError") {
      return null;
    }

    throw error;
  }
}

Even this solution is only one part of the problem. The application still needs correct loading states, error handling, and a decision about what to display when a request fails.

Production debugging requires logs, monitoring, reproduction steps, browser knowledge, and an understanding of the complete system.

The difference: AI can help investigate a bug. It cannot reliably diagnose an environment it cannot observe.

10. Take Responsibility for Security and Long-Term Code Quality

A frontend project is not finished when the interface compiles.

The code needs to be understandable, secure, maintainable, and compatible with the rest of the application.

AI can generate a component quickly, but it may not know all the architectural decisions behind an existing codebase. It might introduce unnecessary dependencies, duplicate existing logic, bypass established patterns, or place too much responsibility inside a single component.

Security deserves particular attention.

For example, consider rendering user-provided content:

element.innerHTML = userInput;

This can create a cross-site scripting vulnerability when untrusted input is interpreted as HTML.

For plain text, use a safer approach:

element.textContent = userInput;

In framework-based applications, use the framework's normal escaped text-rendering mechanisms. Avoid bypassing those protections with raw HTML unless the content has been properly sanitized.

There is another important rule: frontend code is visible and controllable by the user. Business-critical authorization, secrets, and security decisions must not rely on client-side checks.

The OWASP Web Frontend Security Cheat Sheet explains why client-side input, API responses, browser storage, and third-party data should all be treated carefully.

Long-term quality requires more than passing tests today. It means being able to understand the code six months later, update dependencies safely, investigate regressions, and add features without breaking unrelated parts of the application.

The difference: AI can generate and refactor code. Developers remain responsible for the security boundaries, architecture, and consequences of shipping it.

Does This Mean AI Is Bad at Frontend Development?

Not at all.

I use AI as a development tool, and there are plenty of situations where it saves time.

It is useful for generating boilerplate, explaining unfamiliar code, creating prototypes, suggesting CSS solutions, writing tests, and exploring implementation alternatives.

The problem starts when we confuse speed with quality.

A generated component can be technically correct and still create a poor experience. A design can look professional and still be inaccessible. A translation can be understandable and still feel unnatural.

The better approach is to give AI the repetitive work while keeping developers involved in the decisions that affect users.

A practical workflow looks something like this:

  1. Define the user problem and requirements before generating code.
  2. Use AI to create a first implementation or explore alternatives.
  3. Review the code for accessibility, responsiveness, security, and maintainability.
  4. Test the experience with real content, devices, and interaction methods.
  5. Measure performance and fix problems based on actual evidence.
  6. Keep human review in the process before shipping.

AI becomes much more useful when it is part of a feedback loop rather than the final decision-maker.
