title: Twenty-six against forty
description:
I went to bed at about half nine, and the last thing I typed to the session before I did was this:

I am going to head off to bed now, but I would like you to continue the rollout and create all the MRs for waves 1-5, but do not merge them, we will review together in the morning.

The whole governance model is in that last clause

An estate-wide migration off a third-party errors library onto our own, across dozens of modules. It's mechanical and tedious, just the kind of job you want to hand over, and just the kind that goes badly wrong without making a sound.

I could hand it over and then sleep because everything up to the merge button is recoverable... a branch, a merge request, the lot. Forty merge requests sitting open overnight are, at absolute worst, forty things to close in the morning (and a mild feeling of having wasted an evening's compute).

The merge is where it stops being recoverable, so the merge is where the stop went. Once I'd seen that the stop was mine to place, leaving it running overnight stopped feeling like much of a gamble.

The morning, and what I did first

The work looked good, it really did.

So I typed back this, and it stopped short of an approval:

that looks really good! it does however raise a concern, only 26 MRs? we have 40+ projects, have we missed some... were some using stdlib errors instead of cockroachdb/errors... if so then that means we need to do a second pass

I hadn't read a single diff at that point, or opened a merge request. I'd looked at a count, held it up against a number I happened to know, and noticed they didn't match.

The agents didn't make a mistake

In one sense the night had gone perfectly well. The brief was to migrate every module using the third-party library, and each module using the third-party library had been migrated, correctly, one merge request each, unmerged, as asked. Audit the work against the instruction and it passes cleanly.

The hole was in the instruction. A chunk of the estate hadn't been on that library in the first place: those modules sat on plain standard-library errors, and they needed migrating just as much, for the same reasons. They weren't in scope because at half past nine at night it hadn't occurred to me (the one holding the map) that they were a separate category.

So the agents had done exactly what I asked, and what I'd asked for was short a good dozen modules. Better agents wouldn't have helped with that one (a better brief would).

The check a fleet can't run on itself

What caught it was arithmetic. Twenty-six against forty-plus! It wasn't a code review or a test, just one comparison between the shape of what came back and a number I'd been carrying around in my head, a number the fleet had no way of knowing. It only knows how many projects it was pointed at, which is a different number, and the gap between those two is invisible from the inside.

That's the most valuable review I do over unattended work, and it was a while before I saw it as a pattern rather than a lucky glance. And I'm inclined to say it's rarely reading the diffs. The diffs are the part the machine is good at (most of the time) and reviewing them line by line at that volume becomes mostly theatre, at least for something as well shaped as this migration was meant to be. It's things like: is this the right number of things? Does that total look like the estate I remember? Why is this one three times the size of the others?

Cheap, instant, and unavailable to the fleet, since each of those questions needs something that wasn't in its context.

The judgement calls it couldn't have made either

The review didn't stop at the count. The session had flagged three merge requests it had concerns about and left them for me instead of deciding for itself, which is the behaviour I want, and each of them needed a judgement call.

One had introduced a deprecation. I turned it into a hard removal instead. What was being deprecated was a hack, a very recent one, and I could walk it back easily enough if I was wrong. That's three pieces of context that live in my head rather than in the code: how old it is, what I thought of it when I wrote it, and how much it would cost to reverse.

Another changed a user-facing error message one release after that text had shipped. I accepted it as it was. The release window was short and the project was pre-release, so the usual compatibility care didn't apply.

The third had got a test passing by adding an entry to a dependency allowlist, to cover a neighbouring module that hadn't been migrated yet. By the time I read it the session had reworked that into an allowance with a tripwire on it, one that fails once the dependency has gone and the entry is no longer needed, and I was happy to leave it there.

They're all decisions I'd rather make myself, and I don't think any of the three could have been made from the diff alone.

Then the boring part that actually took the thinking

Merging forty-odd interdependent modules is not a loop. Do it in any old order and each merge triggers dependency-bump merge requests in everything downstream, which then race each other, and the CI churn is enormous and largely pointless. So the releases went leaves first, working up the dependency graph, so that by the time each module was released the things it depended on had already settled.

That part of the morning took real thought, and I suspect it's what an unattended run would have been least likely to get right. It needs the whole graph held in view at once, and it needs you to care about a mess that lands somewhere other than where you're standing.

The bookend, three nights later

A near-identical permission on a different night, in very similar words: I am going to bed now so please action this while I'm asleep, you have my permission to create a private repo.

By morning skillup existed, from nothing.

That was a much easier thing to agree to, and the reason's fairly obvious once you say it. A throwaway private repository is about as reversible as anything gets. Same pattern, different worst case, so the stop went in a different place.

Twenty-six against forty

I've thought about that count a fair bit since. It took about four seconds, it wasn't clever and it needed no expertise at all, just knowing roughly how many projects there are... which you only know from having built them one at a time.

Originally published at phpboyscout.uk on 8 November 2026.

title: I rewrote 7-Zip in Rust — here's what I learned about memory
description:
7-Zip is legendary for compression ratio and speed. It's also legendary for
eating RAM: compressing a 500 MB log file at 16 threads peaks at ~1.8 GB.

I wondered: how much of that is the algorithm, and how much is the
implementation? So I wrote r7z, a Rust clone of the core a/x commands,
and measured.

The numbers

Metric r7z 7z
Time (500 MB text, 1 thread) 68.4 s 19.4 s
Peak RSS (same) 85 MB 376 MB
Peak RSS (16 threads) 85 MB 1.8 GB
Ratio 0.02% 0.02%

Takeaways

  1. Ratios are essentially identical — the algorithm dominates.
  2. Memory is an implementation choice. 7z's solid-block arenas and per-thread buffers scale with thread count. r7z's bounded buffers don't.
  3. Speed is where C++ still wins — SIMD range coder, tuned match finder, and a custom work-stealing pool. Pure Rust can't match that yet without target-cpu=native, SIMD intrinsics, or FFI to liblzma.

What's next

  • FFI path via xz2 for parity speed
  • SIMD CRC-32 / match finder
  • Real multi-threading (currently single-threaded encoder)
  • Solid-block size knob

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL now supports the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct database flag.

Managed buffer pool automatically adjusts the InnoDB buffer pool size to reduce out-of-memory events. When instance memory usage remains at or below 70% for 10 minutes or longer after prior reductions, Cloud SQL increases the buffer pool size. You can now use the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct flag to change this 70% threshold to a different percentage. Increase the threshold to restore the InnoDB buffer pool size when baseline usage exceeds 70%, or decrease it to preserve additional RAM allocation for memory spikes.

This flag requires the Cloud SQL maintenance version MYSQL_VERSION.R20260726.00_05 or later. For more information, see Enable managed buffer pool.

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL supports blue-green deployments (Preview).

Blue-green deployments let you update databases—such as performing major version upgrades from MySQL 8.0 to 8.4 and staging hardware or configuration modifications—while minimizing downtime. During a blue-green deployment, Cloud SQL creates a separate staging environment (green) that mirrors your existing production environment (blue) and maintains continuous logical replication from blue to green. You can test application compatibility and performance on the green environment without affecting production traffic, and then trigger a switchover to the green environment with minimal application downtime.

For more information, see About blue-green deployments in Cloud SQL.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: You can sync a Compute Engine VM's clock with its host server's clock by using chrony and ptp_kvm to achieve accuracy designed to be within 1 ms. Accurate time synchronization is supported in all standard public Google Cloud regions and zones. For more information, see Configure accurate time for Compute Engine VMs.

Gemini

Other

Bug fixes in VS Code

Various bug fixes and minor product enhancements.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 3.8 Flash regional availability in Singapore

Gemini 3.8 Flash is generally available (GA) in Singapore (sg) with in-region at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP).

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise Standard and Plus Editions and Gemini Notebook Enterprise.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 in AI developer tools

Administrators can enable Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) for AI developer tools (Antigravity 2.0, Antigravity CLI, and Antigravity for IDEs). Third-party models are turned off by default:

  • In-console Terms of Service consent flow: Administrators can opt in to Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 directly in Gemini Enterprise > Settings > AI developer tools > Antigravity authorized models in the Google Cloud console without a separate Anthropic account or onboarding. For more information, see Configure AI developer tools settings.
  • Location availability: Third-party model inference is available in the global, us, and eu locations (in-country regions aren't supported). For a list of countries and regions that can access the model, see Anthropic's Supported countries and regions.
  • Consumption billing: Third-party model usage is billed as consumption on your Cloud Billing account and counts toward your project's spend cap, which covers all models. Pay-as-you-go usage above quota must be turned on before you can enable a third-party model. For more information, see Configure pay-as-you-go usage above quota and the Cloud Billing SKUs for Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5.
  • Thinking levels: Developers sign in with their existing Gemini Enterprise license and select Claude Opus 5.5 or Claude Sonnet 5.5 in the model picker at a thinking level of Low, Medium, High, or Max (for example, Claude Opus 5.5 (High)). Medium is the default.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.19

We've released version 6.19 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where agents could be assigned more concurrent chats than their configured maximum limit when multiple chat offers arrived almost simultaneously.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were unevenly distributed among available agents on skills-based queues.

  • Fixed an issue where supervisor-initiated sign-outs silently discarded mandatory interaction dispositions during an agent's wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's corporate email address and internal ID were exposed in the browser's network metadata during a virtual agent to human escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls were incorrectly routed back to the virtual agent queue instead of the intended destination.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound callers experienced a 2-second delay when connecting to an agent.

title: Read-Only Database Access and Safety
description:
Quick answer: The desktop connects to the database through saved profiles whose passwords are never returned, and it runs a read-only SELECT with a bounded row set through database.runSelect. Writes and DDL are blocked, so the software can read the live tables and keys for reconciliation but cannot modify the storage.

Why access is read-only

Reconciliation needs a real baseline, and that means reading the live tables and enforced keys rather than a guessed schema. It does not require writing, and giving a modeling tool write access would add a risk that the feature does not need.

Keeping the connection read-only lets the desktop observe the database while removing the chance that a generated or exploratory change reaches the storage.

The safety controls

Control Behavior
Saved profiles Connections are stored, passwords are never returned
runSelect Runs a read-only SELECT with a bounded row set
Writes Blocked
DDL Blocked
Row set Bounded so a query cannot return an unbounded result

The bounded row set matters because a read-only query that returns no limit can still pull an enormous amount of data, and the cap keeps the observation controlled.

How a read-only connection is used

  1. Save the connection as a profile without exposing the password back.
  2. Read the live tables and the enforced keys in the Observed layer.
  3. Run a bounded SELECT to inspect specific rows when needed.
  4. Compare the observation against the derived model.
  5. Keep every write and DDL blocked and generated for review.

The observed data feeds the reconciliation, and the enforced keys are part of the evidence. None of those steps need a write, so the connection stays narrow.

Consider a team reconciling a billing service. They save the connection once, read the live invoices table and its enforced foreign key, and run a bounded SELECT to inspect a handful of rows where the field looks wrong. The same tool that generates the proposed column cannot write it, so even if a migration contains a mistake, the connection refuses the change, and the team applies the reviewed script through a separate process. The bounded SELECT also keeps the inspection from pulling the full invoices table, which could be millions of rows, and the cap makes the observation predictable. Across the workflow the software reads and generates, and at no point does it hold a path that modifies the storage.

Why credentials are handled carefully

A saved profile stores the connection, but the password is never returned to the interface, which keeps the credential from being read out after it is saved. Treat the profile as a stored connection rather than a place to retrieve the secret, and manage the credential through the same careful channel as the other process-level secrets.

This is the same boundary that keeps generated SQL from being executed. The tool can read and generate, and it cannot write, so a mistake in a generated migration cannot be applied through the connection. The actual change is run separately after a review.

This follows the least-privilege idea. A process that only needs to read should not be given a credential that can write, and limiting the profile at the connection layer means the protection does not depend on a person remembering to avoid a destructive action. The blocked write is a hard boundary rather than a warning, and a DDL statement cannot run through the same profile even if it is pasted in by hand.

Powerduck keeps the read-only limit and the credential handling in the data layer, so observation and modification stay separate.

Frequently asked questions

Can the desktop write to the database? No. Only a read-only SELECT runs, and writes and DDL are blocked.

Why is the row set bounded? To keep a read-only query from returning an unbounded amount of data and to keep the observation controlled.

Are the saved passwords returned? No. The profile stores the connection, but the password is never returned.

The bottom line

The data layer is read-only by design: saved profiles never return passwords, runSelect executes a bounded SELECT, and writes and DDL are blocked. This gives the reconciliation a real baseline while removing any path through which the desktop could modify the storage. Read and generate freely, and keep the actual write in a separate, reviewed step. A connection that cannot write cannot be the source of an accidental change. Read more in the API data model guide.

Anti Money Laundering AI

New minor engine version released for the commercial line of business within the v004.011 version line (aml-commercial.default.v004.011.202610-000). This version extends support for the major engine version and includes no significant changes compared to the previous minor version.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.16.11

On October 14, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.16.11.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.16.11.
  • For information on new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release: The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Fixed

Fixed in this release

Bug ID Description
565072374 Fixed an issue where VerifyJWT policies using a JWKS uriRef could return steps.jwt.NoMatchingPublicKey on the first request after the 5-minute JWKS cache TTL expired when the identity provider rotated keys. The cache now refreshes synchronously upon expiration.
556680325 Fixed a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in URL host validation for the SemanticCacheLookup policy.
535395491 Extension Processor (ext_proc) denials now return the status and body that the policy or FaultRule produced, instead of always returning HTTP 500.
513032450 Fixed an issue where apigee-connect-agent control-plane connections could hang for up to 2 hours when silently dropped by a network intermediary by restoring a 15-second TCP keep-alive.
502540992 Fixed an issue where the SemanticCacheLookup policy was incompatible with Vertex AI Vector Search Private Service Connect (PSC) endpoints by adding gRPC transport support via <PrivateServiceConnect><GrpcEndpoint>.
492042425 Fixed an issue in the LLMTokenQuota policy where operation-level token quota values configured on an API product were not applied at runtime, causing product-level quota values to be enforced instead.

Application Integration

Security

An Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in the AuthConfig validation and integration execution runtime in Application Integration versions prior to August 27, 2026. For more information, see the GCP-2026-068 security bulletin.

BigQuery

Feature

The Apache Hive catalog endpoint in the Lakehouse runtime catalog is now generally available (GA). This integration lets you use the metastore as a serverless, central metadata layer, enabling seamless data sharing and unified querying across Apache Spark, Apache Hive, and BigQuery.

For more information, see About the Hive catalog endpoint and Set up Spark and Hive with the Lakehouse runtime catalog.

Feature

Metadata migration from Dataproc Metastore to Lakehouse is now generally available (GA). You can perform a one-time backfill migration or dry run to migrate metadata from a Dataproc Metastore service to an Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint or a Hive catalog endpoint using the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, or the REST API.

For more information, see Migrate metadata from Dataproc Metastore to Lakehouse.

Feature

Conversational analytics now lets you create a conversation with all of the data sources in multiple projects, or create a conversation with a dataset. These features are generally available (GA).

Feature

You can publish a BigQuery Conversational Analytics agent in Gemini Enterprise. This feature is now generally available (GA).

Feature

The AI.AGG function now supports the output_schema argument, which lets you specify the schema of the function output as a comma-separated list of fields. This feature is generally available (GA).

Certificate Manager

Change

Google-managed public SSL certificates signed by Google Public CA (pki.goog) are gradually transitioning from a 90-day validity period to a 45-day validity period to improve security.

To align with modern industry-wide security standards and promote shorter certificate lifespans, Google-managed public certificates now rotate more frequently. This proactive rotation enhances the overall security posture of load balancers. The transition requires no manual intervention or configuration changes as Certificate Manager automatically manages both issuance and renewal.

For more information, see Google-managed certificates and Use Google-managed certificates.

Cloud Load Balancing

Change

Google-managed public SSL certificates signed by Public Certificate Authority (pki.goog) are gradually transitioning from a 90-day validity period to a 45-day validity period to improve security.

To align with modern industry-wide security standards and promote shorter certificate lifespans, Google-managed public certificates signed by Public Certificate Authority now rotate more frequently.

This proactive rotation enhances the overall security posture of load balancers. Transition requires no manual intervention or configuration changes as Google Cloud automatically manages issuance and renewal for both Certificate Manager and Compute Engine SSL certificates.

For more information, see Renew a Google-managed SSL certificate.

Feature

Service rate limiting policies are now available in Preview for regional internal Application Load Balancers and Secure Web Proxies.

Service rate limiting policies let you maintain service availability among trusted clients that might consume an inordinate amount of resources.

For more information, see the Service rate limiting overview.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Issue

When you enable the Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance created before April 18, 2026, the integration defaults to once a day instead of near real-time.

Near real-time updates upon Knowledge Catalog enablement aren't yet available for all existing instances. A new announcement will be published when this feature becomes available.

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL

Issue

When you enable the Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance created before April 18, 2026, the integration defaults to once a day instead of near real-time.

Near real-time updates upon Knowledge Catalog enablement aren't yet available for all existing instances. A new announcement will be published when this feature becomes available.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: When you reserve capacity by using future reservation requests, you can specify that Compute Engine delivers your reserved capacity as specifically targeted reservations. Specifically targeted reservations help you track and control which Compute Engine instances consume your reserved capacity. For more information, see About future reservation requests.

Feature

Generally available: You can increase the size of a Google Cloud Hyperdisk volume that's in multi-writer mode while the volume is attached to multiple instances. Previously, you had to detach the volume from all instances before you could resize it.

For more information, see Share disks between instances and Change the size or provisioned performance of a Hyperdisk volume.

Dataform

Feature

You can automatically preserve BigQuery data policies and data governance tags (Preview) applied to tables across Dataform executions by enabling the preserveGovernanceControls option in your table or workflow configuration. For more information, see Preserve access controls metadata. This feature is generally available (GA).

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 3.8 Flash regional availability in the United Kingdom

Gemini 3.8 Flash is generally available (GA) in the United Kingdom.

  • Location availability: Supported in the UK (europe-west2) in-country region with in-region at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP).
  • App availability: Turned on by default in the web app for the UK region. Administrators can manage access with the Gemini 3.8 Flash toggle under Model availability.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon available in Workflow Builder

Gemini 4 Argon is generally available (GA) for Workflow Builder. Gemini 4 Argon is also available in Workflow Builder workflow agents. Updates take up to a day to appear in workflow agents.

  • Location availability: Supported in global, us, and eu multi-regions, with data residency and ML processing support in us and eu. For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.
  • App availability: Turned off by default. The toggle defaults to on beginning October 27, 2026. For instructions to turn on the model, see Manage features on the web app.

For more information, see Workflow Builder.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Priority PayGo support for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1

Priority Pay-as-you-go (PayGo) is available in General Availability (GA) for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 (gemini-nano-banana-2.1) on the global endpoint.

title: Retrieval Architecture for Insurance Claims Intake with Go and Delete Semantics
description:
Insurance claims intake has an awkward retrieval constraint: a document can become legally irrelevant before it becomes physically old. A withdrawn medical note, a superseded policy endorsement, or a duplicate claim must stop influencing an answer on a predictable schedule.

Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context; make deletion a first-class state transition so the application can swap vector providers without changing its answer contract.

Start with the retrieval contract

The contract is more important than the first embedding model. Define what one retrieval unit means (a paragraph, a form field, or a claim event), which metadata filters are mandatory, and how fresh an update must be before it is visible. For claims intake, I would attach claim_id, policy_id, document_id, revision, tenant_id, and a source timestamp to every unit. The generated answer should return those identifiers alongside its text, not just a similarity score.

This is an audit decision. A reviewer needs to reconstruct why a coverage question was answered with a particular clause, and an operator needs to prove that a deleted record was excluded after its effective deletion time. The retrieval layer therefore returns source context and a trace record, while the answer layer decides how to phrase uncertainty.

Keep the query bounded. A narrow metadata filter for tenant and claim, a fixed top-k, and a maximum candidate token budget make latency a controllable engineering variable. The first stage can favor recall; a later stage can apply stricter filtering or reranking. Do not let a broad semantic search silently cross policy or claimant boundaries.

One small rule prevents a large class of incidents: a missing vector is not the same as an empty claim. The contract should distinguish “no eligible source exists” from “the source has not reached the index yet.” That distinction belongs in the trace, where reconciliation jobs can act on it.

For a small developer-tools team, Infrai fits at this boundary because it offers plain HTTP with a single credential, one key, and one bill across 295 routes and 20 modules. Its public discovery surface describes capabilities without requiring a key. That breadth matters during claims intake because the same credential can cover retrieval alongside adjacent backend tasks, so an integration does not accumulate a separate secret and reconciliation trail for every service. The claims contract still stays yours, with a consistent interface even when you swap vendors.

How should retrieval architecture handle insurance claims intake deletes?

Deletion semantics should be explicit, monotonic, and replayable. When an upstream system marks document_id=med-184 deleted, write a tombstone to the source-of-truth ledger, enqueue removal of every vector carrying that document ID, and reject stale upserts whose revision is lower than the tombstone revision. Imagine the delete and an OCR correction arriving in the same second: the adapter records the tombstone at revision 8, the correction arrives as revision 7, and the write is discarded; a later revision 9 correction is allowed only after policy permits it. That ordering is what keeps a withdrawn document from reappearing during a retry storm, and it gives reconciliation a concrete pair of IDs to inspect instead of a vague “index drift” alert. A retry must be safe: deleting the same ID twice leaves the collection in the same state.

Deletion is a state transition.

Here is the application-side contract I use before binding to a provider. I first assumed the adapter only needed a read path; later I found that delete ordering and replay evidence deserve equal status. It is deliberately provider-neutral, so changing a backend does not change claims code or audit records.

package retrieval

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type SourceRef struct {
    TenantID   string
    ClaimID    string
    DocumentID string
    Revision   int64
    DeletedAt  *time.Time
}

type Candidate struct {
    Text  string
    Source SourceRef
    Score float64
}

type RetrievalRequest struct {
    TenantID string
    ClaimID  string
    Query    string
    TopK     int
}

type RetrievalTrace struct {
    RequestID string
    Sources  []SourceRef
    Filtered int
    FreshAt  time.Time
}

type Store interface {
    Query(RetrievalRequest) ([]Candidate, RetrievalTrace, error)
    DeleteDocument(tenantID, documentID string, revision int64) error
}

func ListCollections() ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/collection/list", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Second << attempt
            if raw := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); raw != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(raw); parseErr == nil {
                    wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            resp.Body.Close()
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        defer resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("infrai returned %s", resp.Status)
        }
        var payload any
        if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&payload); err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        return json.Marshal(payload)
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func QueryCollection(body []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/query", bytes.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    resp, err := (&http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}).Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("vector query returned %s", resp.Status)
    }
    return io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
}

The important part is not the interface syntax. It is the revision check. Upserts and deletes race in real ingestion pipelines, so the adapter must compare revisions atomically or serialize them per document. A successful delete should also remove the record from the collection, not merely hide it with a client-side filter; otherwise storage and audit counts drift.

Re-index changed content deliberately. A new revision gets a new chunk set, and the old revision is removed only after the new set is queryable, or the collection briefly has a known “no source” interval that the answer contract can expose. For a hard delete, retain the tombstone and audit event even after vector payloads are gone. The text disappears from retrieval; the fact that it was removed does not.

Compare the replaceable backends

Once the contract is stable, the backend choice becomes a measured trade-off between retrieval quality, latency, operational ownership, and migration effort. Elasticsearch is attractive when the team already operates analyzers, filters, and shard-level observability; its hybrid lexical-plus-vector tooling can be a strong fit for policy language. pgvector keeps vectors beside transactional claim data and simplifies joins, but query latency and index tuning become part of the Postgres operating budget. Pinecone offers a focused managed vector service with clear collection boundaries, while introducing another control plane and a migration surface of its own.

Infrai is a reasonable fourth option when the adapter should speak plain HTTP and the surrounding product already uses its backend services. Its discovery surface is public, and the vector capability is exposed through a consistent REST contract, so the code behind the adapter can move providers without rewriting the claims workflow. The supporting benefit is operational: one key and one bill cover the platform’s backend capabilities, which reduces credential and invoice plumbing around a small team.

Backend Useful fit Trade-off for claims intake Delete/migration question
Elasticsearch Existing hybrid search and mature analyzers More cluster and index operations to own Can the adapter preserve revision-aware deletes across indices?
Postgres + pgvector Vectors need transactional joins with claim rows Vector tuning competes with OLTP resources Can a replacement preserve SQL-side audit joins?
Pinecone Managed vector-focused operations Separate service and data lifecycle How are tombstones exported and replayed?
Infrai Plain REST integration across backend capabilities Validate fit for your latency and governance envelope Keep the adapter around /v1/vector/collection/list, /v1/vector/collection/get, and /v1/vector/query rather than leaking vendor details

That last row is a recommendation with a boundary, not a verdict. I would ask a team building a multi-service developer tool to try Infrai for the vector adapter when a stable HTTP contract and provider substitution matter more than owning a search cluster. I would stick with Elasticsearch when mature lexical analysis is the primary requirement, and with pgvector when transactional SQL locality outweighs independent scaling.

Measure quality before rollout

Create a small labeled evaluation set from representative claims questions. Label whether the expected policy clause or claim event appears in the top-k, then record false inclusions caused by stale revisions or a missing tenant filter. Measure recall and precision separately from p95 latency; one blended score hides the exact trade-off this architecture is meant to control.

Run the set before and after a delete event. The expected result is boring: the deleted source never appears, the replacement revision does, and the trace identifies the surviving source IDs. I am not sure a single offline set will predict every regional policy variation, so keep a review queue for low-confidence or no-source answers and expand labels from those cases.

A migration-shaped rollout

Start with dual reads behind a feature flag, but keep one canonical answer contract. Compare candidate IDs, freshness, and latency in the trace; do not compare only generated prose. During the cutover, replay tombstones and changed revisions before enabling writes to the new collection, then run the labeled set again.

The catch is governance. A provider that is easy to call is not automatically suitable for every jurisdiction, retention policy, or data-residency requirement. When those constraints are decisive, choose the backend with the evidence and controls your compliance review accepts, even if migration takes longer.

For the REST adapter’s current capability definitions, see the vector documentation. Keep that link at the boundary of the implementation; the rest of the system should depend on your retrieval contract, not on a vendor-shaped data model.

Sources

  • Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • Lewis et al., “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks”: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • Elasticsearch vector search documentation: https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/knn-search.html
  • pgvector project documentation: https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector
  • Pinecone delete records documentation: https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/manage-data/delete-data

title: Comment FORECAST.ETS prévoit-il le pic de ventes de décembre ?
description:
=FORECAST.ETS(...) ressemble à de la magie : on lui donne trois ans de ventes mensuelles et il renvoie un décembre plus haut que tous les autres mois, un janvier qui retombe et un intervalle de confiance autour des deux. En dessous, il y a un lissage exponentiel avec une tendance et une saison qui se répète, une méthode de la fin des années 1950 qui tient en une quarantaine de lignes. La Forecast Sheet de l'éditeur de tableur de l'application de bureau osFoundry écrit cette fonction dans une nouvelle feuille. Cet article reconstruit la même idée en Python, la fait tourner sur les mêmes 36 mois, et regarde où elle concorde avec la feuille et où une méthode plus simple échoue. Les données sont un exemple : les ventes d'une petite boutique avec une hausse régulière, une forme annuelle fixe et environ 4% de bruit, générées pour cette démonstration.

Ce que produit la feuille

Sur 36 mois (de janvier 2023 à décembre 2025), Forecast Sheet avec la saisonnalité sur auto et un niveau de confiance de 95% écrit trois colonnes, Forecast, Lower et Upper Confidence Bound, et un graphique. La cellule C49, décembre 2026, contient =FORECAST.ETS(A49,$B$2:$B$37,$A$2:$A$37,1,1) et affiche $20,654. Les deux bornes à côté sont $19,008 et $22,300.

Ce sont les chiffres à reproduire. Tout ce qui suit s'exécute avec uvx --with numpy --with scipy python -I forecast.py sous Python 3.12, numpy 2.5.4 et scipy 1.18.1.

D'abord, trouver la saison

La saisonnalité auto doit deviner la longueur d'un cycle. Une version simple de cette devinette est l'autocorrélation de la variation d'un mois à l'autre. Une tendance ajoute la même quantité à chaque mois et disparaît dans les différences ; une forme annuelle, non.

d = np.diff(y); d = d - d.mean()
ac = [np.sum(d[:-k] * d[k:]) / np.sum(d * d) for k in range(1, 19)]

Sur ces 36 mois, le décalage 12 donne 0.53, le 6 donne 0.06 et le 13 donne -0.01 : la longueur de saison est donc 12. C'est ma propre règle empirique, pas une description de la façon dont l'éditeur choisit sa longueur de saison ; ce qui peut se comparer, c'est le résultat, plus bas.

Holt-Winters, additif

À chaque nouveau mois, trois choses sont mises à jour : un niveau (où en sont les ventes maintenant, saison retirée), une tendance (de combien elles croissent par mois) et douze valeurs de saison (de combien chaque mois du calendrier se situe au-dessus ou en dessous du niveau). Chacune est un mélange pondéré de la nouvelle observation et de l'ancienne estimation, avec des poids alpha, beta et gamma.

def run(y, a, b, g):
    l, t, s = init(y); s = list(s); err = []
    for i, v in enumerate(y):
        err.append(v - (l + t + s[i % M]))              # one-step-ahead error
        ln = a * (v - s[i % M]) + (1 - a) * (l + t)     # level
        t = b * (ln - l) + (1 - b) * t                  # trend
        s[i % M] = g * (v - ln) + (1 - g) * s[i % M]    # season
        l = ln
    return np.array(err), l, t, s

Les valeurs de départ viennent des deux premières années : la moyenne de la première année comme niveau, la différence entre les moyennes des deux premières années divisée par douze comme tendance, et l'écart de chaque mois à la moyenne de la première année comme saison. Les trois poids sont trouvés en minimisant les erreurs quadratiques à un pas avec scipy.optimize.minimize, depuis trois points de départ pour qu'un mauvais départ ne décide pas de la réponse. Prévoir h mois à l'avance, c'est niveau + k * tendance + saison[mois].

Pour l'intervalle, j'ai utilisé une règle empirique : 1.96 fois l'écart-type des résidus fois la racine carrée de l'horizon. La formule d'intervalle de la feuille n'a pas été examinée, seuls ses chiffres sont donc comparés.

Face à la feuille

Sur les 36 mois complets, l'ajustement donne alpha 0.37, beta 0.01 et gamma 0.42, et un écart-type des résidus de $567. Face à la colonne Forecast de la feuille :

Mois Ce script Forecast Sheet
Janv. 2026 $12,136 $12,260
Déc. 2026 $20,698 $20,654
Différence absolue moyenne, 12 mois $297 (2.0%)
Plus grande différence (juin 2026) $587

Les douze mois concordent en moyenne à moins de 2%, ce qu'on attend de deux implémentations de la même famille de méthodes avec des valeurs de départ et un ajustement différents. Cela ne prouve pas que l'éditeur fasse exactement cela, et c'est un seul jeu de données à la forme propre. Avec des données réelles, un mois manquant ou un changement de niveau, les deux s'écarteront davantage.

Les intervalles ne concordent pas : décembre sort ici de $16,849 à $24,548, contre $19,008 à $22,300 dans la feuille. Le mien est plus large et s'élargit plus vite avec l'horizon : $2,223 en janvier à $7,700 en décembre, contre $1,621 et $3,292 dans la feuille. La règle de la racine carrée est grossière, et rien ici ne dit quelle bande est la mieux calibrée.

Ce que la saison apporte

Faire tourner les mêmes données sans saison, avec seulement un niveau et une tendance (la méthode linéaire de Holt), montre ce que vaut le motif :

no season: Jan 17872   Dec 23159   residual sd 2185

Sans la saison, la prévision de janvier est $17,872, là où la feuille donne $12,260 et où les deux janviers précédents ont chuté d'environ 40% par rapport à décembre. L'écart-type des résidus est 2,185 contre 567 avec la saison. La prévision de décembre se trompe dans l'autre sens, $23,159 contre $20,654, parce qu'une droite de tendance n'a aucun moyen de savoir que décembre est un pic et janvier un creux.

Un test sur un an

On ajuste seulement sur janvier 2023 à décembre 2024, on prévoit 2025 et on compare avec ce qui s'est passé. Erreur absolue moyenne en pourcentage (MAPE) sur les douze mois :

Méthode MAPE Prévision déc. 2025
Moyenne globale 19.4% $10,586
Dernier mois répété 37.3% $17,000
Même mois l'an dernier 12.0% $17,000
Même mois l'an dernier fois la croissance 4.1% $20,025
Holt-Winters (ce script) 3.4% $18,511

En décembre 2025, il s'est vendu en réalité $19,480. Deux choses en ressortent. Une simple copie saisonnière de l'an dernier (12.0%) rate la croissance, et en ajoutant la croissance annuelle observée de 17.8% (4.1%), on est presque au niveau de Holt-Winters (3.4%) ; avec deux ans de données, le lissage exponentiel n'est donc pas un grand pas au-delà d'une formule de tableur soignée. Et la bande à 95% a couvert les douze valeurs réelles, ce qui, avec douze points, dit seulement qu'elle n'est pas trop étroite.

C'est un seul découpage d'une seule série d'exemple. Cela ne dit rien du classement des méthodes sur d'autres données.

Un piège : demander à une bibliothèque de statistiques de tout estimer

Le raccourci évident est statsmodels. Avec l'ajustement par défaut sur les mêmes 36 mois :

ETSModel(series, error='add', trend='add', seasonal='add', seasonal_periods=12).fit()

statsmodels 0.15.0 donne décembre 2026 à $22,738 avec une plage de $17,688 à $27,787, soit 10% au-dessus de la feuille. Dans le test sur un an, le même modèle a eu un MAPE de 33.2%, pire que la moyenne globale. Probablement, un modèle qui estime douze valeurs initiales de saison plus les poids de lissage à partir de 24 ou 36 points a trop de nombres libres, et l'ajustement finit sur quelque chose d'étrange. Le script ci-dessus fixe plutôt les valeurs de départ à partir des premières années, une des différences entre les deux ; cela n'a pas été testé isolément. Mieux vaut comparer toute prévision de bibliothèque à « même mois l'an dernier fois la croissance » avant de lui faire confiance.

À l'usage

Le script (forecast.py) est toute l'expérience. Pour de vrais chiffres de ventes, le plus rapide est la Forecast Sheet de l'application, gratuite sur la page de téléchargement d'osFoundry et qui travaille sur le fichier de l'ordinateur. Écrire la méthode à la main sert à comprendre ce que signifie la plage, et à remarquer quand une prévision doit être jetée.

title: TanStack Router: my admin panel's URLs are type-checked and validated like API input
description:
ParkEase's admin panel is a React and Vite app with nine pages: dashboard, approvals, partners, users, bookings, finance, surge, moderation and the audit log. It routes with TanStack Router, not React Router. The project file says so in capitals, because left alone, an AI will reach for React Router every time; it's what most tutorials use.

(The Android app is different: it uses Expo Router's file-based routing, the native choice for Expo. This post is about the admin.)

Here's what TanStack Router gave the admin, using the real route file.

1. Every link is type-checked

The router registers itself with TypeScript:

export const router = createRouter({ routeTree: tree });

declare module '@tanstack/react-router' {
  interface Register {
    router: typeof router;
  }
}

After that, <Link to="/finanse"> is a compile error, not a 404 an operator finds later. Rename a route and the type checker lists every link that broke. For code an AI writes quickly across many files, that's a safety net you get for one declaration.

2. Search params are validated like API input

This is the feature that sold me.

When the ledger doesn't balance, the dashboard shows a red alert listing the transactions whose debits don't equal their credits. Each is a link into the finance page's ledger explorer, opened on that exact transaction:

<Link key={t} to="/finance" search={{ txnId: t }}>
  {t.slice(0, 8)}
</Link>

On the receiving side, the finance route declares its search params with a Zod schema, the same validation library the whole project uses for API requests:

const financeSearch = z.object({ txnId: z.string().uuid().optional() });
const finance = createRoute({
  getParentRoute: () => admin,
  path: '/finance',
  validateSearch: (search) => financeSearch.parse(search),
  component: function Finance() {
    return <FinancePage txnId={finance.useSearch().txnId} />;
  },
});

?txnId= must be a UUID or absent. The page receives a typed txnId: string | undefined, never a raw string from the URL bar. It's a small thing, but it's the same rule as the API: everything that comes from outside the program gets validated at the boundary. A URL is outside the program.

3. An auth gate without a fake URL

Every admin page needs a signed-in admin. Instead of repeating a check in nine pages, the routes nest under one pathless layout route:

/** Every feature page sits under the admin gate, so none mounts without a session. */
const admin = createRoute({ getParentRoute: () => root, id: 'admin', component: RequireAdmin });

It has an id instead of a path, so it adds no /admin segment to any URL. Its component shows a skeleton while the session loads, redirects to the login page if there isn't one, sends a non-admin to "not authorised", and only then renders the shell with the page inside. One gate, impossible to forget on a new page, because a new page is a child of it.

4. Each page is its own download 

/** Each page is its own chunk: antd tables, MapLibre and the finance screens load on first visit. */
const page = <P extends string>(path: P, component: ReturnType<typeof lazyRouteComponent>) =>
  createRoute({ getParentRoute: () => admin, path, component });

The surge page pulls in a whole map library; the finance page has heavy tables. With lazy route components, an operator who only ever approves spaces never downloads the map. Eight of the nine pages are declared with that one helper. Finance is spelled out because it validates its search params.

Why it was good

  • Mistakes move to compile time. Broken links and wrong search params fail the build, not the operator.
  • URLs got the same rigour as the API. The same Zod library validates the request body and the query string.
  • The structure enforces the rules. Auth is a parent route, code splitting is a helper, deep links are typed.

The cost was small: a route file that's a little more verbose than JSX routes, and having to tell the AI, once, in writing, that this project doesn't use React Router.

Next: the last post in the series, and the one I learned the most from: the AI kept saying "done" when it wasn't.

ParkEase is a peer-to-peer parking marketplace for India, built solo with Claude Code.
Code: https://github.com/Deonkar/parkease

title: Next.js ~revalidateTag~
description:
revalidateTag is a server function that is used for invalidate cache on demand follwing a specific tag of cache.

Key Features and Specifications

• Supported Enviroments: This can be useed only in server function or route handler.（This can't be used in client)

• System of revalidation: The data tagged by a specific tag is marked as 'stale', promote refetching tag latest data in the next or background.

• Second parameter(profile): Afrter Next.js 16, evalidateTag(tag, profile) format is recommended, and assign default or customized cache profile(such as max).

• Difference from revalidatePath: While revalidatePath invalidates the cache by a module of a specific URL path, revalidateTag invalidates at a time crossing multiple pages on base of the data tagged by a specific tag.

Basic Usage

  1. Attach a tag to fetching data: 
const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/posts', {
  next: { tags: ['posts'] }
});
  1. Invalid in server function or route handler: 
import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache';

export async function updatePost() {
  // Update data...
  revalidateTag('posts', 'max');
}

title: Create custom monitors in Vercel Observability
description:
You can now create custom monitors to get alerts based on your Vercel Observability query results.

For example, you can track signals such as AI Gateway costs, Core Web Vitals and other performance metrics, Workflow and external API failure rates, or Vercel Sandbox CPU time.

Each monitor tracks a single metric, such as response time, or a ratio of two metrics, such as errors divided by total requests. Choose statistical anomaly detection or a fixed threshold, then configure the detection window, filters, and grouping.

To create a monitor, inspect a chart’s query in Observability, start from a preset, or open Settings > Alerts for your team.

You can also define a custom monitor in a JSON file and create it with vercel monitors add in the Vercel CLI. Run vercel monitors schema --type custom for the schema and examples.

Receive alerts through email, Slack, Vercel Inbox, push notifications, or team-level webhooks. You can also add context for Vercel Agent to use when investigating an alert.

Custom monitors are available on Pro and Enterprise plans with Observability Plus, at $0.0035 per GB of data scanned. Built-in alerts remain included with Observability Plus.

Create a custom monitor or learn more in the configuration documentation.

Read more

title: Vercel CLI adds Spend Management
description:
You can now view and manage your team's Spend Management budget from the Vercel CLI. Run vercel budgets and you, or the scripts and agents you run, get back your current spend and the active budget.

View, set, and remove a budget

This is the same On-Demand Budget shown in your team's billing settings. Setting a budget does not stop usage on its own. The --pause flag pauses production deployments of all projects when spend reaches 100%.

List budget alert history

You can now see your budget alert history. Run vercel budgets alerts for the full log, filtered with --since, --until, --limit, and --json. A bare vercel budgets prints the three most recent alerts.

Managing budgets requires the Owner or Billing role. Spend Management is available at no additional cost to Pro teams and to Enterprise teams on the Flexible Commitment plan.

Full reference now available in the vercel budgets CLI reference. Read more about Spend Management.

title: Three front-end bugs my build said were fine
description:
I run a static browser-games site. Every page exists twice: once as prerendered HTML for search engines, and once as a React app for people clicking around. The build is a babel bundle plus a generator script. Here are three bugs that went through that build without a single error and broke the page people actually saw.

1. <img width="700" height="700"> means height: 700px

Every game card has an image with width and height attributes. That is the standard advice: the browser reserves the right space before the image loads, so the layout does not jump.

My CSS made the image fill its card and kept it square:

.grid img, .cards img { width: 100%; aspect-ratio: 1/1; object-fit: cover; display: block; }

The cards were about 176 px wide, so I expected 176 × 176.

The browser drew 176 × 700 on every category, tag and collection page. Everything below the first row was pushed off the screen.

The reason: the height attribute is not just a hint for the aspect ratio. It maps to a CSS height: 700px, and aspect-ratio only takes effect while height is auto. My rule set the width and said nothing about the height, so the attribute won.

The fix is two words in the same rule:

.grid img, .cards img { width: 100%; height: auto; aspect-ratio: 1/1; object-fit: cover; display: block; }

Keep the attributes, because they still prevent layout shift. Just never set a width on an image without also saying height: auto.

2. Two class names for one grid

The generator that writes the static pages had grown in pieces. Some templates wrote <ul class="grid">, others <ul class="cards">. Only .grid had styles.

Every .cards list rendered as one full-width thumbnail per row. That included the "related games" strip at the bottom of every game page, which nobody looked at closely because it was at the bottom.

Nothing failed. The HTML was valid, the CSS was valid, and the pages returned 200. The fix was to style both names together:

.grid, .cards { list-style: none; padding: 0; display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(158px, 1fr)); gap: 16px; }

Better still is one class name everywhere, but until then, anything shaped like a grid gets both selectors.

3. Deleting a feature deleted a neighbour

I removed an ad integration from one large component file. The change was one hunk of about 240 lines. It ran a little past the end of the ad code and also deleted the Logo component that sat right below it.

The bundle compiled. Babel transforms syntax; it does not know whether a name you use is defined anywhere. The prerendered pages have no React in them, so they looked perfect.

The React app threw ReferenceError: Logo is not defined on load. For a day the homepage showed only its no-JavaScript fallback: a list of popular games with no header, no search, no navigation and no footer. From a distance it looked like a page, which is why it survived a quick look.

Two checks catch this now:

  1. After deleting code, compare the top-level definitions before and after: 
git show HEAD~1:components.jsx | grep -oE "^(function|const|let) +\w+" > before.txt
grep -oE "^(function|const|let) +\w+" components.jsx > after.txt
diff before.txt after.txt

Anything in the diff that you did not mean to remove is the bug.

  1. Load the page in a real browser with a listener on pageerror. A static check cannot tell you that a name is missing at run time; the browser can, in one line of output.

What the three have in common

Each bug produced valid output. The build, the validator and the HTTP status code all agreed things were fine. What caught them was looking at the rendered page: a screenshot at phone and desktop width, and the browser's error log.

That is now the last step before anything ships on 360 PlayZone: screenshot a few pages both ways, including the full games list, and read the console.

Written by an AI assistant from my own build notes.

title: We've Made Software More Powerful. Have We Made It Harder to Use?
description:
I've always cared about two things in software engineering: the experience of the people using an application, and the experience of the developers building it. I've always believed there should be a reasonable balance between the two.

But after years of building software across different industries, I've noticed a recurring problem. As applications become more sophisticated, they often become harder to use for the very people they're built to serve.

That usually isn't because the software is poorly built. It's simply how software evolves.

The Problem with Growing Software

Imagine a healthcare application used by doctors, nurses and administrative staff.

At launch, it might have a handful of features: patient records, appointments, consultations and billing. Over time, customers request more. The engineering team responds with new pages, menus, settings and workflows. An application that started with five major features can quickly grow to fifty, and it certainly doesn't stop there.

From the engineering team's perspective, the product has improved considerably. But a doctor who only wants to review a patient's history now goes through several pages. A receptionist trying to reschedule an appointment might need several clicks to carry out what they consider a simple, routine task.

The functionality exists. Reaching it has become unnecessarily complicated.

My brother and I have run into versions of this problem while working on applications in property management, human healthcare and veterinary healthcare. We've heard it in feedback from users and in conversations with product and customer success teams. The complaints come down to the same things: too many clicks, too many screens and too much navigation for relatively simple tasks.

None of this means developers aren't doing their jobs. They're responding to legitimate customer requests while keeping one application that works for everyone.

The industry has been working on this. Companies like Pendo and WalkMe help users through complex applications with in-app guides, walkthroughs and contextual assistance, and those tools have an important place.

But I've often wondered whether we could approach the problem from another angle.

Instead of helping users figure out where to go and what to click, what if we reduced the need for that navigation altogether?

One Application, Different Users, Different Needs

Most applications are built around predefined interfaces and workflows. Product managers, designers and developers decide how information is presented, how features are organised and how users navigate between them. That's necessary: an application needs structure.

Modern applications already accommodate different users in some ways. Role-Based Access Control decides which pages, features and actions each role can reach. Some applications add custom dashboards, saved views and configurable workflows.

But controlling what a user is allowed to access isn't the same as letting them decide how they work with what they can access.

Consider two doctors in the same hospital with identical roles and permissions. One spends most of the day reviewing patient histories; the other works mostly with prescriptions and treatment plans. Same functionality, very different routines.

Where customisation exists, it's limited to what the developers anticipated, and using it often means finding the right settings page and working out which option affects which part of the application. Some preferences, such as themes or font sizes, apply everywhere even when a user only wants a change on one page.

So when a user wants something slightly different, they adapt to the interface, request a feature or find a workaround.

Why must users always be the ones adapting?

What If Users Could Simply Ask?

For decades we've used graphical software through menus, buttons and links. Need something? Navigate to it. Want to change something? Find the setting. Need to do something? Follow the sequence of clicks.

Click, click, click.

Those methods have served us well, and they aren't going anywhere. But why should they be the only practical way to use increasingly sophisticated applications?

We're already seeing approaches that let AI interact with existing software. The Model Context Protocol (MCP), for example, allows applications to expose tools and functionality to AI assistants. That's useful, and it opens up interesting possibilities. But I've also wondered why users should have to rely on a separate assistant when they could interact just as intelligently within the applications they already use every day.

What if users could also tell the software what they want, in ordinary text or speech, without leaving the interface they're already familiar with?

"Put today's appointments first."

"Hide these columns. I don't need them."

"Show me all outstanding invoices from last month."

The application understands the request and carries it out, provided the user has the permissions to do so. Users could rearrange their dashboard, resize sections and change how information is displayed, without the development team building a feature specifically for them. And tomorrow, their layout is still there.

This isn't about replacing buttons with a chatbot. Sometimes clicking a button is much faster than typing a sentence. The point is choice: navigate the interface yourself, or say what you want done.

Most of the functionality users want already exists in their applications. The problem is how they reach it.

But Should Everyone Be Able to Redesign Their Application?

Giving users more control sounds appealing, but without boundaries it creates a different problem.

Imagine a support agent helping a customer. Ordinarily they'd say "open this page, find this section, click this button." But if every user can generate entirely new interfaces, introduce arbitrary components or change how the application works, support faces countless variations nobody else has seen. What works for one customer may not resemble what another sees.

Some newer approaches even allow AI to generate new interface code dynamically. That's powerful, but it can also introduce interface variations and code paths developers haven't individually reviewed.

I don't think the answer is to make every user a software designer. What users need is a contract, not source code.

Developers declare which existing components can be personalised and which existing actions can be performed. Users rearrange approved sections, hide columns they don't need or change how supported information is displayed. They never generate application code, invent backend functionality or bypass their permissions.

That keeps the variations knowable. Every change is one of a small set of known operations, so it can be reset, restored to defaults or undone. A support agent may still need to know which layout a customer is using, but that's a far more manageable problem than supporting an unlimited number of generated interfaces.

Greater flexibility, without sacrificing predictability.

What About the Developers?

As much as I want users to have more control, it shouldn't come at the cost of developers building and maintaining a whole new interaction system.

Making these interactions possible is one thing, making them reliable enough for everyday use is another. There are existing permissions to respect, user preferences to save, actions to validate, changes to confirm and interfaces to integrate with. And all of that needs to keep working as the application evolves.

Should every software company build and maintain that infrastructure itself?

We've faced this choice before with cloud infrastructure, authentication, version control, feature flags and in-app guidances. Some companies build their own, for good reasons. Many rely on specialised solutions because that's not where they want their engineering effort to go.

What We're Building

These questions led my brother and I to build ClickLess, an SDK that helps software companies give their users more control over how they use existing applications.

Developers wrap their existing components and declare what may change: which sections can move, resize or hide, which settings users can adjust and within what limits, and which existing actions users can perform. Users then ask, by typing or speaking.

The AI never gets unrestricted control. The model only proposes changes from a small, fixed set of operations, and ordinary code checks every one against what the developer declared before anything appears on screen. Users preview a change before keeping it, can undo it later, and their layout is saved for them alone. When the application ships a new release, their changes carry over to the sections that are still there. New sections appear as the developers designed them, and a section that has been rebuilt starts fresh. Actions run through the application's own code with the user's own sign-in, so existing permissions apply unchanged, and anything that modifies data asks for confirmation first.

A few safeguards matter as much as the features:

  • ClickLess checks every request, typed or spoken, for anything that looks like a password, PIN, card number or key. A request that seems to contain one is turned away: it isn't used to plan a change, and it isn't stored.
  • If ClickLess goes down, the application keeps working. Users still see their saved layout, and the application's own buttons and menus still respond. Only requests to ClickLess have to wait until it's back.

We've built the engine, a React SDK, a demo application and an administration dashboard.

How much work is it to integrate? We tested ClickLess on five open-source admin templates using different frameworks and UI libraries, including Next.js with Material UI, Bootstrap, react-admin, Ant Design Pro and plain Tailwind. We integrated ClickLess without replacing or maintaining separate versions of the existing UI components. The first working change took between two and six minutes, and covering the main pages took between sixteen and thirty-eight minutes. Across these tests, ClickLess handled about 950 requests.

These were internal trials using an AI coding agent following our integration guide, not independent developer benchmarks. But they gave us an encouraging starting point.

We've also integrated it into selected pages of a clinic application built on Medplum, an open-source healthcare platform, to see how it holds up in a realistic product.

You can learn more about what we're building at clicklessapp.com. We also have a working demo, with access currently limited while we gather feedback and prepare for wider testing.

An Unexpected Benefit: Understanding What Users Actually Want

Product teams learn what users want through interviews, support tickets, usage analytics and feature requests. All useful, all limited.

A user can be frustrated every day without raising a ticket. They might navigate through several screens without knowing there's a better way, or never request a change, because it seems too small.

In an application where users can simply say what they want, those preferences surface:

"Keep my upcoming appointments visible."

"I wish I could see patient history and previous treatments together."

Even when the application can't do something, the request itself is useful.

What if product teams could learn not only how people use their software, but how they wish they could use it?

ClickLess's administration dashboard records the changes users make and keep, and the requests the application couldn't fulfil, grouped by screen. A team might find many users asking to see information from two pages together, which points to a workflow worth improving. Or they might find a section users often hide, which is worth a closer look.

These signals need careful interpretation. Hiding a section doesn't mean a feature is unnecessary, and requests aren't a substitute for research. But alongside analytics and customer feedback, they show what users are actively trying to accomplish.

Could Developers Just Build This Themselves?

Absolutely. Developers can build most of the tools they currently rely on others to maintain.

The question is whether it makes sense for the company. If a team can build exactly what it needs quickly and maintain it cheaply, building it in-house might be the right choice. If another team would rather integrate something and focus on its core product, that should be an option too.

The value isn't just in the technology we've built, but in what it makes possible: less complexity for developers, better experiences for users, and deeper insights for product teams. Those are things we still need to prove beyond our own testing.

Putting the Idea Out There

You can spend an enormous amount of time trying to get everything right before showing anyone. There's always another feature, another improvement, another edge case. You never reach a point where everything is completely ready.

We've seen this usability problem repeatedly, built a first approach to it, and the next step is to put it in front of developers and software companies outside our own circle.

Some will think it's unnecessary. Some will prefer to build their own. Some may have solved this internally already. Hopefully, some will find it useful enough to try. I want to hear from all of them.

Identifying a problem doesn't mean you've found the right solution, and a working solution doesn't mean companies will adopt it. The only way to find out is to let people try it, challenge it and tell us what we're missing.

Final Thoughts

Traditional interfaces aren't going away, and not every interaction needs AI. Buttons, menus, forms and carefully designed workflows still serve important purposes.

But there's an opportunity to make software less rigid:

  • For users, less time navigating and more time getting things done.
  • For developers, delivering that without building the infrastructure themselves.
  • For support teams, more control for users without unpredictable, AI-generated applications to troubleshoot.
  • For product teams, a clearer picture of what users want, including what their applications don't yet do.

I believe software should become more powerful without becoming more difficult to use.

If you build or maintain a SaaS application, I'd love to hear your thoughts. Would you give your users this level of control? Have you tried building something similar? And what would concern you most about integrating an SDK like ClickLess into your application?

title: When a 200 Response Still Breaks the Contract
description:
Quick answer: A 200 status only means the request was accepted and returned a response. It does not confirm the body matches the contract, so a wrong field, a bad type, or a missing value can break the spec while the status stays green. Assert the response fields and check them against the schema, and keep contract evidence separate from the status code so a 200 cannot mask drift.

Why status and contract are different checks

The HTTP status lives at the transport layer. It answers whether the call succeeded, was rejected, or hit an error. The contract lives at the schema layer and answers whether the response shape and values match what the spec declares. Those are independent questions, and a 200 says nothing about the second one.

A response can break the contract in several ways.

  • A required field is missing from the body.
  • A field returns the wrong type, such as a number where a string is declared.
  • A value has a shape the schema does not allow.
  • A later step consumes the field and fails because it is wrong.

How a 200 still breaks a flow

Inside a scenario, a bad body often surfaces at the step that tries to use it rather than at the step that returned it.

Situation Status Contract result Downstream effect
Missing required field 200 Schema violation A later step reads an undefined value
Wrong field type 200 Type drift Processing or assertion fails
Unexpected value shape 200 Contract break The extracted variable is unusable
Correct body 200 Matches schema The flow proceeds

Per-step field assertions catch these cases at the response that produced them, instead of waiting for a later request to fail.

Assert against the spec, not just the code

Treat the declared spec version as the reference and check the response against it rather than against a lowest-common-denominator assumption.

  1. Assert the status to confirm the call was accepted.
  2. Assert the required fields are present.
  3. Check field types and shapes against the schema.
  4. Confirm any extracted variable matches the expected form.
  5. Let the next step consume the verified value.

Contract evidence is its own class, alongside static, dynamic, and model-only hypothesis evidence. The deterministic verdict fails on real drift, and a lack of verified evidence reads inconclusive rather than passing. The model cannot talk a schema violation into a pass.

Honest limits

A field assertion only covers the fields you check, so an unasserted part of the response carries no evidence. A passing run says the asserted fields and schema held, not that every possible value is valid. Keep the checks focused on the fields the flow and the contract depend on, and remember that static and contract signals are not guarantees about runtime behavior outside the run.

Scenarios stay outside the OpenAPI document with no x-scenarios keys and run against real connected requests. A mock returning fixed 200 answers cannot confirm the real backend conforms to the schema.

Powerduck keeps the contract checks and per-step assertions visible, so a 200 with a bad body is reported against the response rather than hidden behind a green status.

Frequently asked questions

Does a 200 mean the response matches the spec? No. It only means the call was accepted. A missing field or wrong type can break the contract while the status stays 200.

How do I catch a contract break behind a green status? Assert the response fields and check them against the schema, not just the status code, so type drift and missing fields are caught at that step.

What happens to a later step that consumes the bad field? It often fails when it reads the wrong or missing value, which is why asserting at the earlier response is more precise than debugging the downstream failure.

The bottom line

Never treat a 200 as a contract check. The status confirms the call was accepted, while the schema decides whether the body conforms, and a missing field or wrong type can break both the spec and a later step while the status stays green. Assert the fields against the declared spec, keep contract evidence separate, and remember that unchecked fields carry no evidence. A green status is a starting point, not proof that the response is valid. More in the API scenario testing guide.
