title: Python और PyMuPDF से PDF को Word में कैसे बदलें
description:
PDF में पैराग्राफ, हेडिंग या टेबल जैसी कोई चीज़ नहीं होती। उसमें ग्लिफ़ होते हैं, जिनमें से हर एक पेज पर किसी x और y स्थिति पर खींचा गया है, और कुछ आयत और रेखाएँ। इसलिए PDF से Word में बदलने वाला हर कन्वर्टर असल में लेआउट विश्लेषण का एक छोटा प्रोग्राम है: ग्लिफ़ को लाइनों में समूहित करना, तय करना कि कौन-सी लाइनें साथ हैं, और नतीजे को स्टाइल वाले .docx ऑब्जेक्ट के रूप में लिखना। osFoundry डेस्कटॉप ऐप के PDF Editor में यह एक एक्सपोर्ट के रूप में है (All tools, Export a PDF, Microsoft Word)। एडिटर कंपाइल किए हुए मॉड्यूल के रूप में आता है, इसलिए उद्धृत करने के लिए सोर्स कोड नहीं है। नीचे वही काम PyMuPDF और python-docx के साथ लगभग 50 लाइनों के Python में दोबारा बनाया गया है, उसी एक पेज की सूचना पर चलाया गया है, और फिर ऐप ने उस PDF से जो .docx लिखा उससे मिलाया गया है।

माप Apple M1 पर Python 3.12, MuPDF 1.28.6 और python-docx 1.2.0 के साथ लिए गए। टेस्ट पेज एक काल्पनिक एक पेज की सूचना है (उदाहरण दस्तावेज़): कंपनी का नाम, एक शीर्षक, दो परिचय लाइनें, "Details" हेडिंग, लेबल और मान की पाँच पंक्तियाँ, और एक फ़ुटर लाइन।

फ़ाइल असल में क्या स्टोर करती है

पेज के ग्लिफ़ डंप करने पर दिखता है कि उसमें कितना कम है। शीर्षक के पहले अक्षर:

import pymupdf
page = pymupdf.open("Holiday party 2025.pdf")[0]
for b in page.get_text("rawdict")["blocks"]:
    for line in b.get("lines", []):
        for span in line["spans"]:
            for ch in span["chars"]:
                print(ch["c"], round(ch["origin"][0], 1), round(ch["origin"][1], 1), span["size"])

H 56.0 118.0 26.0
o 74.8 118.0 26.0
l 90.6 118.0 26.0
i 97.8 118.0 26.0
d 105.0 118.0 26.0

पूरा पेज 327 ग्लिफ़ का है, जिनमें 277 स्पेस नहीं हैं, और 16 लाइनों में बँटा है। कहीं नहीं लिखा कि "Holiday Party 2025" शीर्षक है। वह y = 118 पर 26 पॉइंट का टेक्स्ट है, और एकमात्र सुराग यही है। स्पेस का होना भी पक्का नहीं है। मैंने एक ऐसा PDF लिखा जिसमें हर शब्द x ऑफ़सेट पर अलग से रखा गया था, जैसा कई जनरेटर करते हैं, और फ़ाइल में एक भी स्पेस कैरेक्टर नहीं था। फिर भी page.get_text() ने Thank you all for a great year लौटाया, क्योंकि जब दो ग्लिफ़ के बीच का अंतर फ़ॉन्ट साइज़ के एक अंश से ज़्यादा होता है, तो MuPDF स्पेस जोड़ देता है।

सीधा तरीका, यानी page.get_text() और हर लाइन पर एक पैराग्राफ, इस पेज के लिए 16 पैराग्राफ देता है: लेबल "Date" और उसका मान दो पैराग्राफ बन जाते हैं, और दोनों परिचय लाइनें भी।

लाइनों को ढाँचे में समूहित करना

साफ़ पेज के लिए तीन संकेत काफ़ी हैं, और तीनों वे संख्याएँ हैं जो डंप में पहले से हैं।

फ़ॉन्ट साइज़ हेडिंग को बॉडी टेक्स्ट से अलग करता है। बॉडी का साइज़ पेज पर सबसे आम साइज़ है (यहाँ 12 pt: परिचय लाइनें और लेबल-मान की दस लाइनें), और जो भी साफ़ तौर पर बड़ा है वह हेडिंग है। साइज़ का अनुपात स्तर तय करता है।

बेसलाइन टेबल के सेल को टेक्स्ट से अलग करती है। समान y पर पर x में बड़े अंतर वाली दो टेक्स्ट लाइनें एक पंक्ति के दो सेल हैं।

लाइन की दूरी पैराग्राफ को लाइनों के ढेर से अलग करती है। समान साइज़ की लगातार दो लाइनें, जिनके बीच की दूरी फ़ॉन्ट साइज़ के दोगुने से कम है, एक पैराग्राफ हैं।

import collections, statistics, pymupdf, docx

def is_cjk(ch):
    return "　" <= ch <= "鿿" or "＀" <= ch <= "￯"

def join(prev, nxt):
    # a line break is a space between Latin words and nothing between Japanese characters
    return nxt if is_cjk(prev[-1]) or is_cjk(nxt[0]) else " " + nxt

def read_lines(page):
    out = []
    for b in page.get_text("dict")["blocks"]:
        for ln in b.get("lines", []):
            spans = [s for s in ln["spans"] if s["text"].strip()]
            if spans:
                out.append({"text": "".join(s["text"] for s in ln["spans"]).strip(),
                            "x": ln["bbox"][0], "y": ln["bbox"][1],
                            "size": round(spans[0]["size"], 1)})
    return sorted(out, key=lambda l: (round(l["y"]), l["x"]))

def rebuild(pdf_path, out_path):
    lines = read_lines(pymupdf.open(pdf_path)[0])
    body = statistics.mode([l["size"] for l in lines])
    rows = collections.defaultdict(list)
    for l in lines:
        rows[round(l["y"])].append(l)

    doc, para, prev, table = docx.Document(), None, None, None
    for y in sorted(rows):
        cells = sorted(rows[y], key=lambda l: l["x"])
        if len(cells) >= 2:                      # label and value on one baseline
            if table is None:
                table = doc.add_table(rows=0, cols=2)
            r = table.add_row().cells
            r[0].text, r[1].text = cells[0]["text"], cells[1]["text"]
            para = prev = None
            continue
        l, table = cells[0], None
        if l["size"] > body * 1.2:               # clearly larger than body text
            doc.add_heading(l["text"], level=1 if l["size"] >= body * 1.8 else 2)
            para = None
        elif para and l["y"] - prev["y"] < 2.0 * l["size"] and l["size"] == prev["size"]:
            para.add_run(join(para.text, l["text"]))
        else:
            para = doc.add_paragraph(l["text"])
        prev = l
    doc.save(out_path)

अंग्रेज़ी सूचना पर चलाने पर यह देता है: कंपनी के नाम के लिए एक Normal पैराग्राफ, "Holiday Party 2025" के लिए Heading 1, दो परिचय लाइनों के लिए एक Normal पैराग्राफ, "Details" के लिए Heading 2, 5 पंक्तियों की टेबल, और फ़ुटर सामान्य पैराग्राफ के रूप में। उसी सूचना का जापानी संस्करण, जिसमें 15 लाइनों में 149 बिना-स्पेस ग्लिफ़ हैं, उसी रूप में निकलता है।

ऐप के एक्सपोर्ट से तुलना

मैंने उन्हीं दो PDF को ऐप से एक्सपोर्ट किया और .docx फ़ाइलें python-docx से वापस पढ़ीं। पैराग्राफ और स्टाइल मेरे बनाए हुए से लाइन-दर-लाइन मेल खाते हैं: वही टेक्स्ट, Normal, Heading 1 और Heading 2 का वही बँटवारा, दो परिचय लाइनों का वही एक पैराग्राफ, और टेबल की वही पाँच पंक्तियाँ।

ग्लिफ़ (स्पेस छोड़कर) लाइनें समूहन के बाद पैराग्राफ टेबल की पंक्तियाँ एक्सपोर्ट का साइज़
अंग्रेज़ी सूचना 277 16 5 (2 हेडिंग) 5 2,737 बाइट (ऐप)
जापानी सूचना 149 15 5 (2 हेडिंग) 5 2,882 बाइट (ऐप)

दोबारा बनाने में अंग्रेज़ी सूचना के लिए प्रति पेज औसत (मीडियन) 16.9 ms और जापानी के लिए 16.7 ms लगे (हर एक के 50 रन, .docx को डिस्क पर लिखना शामिल)।

जहाँ ये अनुमान टूट जाते हैं

मैंने तीन मामले आज़माए, जिनमें एक सीधा नियम ग़लत नतीजा देता है।

स्कैन किए गए पेज में कोई ग्लिफ़ ही नहीं होता। मैंने टेस्ट पेज को 150 dpi पर रास्टराइज़ किया और नए PDF में लपेट दिया: rawdict ने 0 ग्लिफ़ और 1 इमेज लौटाई। जब तक OCR इमेज को स्थिति वाले टेक्स्ट में नहीं बदल देता, ऊपर के नियमों के पास काम करने को कुछ नहीं है।

टेक्स्ट के दो कॉलम टेबल जैसे दिखते हैं। बॉडी टेक्स्ट के दो कॉलम वाला पेज, हर एक में चार लाइनें, rebuild से 4 पंक्ति और 2 कॉलम की टेबल और शून्य पैराग्राफ के रूप में निकला, क्योंकि "समान बेसलाइन, x में बड़ा अंतर" ठीक वही है जो टेबल की पंक्ति होती है। असली कन्वर्टर को किसी चीज़ को टेबल कहने से पहले कई पंक्तियों में रूलिंग लाइनें या एक जैसे कॉलम किनारे जाँचने पड़ते हैं।

लाइनें जोड़ते समय लिपि का पता होना चाहिए। हर जोड़ी गई लाइन के बीच स्पेस रखने पर, PDF में टूटा हुआ जापानी वाक्य बीच में स्पेस पा लेगा। ऊपर का join फ़ंक्शन तब स्पेस छोड़ देता है जब लाइन टूटने के किसी भी ओर जापानी अक्षर हो। मेरे टेस्ट में दो लाइन का जापानी पैराग्राफ एक अटूट वाक्य के रूप में निकला।

दोबारा बनी फ़ाइल किस काम की है

दोबारा बनाने का मकसद फ़ाइल फ़ॉर्मेट नहीं है। असली Heading 1 और Heading 2 स्टाइल और असली टेबल के साथ दस्तावेज़ खोजा जा सकता है, उसकी स्टाइल बदली जा सकती है और उसे दोबारा फ़्लो कराया जा सकता है, और किसी साल को खोजकर बदलने से हर जगह वह बदल जाता है। स्थिति के हिसाब से रखा गया टेक्स्ट इनमें से कुछ नहीं देता; PDF से कॉपी करने पर लाइनों का एक ढेर मिलता है जिसे हाथ से दोबारा फ़ॉर्मेट करना पड़ता है। ऊपर की सूचना जैसा पेज इतना छोटा भी है कि नतीजा वापस पढ़कर जाँचा जा सके, जिसके लिए python-docx की कुछ ही लाइनें चाहिए:

d = docx.Document("Holiday party 2025.docx")
print([(p.style.name, p.text) for p in d.paragraphs if p.text.strip()])
print([[c.text for c in r.cells] for r in d.tables[0].rows])

यह एक्सपोर्ट osFoundry डेस्कटॉप ऐप के PDF Editor में है, जो डाउनलोड पेज से मुफ़्त मिलता है और कंप्यूटर पर ही चलता है, उसी local-first तरीके के अनुरूप जिस पर ऐप बना है।

title: Four transactions, eight transfers: an ERC-20 ingestion regression fixture
description:
A transfer table keyed only by transaction hash can lose valid rows while every RPC call succeeds.

Here is a small, real fixture that catches that mistake: eight ERC-20 Transfer logs across four Base transactions. The per-transaction counts are 1, 1, 2 and 4. Put those logs into a dictionary keyed only by transaction hash and only four rows survive.

Run the check without an RPC key

Download cadd-raw-logs.jsonl from the fixed sample revision. Save the following as verify-sample.py in the same directory and run it with Python 3:

import json
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

logs = [json.loads(line) for line in
        Path("cadd-raw-logs.jsonl").read_text().splitlines() if line.strip()]

by_transaction = {log["transactionHash"].lower(): log for log in logs}
event_keys = [(log["transactionHash"].lower(), int(log["logIndex"], 16))
              for log in logs]

assert len(logs) == 8
assert len(by_transaction) == 4
assert len(set(event_keys)) == 8
assert sorted(Counter(key[0] for key in event_keys).values()) == [1, 1, 2, 4]
print("8 logs; 4 transactions; 8 distinct event keys")

The code intentionally constructs the lossy transaction-keyed dictionary, then checks the event-level keys separately. No package installation, wallet, key or network request is needed once the sample is downloaded.

For this single-chain fixture, use transaction hash and log index to distinguish events. A dataset spanning chains should also carry chain identity. Keep block identity and removed/reorg handling as separate concerns: a distinct row key does not prove that an event is still canonical.

What the sample actually contains

BlockVectra's keyed Base endpoint returned these eight logs on November 8, 2026 at 04:25 UTC, for CADD at:

0x16f93ebc5320c89efc8701577efe49d14a276a06

The request filtered the ERC-20 Transfer topic over the inclusive range 53,758,000–53,758,999. The sample includes the raw result entries and expected rows from the unchanged decoder in this pinned upstream loader.

Only one event was independently compared with BaseScan: block 53,758,011, log index 6, contract/from/to, and raw amount 57370140000000000000000. The other seven are provider-returned samples. This does not establish that the window contains every event.

Keep raw amounts as integers or decimal strings. The fixture does not use floating-point conversion to normalize token amounts.

Timestamp and receipt checks are separate

At 05:02 UTC, two additional calls returned:

  • decimals() at latest: 18, agreeing with the project seed.
  • A one-element JSON-RPC batch for block 53,758,011: timestamp 1793941977, or 2026-11-06T05:12:57Z, matching the independently saved BaseScan time.

Those request/response bodies are in loader-method-requests-responses.json in the same sample. The header hash agrees with the earlier log response, which is a same-provider cross-check rather than independent canonical verification. One batch item does not establish compatibility for the loader's usual 50-item batches.

The earlier lookup of that transaction's receipt returned null. That result remains tracked separately; the upstream log loader does not directly call receipts. Safe-head selection, timestamps for the other sample blocks, February-onward history and the full database backfill have not been validated here.

This fixture is useful for a narrow regression: preserving multiple transfers in one transaction. It is not a backfill benchmark, a complete ingestion test or evidence of customer adoption.

Agent Registry

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.16.13

On October 30, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.16.13.

  • For information about upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to v1.16.13.
  • For information about new installations, see The big picture.

Bug ID Description
578314600 Fixed an issue where apigee-connect-agent ignored HTTPS_PROXY and failed to establish a tether in clusters that require an HTTP forward proxy for egress; the agent now uses HTTP/2 keepalive pings on the control-plane connection while honoring HTTPS_PROXY (including proxy credentials).
576707253 Removed the compromised emSign roots and the cross-signing Comodo AAA Services root from the system and Java (cacerts) trust stores across containers.
573622417 Fixed an issue where apigee-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
492041991 Fixed an issue where VerifyAPIKey and VerifyAccessToken set the apiproduct.operation.llmTokenQuota.* flow variables from unmatched LLM operations; they are now set only from the LLM operations that matched the request.

The following library updates are available for the backup/recovery appliance:

Stored timestamp data isn't modified.

What should I do?

Before November 1, 2026, do one of the following fixes:

    Updated time zone rules that reflect permanent standard daylight offsets across Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Northwest Territories are supported in Cloud SQL for MySQL maintenance release *.R20260726.00_36 or later.

    For more information, see Perform self-service maintenance.

  • Database configuration stopgap: If your organization can't restart instances before November 1, 2026, then you can set the time zone for your database session without causing downtime for your instance. Set the default_time_zone flag for the database session to your target fixed numeric offset (for example, '-06:00' for Alberta, '-07:00' for British Columbia, or '-05:00' for Manitoba).

title: Rebuilding Praecepta: From a Trie to Bitsets, and a Fair Benchmark Against Camunda and Drools
description:
In January 2023 I wrote about optimizing decision-making with a trie. The idea worked in principle: part of it was implemented, and is still maintained, at Pictet Tech. The numbers looked great, as you can see in my previous post.

Going through my old repositories for opportunities to test Claude, I decided to explore the major problem of that solution: the trie's memory exploded as tables grew; a generated table of 1,000 rules took over 1 GB. And during the development process, Claude told me that the first benchmark was not entirely fair, as Praecepta ran a different hit policy from Camunda and Kogito, and two of the services read one input from the wrong field.

So I refactored the engine and the benchmark, and completed the Maven plugin that compiles tables at build time. The result of the refactoring can be found in Praecepta 0.1.0 on Maven Central. The principles are still the same: a small, dependency-free Java engine for DMN decision tables. It now also has a website for the guide and the API documentation.

This post covers what changed, a benchmark against Camunda and Drools that I tried hard to make fair (including where it flatters Praecepta, and where Praecepta is slower), and what those engines do that Praecepta does not. This post also covers how open Praecepta is, and what could come next. That last part is where I would love your opinion.

From a trie to bitsets

A decision table is a simple list of rules. Each rule tests some input columns (country is "PT" or "ES", age in [18..65), or "anything") and produces outputs. The previous solution, a custom implementation of a trie, stored every possible path through the columns, and every "anything" cell multiplied the paths. That multiplication was the memory problem!

I tried a couple of things back then, including quantum computing via qengine: encoding the input as bits and each rule as quantum logic gates, to see whether a quantum circuit could beat the trie. It ran only on a simulator, but the thought stayed with me: rule matching is boolean logic over bits. The bitset index is the classical, practical version of that thought.

In the end, I stopped thinking about it. But now, in 2026, and with Claude's support, the new core uses bitsets. Every rule gets one bit. For every column, each distinct value the rules can tell apart gets a mask: the set of rules that accept it.

Column country rule 1 rule 2 rule 3 rule 4
"PT" 1 0 1 1
"FR" 0 1 1 0
any other value 0 0 1 1

Rule 1 tests "PT", rule 2 tests "FR", rule 3 is "anything" (so it is in every mask), and rule 4 is not("FR"). Evaluating an input looks up one mask per column and ANDs them together. A 64-bit AND checks 64 rules at once, and the bundled 119-rule table fits in two words. Memory grows with columns × values × rules, never with the product of values, and the 1,000-rule table that needed 1 GB now takes 0.6 MB, and reading it from DMN and building it takes about a quarter of a second in a fresh JVM.

And the best part: the hit policy falls out of the bits too. Bits are numbered in rule order (or priority order), so FIRST is "lowest set bit", which is a single CPU instruction.

Numbers and dates work the same way: the boundaries the rules mention (18, 65, date("2025-01-01")) split each column into intervals, a binary search finds the interval, and each interval has its mask.

What else changed

The core was not the only change. Praecepta now also has:

  • Strict DMN 1.3 hit policies: UNIQUE, ANY, PRIORITY, FIRST, OUTPUT ORDER, RULE ORDER, and COLLECT with SUM, MIN and MAX.
  • FEEL cells on string, number and date columns: lists, not(...), comparisons, intervals and null.
  • Validation when the table is built: overlapping rules, conflicting outputs, rules that can never fire, and gaps (inputs no rule covers, with an example).
  • DMN import and export: Praecepta reads DMN 1.1–1.5 files, including those from Camunda Modeler.
  • A Maven plugin that validates tables at build time and generates typed input and output records, so your application ships only the engine.
  • Java 21+, with the engine as a JPMS module. Everything is tested on Java 21, 25 and 27.

The benchmark

Since the first benchmark was not fair, I rebuilt it from scratch. This time Praecepta runs against Camunda 8 and Drools (the DMN engine inside Kogito), and every engine gets exactly the same work.

How I measured it

  • Same rules, same file, for every engine. Each table is written once as a DMN document, and every engine, Praecepta included, reads that document, as an application loading a .dmn file would. Before any timing, every engine evaluates the whole workload and its answers are compared with Praecepta built straight from the rules. The run aborts if any engine disagrees.
  • Supported, default setups: Camunda 8's DMN engine (dmn-scala 1.12.6, the one Zeebe embeds) and Drools 10.2.0's DMN runtime.
  • The same input for all: a Map of values. Praecepta's fastest path (generated classes with enums) is shown separately and labelled as its best case.
  • Many tables:
    • Real: the 119-rule table from 2023 (values blurred, FIRST hit policy).
    • Generated, synthetic: string columns only.
    • Generated, mixed: string, number and date columns, with comparisons, intervals and not(...).
    • Sizes: the generated tables run from 10 to 10,000 rules and from 5 to 20 columns. The same 1,000 rules are also run under each hit policy, and with inputs that match no rule.
  • More than an average: latency percentiles, memory allocated per decision, throughput with 1, 4 and 8 threads sharing one engine, the time to build an engine, and the time to the first decision in a fresh JVM.
  • The released engine: I measured the same engine code that is in the 0.1.0 release.
  • Machine: Apple M2 Pro (8 performance cores), 16 GB, macOS 26.7.1, OpenJDK 27.0.1. JMH: 5 × 2 s warm-up and 5 × 3 s measurement iterations, 3 forks.
  • Everything is public: the results keep every log, the raw JMH output and the environment, and one script reruns the whole suite in about 2.5 hours. To check that the picture is not an artefact of my machine, I also ran the short profile on a GitHub Actions runner (AMD EPYC, 4 vCPUs, Linux, Java 25). It used one fork, so its numbers are noisy, and its absolute times are 1.5–3× higher, but the ranking holds on every table. On mixed-1000, for example, Praecepta took 1.0 µs, Camunda 519 µs and Drools 421 µs.

Latency as tables grow

µs per evaluation Praecepta 0.1.0 Camunda 8 Drools 10.2.0
real (119 rules) 0.19 19.3 43.5
synthetic-10 0.15 4.20 5.89
synthetic-100 0.16 19.1 14.5
synthetic-1000 0.25 146 126
synthetic-10000 0.67 1,333 1,419
mixed-10 0.31 7.05 7.95
mixed-100 0.44 33.2 31.3
mixed-1000 0.64 263 256
mixed-10000 1.51 3,118 3,122

The bigger the table, the bigger the gap:

  • Praecepta: from 10 to 10,000 mixed rules, its time goes from 0.31 to 1.51 µs, 5× slower for 1,000× more rules.
  • Camunda and Drools: their time grows roughly with the number of rules, from about 7 µs to about 3,100 µs.
  • The ratio: Praecepta is 25–40× faster on 10 rules, 70–120× on 100, 400–600× on 1,000 and about 2,000× on 10,000. On the real table it is 104× faster than Camunda and 233× faster than Drools.

More columns cost Praecepta little: with 1,000 rules, going from 6 to 18 mixed columns takes it from 0.62 to 1.12 µs. Number and date columns cost it 2–3× string columns, because a binary search over decimals is slower than a hash lookup; that one has an issue.

Not every number is equally precise: 51 of the 63 latency measurements have a 99.9% confidence interval within ±10%. The widest is Drools on synthetic-10000, at ±33%. All of them are in the results, if you want to check.

Hit policies, and inputs that match no rule

µs per evaluation, 1,000 mixed rules Praecepta 0.1.0 Camunda 8 Drools 10.2.0
COLLECT 0.64 263 256
FIRST 0.53 49.6 248
PRIORITY 0.55 287 252
RULE ORDER 0.64 285 257
UNIQUE (1,000 rules that never overlap) 0.23 161 128
No rule matches (COLLECT) 0.32 261 197
  • Praecepta: the hit policy barely changes its time, because it is one operation on the bits that matched. An input that matches nothing costs no more than one that matches.
  • Camunda: it is 5× faster under FIRST, which suggests it stops at the first match.
  • Drools: it takes about the same time under every policy. When nothing matches, it still pays about three quarters of the time of a match, and Camunda nearly all of it.
  • The real table has no such inputs: its last rule matches anything.

Tail latency and memory per decision

µs per evaluation p50 p99 p99.9
Praecepta, real 0.17 0.29 0.54
Camunda 8, real 17.7 32.4 41.1
Drools 10.2.0, real 51.8 69.8 85.5
Praecepta, mixed-1000 0.67 1.00 2.57
Camunda 8, mixed-1000 250 323 444
Drools 10.2.0, mixed-1000 260 309 386
  • Tails: Praecepta's 99.9th percentile on mixed-1000 (2.6 µs) is still about 100× below the others' median.
  • The slowest decisions: each engine's single slowest decision took up to a few milliseconds, most likely from pauses in the JVM or the operating system, which every engine sees.
  • Allocation: on tables of up to 1,000 rules, Praecepta allocates 32 to 466 bytes per decision. Camunda allocates 22 KB to 1.5 MB, and Drools 16 KB to 375 KB. Less garbage means less garbage collection under load.

Throughput with threads

Here, all three engines do well: they can be shared between threads, and all of them scale.

  • From 1 to 8 threads: Praecepta goes from 5,374 to 33,796 decisions per millisecond (6.3×), Camunda from 61 to 451 (7.4×) and Drools from 21 to 146 (7.0×).
  • Locks: Praecepta's engine is immutable, so threads share it without any.
  • mixed-1000, 8 threads: 11,721 decisions per millisecond for Praecepta, against 29 for Camunda and 23 for Drools.

Start-up and building

ms Praecepta 0.1.0 Camunda 8 Drools 10.2.0
Read the DMN and build the engine, warm JVM: real 6.5 22.6 36.1
Read the DMN and build the engine, warm JVM: mixed-1000 45 57 437
First decision in a fresh JVM: real 76 469 379
First decision in a fresh JVM: mixed-1000 240 774 1,005

"First decision" starts a new JVM, reads the DMN file, builds the engine and evaluates one input. On the real table, Praecepta answers in 76 ms, 5–6× sooner than the others. That matters for command-line tools, serverless functions and test suites, and much less for long-running services.

Memory

"Retained heap" is the heap still in use after building the engine in a fresh JVM and running a garbage collection.

  • At 10,000 rules: Praecepta holds 5 MB, against 133 MB for Camunda and 108 MB for Drools.
  • Across all the generated tables: it uses 6 to 88 times less.
  • The real table: Praecepta's footprint there was too small for the measurement to resolve (under 0.5 MB).

Where Praecepta is slower: building FIRST and PRIORITY tables

Build time in a fresh JVM, 1,000 mixed rules Praecepta 0.1.0 Camunda 8 Drools 10.2.0
COLLECT 0.30 s 0.87 s 1.17 s
RULE ORDER 0.27 s 0.83 s 1.07 s
FIRST 3.6 s 0.85 s 1.15 s
PRIORITY 68.7 s 0.82 s 1.12 s

When it builds a FIRST or PRIORITY table, Praecepta looks for rules that can never fire: the validation described above. The check is exact, and on 1,000 random, overlapping rules it is expensive: 3.6 s under FIRST, and over a minute under PRIORITY. Evaluation is not affected, and the real 119-rule FIRST table builds in 74 ms. Still, a minute is not acceptable, and fixing it is on my list: issue #29 tracks making the check optional, bounded or cheaper.

Praecepta's best case

Feeding a Map costs two hash lookups per column: one to read the value, one to find its mask. With the Maven plugin, inputs are generated records, and string columns with a value list become enums, whose masks are found by position instead of by hashing:

That is about 100 ns per decision on the real table, from an earlier run of the same code. But to keep the comparison fair, everything above uses Map inputs for every engine, Praecepta included.

Being fair: what the numbers do not say

Numbers like these are easy to oversell, so here is what they do not say.

Where the comparison flatters Praecepta, or is limited:

  • Praecepta does less work. Camunda and Drools are general FEEL interpreters. Even when a cell is a simple test, they evaluate it through machinery that can handle arbitrary expressions, and they return richer results. Praecepta only supports what it can index.
  • It is still a microbenchmark. It runs in-process, on one machine. A real service adds HTTP and serialisation, which usually cost far more than 20 µs, so in many systems the engine is not the bottleneck at all.
  • Generated tables are not real ones. Their rules are random, so they overlap in ways real tables may not. Only one real table was measured: the DMN conformance kit's tables all use boolean columns, which Praecepta does not support yet.
  • Not every option was measured. Drools' compiled (executable) model, generated at build time by Kogito, was not measured; it may be faster than the runtime DMN path I used. Drools' experimental "alpha network" option gave wrong answers on these tables in 10.2.0, so the harness refused to time it.

What Camunda and Drools do that Praecepta does not:

  • Full FEEL: functions, arithmetic, contexts, lists, and tests across several columns (income > 2 * rent). Praecepta cells are FEEL simple unary tests on one column.
  • Decision requirement graphs: decisions feeding other decisions, business knowledge models and boxed expressions.
  • More types: boolean, time and date-time columns (planned).
  • Tooling and services: visual modellers, decision services, process engines, audit and explanation of decisions.
  • Proven conformance: Drools runs the official DMN conformance kit; Praecepta has not been run against it yet.
  • Maturity: large communities, years of production use, and commercial support.

So, if your decisions are mostly decision tables with simple cell tests, and latency, memory or start-up matter to you, give Praecepta a try. If you need full DMN, Camunda and Drools are the better choice.

How to use it

Using it is simple. First, add the engine (it has no dependencies):

<dependency>
  <groupId>io.github.brunopacheco1</groupId>
  <artifactId>praecepta-engine</artifactId>
  <version>0.1.0</version>
</dependency>

Then load a DMN file, bind the inputs, and evaluate:

record Customer(String country, Integer age) {}

DecisionTable table;
try (var dmn = Files.newInputStream(Path.of("discount.dmn"))) {
    table = DmnReader.read(dmn);
}
var engine = PraeceptaEngine.<Customer, String>builder()
        .table(table)                              // hit policy, column types, value lists, rules
        .input("country", Customer::country)
        .numberInput("age", Customer::age)
        .output(output -> output.values().get("tier"))
        .build();

engine.evaluate(new Customer("PT", 30));          // e.g. [gold]
engine.validationReport();                         // overlaps, unreachable rules, gaps

Or let the Maven plugin compile your tables (Excel, CSV or DMN) at build time:

<plugin>
  <groupId>io.github.brunopacheco1</groupId>
  <artifactId>praecepta-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>0.1.0</version>
  <executions><execution><goals><goal>generate</goal></goals></execution></executions>
  <configuration>
    <packageName>com.acme.pricing</packageName>
    <tables>
      <table><source>src/main/rules/discount.dmn</source></table>
    </tables>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

Optional<DiscountOutput> discount = Discount.evaluate(new DiscountInput(DiscountInput.Country.PT, new BigDecimal(30)));

The build fails if the table has errors (for example, two UNIQUE rules that overlap), and only the engine is needed at runtime. The README has the details.

How open is it?

I wanted a small project that is easy to trust. Here is what that means in practice:

  • Licence: Apache-2.0. The repository is REUSE-compliant: every file says who wrote it and under which licence.
  • Everything in public: the code, the CI, the modernisation plan phase by phase, the benchmark harness and every result, and the issues. So are the roadmap, the architecture, the security assurance case and the governance, which also says who takes over if I stop.
  • Release integrity: every artifact is GPG-signed and ships with an SBOM (CycloneDX), build provenance (SLSA, verifiable with gh attestation verify) and third-party notices. The builds are reproducible.
  • Checks on every change: tests on three Java versions, plugin tests on three Maven versions, an enforced code style with compiler warnings as errors, a SonarCloud quality gate, CodeQL, dependency licence and vulnerability checks, and fuzzing of the two parsers that read untrusted input, on every pull request that touches the engine and for longer every week.
  • A protected main: signed commits only, and every change arrives through a pull request that passes the checks and is approved by a code owner.
  • Badges from independent issuers: the OpenSSF Best Practices silver badge and OpenSSF Baseline level 1 (every answer links to its evidence), REUSE compliance checked by the FSFE, and the OpenSSF Scorecard, which rechecks the repository every week: 8.8 / 10.

The lowest Scorecard item is code review, and it is worth explaining. Anyone can fork the project and open a pull request. The check measures something else: whether each change that reached main was approved by someone other than its author. Today that is zero, because I am the only maintainer, and nobody can approve their own changes. The same reason keeps branch protection from a full score: I merge my own pull requests with an administrator's bypass. Every contribution I review raises the first, and a second maintainer would close both. The governance explains how to become one. Which brings me to the next part.

Want to help?

If you would like to contribute, the website gathers the guide, the API documentation and how the engine works, and the contributing guide explains how to build and test it. Here are some good first issues:

  • string ranges in cells;
  • a COUNT aggregation;
  • running the DMN conformance kit.

I would also welcome reviewers and a co-maintainer: the governance describes the roles and how decisions are made.

What could come next?

These are the features I think would be useful; the roadmap puts them in order for the next year. Tell me which ones you would use: a 👍 on the issue is enough, and a comment if you would like to build it.

  • Boolean, time and date-time columns
  • String ranges in cells
  • Inputs with several values, e.g. more than one nationality
  • Decision requirement graphs (chained decisions)
  • A COUNT aggregation
  • Faster number and date columns
  • Compressed bitmaps for very large tables
  • A Gradle plugin
  • GraalVM native-image support
  • A Spring Boot starter
  • An online playground
  • Running the DMN conformance kit

Wrapping up

The 2023 trie proved the idea and hit a wall. Bitsets took it further: on these tables, 20 to 2,000 times faster than general-purpose DMN engines, with 6 to 88 times less memory, and honest about what it does not do, including a build that is still slow for large FIRST and PRIORITY tables. Give it a try, tell me where it breaks, and tell me what you would like it to do next.

Namárië | See you | Bis geschwënn | Até mais | À bientôt

title: Cheapest Way to Host a Node.js + Postgres App in 2026
description:
Originally published at LeanStack.

Every week someone asks the same question on Reddit: what is the cheapest way to host a Node.js API with a Postgres database that is not a toy? The honest answer depends on how much downtime and maintenance you can accept, so this guide gives you real 2026 prices for five options and tells you which one fits which situation.

Short answer:

  • About $3/month: a PC you already own + Cloudflare Tunnel (you pay only electricity and the domain). Fast, but you are the ops team. I ran my production app this way for 12 days (full setup here).
  • $0/month, always on: Google Cloud's free e2-micro, if 1 GB of RAM, a shared CPU and a U.S. region are acceptable. My app runs there now.
  • About $6/month: one small VPS running both Node.js and Postgres. The cheapest always-on option if you can do basic Linux admin.
  • About $13/month: Render with a paid web service and database. No servers to manage, predictable bill.
  • $5 and up: Railway, billed by usage. Great for small, spiky apps; watch the meter.
  • Free database: Neon's permanent free Postgres pairs well with any of the above.

Quick comparison

Prices checked on November 8, 2026 on each provider's official pricing page. Taxes not included.

Option Monthly cost Always on? You manage Best for
Home PC + Cloudflare Tunnel ~$3 (electricity + domain) Only while your PC and internet are up Everything Side projects, pilots
Google Cloud e2-micro (Always Free) $0 within free limits Yes OS, Postgres, backups Low-traffic apps, U.S. regions only
DigitalOcean Droplet 1 GiB $6 Yes OS, Postgres, backups Cheapest reliable always-on
Hetzner CPX02 (EU only) €6.49 + VAT Yes OS, Postgres, backups EU users
Hostinger KVM 1 (4 GB RAM) $6.49 intro (24-month prepay), $11.99 renewal Yes OS, Postgres, backups Most RAM per dollar up front
Render web + Postgres $7 + $6 = $13 Yes Nothing No-ops, fixed bill
Railway Hobby $5 incl. $5 usage, then metered Yes Nothing Small or spiky apps
Neon Free (database only) $0 Scales to zero after 5 min idle Nothing Free Postgres that does not expire

Where these numbers come from

Prices come from each provider's official pricing page and documentation on November 8, 2026; I did not open a paid account on every platform just to collect invoices. The home-PC and small-VM numbers come from my own production app, a multi-school exam platform built with Node.js, Express and PostgreSQL: it ran for 12 days on a laptop at home, and now runs on a 1 GB cloud VM. Where I estimate a bill, I show the math so you can plug in your own usage.

There is also one more $0 option that stays always on: Google Cloud's Always Free e2-micro (2 shared vCPUs, 1 GB RAM, 30 GB standard disk, 1 GB of egress per month from North America) in us-west1, us-central1 or us-east1. That is where my app runs today; the catches are a weak shared CPU and U.S.-only regions.

Option 1: A PC you already own + Cloudflare Tunnel (~$3)

If you have a spare PC or laptop, Cloudflare Tunnel publishes a local app on your domain without opening router ports, and the tunnel is free. My production exam platform ran this way on a laptop CPU from 2016 and handled 1,000 simulated users with zero errors and p95 around 100 ms. Electricity and the domain came to about $3 a month.

The catch is uptime: sleep, Windows Update reboots, power cuts and ISP outages all take your app down, and backups are entirely on you. In 12 days my laptop went to sleep twice and the app was offline for about 12 hours in total. I wrote up the whole setup, the load test and the risks in Hosting a Node.js + Postgres App From a Home PC.

Option 2: One small VPS for both Node.js and Postgres (~$6)

This is the cheapest option that stays online when your laptop is closed. You rent a small Linux server, install Node.js and PostgreSQL on it, and run your app with a process manager like PM2 or systemd.

What you get for about $6 a month:

Provider Plan vCPU RAM Disk Traffic Price
DigitalOcean Basic Droplet 1 1 GiB 25 GiB SSD 1,000 GiB $6
Hetzner CPX02 (Germany/Finland) 1 1 GB 20 GB NVMe 20 TB €6.49 + VAT
Hostinger KVM 1 1 4 GB 50 GB NVMe 4 TB $6.49 intro, $11.99 renewal

Things the price tables do not tell you:

  • Hetzner's US locations cost much more. The cheapest cloud plan in Ashburn or Hillsboro was CPX11 at €17.99/month when I checked, versus €6.49 for CPX02 in Europe. If your users are in the U.S., latency to Germany matters.
  • Hostinger's $6.49 requires paying 24 months up front, and the plan renews at $11.99/month.
  • 1 GB of RAM is tight for Node.js plus Postgres. It works for small apps if you lower Postgres memory settings and add a swap file; 2 GB is more comfortable (DigitalOcean's 2 GiB Droplet is $12).

How tight is 1 GB in practice? My app runs on a 1 GB VM (Google Cloud's free e2-micro) with Node.js in cluster mode (2 workers), PostgreSQL 16 and cloudflared. With Postgres set to shared_buffers = 128MB and max_connections = 40, plus a 2 GB swap file, free -m shows:

               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:             969         519         373          26         239         450
Swap:           2047          32        2015

About half the RAM is used and swap is barely touched, so 1 GB is enough for a small app if you tune Postgres down. It will not be enough if you add Redis, a search engine or a big in-memory cache.

Do not skip backups on a VPS. A cron job running pg_dump to another machine or cloud storage every night is the minimum. Most providers also sell automatic server snapshots for a small extra fee.

Option 3: Render (~$13, fully managed)

Render runs your app from a Git repo and handles TLS, deploys and restarts. The Hobby workspace itself is free; you pay per service:

Render service Specs Price
Web service (free) 512 MB $0, spins down after 15 min idle
Web service 0.5 CPU, 512 MB $7/month
Postgres (free) 256 MB, 1 GB storage $0, expires after 30 days
Postgres 0.1 CPU, 256 MB $6/month + $0.30 per GB storage

So the realistic floor for an always-on app with a database you keep is $13/month. The free tier is fine for demos, but two details bite people:

  • A free web service sleeps after 15 minutes without traffic and takes about a minute to wake up.
  • A free Postgres database expires 30 days after creation. You get a 14-day grace period to upgrade; after that Render deletes it, data included.

Render's docs put the wake-up at about a minute, and community reports go higher for bigger apps. Since February 2026, a free service also stays awake while it receives WebSocket messages, not only HTTP requests. Free services lose any files written to local disk when they spin down, so keep uploads in a database or object storage.

Option 4: Railway (from $5, usage-based)

Railway bills by the second for the resources your services actually use. The Hobby plan costs $5/month and includes $5 of usage. Beyond that:

  • Memory: about $10 per GB per month
  • CPU: about $20 per vCPU per month
  • Volume storage (for Postgres data): about $0.15 per GB per month
  • Egress: $0.05 per GB

You can estimate your bill as average RAM (GB) × $10 + average CPU (vCPU) × $20 + storage. An app and database that together average a few hundred MB of RAM and little CPU can stay close to the $5 included credit. A busy app, or one with a memory leak, will not.

A worked example using my own app's real footprint: Node.js plus Postgres use about 0.5 GB of RAM together and almost no CPU when idle. On Railway that is roughly 0.5 GB × $10 = $5 for memory, plus perhaps 0.05 vCPU × $20 = $1 for CPU, plus 1 GB of Postgres volume at $0.15. That is about $6.15 a month, or $1.15 above the included $5. An exam with 1,000 students logging in at once would push CPU, and the bill, up for that hour.

There is also a free plan with $1 of usage per month and a one-time $5 trial credit, which is enough to try it but not to run anything permanent.

Option 5: A free managed database with Neon

If the database is what pushes you onto a paid plan, Neon offers serverless Postgres with a permanent free plan:

  • 100 compute-hours per project per month (autoscaling up to 2 compute units)
  • 1 GB storage per project (20 GB across up to 100 projects)
  • Scales to zero after 5 minutes idle, which adds a short delay on the first query after a pause

The paid Launch plan has no monthly minimum: $0.106 per compute-hour and $0.35 per GB-month of storage. Neon's own estimate for a small database with intermittent load is about $15/month.

A common cheap combination: Node.js on Render's free web service or a small VPS, with the database on Neon's free plan. Just remember both the free web service and the free database go to sleep, so the first request after a quiet period is slow.

How slow is slow? Neon describes its cold starts as subsecond, around 500 ms on average, which is far less painful than Render's one-minute wake-up. Still, set your Postgres client's connection timeout to a few seconds (the pg default is no timeout, but many ORMs use shorter ones) so the first query after a pause does not fail.

Which one should you choose?

  • Learning, demo or early pilot: home PC + Cloudflare Tunnel, or Render free + Neon free. Accept the sleeps and the downtime.
  • First paying users, and you know some Linux: a $6 VPS (DigitalOcean for U.S. users, Hetzner for Europe) with nightly pg_dump backups. Cheapest always-on option by far.
  • You never want to SSH into a server: Render at about $13/month for a fixed, predictable bill.
  • Small app with uneven traffic: Railway, as long as you check the usage graph in the first weeks.
  • Database is the expensive part: move it to Neon's free plan first and see if that is enough.

My own path: I started on a home laptop at about $3 a month, then moved to Google Cloud's free e2-micro once sleep-related outages started to matter. When my exams outgrow it, I will pay for a VPS with 2–4 vCPUs rather than a managed platform, because my bottleneck is password hashing, and that needs cores, not convenience.

Common problems

  • "My free database disappeared." Render free Postgres expires after 30 days. Export it with pg_dump before then or move to a paid plan.
  • "The first request takes 30–60 seconds." That is a sleeping free web service waking up. Pay for an always-on instance, or use a VPS.
  • "My VPS bill went up." Many providers repriced in 2026, and intro prices like Hostinger's renew higher. Check the renewal price before you prepay.
  • "Out of memory on a 1 GB VPS." Lower Postgres shared_buffers and max_connections, add a 1–2 GB swap file, or move up to 2 GB RAM.

title: Nobody asked for this
description:
Originally published on hayatibis.dev, where the figures move and the toys are interactive.

I’ve run into the gap between an idea and what gets built many times. An illustration:

A dental clinic finds a freelance developer through a friend and asks for “an online booking system”. The developer builds a calendar, patient records and an admin panel. At the handover the clinic says “we didn’t ask for this”. Their real problem was patients who don’t show up, chairs sitting empty in the middle of the day. A reminder sent the day before would have solved most of it.

In a product company, again as an illustration, the same gap comes in other clothes. Sales asks for an “export to Excel” button, and the team builds a filtered export on every table. What sales wanted was a list, every Monday, of the customers whose usage dropped, so they’d know whom to call.

Nobody said anything misleading, but the meaning got lost on the way.

Illustrative. After the tree swing cartoon engineers have passed around for decades, redrawn for the clinic. (interactive version)

Why it shows at the end

The misunderstanding happens at the start, but it only shows at the end, so the last person in the chain pays for it. Even a contract usually writes down the sentence that was asked for, not the need behind it.

Illustrative. The same request passes through four hands. Without the questions, the sentence survives and the need doesn’t: every hand builds a little further from it, and the agent’s green checks only prove it built what it was told. Ask first, at the clinic, and the need travels with the work as an example the clinic approved and a test can check. (interactive version)

Fred Brooks saw this in 1986. In No Silver Bullet, his essay on why no single tool would make software ten times easier to build, he writes: “The hardest single part of building a software system is deciding precisely what to build.” A paragraph later he adds that clients “usually do not know what questions must be answered”.

So someone has to ask them. Most of us do ask, just too late, in the design review or at the handover.

The right time, the right place, the right questions

The right time is before anyone talks about a solution. Once “a booking system” is on the table, every question starts circling it.

The right place is the desk of the person who does the job. Watch how the clinic’s receptionist keeps appointments today, and how they notice a patient who didn’t come, with whatever they use now.

The questions are plain:

  • What decision will you make when you open this screen?
  • How do you make that decision today?
  • Can you show me a real case from last week?

At the decision points, the questions that come up while building aside, I try to stay with one sentence:

you can outsource your thinking
but you cannot outsource your understanding

— kache (@yacineMTB), 4 February 2026

In April Karpathy said in a talk at Sequoia that he keeps thinking about it “like every other day”, and a day after the video went up he quoted it as the quote he’d been citing a lot recently. In the talk he adds: “the LLMs certainly don’t excel at understanding. You still are uniquely in charge of that.” You can hand the thinking to an agent; you can’t hand over the understanding. An agent writes the calendar in a few hours. Understanding that the clinic’s problem is empty chairs is something else.

Then turn the answers into a few concrete examples the people who asked have approved, like “every patient with an appointment tomorrow gets a message today at 18:00” (illustrative), and turn the examples into tests. The argument stops being about who said what and becomes about whether the example passes.

We used to work hard to keep the developer’s part limited to technical questions. But times have changed: the person who designs a feature and the person who builds it are slowly becoming the same person. I don’t know if that separation is still needed; the developer doesn’t seem to be a separate role any more. So asking the question and understanding the answer land on the same person.

When the last hand is a loop

More and more often the hand that builds is an agent. First came vibe coding, where you describe what you want and the model writes it, then agents writing and reviewing while a person steers. Now we talk about loops that run for hours on a goal without anyone in between.

Karpathy’s autoresearch is the cleanest example I know. The idea, in its own words: “give an AI agent a small but real LLM training setup and let it experiment autonomously overnight.” The agent changes the training code, trains for five minutes, checks if a single metric got better, keeps or discards the change, and repeats.[1] “You wake up in the morning to a log of experiments and (hopefully) a better model.”

It works because the task is verifiable. Karpathy wrote about this in a short post, Verifiability: for a task to be automated this way, the environment has to be resettable, efficient and “rewardable (there is some automated process to reward any specific attempt that was made)”. He sums it up in two lines: “Software 1.0 easily automates what you can specify. Software 2.0 easily automates what you can verify.”

Now put the clinic’s booking system in that loop. The tests pass, the calendar shows every appointment, the lint is green. But whether the chairs stay empty can’t be measured overnight; the answer comes weeks later, at the clinic.

Illustrative numbers. autoresearch trains for five minutes per experiment, about 12 an hour and about 100 while you sleep (its README), and keeps a change only if val_bpb goes down. Switch to the clinic and the same tireless loop has only the tests to go by: they stay green all night while it adds screens, and the empty chairs never reach its log. (interactive version)

A loop that never gets tired keeps chasing the question it was given. If the question is wrong, it grows the wrong answer with the same patience.

When I vibe code a part I don’t understand, building something many people will use and get value from is, I think, very hard.

Can the agent ask instead?

Partly. This essay is a small example. While I was preparing it, an agent asked me one question at a time, because a skill file someone wrote tells it to ask first and build later. Nothing it asked changed my mind, but it let the idea cook and mature. The answers, what I’d seen and what bothered me about it, it couldn’t find anywhere; they had to come from me.

So an agent can ask the right questions if we show it how. Unless someone brings the problem into its context, it can’t go to the clinic and ask the receptionist the right question, for now :)

Where the work is going

Karpathy’s MenuGen story is a good example here. He often got stuck on restaurant menus, not knowing what the dishes were, so he built an app that shows a picture of each dish when you photograph the menu, without writing a line of it himself: MenuGen. In the same talk he told the rest. Later it was enough to give the photo to Gemini and ask Nano Banana to draw the dishes onto the menu; the model gave back the same photo of the menu with the dishes rendered into it. In his words, “all of my MenuGen is spurious”, and “that app shouldn’t exist”.

Karpathy’s story from his Sequoia talk, redrawn; the menu and the drawings are illustrative. The app went away, and the need stayed: seeing what a dish looks like. (interactive version)

In the same talk he describes the LLM as a new kind of computer. Today neural nets run “virtualized on existing computers”; one day that may flip, and “the neural net becomes kind of like the host process” with the CPUs as the co-processor. Going on from MenuGen, he says “a lot of this code shouldn’t exist and it’s just neural networks doing most of the work”.

The app went away, but the need stayed: seeing what a dish looks like. The clinic’s problem wasn’t a booking system either; it was empty chairs.

What we build can change, and like MenuGen it may one day not be needed at all; what doesn’t change is understanding what’s needed.

As writing code gets cheaper, the part before it gets more valuable: asking at the right time and in the right place, and turning the answer into something a loop can check.

The card

Five lines to fill before work starts, by a person or by an agent, a small checklist. I filled this one in with the clinic’s request; tap a line to call it out.

Fig. 5 · Illustrative. A card filled in with the clinic's request. The fourth line is written so a test can check it. (interactive version)

The fourth line is also a very good instruction you can give an agent: it turns “build a booking system” into something it can verify.

Back at the clinic, the calendar worked, and nobody had asked for it. When did your agent last ask you, without you telling it to, who is going to use this, and for what?

Stands on

  • Frederick P. Brooks, Jr., No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering (Proceedings of the IFIP Tenth World Computing Conference, pp. 1069–76) (1986)
  • kache (@yacineMTB) on X (4 February 2026)
  • Andrej Karpathy on X, quoting it (30 April 2026)
  • Andrej Karpathy: From Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering, with Stephanie Zhan (Sequoia AI Ascent, 20 April 2026; video 29 April 2026)
  • Andrej Karpathy: Vibe coding MenuGen (27 April 2025)
  • Andrej Karpathy: Verifiability (17 November 2025)
  • Andrej Karpathy: autoresearch (GitHub, March 2026)

Notes

  1. The metric is val_bpb, validation bits per byte, and lower is better. The human edits one file, program.md, which tells the agent how to run the research; the agent edits train.py.

A new essay every Sunday: get it by email. If you'd like more of these, you can support the writing on Patreon, or buy me a coffee once.

title: Two agents, one room: how we caught a bug neither repo's tests could see
description:
Two teammates, two coding agents, one Switch room. One agent owns the
backend (a small checkout API). The other checks that the clients (a web page and
an older mobile app, represented in the repo by a pinned fixture,
clients/mobile-client-v1.js, that stands in for the shipped v1.2 binaries) still
work against it. The room is where their requirements, handoffs and evidence
meet. In the live run one room owner played both teammate roles, so the two
human "teammates" were the same account; the two agents were separate.

The 80-second change

At 01:30 (GMT, 8 Nov) the backend owner asked their agent to rename one field in
the checkout response, total to grandTotal, and add a tax and shipping
breakdown. 80 seconds later: PR #5, commit fd023c7, 25 of 25 tests green. We
re-ran the suite at that commit while writing this post: still 25 of 25.

The break

The second teammate role asked the checking agent to test it before the mobile
release. Its verdict: do not ship. The old app reads total; the new
response doesn't have it, so the app gets undefined. The backend's own suite could not see this.

The part we find most interesting is why the tests stayed green. The only test
that read total had been rewritten to read grandTotal in the same commit. The
change erased the check on the old behaviour while breaking the old behaviour.
The checking agent added a regression test, fe4c9c3. We ran it against both
versions: it fails on PR #5 (Received: undefined) and passes on the fix.

The fix, and the human in the loop

The backend owner replied in the room: "my suite was 25/25 and I still broke your
clients." The backend agent put total back next to grandTotal and added a
version header: nothing removed, 28 of 28 tests (commit b13234f, merged as
405f440). The checking agent re-ran everything against those exact commits and
reported all clear. A human typed /approve. From the check request (01:33) to
approval (01:45): 12 minutes.

Why this needed Switch

  • The requirement lived in chat. "Older mobile clients MUST keep working" was a sentence from a person. The checking agent turned it into a test.
  • Evidence moved like teammate messages. Verdicts named exact commits, so a human could read them at a glance.
  • Roles were written down. The room's Instructions say the verifier never merges anything, the fixer never approves its own fix, and only the human merges.

Try it

Clone the repo and run ./run-demo.sh. The page has a panel that calls the real
backend; tick "Replay PR #5" to watch the old app break.

Repo: https://github.com/shahaman098/proofroom

Built for the Flip the Switch hackathon, Best Business Workflow track with Switch.

title: AI Gateway logs now show session affinity
description:
AI Gateway logs now have a Sessions view that groups requests into sessions and shows how session affinity routed each one. Each row shows the coding agent or app that ran the session, such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, along with its cost, models, providers, and how much of its input was cached across every turn.

Open a session to see its cache hit rate, duration, and path. The path lists each turn with its model and timing, and names the provider serving the session along with any earlier ones. Session affinity sends each turn to the provider that served the one before it, so the provider already has most of the prompt in cache. A session that stays on one provider reads more of each prompt from cache.

Filter sessions by turns, client, model, provider, authentication, or cost. Single-turn sessions are hidden until you clear the minimum turns filter.

Session affinity runs by default on text and chat requests. To group requests yourself, send the same sessionId in providerOptions.gateway, or the same x-session-id header, on every request in a conversation. Requests without one are grouped by a fingerprint of the conversation's opening and appear as fingerprinted sessions.

Read the session affinity documentation for more information on how AI Gateway identifies sessions.

title: Mobile-First SCSS Architecture with Dart Sass in Docker
description:
Our SCSS is split into three folders and compiled by tools inside Docker, so developers do not need Sass installed on the host. The source and generated files still live on a bind-mounted project directory. Here's the setup and why it matters.

The Directory Structure 

assets/scss/site/
├── common/          ← variables, breakpoints, shared partials
├── mobile/          ← base styles and small-screen adjustments
│   ├── _catalog_list.scss
│   ├── _catalog_item.scss
│   ├── _account.scss
│   └── _main.scss
└── desktop/         ← wider-screen overrides
    ├── _catalog_list.scss
    ├── _catalog_item.scss
    └── _main.scss

The mobile folder contains the base appearance. It still has a few targeted media and accessibility queries; “mobile-first” does not have to mean “no media queries.”

The desktop folder primarily contains wider-screen overrides. If a component does not change at the desktop breakpoint, it usually needs no matching desktop partial.

Why This Matters

The separation makes the cascade and ownership clear: base rules live in one place, and desktop files describe the delta. We compile separate outputs and apply the desktop stylesheet conditionally:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="/storage/static/css/site/main_catalog_list_mobile.css">
<link rel="stylesheet"
      href="/storage/static/css/site/main_catalog_list_desktop.css"
      media="(min-width: 641px) and (min-height: 500px)">

The media attribute controls when the desktop CSS applies. Browsers may fetch a nonmatching stylesheet at lower priority, but it does not guarantee that the file will not be downloaded. Verify transfer behavior with browser tooling instead of treating file separation as an automatic bandwidth saving.

Building Inside Docker

We never run sass on the host machine. The Docker container has Dart Sass installed:

# docker-compose.yml (simplified)
site:
  build:
    context: .
    dockerfile: .docker/site/site.dockerfile
  command: ["make", "-f", "/Makefile", "dev"]
  volumes:
    - ./src:/app
    - ./Makefile:/Makefile

The development target builds assets once, then runs Air and Sass concurrently:

dev: build-css-dev build-js-dev
    $(MAKE) -j 2 run-air watch-css

run-air:
    cd $(SRC_DIR) && air -c .air.site.toml

watch-css:
    sass --watch --poll $(SCSS_INPUTS) --style=expanded --no-source-map

We use --poll because filesystem event delivery from bind mounts varies across host and Docker combinations. Polling is not universally required, so test both modes in your own environment.

Compiled Output 

storage/static/css/site/
├── main_catalog_list_mobile.css
├── main_catalog_list_desktop.css
├── main_catalog_item_mobile.css
├── main_catalog_item_desktop.css
├── main_account_mobile.css
├── main_account_desktop.css
├── bundle_mobile.css
└── bundle_desktop.css

Our static web server serves the compiled files directly, without routing them through the Go application.

The Gotcha: Air Doesn't Watch SCSS

Air's config explicitly excludes assets/ and storage/:

[build]
  exclude_dir = ["assets", "storage", "tmp"]

This is intentional. SCSS changes are handled by sass --watch, which runs in parallel. If Air watched SCSS files too, it would rebuild the Go binary on every CSS edit — pointless and slow.

JavaScript has no watcher in this setup. After editing an entry file, we run:

docker compose exec -T site make -f /Makefile build-js-dev

This is a deliberate project trade-off, not a requirement of Docker or Sass.

What We'd Change

If starting over, we would evaluate native CSS plus Lightning CSS, or keep Sass and add a separate post-processing step. Lightning CSS can transform, prefix, bundle, and minify CSS, but it is not a drop-in compiler for SCSS syntax.

Dart Sass remains a good fit for the current partials, and keeping the toolchain in Docker gives every developer the same compiler version.

This article is based on lessons from building Towami, a multi-country marketplace and white-label storefront platform. Follow for more practical notes on Go, HTMX, infrastructure, and SaaS.

title: Same AI, two answers: what happened when we gave our on-call agent a memory
description:
Picture the person who uses an incident tool. It's the middle of the night. An alert just woke them up. Customers are affected, a manager is asking for updates, and they are trying to read logs with half-open eyes.

That person doesn't need a clever chatbot. They need an answer they can trust in seconds, and proof they can check.

Our team built DejaVu, an AI on-call agent that remembers how past outages were fixed. This post is about the design side: how we made an invisible thing, memory, visible and useful.

The engine underneath

DejaVu's memory is powered by Hindsight, an open-source agent memory system by Vectorize. Every past incident is stored in Hindsight. When a new error comes in, DejaVu recalls similar incidents, an LLM (GPT-OSS 120B on Groq) reasons over them, and the engineer's feedback is retained as a new memory.

If you're curious why memory is different from just searching documents, Vectorize explains it well in what is agent memory.

The challenge for design: memory works in the background. How do you show a stressed engineer why the agent is so sure?

1. A live memory map

The first thing you see is a map of dots. Each dot is a past incident, sized by how long it took to fix, and grouped by type of failure: cache, database, bad config, queues.

When DejaVu recalls incidents for a new error, the matching dots light up and lines draw out to them. You don't have to read anything to understand "this has happened before, many times." A failed fix shows as a red dot, and a newly learned incident appears as a green one.

2. Show the comparison, not just the answer

We added a button: Compare without vs with memory. It runs the same model twice, side by side. Without memory: 20% confident, a generic guess. With memory: 98%, with the exact fix.

This turned out to be the clearest way to explain the product to anyone, technical or not. One glance, and the value of memory is obvious.

3. Proof under every claim

The confidence ring never stands alone. Under it is a sentence in plain words, like "5 of 5 matching past incidents were fixed this way," and chips for each cited incident. On the right, each recalled incident has a card: the service, what happened, how strongly it matches, how long it took to fix, and why it matches.

The rule we followed: if the agent claims it, the screen shows where it came from.

4. One click to teach it

Feedback has to be effortless at 3 a.m. So it's two big buttons: Fix worked and Fix failed. One click saves the outcome to Hindsight in the background, and the interface never freezes:

learn_new_incident({
    "id": new_id,
    "service": ss.service,
    "error_signature": ss.error,
    "root_cause": answer["probable_cause"],
    "resolution_steps": answer["fix_steps"],
    "fix_successful": outcome,          # True or False from the button
    "time_to_resolve_minutes": minutes_since(ss.diag_at),
    "occurred_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
})

Inside, this calls Hindsight's retain with retain_async=True. A small celebration, a toast and a new green dot confirm it worked. We also record the real minutes from diagnosis to fix, not the AI's guess, so the learning curve stays honest.

5. Calm colours, red only for alerts

Our first version had neon colours everywhere, and it felt stressful. We switched to a calm black and champagne-gold theme. Red is used only for real alerts and failed fixes, so when you see red, it means something. Animations respect the "reduce motion" setting, and the layout works on a phone, because on-call engineers aren't always at a desk.

6. Fitting into a real team

Good design also means fitting how teams already work. Our path to adoption:

  1. Import history: load past postmortems into Hindsight.
  2. Alert in: a PagerDuty or Grafana webhook sends each alert to DejaVu.
  3. Fix plan out: the cited diagnosis is posted to the team's Slack or Teams channel.
  4. Close the loop: each "fix worked" becomes memory, and a weekly reflect report tells the team lead what keeps breaking.

Steps 1 and 4 work today. The Hindsight docs cover the reflect feature that powers that weekly report.

What I learned

  • Make the invisible visible. Memory is the core of the product, so we gave it a picture.
  • Proof builds trust faster than polish.
  • Design for the worst moment, not the demo moment.

Small details that made a big difference

A few smaller choices helped more than we expected:

  • Quick-pick alerts. Three buttons replay common outages (cache error after a deploy, database out of connections, login rate limits), so anyone can try the product without typing an error.
  • A downloadable postmortem. One click writes a blameless postmortem in Markdown, because writing it is the task everyone puts off after an outage.
  • A learning curve chart. It shows time-to-fix for every incident, with the average dropping from 44 minutes to 6 as memory grew. It answers "is this actually helping?" without a single word.
  • Friendly errors. When the free AI tier is busy, the app says "wait 30 seconds" instead of showing a stack trace.

None of these are about AI. They're about respecting the person using the tool.

Try it

  • Code: https://github.com/Pratheeksh-7S/dejavu-incident-agent
  • Demo video: https://youtu.be/Nu_sktguGMk
  • Hindsight: https://github.com/vectorize-io/hindsight

The best incident tool is the one a tired engineer can understand in five seconds.

title: Deleted deployments are permanently removed sooner
description:
Deployments deleted before they are 30 days old now have a shorter recovery period before permanent deletion. As developers deploy more frequently on Vercel, this reduces the buildup of old deployments on the Recently Deleted page.

For successfully built deployments, the recovery period is the time you have to restore them after deletion:

When the deployment is deleted

Time to restore after deletion

By retention policy before it reaches 30 days old

Same length as the policy. A 7-day policy gives you 7 more days.

Manually, less than 1 day after creation

1 more day

Manually, at least 1 day but less than 30 days after creation

Same as its age at deletion. Delete it 3 days after creation, and you have 3 more days.

Manually or by retention policy, 30 days or more after creation

30 more days, unchanged

After this time, deployments are permanently deleted and cannot be restored. Unsuccessful deployments may be permanently deleted sooner.

Learn more in the deployment retention documentation.

title: From 100 Million Cells to One Molecule You Can Walk Inside — Why Cascade Makes NexoPeek Essential Now
description:
From 100 Million Cells to One Molecule You Can Walk Inside — Why Cascade Makes NexoPeek Essential Now

I still remember the night the data dump landed on my laptop. A single CSV, 100 million rows, each row a cell from a spatial transcriptomics experiment. The file was 27 GB, the kind of thing that makes a laptop fan sound like a jet engine. I had a deadline in two days, a grant review looming, and a sinking feeling that the usual “load‑into‑pandas‑and‑plot” workflow would never finish in time.

The viral post that popped up on Hacker News that morning — “From 100 Million Cells to One Molecule You Can Walk Inside” — felt like a personal message. It described a pipeline called Cascade that breaks a massive cellular atlas into hierarchical tiles, each tile small enough to stream to a browser, yet preserving the full resolution needed to zoom down to a single transcript. The article claimed that NexoPeek, a web‑based viewer built on top of Cascade, lets you “walk inside” a molecule, rotating, slicing, and measuring distances in real time.

I clicked the link, half‑expecting marketing fluff. Instead I found a technical deep‑dive: a description of a quad‑tree‑like spatial index stored as Parquet files on object storage, a WebAssembly‑compiled rendering engine that streams only the visible tiles, and a WebGPU‑accelerated shader that draws point clouds at 60 fps even on a modest GPU. The numbers were concrete — 1.2 ms per tile fetch, 0.8 ms decode, 0.4 ms raster — and the benchmarks were run on a single‑core Cloud Run instance. No hidden clusters, no proprietary magic.

That night I cloned the open‑source Cascade repo, spun up a local MinIO bucket, and ran the ingestion script on a 4‑core VM. The ingestion took 3 hours, wrote 12 TB of tiled Parquet, and produced a manifest JSON that NexoPeek reads at load time. The first time I opened the viewer in Chrome, the 100 million‑cell dataset appeared as a faint cloud. I hovered, the tile loader fetched the next level, and suddenly individual nuclei resolved. Another zoom, and a single mRNA molecule glowed, its coordinates exact to the nanometer.

The experience was visceral. I could rotate the molecule with a mouse drag, slice it with a plane slider, and measure the distance between two transcripts by clicking two points — a feature the demo highlighted as “spatial ruler”. The UI never froze; the frame‑time graph in DevTools stayed flat at 16 ms. I realized the cascade architecture does two things that matter for any large‑scale spatial data product:

  1. Progressive refinement — the index guarantees that the first tile you see is a coarse summary, and each subsequent tile adds detail only where you look.
  2. Stateless streaming — tiles are immutable objects in object storage; the viewer never needs a persistent server session, just signed URLs.

For a team like mine — a handful of bio‑informaticians, a shared cloud budget, and a need to ship interactive figures to reviewers — this meant we could publish a live, explorable supplement instead of a static PNG. The grant reviewers could open the link, zoom to the exact region we highlighted in the paper, and verify the spatial colocalization themselves. No more “supplementary movie” that never plays on the conference Wi‑Fi.

There were hiccups. The first ingestion run crashed because the Parquet writer hit a 2 GB row‑group limit; I had to patch the writer to split row groups at 500 MB. The WebGPU shader failed on Safari until I added a fallback to WebGL2. The signed‑URL expiration was set to 1 hour, which broke long‑running explorer sessions; a quick lambda refresher fixed it. Each fix felt like a small victory, the kind you only get when the stack is transparent enough to debug.

What struck me most was how Cascade’s design mirrors the biology: just as a tissue is organized into organs, then cells, then molecules, the data is organized into tiles, then sub‑tiles, then points. The same hierarchy that lets a pathologist zoom from a whole‑slide image to a single nucleus now lets a computational biologist zoom from a million‑cell atlas to a single transcript. The tool didn’t invent that hierarchy; it exposed it.

Now, when a new dataset lands — a 200 million‑cell atlas from a collaborator — I don’t reach for a heavier cluster. I spin up the same ingestion pipeline, point it at a new bucket, and hand the manifest URL to NexoPeek. The viewer loads in seconds, the first tile paints in milliseconds, and I can start asking scientific questions instead of engineering ones.

If you’re wrestling with spatial data that feels too big for a browser, give the cascade‑tiling approach a try. The open‑source repo, the ingestion scripts, and a minimal NexoPeek starter are all on GitHub. Clone, run the demo on a tiny subset, and see the first tile appear. Then scale up. The architecture does the heavy lifting; you just bring the biology.

Explore the cascade, walk the molecule, and let the data tell its story.
