title: DDL for MySQL, SQL Server, or Oracle from One Spec
description:
Quick answer: One OpenAPI spec generates dialect-specific DDL, indexes, deterministic seed data, and deployment scripts for MySQL, SQL Server, and Oracle. The relational design is derived once from the schemas, then emitted in the dialect each database requires, rather than hand-writing and maintaining a separate design per engine. The generated SQL is for review and is never executed by the modeling package.

Why one source matters

Maintaining three hand-written designs is slow and invites drift. A change made to one dialect can be missed on the others, and a type or key that works on one engine may need a different form on the next. Building the relational model once and generating the dialect output keeps the three databases aligned against the same source.

The OpenAPI schemas are that source, and the derived entities, foreign keys, and link tables are shared before the dialect-specific rendering.

What each dialect receives

Output MySQL SQL Server Oracle
Table DDL Yes Yes Yes
Indexes Yes Yes Yes
Foreign keys Yes Yes Yes
Deterministic seed data Yes Yes Yes
Deployment script Yes Yes Yes

The same logical table is rendered with the data types and syntax the target engine expects, so the dialect differences are handled at generation rather than by separate manual edits.

How the generation works

  1. Derive the relational entities and keys from the schemas.
  2. Infer the link tables and resolve the open questions.
  3. Reconcile the model against the live database when a profile exists.
  4. Render the DDL, indexes, and seed data for each dialect.
  5. Produce the idempotent, forward-only deployment script.
  6. Review the output before running it.

The seed data is deterministic, so a fresh deployment produces the same starting values rather than random or environment-dependent rows, and the deployment script is idempotent so a repeated run does not create duplicate objects.

Take a table that stores a timestamp and a fixed-length code. The shared model declares the two fields once, and the generator renders each in the dialect the engine accepts: the date type and the string type take the form MySQL expects, then the equivalent forms for SQL Server and Oracle. The foreign keys and the indexes are emitted the same way, so a change to a field is made once and all three outputs move together. A reviewer still opens the dialect-specific rendering, because a type that maps cleanly on one engine can carry a length or precision difference on another, and the review happens before the forward-only script runs. None of the three sets executes itself, and the deterministic seed data keeps a fresh deployment identical across the engines.

Honest limits

The dialect output is generated for review, and the modeling package has no executing driver, so none of the three sets of DDL runs automatically. A dialect-specific edge case, such as a type that maps differently under a particular engine, still deserves a review against the target database rather than blind trust.

When the business logic is ambiguous, the result raises an open question rather than guessing across all three dialects, and the inferred link tables stay labeled until confirmed. This is the same boundary that keeps a static signal from being written as a guarantee.

Powerduck keeps the three dialects and the shared source model in the desktop, so the databases stay aligned while the execution remains a separate, reviewed step.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a separate design for each database? No. The relational model is derived once and rendered as DDL for MySQL, SQL Server, and Oracle.

What handles dialect differences? The generator emits the data types and syntax each engine expects, rather than using one generic form.

Does the tool run the DDL? No. It is generated for review, and the deployment script is idempotent and forward-only when you run it.

The bottom line

A single OpenAPI spec can drive three databases, deriving the relational model once and generating dialect-specific DDL, indexes, seed data, and deployment scripts for MySQL, SQL Server, and Oracle. This keeps the engines aligned and removes the drift of three hand-written designs, while the SQL stays reviewed rather than executed and ambiguous logic stays an open question. One source, three dialects, and the execution decision stays with the team. Read more in the API data model guide.

title: Electron vs GPUI: What Discord's 290 MB Rust Rewrite Can and Cannot Prove
description:
A screenshot can make a framework debate look settled. Discord's co-founder and CTO showed an early Windows build of a rewritten client using about 290 MB of memory, and suddenly the question became: was Electron the problem all along?

Not so fast. The screenshot is a real data point shared by Discord's leadership, but it is not a controlled benchmark. It does not tell us what the old client used under the same workload, which background tasks were running, or how the new build behaves during a busy voice call, screen share, or large server session. Discord has not published a repeatable performance comparison.

The news is still worth paying attention to. On November 4, 2026, Stanislav Vishnevskiy said Discord was moving its desktop client from Electron to Rust, with GPUI, the Rust UI framework developed by the Zed team. He said the company had used Rust since 2018 in infrastructure, voice technology, and parts of the existing client. He also said React Native would leave the mobile stack, while mobile would keep native interfaces and share app logic with desktop through Rust. The team hopes to put the new client into user testing soon, but no release date was announced. (Vishnevskiy's post on X)

That makes this a useful comparison, not a verdict. Electron and GPUI solve different problems. Electron makes it practical to ship desktop software with web technologies. GPUI gives a team more control over a Rust-based, GPU-accelerated interface, but it also asks that team to own more of the application stack.

The short version

  • Choose Electron when a web team needs to ship a cross-platform desktop app quickly, reuse web skills and components, and rely on a mature ecosystem.
  • Consider a native Rust UI such as GPUI when profiling shows that the current architecture is holding back a product, the team can support Rust and platform-specific work, and the product benefits from a more integrated native rendering stack.
  • Do not choose either from one RAM screenshot. Compare equivalent builds under the same user actions, operating system, hardware, and measurement method.
  • Consider Tauri separately. It uses Rust for the application backend and a system webview for HTML-based UI. It is not the same architectural choice as GPUI, and Discord's CTO explicitly said the rewrite uses GPUI, not Tauri. (Tauri architecture, Vishnevskiy's post)

Electron is a browser-shaped application platform

Electron is not simply “a website in a window.” Its process model inherits ideas from Chromium. An Electron application has a main process that manages the app lifecycle and windows, and renderer processes that display web content. Each BrowserWindow has a separate renderer. Electron's documentation explains that renderers behave much like web pages, while the main process runs in a Node.js environment and can access operating-system APIs. (Electron process model)

That architecture is a deliberate bargain. A team can use JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and its existing front-end framework to build for Windows, macOS, and Linux. The same browser technology that powers the web becomes the interface layer for a desktop product. Teams can move quickly, reuse knowledge, and build UI surfaces without requiring every contributor to understand native toolkits.

There is a cost. Chromium and Node.js are not free, and Electron applications carry a multi-process runtime. Several apps running side by side can each bring their own framework and rendering work. But that does not mean every Electron app is inherently wasteful or doomed to consume gigabytes. Electron's own performance guide emphasizes profiling the actual application, deferring expensive work, avoiding blocked processes, and reducing unnecessary dependencies. It notes that performance depends substantially on how the app is built. (Electron performance guide)

For Discord, the comparison is also not “Rust versus JavaScript” in a clean lab. The current client already contains Rust components, according to its CTO. The proposed change is about moving more of the client logic into Rust and replacing Electron's UI runtime with GPUI. The results will depend on what is moved, what remains web-based, how features are implemented, and how much work the new framework takes over.

GPUI changes the UI ownership model

GPUI is an open-source Rust UI framework created for Zed. Its project describes it as a GPU-accelerated framework with a hybrid immediate and retained rendering model. Zed's team says it built GPUI because it wanted control over the editor's interface and rendering approach. (GPUI project README, Zed 1.0 engineering post)

That direction can offer a different performance envelope. Instead of treating the product primarily as a web interface running inside a packaged browser runtime, a team can build UI and application behavior around its chosen Rust framework and native platform integrations. The potential benefits include tighter control of rendering, lower overhead for some workloads, and sharing business logic across desktop and mobile while retaining native mobile interfaces.

Those are possibilities, not automatic results. Discord's 290 MB figure comes from a single early-build screenshot. The number does not establish typical idle usage, peak usage, battery consumption, startup time across machines, memory while playing video, or stability under long sessions. Even the app state matters: the CTO said the screenshot build had two accounts open, but that still leaves many workload details unspecified. (Vishnevskiy's post on X)

There is also framework maturity to consider. GPUI's public README says the framework is in active development and pre-1.0, with breaking changes possible. Discord has said it maintains patches on top of GPUI and will consider upstreaming relevant changes. A large company can invest in a fork, employ framework specialists, and carry long-term maintenance costs that a small product team may not be able to absorb. (GPUI project README, Vishnevskiy's post on X)

That is the hidden comparison: Electron gives up some runtime efficiency in exchange for a mature web-based development model. GPUI can give the product team more control, but the team must take responsibility for a less mature and more specialized UI stack.

Electron vs GPUI, by decision axis

  • Team skills: Electron fits teams with strong web engineering skills. GPUI requires meaningful Rust capability and willingness to learn the framework's UI model.
  • Cross-platform consistency: Electron brings a consistent Chromium engine across supported desktop platforms. GPUI aims for a Rust-native interface, but platform behavior, accessibility, text rendering, and input details still need careful validation.
  • Runtime footprint: Electron includes Chromium and Node.js components. A native Rust UI may avoid much of that browser runtime overhead. Actual app memory depends on implementation and workload, so benchmark instead of assuming.
  • Development speed: Electron can reuse web components, libraries, and hiring pools. GPUI may deliver a better fit for a product with demanding interaction or rendering needs, but a rewrite adds migration and framework costs.
  • Embedded web experiences: Discord's CTO said some experiences such as video and Activities will still use a native webview. A Rust rewrite does not imply that every part of the product stops using web technology. (Vishnevskiy's post on X)
  • Long-term maintenance: Electron teams track Electron, Chromium, and Node.js updates. GPUI teams own more of the UI integration and may need to maintain patches. Neither route removes maintenance; it changes what the team maintains.
  • Security boundaries: Electron's process model and security controls need correct configuration. Its official guidance recommends context isolation and renderer sandboxing. A native UI can reduce reliance on a browser renderer, but Rust does not eliminate bugs in networking, parsing, permissions, dependencies, or application logic. (Electron security guide, Electron sandbox guide)

Where Tauri fits, and where it does not

Tauri is an important option for teams that want to keep an HTML and JavaScript interface while using Rust for application logic and native capabilities. Its architecture uses the operating system's webview rather than shipping the same bundled browser runtime approach as Electron. That can reduce installer size, but it means behavior can vary with the webview available on each operating system. (Tauri architecture)

So the real menu is not a simple Electron-versus-Rust binary:

  • Electron: bundled Chromium-based runtime with a web UI and Node.js main process.
  • Tauri: web UI in a system webview, with Rust backend and message passing.
  • GPUI: Rust UI framework with a more native, GPU-focused rendering approach.

Tauri may be a sensible middle ground when the team wants to reuse web UI skills and reduce runtime bundling. GPUI is a more substantial commitment to Rust as the interface layer. Discord's choice should not be misread as proof that Tauri failed. The company chose a different architecture for its own product and organizational needs.

What a fair benchmark should measure

A meaningful comparison should answer more than “how many megabytes does Task Manager show?” Before replacing a mature client, build the same test plan for old and new versions:

  1. Define matching workloads. Test cold start, warm start, idle, a large server, multiple accounts, voice, video, screen sharing, and a realistic long session.
  2. Use the same machine and operating system. Record hardware, OS version, display scaling, network conditions, and power mode.
  3. Measure the whole application. Include child processes, helper processes, GPU use, and webview components. Do not compare one process from one architecture with a process tree from another.
  4. Track more than memory. Record startup time, CPU, GPU, responsiveness during interaction, battery draw on laptops, crash rates, and update size.
  5. Repeat and report distributions. One run can be noisy. Publish medians and ranges across repeated runs rather than selecting the best screenshot.
  6. Check feature parity. Make sure both versions do the same work. A lightweight build that has not yet implemented every feature is not a like-for-like replacement.
  7. Test accessibility and reliability. Keyboard navigation, screen readers, localization, multi-monitor behavior, and recovery after sleep matter as much as a low idle number.
  8. Keep the measurements reproducible. Publish the test steps, version identifiers, and tooling so other teams can repeat the comparison.

This is the standard a framework debate needs. If a new build is faster and lighter while preserving the same feature set and reliability, that is strong evidence. A single screenshot is a promising hint, not the conclusion.

The practical verdict

Electron remains a rational choice for many desktop products. If the app's memory use is acceptable, the team ships quickly, and performance problems can be fixed through profiling and targeted optimization, a full rewrite may cost more than it returns. Electron's own guidance is to measure real bottlenecks, not optimize based on framework reputation alone. (Electron performance guide)

GPUI or another native Rust UI deserves a serious evaluation when the product has measured performance constraints, the team has Rust expertise, or the application needs a level of rendering control that its web-based architecture makes difficult. Discord has a distinctive scale, existing Rust experience, and an existing engineering investment in the language. Its decision is not a universal migration recipe.

The 290 MB screenshot is interesting because it demonstrates a real early build, not because it settles the debate. Watch for a public test, feature parity, repeated measurements, and the application's behavior under real voice, video, and multi-account use. Until then, treat the number as an early signal and keep Electron, Tauri, and GPUI in their proper architectural categories.

I write about software engineering, developer tools, and practical architecture. Subscribe if you want more source-checked comparisons and hands-on guides.

Have you shipped a desktop app with Electron, Tauri, or a native UI framework? What mattered most in your choice: team speed, runtime cost, or control over the interface?

Save the benchmark checklist for your next desktop architecture review.

Sources:

  • Discord CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy's November 4 post on X
  • Electron process model documentation
  • Electron performance documentation
  • Electron security documentation
  • Electron sandbox documentation
  • Tauri architecture documentation
  • GPUI project README
  • Zed: Zed is 1.0

title: Human in the Loop Is Not a Checkbox
description:
Why approval steps fail when they are added at the end instead of designed into the workflow

Every serious enterprise AI design eventually adds the same box to the diagram.

It usually sits just before execution, and it says: Human Approval.

It makes everyone feel better. Security is satisfied. Compliance is satisfied. The business is satisfied. The model can make mistakes, but a person will check before anything important happens.

Then the system goes live.

In the first week, reviewers read every recommendation carefully. In the second week, they skim. By the end of the month, they approve forty requests in ten minutes, because the model is right most of the time and the queue keeps growing.

The box is still on the diagram.

The control is gone.

This is a hypothetical example, but anyone who has worked with approval workflows in ERP, finance, or sales operations has seen the pattern long before AI arrived.

AI makes it more important, not less.

In earlier articles, I wrote that a recommendation is not an authorization, and that high-impact actions should require human approval. Both statements are still true. But they leave an important question open:

What makes a human approval actually work?

A Human Who Approves Everything Is Not a Control

We often treat human approval as a safety property of the system. If a person approves the action, the action is safe.

But approval is not a property. It is a behavior.

And human behavior adapts to the workload and the feedback it receives.

When the model is right most of the time, reviewers learn that approving is almost always correct. When the queue is long, they learn that reading carefully is expensive. When nobody ever checks the quality of their reviews, they learn that speed is what matters.

None of this is laziness. It is a rational response to the way the workflow was designed.

The result has a familiar name: automation bias. People tend to trust the output of an automated system, especially when it is usually correct and when disagreeing requires extra effort.

This creates an uncomfortable situation:

Model is usually right
  ↓
Reviewers approve faster
  ↓
Reviews become shallow
  ↓
Rare model errors pass through
  ↓
The errors that matter most are the ones nobody catches

The human is still in the loop.

But the loop no longer contains judgment.

What remains is a name in the audit record: someone who formally approved the action, but no longer had the time, context, or incentive to say no.

Decide Where the Human Belongs

The first design mistake is putting a human approval step in front of everything.

It feels safe. In practice, it spreads human attention so thin that the important decisions receive the same three seconds as the trivial ones.

Human attention is a limited resource. It should be spent where it changes the outcome.

Three questions help decide where that is:

  • How much damage can a wrong action cause? A wrong tag on a CRM note is not the same as a wrong credit limit.
  • Can the action be reversed? Updating a draft can be undone. Sending an email to a customer, posting an invoice, or deleting data often cannot.
  • How uncertain is the model, and how unusual is the case? A familiar request with complete data is different from an edge case the system has never seen.

Combining the first two gives a simple map:

Easy to reverse Hard to reverse
Low impact Automate. Log it and sample it later. Automate with strict validation and clear limits.
High impact Automate with notification and a fast undo path. Human approval, with real context and clear authority.

Uncertainty then moves individual cases between these zones. A low-impact action can still be routed to a person if the input is incomplete or the model's output fails a validation rule. A high-impact action with very predictable inputs may eventually need only sampling, once the system has earned that trust with data.

The goal is not to remove humans.

The goal is to make sure that when a person is asked to decide, the decision actually deserves a person.

Design the Review, Not the Button

Most approval screens are designed around a button.

The model produces a recommendation. The screen shows it. There is a green button and a red button.

That is not a review. It is a confirmation dialog.

A reviewer can only make a good decision if the screen gives them what they need to disagree. In practice, that usually means:

  • The proposed action, in business terms. Not "call update_credit_limit with payload X", but "increase Acme's credit limit from 50,000 to 80,000".
  • The evidence. Which records, documents, or messages the recommendation is based on, with links to the originals.
  • What is unusual. A larger amount than usual, a customer with overdue invoices, missing data, a rule that was close to its limit.
  • The consequence. What will happen if this is approved, and whether it can be undone.
  • The alternatives. Approve, reject, edit, or send back with a question. A binary choice pushes people toward the default.

The third item is the most important and the most often missing.

A reviewer looking at forty similar requests cannot find the one that matters by reading forty summaries. The system has to help them see it. Highlight the differences, not the similarities.

There is also a subtle design question: should the reviewer see the model's recommendation before forming their own view?

For routine decisions, showing it saves time. For high-impact decisions, it can anchor the reviewer. Some teams ask the reviewer to look at the key facts first and only then show the recommendation. It is slower, but it keeps the human judgment independent.

The principle is simple:

If the approval screen makes approving easier than thinking, people will approve without thinking.

Approval Is Authority, Not Just a UI Step

An approval step is not only a screen. It is a transfer of responsibility.

When someone approves an AI-recommended action, the organization is saying: this person had the authority to make this decision, and they made it.

That statement only holds if the system enforces it.

This means the approval has to be part of the application's authorization model, not a flag the model or the frontend can set:

  • The approver must have the authority. A sales representative should not approve a discount that requires a regional manager, just because the AI routed the request to the wrong queue.
  • The approval must match what is executed. If the action changes after approval, for example a different amount or a different customer, the approval no longer applies.
  • The approval must be fresh. An approval from last week may not be valid if the underlying data has changed since then.
  • The requester should not approve their own request. Separation of duties does not disappear because an AI is involved.

The audit record should capture the whole decision, not only the click:

Request received
  → Model recommendation (with model and prompt version)
  → Evidence shown to reviewer
  → Reviewer identity and authority
  → Decision: approved, rejected, or edited
  → Reason, if rejected or edited
  → Action executed, and its result

This is what makes it possible to answer the question that eventually comes from an auditor, a customer, or a manager:

Who decided this, based on what?

"The AI recommended it and someone clicked approve" is not a good answer.

Measure the Loop

If human review is a control, it should be measured like one.

Most teams measure the model. Very few measure the reviewers. But the combined system is what produces the outcome.

A few signals tell you whether the loop is still working:

  • Approval rate. If it is 99.8%, the reviewers are either looking at a perfect model or not really reviewing.
  • Time per decision. Two seconds for a high-impact approval is a warning sign.
  • Edit rate. How often reviewers change the recommendation instead of simply accepting or rejecting it. Edits are often the most valuable feedback the system gets.
  • Errors found later. Approved actions that were corrected, reversed, or complained about afterward.
  • Queue size and waiting time. A loop that delays every decision by two days will eventually be bypassed.

One useful technique is to occasionally insert known cases into the review queue: requests where the correct answer is already known, including some that should be rejected. It tells you whether reviewers catch real problems, not just whether they click.

And every rejection or edit should flow back into the evaluation set. A reviewer who says no is giving the system a lesson for free.

The strongest argument for removing the human

There is a fair objection to all of this.

Human review is slow and expensive. People are inconsistent. They get tired. In some workflows, a well-tested model with strong validation may make fewer mistakes than a hurried reviewer.

That can be true.

If the data shows that reviewers almost never change the outcome, keeping them in the loop may be costing time without adding safety. In that case, the honest answer is not to pretend the approval step is a control. It is to redesign it: automate the action, strengthen validation, add sampling, and keep a fast way to undo mistakes.

Removing a human from a step should be a decision based on evidence, just like adding one.

What is not acceptable is the middle state: a human who is formally responsible but practically absent.

A Practical Checklist

Before adding a human approval step to an AI workflow, it is worth asking:

  • Which actions actually need a human, based on impact and reversibility?
  • Which cases are routed to a person because they are unusual or uncertain?
  • Does the reviewer see the proposed action in business terms, not as a tool call?
  • Does the screen show the evidence and highlight what is unusual?
  • Can the reviewer edit, reject, or ask a question, not just approve?
  • Is the approver's authority enforced by the application, not by the routing?
  • Is the approval tied to the exact action that will be executed?
  • Does the audit record show who decided, based on what, with which model version?
  • Do we measure approval rates, decision times, edits, and errors found later?
  • Do rejections and edits flow back into the evaluation set?

If the answer to most of these is no, the approval step is probably a checkbox.

And a checkbox is not a control.

Conclusion

Adding a human to an AI workflow is easy. It takes one box on a diagram and one button on a screen.

Keeping that human meaningfully involved is much harder.

It requires deciding where human judgment actually changes the outcome. It requires review screens that make disagreement possible. It requires authorization rules that the application enforces, audit records that explain the decision, and metrics that show whether the loop still works.

This is not a new problem. Enterprise software has always had approvals that nobody really reads. AI simply increases the number of decisions and makes the recommendations more convincing.

The goal is not to put a human in front of every AI action.

The goal is to make sure that when a human decides, it is a real decision.

A human in the loop should be a source of judgment, not a signature on the model's work.

title: How to scrape Workday job postings (and the 2,000-job trap)
description:
Thousands of large employers (Nvidia, Salesforce, Adobe and much of the Fortune 500) publish their jobs on Workday. Unlike Greenhouse or Lever, Workday has no documented public API and no global directory, so most job scrapers skip it. But every Workday careers site loads its jobs from a small JSON endpoint that anyone can call. Here is how it works, the two traps that silently break most scripts, and a ready-made option if you don't want to maintain it.

1. Find the careers site

A Workday careers URL looks like this:

https://nvidia.wd5.myworkdayjobs.com/NVIDIAExternalCareerSite

Three parts matter: the tenant (nvidia), the data center (wd5) and the site name (NVIDIAExternalCareerSite). There is no way to list all tenants, so you need each company's careers URL. Google site:myworkdayjobs.com <company> usually finds it.

2. Call the jobs endpoint

The careers page calls this endpoint with a POST:

import httpx

tenant, wd, site = "nvidia", "wd5", "NVIDIAExternalCareerSite"
url = f"https://{tenant}.{wd}.myworkdayjobs.com/wday/cxs/{tenant}/{site}/jobs"
r = httpx.post(url, json={"appliedFacets": {}, "limit": 20, "offset": 0, "searchText": ""})
data = r.json()
print(data\["total"], data\["jobPostings"]\[0]\["title"])

Each posting has title, locationsText, postedOn ("Posted 3 Days Ago") and externalPath. For the full description, exact posting date and every location, GET the detail endpoint:

detail = httpx.get(f"https://{tenant}.{wd}.myworkdayjobs.com/wday/cxs/{tenant}/{site}{path}").json()
info = detail\["jobPostingInfo"]  # jobDescription (HTML), startDate, location, timeType, jobReqId (+ additionalLocations when there are several)

3. The two traps

Trap 1: the 2,000-job wall. total never goes above 2,000, and it is only reported on the first page. Worse: past offset 2,000, Workday does not return an error. It quietly starts again from page 1. A naive "paginate until the page is empty" loop never ends and fills your dataset with duplicates. Keep a set of externalPath values and stop at the first page with nothing new. For employers with more than 2,000 openings, split the search with searchText or location facets.

Trap 2: relative dates. The list only says "Posted Today", "Posted Yesterday" or "Posted 30+ Days Ago". Use startDate from the detail endpoint when you need the real date.

Also: a 422 response means the tenant does not exist and a 404 means the site name is wrong. A 401 or 403 means that site does not allow anonymous access: respect it. Keep a few requests in parallel at most, and back off on 429.

4. Or skip the maintenance

If you need Workday next to Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workable, Recruitee and SmartRecruiters in one unified format, the ATS Jobs Scraper on Apify does all of the above: paste Workday careers URLs or just type company names for the other platforms. It handles the 2,000 wall without duplicates, returns exact dates and full descriptions, and costs $1 per 1,000 jobs. Companies not found and blocked sites are free.

{
  "companies": \["https://nvidia.wd5.myworkdayjobs.com/NVIDIAExternalCareerSite", "Stripe", "notion.so"],
  "titleKeywords": \["engineer"],
  "postedWithinDays": 7
}

Typical uses: hiring signals for sales teams, niche job boards and newsletters, and tracking competitors' hiring.

title: 9955 Icons, Every Single One Animated. PulsoIcon Hands-on
description:
The problem: buttons that feel dead

If you build with Lucide like I do, your icons look clean — and do absolutely nothing.

Hover a button, click a tab, and the icon just sits there. It's a small thing, but it's the kind of small thing that makes an interface feel static.

PulsoIcon is what happens when someone decides every icon deserves its own motion.

Not one generic hover effect stamped onto everything — a motion written for that specific icon.

The bell rings. The trash can opens its lid. The clock's hand goes around.

What it is

  • 9,955 animated icons, each with a hand-written motion.
  • Five platforms from one source: React, Vue, Svelte, Jetpack Compose, and SwiftUI.
  • About 3,700 custom-drawn icons, including approximately 2,770 line-art brand logos. The rest build on Lucide, Tabler, and Iconoir shapes, all credited in the LICENSE.
  • Automatic hover and focus animations: Icons respond when you hover over or focus on the nearest interactive button, link, or tab.
  • Accessibility built in: Animations respect the user's prefers-reduced-motion system setting.

You can browse and try all the icons live here:

Explore the PulsoIcon Playground

The part that sold me: it's a one-line switch

The React package is designed as a drop-in replacement for lucide-react.

Same component names. Same props.

Before:

import { Bell, Trash2 } from "lucide-react";

After:

import { Bell, Trash2 } from "pulsoicon-react";

That's the whole migration for most components.

Your existing size, color, and strokeWidth props keep working.

No need to manually write animation code for every icon.

How it's built (for the curious)

Every icon is defined in a single data file within a core package.

Each file contains the icon's shapes and optional motion settings for individual shapes:

  • 36 motion recipes, including draw, swing, lift, and more.
  • Delay, controlling when the animation begins.
  • Direction, determining how elements move.
  • Amplitude, controlling the intensity of the motion.
  • Pivot points, defining where a shape rotates or transforms on the 24×24 grid.

A generator takes this single source and produces packages for all five supported frameworks:

  • React
  • Vue
  • Svelte
  • Jetpack Compose
  • SwiftUI

Browser tests also run icons side by side in React, Vue, and Svelte to help verify that animations behave consistently across frameworks.

Open source on GitHub

CityPulso / PulsoIcon

Animated React icons — every Lucide icon plus extra icons and brand logos, each with its own hand-written motion. Drop-in replacement for lucide-react, built on Motion.

PulsoIcon

9955 animated icons. Every one has its own motion.
For React, Vue, Svelte, Jetpack Compose and SwiftUI. Icons come alive on hover; in React they replace lucide-react in one line

pulsoicon.com: browse all icons, try them live and copy the code · Playground · Documentation

Docs: React · Vue · Svelte · Android (Compose) · iOS / macOS (SwiftUI) · Core data

A bell rings. A calendar lifts its rings. A trash can opens its lid. A clock's hand goes round.

PulsoIcon gives every icon a motion written for that icon, not one effect stamped on all of them. At rest each icon is a clean 24×24 icon; it plays when someone hovers or focuses the button, link or tab it sits in.

Every one of the 9955 motions is written for this set. About 3,700 icons are drawn here, including the line-art brand logos; the rest build…


View on GitHub


The project is available under the ISC License.

Current limitations

There are a couple of things worth mentioning:

  • Web packages are the most polished. React, Vue, and Svelte have received the most refinement. The Jetpack Compose and SwiftUI ports are newer.
  • Animation quality can vary. With 9,955 individually tuned motions, some animations naturally feel better than others.

If you find an icon whose animation feels unnatural or doesn't match its meaning, opening an issue with the specific icon name would be genuinely helpful.

Verdict

If your UI already uses Lucide and feels more static than you'd like, PulsoIcon offers a straightforward way to introduce meaningful micro-interactions.

For many React components, all it takes is changing one import statement.

No complex animation setup. No manually defining hover effects for hundreds of icons.

Just icons that respond to the interface around them.

Try it yourself:

  • Playground: https://pulsoicon.com
  • GitHub: https://github.com/CityPulso/PulsoIcon

I'd love your feedback

Two things I'm especially interested in:

  1. Does the parent-hover animation model fit your workflow? Would you prefer icons to animate automatically when hovering over their parent button, or would you rather control animation triggers manually?

  2. Which icon animations feel wrong? If you notice an animation that seems unnatural, distracting, or inconsistent with the icon's meaning, I'd love to know which one.

And if you try the playground, let me know which icon's animation is your favorite.

Mine's the trash can. 🗑️

title: Real faces on Seedance: standard vs ultra-wide, in practice
description:
Answer: Seedance's standard route handles most real-face references — a clean photograph of a person usually conditions the shot without complaint. The ultra-wide route exists for the cases the standard review refuses: it is a broader moderation path, supports real-face references by design, and costs 1.5× to 2.1× the standard rate at the same resolution.

The published moderation page reads conservatively on this — it lists real-person depictions as prohibited — and that wording is why people assume the model cannot hold a face at all. In practice the standard route passes the majority of ordinary real-face jobs; the refusal is the model's review being stricter than the brief, not a blanket ban.

What the two routes actually do

Standard route Ultra-wide route
Real-face references usually accepted the intended use
Review path the model's own check broader moderation
Price, 2.0 Mini 480P 2 credits / s 3 credits / s
Price, 2.5 1080P 21 credits / s 45 credits / s
Subscription needed Starter or higher Starter or higher
Refund on refusal automatic automatic

So the working rule is: try standard first, move to ultra-wide when the review says no. Standard is cheaper and, for ordinary ports of a real photograph into a shot, it is where most jobs succeed.

The checklist that gets a real-face job through

  1. One clean reference per person. Frontal, evenly lit, no sunglasses, no heavy filter. Two photos of the same face average into a third person.
  2. Give the image a job. "The woman from @Image1" beats "use the reference". It tells the model which decision that photograph owns.
  3. State what must not change, then what should. Identity, wardrobe and framing first; camera, light and environment second.
  4. Write the beat, not the vibe. A shot that says what happens reads better than four adjectives: "she turns from the window, the coat catches the light, she looks at the door".
  5. Consent is yours to hold. Uploading a photograph of someone else is a representation that you have the right to use it. The acceptable-use policy applies on both routes, and a wider review path is not a licence.
  6. No public figures. Even on ultra-wide, recognisable third parties are a liability rather than a feature.

What it costs, concretely

Job Route Credits USD at settlement
5 s · 2.0 Mini · 480P standard 10 $0.10
5 s · 2.0 Mini · 480P fallback ultra-wide 15 $0.15
5 s · 2.0 Mini · 720P ultra-wide 30 $0.30
10 s · 2.5 · 720P standard 120 $1.20
10 s · 2.5 · 1080P ultra-wide 450 $4.50

A reference video adds an input-duration charge on top. Twice the resolution is not twice the price here — it is 2.5×.

The failure you will see, and what to do with it

If the standard review refuses the job, it is a guideline refusal rather than a silent downgrade:

Your content violated community guidelines.

No task is created at the prompt-screening stage, so nothing is charged. If a job passes screening and fails later, the credits are refunded automatically after reconciliation and the activity page shows a refund note.

The response is not to rewrite adjectives. Change one of three things: the route (ultra-wide), the reference (a synthetic face, or a different photograph of the same person), or the subject (a scene that does not hinge on a recognisable individual).

When ultra-wide is the wrong choice

  • The standard route already passes. You are paying 1.5–2.1× for a path you did not need.
  • Fully synthetic people. If the character is generated rather than photographed, standard is cheaper and the review is the one designed for it.
  • You are still testing composition. Draft framing with a synthetic face, then re-run the approved shot with the real reference.
  • The brief needs a brand. Neither route passes trademark-heavy prompts reliably; generic descriptions travel further.

FAQ

Does the standard route accept real faces? In most cases, yes. It is the cheapest route that does, and ultra-wide is the fallback for refusals.

Does ultra-wide guarantee a pass? No. It is a broader path with a review, not automatic approval.

Can I use real faces without a subscription? No. Both routes require an active Starter plan or higher.

What if the prompt passes but the frames fail? That is the visual layer: the job fails during or after generation and the credits are refunded after reconciliation.

The six worked real-face examples are on Callirra's wide-limit page, the review rules are published at the Seedance community guidelines, and both routes run from the video generator. If you have a reference set that passes on standard every time, the prompt and the photograph are the two things worth sharing.

title: Deploy your first Docker container for free: an Express app from empty folder to live URL
description:
TL;DR: A step-by-step walkthrough from an empty folder to a live HTTPS URL: a small Express app, a Dockerfile and a .dockerignore, a local test, a push to GitHub, the deploy itself, environment variables, an optional $1 managed database, and the checks that tell you it worked. No card and no DevOps background needed.

This hands-on guide walks you through deploying your first Docker container for free. We'll cover project setup, Dockerfile creation, environment configuration, and the actual deployment process with real code examples.

Prerequisites

  • A GitHub account
  • Basic familiarity with the command line
  • A simple application (we'll use a Node.js example)

Step 1: Prepare Your Application

Let's create a simple Express.js application. Create these files in your project:

{
  "name": "my-free-container",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "index.js",
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node index.js"
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "express": "^4.18.2"
  }
}

const express = require('express');
const app = express();
const PORT = process.env.PORT || 3000;

app.get('/', (req, res) => {
  res.json({
    status: 'running',
    message: 'Hello from my free container!',
    timestamp: new Date().toISOString()
  });
});

app.get('/health', (req, res) => {
  res.status(200).send('OK');
});

app.listen(PORT, () => {
  console.log(`Server running on port ${PORT}`);
});

Step 2: Create a Dockerfile

Add a Dockerfile to your project root:

# Use official Node.js LTS image
FROM node:22-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first (for better caching)
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app runs on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]

Dockerfile Best Practices

  • Use Alpine images — Smaller size means faster builds
  • Copy package.json first — Enables Docker layer caching
  • Use npm ci — Faster and more reliable than npm install
  • Don't run as root — Add a non-root user for production

Step 3: Add a .dockerignore File

Create .dockerignore to exclude unnecessary files:

node_modules
npm-debug.log
.git
.gitignore
.env
*.md
.DS_Store

Step 4: Test Locally (Optional)

Before deploying, verify your container works locally:

# Build the image
docker build -t my-app .

# Run the container
docker run -p 3000:3000 my-app

# Test it
curl http://localhost:3000

Step 5: Push to GitHub

Initialize a git repository and push your code:

git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit with Dockerfile"
git remote add origin https://github.com/yourusername/my-app.git
git push -u origin main

Step 6: Deploy to SnapDeploy

Now deploy your containerized application:

  1. Create account — Go to snapdeploy.dev and sign up (no credit card)
  2. New Container — Click "New Container" in the dashboard
  3. Connect GitHub — Authorize access and select your repository
  4. Configure — Set container name (becomes your-app.containers.snapdeploy.app)
  5. Deploy — Click Deploy and watch the build logs

Step 7: Configure Environment Variables

If your app needs environment variables, add them in the dashboard:

# Example environment variables
NODE_ENV=production
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/db
API_KEY=your-secret-key

Access them in your code with process.env.VARIABLE_NAME.

Step 7b (Optional): Add a Managed Database for $1

Your free container is stateless — data inside the container resets on every deploy. For persistent data, add a managed database. You have two paths:

  • Test first with the DB Sprint Pack — $1 for 12 hours. Pick any of six engines (PostgreSQL 16, MySQL 8, MariaDB 11, MongoDB 7, Redis 7, RabbitMQ 3) at full Mini-tier capacity. Persistent EFS storage, daily backups, full privileged access. Convert to monthly anytime during the 12-hour window or the 24-hour grace afterward — same EFS volume re-attaches, zero data migration.
  • Or go straight to a monthly subscription: Mini from $29/mo (SQL), $12/mo (Redis), $14/mo (RabbitMQ). Auto-injected connection strings.

Once provisioned, SnapDeploy injects the database connection string into your container as an environment variable (DATABASE_URL for SQL, REDIS_URL for Redis, etc.) — your app reads it the same way as the example above.

Read the DB Sprint Pack guide →

Step 8: Verify Deployment

Once deployed, test your live container:

# Test the root endpoint
curl https://your-app.containers.snapdeploy.app

# Expected response:
{
  "status": "running",
  "message": "Hello from my free container!",
  "timestamp": "2026-01-06T10:30:00.000Z"
}

Troubleshooting Common Issues

Ensure package-lock.json is committed. Run npm install locally first.

Check that your app listens on the PORT environment variable, not a hardcoded port.

Check the logs in the dashboard. Common cause: missing environment variables or database connection failures.

⚡ Need it online 24/7? Skip the cold starts.

Your free container sleeps when idle and wakes when a visitor opens it — perfect for side projects. But for a client demo, an interview review, or a weekend launch that has to stay up, drop a Sprint Pack on it: $1 / ₹99 for 24 hours of unlimited deploys plus Always-On. One-time, no subscription, no auto-renewal.

Next Steps

  • Configure environment variables for secrets and config
  • Add a custom domain to your container
  • Set up monitoring to track container health

You now have a containerized application running for free. Free deploy includes auto-sleep when idle and auto-wake on visits — your container is there when someone opens it. For 24/7 uptime, add Always-On starting at $12/month.

title: Why an Empty Test Result Is Not a Pass
description:
Quick answer: An empty test result means no evidence was collected, so it cannot be treated as a pass. When a check does not run, there is no output showing the code worked, and the correct verdict is inconclusive. A missing script is reported as unverified, and a lack of verified evidence stays open until a real run produces something you can trust.

The difference between silence and success

A pass is a positive claim. It says a command ran and produced evidence that the behavior holds. An empty result makes no such claim, because nothing executed, nothing was measured, and there is no raw output to inspect.

Situation What it means Verdict
A test runs and passes Positive evidence the covered path works Pass
A test runs and fails Evidence the behavior is broken Fail
Some checks pass, others cannot run Partial coverage Partial
No check runs, no output No evidence at all Inconclusive

The verdict is produced deterministically with no model involved. With no verified evidence, the result is inconclusive because an empty result is not a pass. Treating silence as a green check invents evidence that was never collected.

Why empty results happen

Empty or missing results are common in real projects, and they usually point to a process gap rather than clean code.

  • A project has no test script, so the check cannot start.
  • A command is configured but produces no runnable output in the current environment.
  • A dynamic run never reaches the branch under review, so that branch gets no evidence.
  • A service the check depends on is not running, leaving the run unconfirmed.

Run checks execute detected project commands explicitly. When a script is missing, the result is unverified rather than passed. If a dynamic suite never enters a branch, you have no evidence about that branch, which is not the same as evidence that it works.

The cost of treating empty as a pass

When an empty result is misread as success, defects hide behind a green-looking label. The team assumes a check exists when it does not, and the gap only surfaces later, often in production. This is especially risky with AI-generated code, where a confident summary can imply verification that never happened.

The safer reading is to keep the absence visible. Label the item as unverified or inconclusive, state which command was missing or did not run, and treat it as work to close rather than a result to trust. Each evidence item is supposed to carry a reproducible command and raw process output, so an item with neither is easy to spot.

How to close the gap

Move an inconclusive item toward a real verdict by giving it a runnable check.

  1. Add or fix the missing script so the command can actually execute.
  2. Run it and capture the raw output.
  3. Confirm the check covers the branch or behavior under review.
  4. Re-run the review so the deterministic verdict updates.

Partial verification stays partial until the remaining checks run, and only fully verified evidence passes. A model-only note never fills this gap, because an AI hypothesis is not a substitute for a measured result.

Powerduck does not promote an empty run to success; it keeps the missing evidence on screen so you can see exactly which command needs to be added.

Frequently asked questions

What if there are simply no tests in the project? Then the review has no dynamic evidence and reports the check as unverified rather than passed. The absence of tests is a gap to close, not a reason to call the code safe.

Can an AI hypothesis replace a missing test? No. A model-only claim is always a hypothesis and does not count as verified evidence. It can point you where to look, but it cannot confirm behavior.

Does inconclusive mean the code is broken? No. It means there is not enough evidence to say either way. The code may be fine, but you have not verified it.

The bottom line

A pass needs real evidence from a command that actually ran, and an empty result offers none. Keep missing scripts unverified, keep unexercised branches without evidence, and let the deterministic verdict read inconclusive rather than green. Treating silence as approval is how unverified code gets mistaken for tested code, and it hides the very gap the review is meant to expose. See the AI code review guide for more.

title: Findings from the $1M Vercel Sandbox challenge
description:
In August, we launched the $1M hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox, inviting security researchers to try and escape Vercel Sandbox. We also coordinated with cybersecurity experts Trail of Bits to review the source code and security architecture.

Here is a summary of the challenge:

  • 1,285 reports over two weeks

  • $242,000 in bounties paid out

  • One Linux kernel zeroday vulnerability uncovered

No reports showed anyone accessing customer data in Vercel Sandbox. The most severe finding was the defect in the upstream Linux kernel.

The kernel zero day

The program's most important report arrived on day three.

Paulos Yibelo of pwn.ai, a HackerOne researcher working from a standard sandbox with no special access, found a defect in the Linux kernel's networking stack. Paulos discovered that specially crafted packets sent from within the microVM enabled three different attacks:

  1. Leak host memory over the network

  2. Crash the host machine

  3. Execute code on the host

Leaking host memory

In the first attack, memory from the host, the machine your sandbox shares with other tenants, shows up in packets the guest sends over the internet. This can happen continuously, for as long as the guest keeps sending.

This attack was demonstrated against Vercel production sandboxes.

Crashing the host and executing code on the host

The researcher also found that by sending specific packets, they could compromise the host.

First, by sending two packets, the researcher crashed the host machine, shutting down every sandbox running on it. Second, using the same flaw, they were able to run commands with full administrator privileges on the host, breaking out of the sandbox’s isolation boundary.

The packet-related crash and code execution attacks were demonstrated on the researcher’s own KVM and Firecracker machines matching Vercel Sandbox configuration.

Responsibly disclosing the kernel vulnerability

Almost every major cloud provider isolates customer workloads on this same layer of the Linux kernel, so any defect is shared-infrastructure risk.

Immediately after being notified, we collaborated with the researcher to understand and mitigate the vulnerability, working with AWS and other industry partners to prioritize a fix, and ensuring that Vercel customers and other developers using the kernel were safe.

The researcher also contacted the kernel maintainers and worked with them to create candidate patches. Fixes are under private review and CVEs are pending, so we are not publishing additional details until the patches are public. We are disclosing the existence of the vulnerability because it was separately disclosed in public.

Our approach to pressure-testing Vercel Sandbox

The HackerOne challenge made bounties available to any researcher, but we also extended our program to include internal evaluations and an independent investigation.

Before launching the public bounty, we performed live security assessments internally with full source access and support from the engineers who created and maintain Vercel Sandbox. We also engaged Trail of Bits, bringing on two engineers to evaluate our security architecture.

Not every finding came from the outside. Marcos Hernanz, a Vercel intern, found a cross-tenant data leak in the Linux device-mapper storage layer. This vulnerability let any sandbox read recycled disk blocks from previously deleted sandboxes.

The white-box deep dive

Trail of Bits spent four engineer-weeks inside our source code, with full access to the repositories and two enterprise test teams. They delivered 20 findings, and each was tested, confirmed, and referenced to the exact code.

They also performed an architectural review and concluded that our virtualization boundary is sound. Each sandbox runs on its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and the device model is deliberately tiny. No guest shares a running kernel with the host, or with another tenant.

On top of that foundation, they gave us three structural recommendations, which we implemented:

  • Find and eliminate all trust in the guest. Our control plane accepted values returned by software running inside the microVM, and every one of those values is tenant input. Anything that crosses the boundary should be derived server-side or signed with a key the guest cannot reach.

  • One policy, one decider. Egress enforcement was split across subsystems that each parsed the same network policy independently, and they did not always agree. We now use one canonicalization routine per data type, one component per decision, and revalidate connections when policy changes.

  • Assume the next zero day. Keep host and guest kernels up to date, reduce the kernel attack surface via build and runtime configs, disable nested virtualization, and use Firecracker’s jailer to run each microVM process with restricted permissions and isolate it from the rest of the host.

Vercel Sandbox findings

We received 1,285 reports in two weeks. This volume is only possible because researchers now hunt at AI speed.

Here is a breakdown of reports by category:

  • 877 duplicates

  • 319 not applicable

  • 57 valid

  • 32 informative

In our report triage we have validated:

  • 1 Critical finding

  • 5 High findings

  • 9 Medium findings

  • 42 Low findings

  • 32 Informative findings

We have paid out $242,000 in bug bounties.

The medium, Low, and Informative findings are small policy-boundary gaps, like a firewall rule that behaved differently than documented and a field that trusted the guest more than it should.

The most severe finding was the Linux kernel zero day defect, and no reports showed anyone reading a customer’s files, secrets, or application data.

We were most impressed with the heterogeneity of the reports. It was clear that researchers used different setups and have different obsessions. Some clearly know Linux namespaces and steered their agents straight at the kernel boundary. Others went after the network policies, and many went after areas we didn’t think to put on the menu.

That variety is what you're funding with a public challenge. Here's one of the more interesting findings it produced.

Cross-tenant disk snapshot restore (with limits)

Filed on day one of the challenge, this report is our favorite example of why we run a public bug bounty, even after internal assessments and a white-box engagement.

When you snapshot a sandbox, the control plane has to record where the snapshot data landed: {storage_url, size, checksum}. The flaw the researcher found was subtle: that answer came from software running inside the guest, and services running on the host trusted it. That is a trust-boundary violation. The guest is where our customers (and hackers) run untrusted code, so the host can never take its word as authoritative.

The researcher combined a known, documented container-escape primitive with this trust flaw. They intercepted the snapshot response inside their own sandbox and rewrote it, swapping the storage objects of two snapshots belonging to two separate accounts they owned. That meant restoring "your" snapshot materialized the other account's entire filesystem.

The researcher demonstrated that each account could read and modify the other’s files, verified the results using hashes, and preserved the test resources so we could independently reproduce the findings.

The limits of this attack matter. Aiming the swap at a specific victim required knowing that victim's internal snapshot storage key, a random 96-bit identifier the platform generates per snapshot and never exposes through the API. The only place that key appears is inside the victim's own sandbox. The researcher owned both accounts, which is what made the proof possible; there was no demonstrated path for a stranger to target another tenant. We still treated it as a priority fix, because a boundary that depends on a secret staying secret is not a boundary.

Trail of Bits independently flagged the same root cause in their assessment, which told us the finding was real, important, and discoverable from two completely different angles.

The fix shipped within a week, and the control plane now binds every snapshot object to the project that created it and rejects anything else. Snapshot creation moved out of the guest-reachable environment into a host-side service, and storage paths are project-scoped with strictly validated URLs.

Thank you to the research community

We would like to thank every researcher who filed a report, whether their finding was a zero day or a duplicate. Every technique discovered in the challenge informs how we protect the workloads running on Vercel Sandbox.

Thank you also to Trail of Bits for your comprehensive internal investigation and guidance.

Read the original challenge announcement and learn more about Vercel Sandbox in the documentation.

title: Construimos REMEMBER, una app de escritorio local-first para estudiar (y esto aprendimos)
description:
Estudiar con cinco apps abiertas no funciona. Las notas en una, las tareas en otra, las fechas en el calendario del celular y las flashcards en una cuarta. Al final, lo que se pierde no es información: es el tiempo buscando dónde quedó cada cosa.

Por eso construimos REMEMBER: una app de escritorio para estudiar y organizarte, todo en un solo lugar. Notas en Markdown, tareas y calendario, flashcards con repetición espaciada SM-2 y Google Classroom. Local-first: tus datos quedan en tu equipo. Está en beta gratuita v0.1.3 para Windows y Linux, y la pueden descargar en isremember.com.

Somos dos estudiantes de Ingeniería de Sistemas y esto es lo que aprendimos construyéndola.

1. Local-first no es un eslogan, es una decisión de arquitectura

REMEMBER corre sobre Tauri v2 + Rust + SQLite. La base de datos local es la única fuente de verdad: WAL activado, claves foráneas, y búsqueda con FTS5 (índice invertido con BM25), así que buscar entre notas y tarjetas responde en milisegundos sin salir del equipo.

Elegir escritorio antes que web nos obligó a pensar en serio en el arranque en frío, el consumo en reposo y el tamaño del binario. Delegar el trabajo pesado al binario de Rust — el scheduler, las notificaciones y las consultas SQL — fue lo que mantuvo la app ligera.

2. SM-2 de verdad, no "repasa cuando quieras"

Las flashcards usan repetición espaciada SM-2, con tres calificaciones: Difícil, Bien y Fácil. El factor de facilidad (EF) empieza en 2.5, con piso en 1.30, y los intervalos reales son: si te sale Bien, vuelve en 1 día y luego en 6; si te sale Fácil, en 2 y luego en 7; si te sale Difícil, vuelve a 1 día.

Documentamos el algoritmo en el repositorio (docs/explicacion/algoritmo-sm2.md) porque descubrimos algo incómodo: es fácil decir "usamos SM-2" y que cada implementación haga una variante distinta sin decirlo. La nuestra está escrita, con sus intervalos y sus límites.

Una tarjeta se considera dominada solo con 3 o más repasos, un intervalo de 21 días o más y un EF de 2.5 o más. Nada de contadores inventados.

3. Google Classroom, pero solo en lectura

La integración con Google Classroom trae tus entregas como tareas con fecha y alerta. Pero fue una decisión consciente: solo lectura. Los cursos activos se mapean como materias y las actividades con fecha de entrega como tareas. No escribimos nada en Classroom.

Y hay un límite que preferimos declarar antes de que alguien lo descubra solo: la importación cubre los últimos 30 días. Lo que ya venció entra en Pendientes marcado como Vencida / Tarde: no se borra ni se da por hecho. Antes, un bug marcaba las vencidas como completadas. Lo corregimos y lo dejamos por escrito.

4. La nube existe, pero es opcional y manual

Aquí va el matiz que más nos costó explicar: REMEMBER sí tiene sincronización en la nube, pero no es automática ni obligatoria.

Funciona así: si inicias sesión, puedes activar el modo nube. Entonces un motor de sincronización en Rust (con outbox, RPCs en Supabase y resolución de conflictos Last-Write-Wins) sincroniza notas, tareas, proyectos y flashcards con PostgreSQL en Supabase, con cada cuenta viendo solo sus filas.

Pero quitamos el ciclo automático de cada 30 segundos. Ahora la sincronización es manual — un botón Sync cuando hay cambios pendientes — más un disparo al iniciar sesión. Por defecto, todo queda local. Si no sincronizas, no pierdes nada.

5. Lo que salió mal (y qué hicimos)

  • El token de Google vivía en texto plano. En la primera versión, el refresh token de Google se guardaba en localStorage y en Supabase sin protección. Una auditoría lo marcó como crítico y lo corregimos: el token de acceso vive solo en memoria y se renueva con una edge function. Todavía no hay keyring del sistema operativo; es una deuda conocida, no un secreto.
  • El audio de Pomodoro se fue. Los archivos de sonido y mezcla del Pomodoro eran código muerto que no aportaba nada. Los eliminamos y dejamos solo la alerta de fin de sesión. Menos código, menos superficie de error.
  • La landing prometía más de lo que había. La primera versión del sitio mencionaba cosas que la app no tenía. La corregimos para que solo diga lo verificado: beta v0.1.3, Windows y Linux, y macOS en preparación.

Qué sigue

  • macOS, que está en preparación.
  • Pulir la sincronización y probarla entre dispositivos con usuarios reales.
  • Seguir con el plan de contenido: un post de función y uno de consejo por semana.

Pruébala y dinos qué está mal

REMEMBER está en beta gratuita para Windows y Linux en isremember.com. Nos sirve mucho el feedback honesto: qué les funciona, qué les falta, qué les sobra. Si la prueban, cuéntennos en los comentarios.

Nota: este artículo describe la beta v0.1.3. La app es de escritorio para Windows y Linux; macOS está en preparación. No hay app móvil.
