title: Spring Boot: migrations at startup, health checks and metrics
description:
Migrations are written in development, but they have to run wherever the application runs: on a colleague's laptop, in CI, in staging, in production. The simplest way to get there is to let the application apply them itself, each time it starts, before anything else touches the database.

This article adds the Migrax starter to a Spring Boot application, follows what happens at startup, starts two instances at once, and looks at what Actuator shows: a health check and Prometheus metrics. At the end, the pipeline runs the migrations instead of the application.

Tested with: Migrax 0.17.1, Spring Boot 3.5.7, Hibernate 6.6.33, Micrometer 1.15.5, PostgreSQL 17. Every output below was copied from a real run; log lines are shortened to the message.

The setup

A shop with two entities, Customer and PurchaseOrder. Besides the usual web and JPA starters, the application has Actuator, the Prometheus registry and the Migrax starter:

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
  <artifactId>micrometer-registry-prometheus</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.migrax</groupId>
  <artifactId>migrax-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
  <version>0.17.1</version>
</dependency>

application.properties has the database, Hibernate set to only check the schema, and the two Actuator endpoints used below:

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
spring.datasource.username=shop
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate

management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,prometheus
management.endpoint.health.show-details=always

The migrations come from the entities. migrax init sets up the project (it reads the database settings from application.properties), and generate writes the first migration:

$ migrax generate
No snapshot yet: using the current database schema as the baseline.
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0001_initial.sql:
  - create table customers
  - create table purchase_orders
  - add foreign key fk_purchase_orders_cu_1ba47d9c on purchase_orders
Rollback script written to src/main/resources/db/migration/rollback.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.

The file sits in src/main/resources/db/migration, so it is packaged into the jar. That is where the starter looks.

What happens at startup

Start the application on the empty database:

HikariPool-1 - Start completed.
Migrax: Applying migration '0001_initial.sql'...
Migrax: Successfully applied migration '0001_initial.sql'.
Migrax: applied 1 migration(s)
Tomcat started on port 8080 (http) with context path '/'
Started ShopApplication in 9.05 seconds (process running for 10.302)

The order matters. The starter runs as soon as the connection pool is there and before JPA starts, so when Hibernate validates the schema, the tables already exist. With ddl-auto=validate, a database that doesn't match the entities stops the start, instead of failing on the first request.

Start it again and there is nothing to do:

Migrax: schema is up to date
Started ShopApplication in 8.571 seconds (process running for 9.58)

The application never needs the migrax command. It reads the migration files from the jar and records each one in the history table in the database, with a checksum.

Several instances starting together

A new field on Customer:

@Column(nullable = false, length = 2)
@ColumnDefault("'GB'")
private String country = "GB";

migrax generate writes 0002_add_customers_country.sql:

ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN country varchar(2) DEFAULT 'GB' NOT NULL;

In production, the new version rarely starts alone: two or more instances start at the same moment. Only one of them may apply the migration. Migrax takes a lock in the database first (on PostgreSQL an advisory lock), and by default an instance that doesn't get it stops at once. Here are the two instances, started together:

--- instance 1
Migrax: Applying migration '0002_add_customers_country.sql'...
Migrax: Successfully applied migration '0002_add_customers_country.sql'.
Migrax: applied 1 migration(s)
Started ShopApplication in 10.515 seconds (process running for 11.809)

--- instance 2
Caused by: org.migrax.dialect.MigrationLockHeldException: Another Migrax process is applying migrations.

Nothing is broken: the migration ran once. But the second instance failed and has to be restarted, and an orchestrator counts that as a crash. Tell the instances to wait for each other instead:

migrax.lock-timeout=2m

To make the wait visible, the next run has more to do. The table now has two million customers, and an index on full_name is added to the entity (@Table(indexes = @Index(columnList = "fullName"))). generate writes it as 0003_index_customers.sql, and warns about it:

src/main/resources/db/migration/0003_index_customers.sql, statement 1: warning MX001
  CREATE INDEX idx_customers_full_name ON customers (full_name)
  Building this index blocks writes to customers until it finishes.
  Fix: Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in its own migration that starts with '-- migrax:no-transaction' ('migrax generate --safe' does this).

Worth knowing on a busy table. Here it is fine. Both instances start again, with 0002 and 0003 pending (0002 was rolled back to run again):

--- instance 1
Migrax: Applying migration '0002_add_customers_country.sql'...
Migrax: Successfully applied migration '0002_add_customers_country.sql'.
Migrax: Applying migration '0003_index_customers.sql'...
Migrax: Successfully applied migration '0003_index_customers.sql'.
Migrax: applied 2 migration(s)
Started ShopApplication in 17.185 seconds (process running for 18.461)

--- instance 2
Migrax: Another Migrax process holds the migration lock; waiting up to 2m...
Migrax: schema is up to date
Started ShopApplication in 18.851 seconds (process running for 20.138)

The second instance waited until the first had built the index, found nothing left to do, and started. Set the timeout longer than your slowest migration takes; when it runs out, the instance stops as before.

The health check

With Actuator in the application, the starter adds a migrax health component:

$ curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/health/migrax
{"status":"UP","details":{"applied":3,"pending":0,"problems":0}}

problems counts migrations that failed, were edited after they were applied, or are in the history but no longer in the jar. Any of those, or a pending migration, makes the component DOWN. Turn it off with management.health.migrax.enabled=false.

An edited migration is the one people run into. Someone changes varchar(20) to varchar(30) in a migration that production has already applied, and the next start stops:

Caused by: org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'migraxMigrator' defined in class path resource [org/migrax/spring/MigraxAutoConfiguration.class]: Checksum changed for applied migration 0004_add_purchase_orders_status.sql

The database already has the old version of that migration, and it never gets the new one. Leave applied migrations alone; a change goes into a new migration.

Metrics

The application has a Micrometer registry (here Prometheus), so Migrax records its migrations there without any setting. After the run above, the first instance shows:

$ curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/prometheus | grep ^migrax
migrax_lock_wait_seconds_max{database="default"} 0.044737607
migrax_migration_seconds_max{database="default",migration="0002_add_customers_country.sql",outcome="success"} 0.005012614
migrax_migration_seconds_max{database="default",migration="0003_index_customers.sql",outcome="success"} 6.10576425
migrax_migrations_applied_total{database="default"} 2.0
migrax_migrations_pending{database="default"} 0.0
migrax_run_seconds_max{database="default",outcome="success"} 6.212559502

(Only the _max lines of each timer are shown; _count and _sum are there too.) The second instance, the one that waited:

migrax_lock_wait_seconds_max{database="default"} 7.803599713
migrax_run_seconds_max{database="default",outcome="success"} 7.843474718

That answers the questions that come up after a slow deployment: which migration took the time (the index, 6.1 seconds), and how long the other instances waited for it (7.8 seconds). For an alert, the counter of failed migrations is the one to watch:

- alert: MigraxMigrationFailed
  expr: increase(migrax_migrations_failed_total[15m]) > 0

With an OpenTelemetry bean, each run and each migration also becomes a span in the trace of the startup. migrax.metrics.enabled=false and migrax.tracing.enabled=false turn them off.

When a pipeline migrates

Some teams don't let the application change the schema. A deployment pipeline or a DBA runs the migrations, and the application only reads. One setting:

migrax.migrate-at-startup=false

The order then becomes the pipeline's job. A new status column on PurchaseOrder, deployed before the pipeline has migrated, doesn't get far:

Migrax: not migrating at startup (migrax.migrate-at-startup=false); 1 migration(s) pending
Caused by: org.hibernate.tool.schema.spi.SchemaManagementException: Schema-validation: missing column [status] in table [purchase_orders]

That is ddl-auto=validate doing its job. So: run migrax migrate (or the Maven goal migrax:migrate) as a step before the new version starts:

$ migrax migrate
Applying migration '0004_add_purchase_orders_status.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0004_add_purchase_orders_status.sql'.
Applied 1 migration(s); 4 total in src/main/resources/db/migration.

Not every pending migration stops the start. An index isn't checked by Hibernate's validation, so a release with a forgotten index migration (0005) starts fine, and is slow. That is where the health check and the pending gauge come in, because they keep working when the application doesn't migrate:

$ curl -s -w ' HTTP %{http_code}\n' localhost:8080/actuator/health/migrax
{"status":"DOWN","details":{"applied":4,"pending":1,"problems":0}} HTTP 503

$ curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/prometheus | grep ^migrax
migrax_migrations_pending{database="default"} 1.0

An alert on the gauge catches a pipeline step that was skipped:

- alert: MigraxMigrationsPending
  expr: migrax_migrations_pending > 0
  for: 30m

To keep traffic away from such an instance on Kubernetes, add the component to the readiness group:

management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true
management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include=readinessState,migrax

Once the pipeline has run migrax migrate, the application notices on its own. It asks the database at most every 10 seconds, so no restart is needed:

$ curl -s -w ' HTTP %{http_code}\n' localhost:8080/actuator/health/migrax
{"status":"UP","details":{"applied":5,"pending":0,"problems":0}} HTTP 200

Summary

  • Add migrax-spring-boot-starter, keep the migrations in src/main/resources/db/migration, and the application applies them each time it starts, before JPA, so ddl-auto=validate checks the migrated schema.
  • Several instances: set migrax.lock-timeout (for example 2m). One instance migrates, the others wait and then start.
  • With Actuator, the migrax health component is DOWN for a pending, failed, edited or missing migration. With Micrometer, metrics show how long each migration took and how long the instances waited.
  • When a pipeline migrates, set migrax.migrate-at-startup=false, run migrax migrate before the new version starts, and alert on migrax_migrations_pending.

More in the docs: Spring Boot, Metrics and tracing and Containers and Kubernetes.

Originally published at migrax.org.

title: Bare-Metal Kubernetes: Talos, MetalLB BGP & Cilium L2 Architecture
description:
Originally published on the HostingPodium Enterprise Engineering Blog.

Free SRE & Developer Diagnostics: Test your stack live with our DMARC Record Checker, Generator & SPF/DKIM Validator, Free Website Speed & Core Web Vitals Checker, or explore all 9 Free Webmaster & Cloud Engineering Tools.

Deploy an enterprise-grade bare-metal Kubernetes cluster leveraging immutable Talos Linux, MetalLB BGP routing, Cilium eBPF networking, and local NVMe storage.

Architectural Foundations for Bare-Metal Kubernetes Infrastructure

Deploying production-grade Kubernetes on bare-metal infrastructure requires eliminating traditional OS-level maintenance overhead while maximizing deterministic state management. In enterprise edge and hyper-converged core deployments, classical distributions running on general-purpose Linux variants introduce configuration drift, package manager vulnerabilities, and mutable kernel modules that undermine cluster stability. This engineering guide details the design, provisioning, and operational lifecycle of a production Kubernetes cluster utilizing Talos Linux as an immutable operating system, MetalLB operating in Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) mode with Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing, Cilium for high-performance eBPF-based networking with L2 announcements, and local persistent storage backed by NVMe arrays.

Building an immutable infrastructure pipeline mandates the separation of the control plane from runtime mutable states. Talos Linux completely removes the shell, SSH daemon, and package manager from the node image, replacing operational access with a cryptographically authenticated gRPC API. Node provisioning leverages declarative machine configurations serialized as YAML documents, translated into kernel boot parameters, and applied via ISO, PXE, or disk image injection. By shifting system configuration to an immutable API-driven model, infrastructure drift is structurally impossible; modifying a sysctl kernel parameter or updating a certificate requires a rolling immutable machine configuration replacement.

Immutable Infrastructure with Talos Linux

Talos Linux transforms node management by treating the operating system as a single static artifact. The root filesystem is mounted read-only, and state is strictly isolated to persistent partitions (STATE and EPHEMERAL). Configuration management is driven entirely through the talosctl CLI interacting with port 50000 over mutual TLS (mTLS). This eliminates the attack surface commonly exposed by SSH keys, unauthorized PAM modules, and legacy cron jobs.

To configure a control plane node, the machine configuration must define essential kernel arguments, disk layouts, and network interfaces. Below is an excerpt of a production-grade Talos machine configuration tailored for high-performance bare-metal servers:


bash
version: v1.5.0
debug: false
machine:
 type: controlplane
 token: "abc123.xyz789..."
 certSANs:
 - "k8s-api.hostingpodium.internal"
 - "10.100.0.10"
 kubelet:
 extraArgs:
 allowed-unsafe-sysctls: "net.core.somaxconn,net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range"
 eviction-hard: "memory.available

---

title: It passed the scan. It did not boot.
description:
Originally published at tothenoc.substack.com

Why every ToTheNOC image is launched on a real instance before it is listed.

We build hardened Linux images. AlmaLinux, Rocky Linux and Debian, x86 and ARM.

In October one of our AlmaLinux 9 builds passed the hardening scan. Clean. Then we launched it on a real instance and it never came up. No SSH. The serial console said "Read-only file system", and after that cloud-init, auditd and sshd all failed.

The cause was one line. The hardening profile wants /tmp on its own mount, so the recipe added a tmpfs line in fstab. On the AlmaLinux base image, tmp.mount is masked. systemd puts that masked unit in the boot transaction, the branch falls out, the root filesystem is never remounted read-write. Everything that needs to write to disk dies, sshd included.

Nothing in the build told us. The scan checks files. It does not boot the system.

A few weeks later, same story on ARM. The image was "running" on x86 and "degraded" on Graviton, because a service waited for a hardware random source that the ARM instance does not have.

So we changed the rule. An image is ready only after:

  • it boots on a real instance,
  • SSH answers,
  • systemctl is-system-running says "running", not "degraded",
  • the same OpenSCAP / ComplianceAsCode profile runs again on the live system.

For AlmaLinux 9 today that is 265 of 265 automated checks of our Level 1 server hardening profile (OpenSCAP / ComplianceAsCode), measured on a running instance. The raw results, the tailoring file and the checksums are public for every release.

This is what "verified on boot" means for us. Not a badge. A boot.

Short video (88 s): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IET97Z8aREo

The images are on AWS Marketplace, 17 regions: search "ToTheNOC".

How we build and verify every release: tothenoc.com/hardened-images.

-- Alex

title: Deriving a Data Model from OpenAPI
description:
Quick answer: Deriving a data model from OpenAPI means turning the schemas into relational entities, foreign keys, and many-to-many link tables, then generating DDL, indexes, deterministic seed data, and deployment scripts for MySQL, SQL Server, and Oracle. This closes the gap between the API contract and the database. When business logic cannot be inferred unambiguously, the result raises an open question rather than guessing.

Why the API and the database drift apart

The OpenAPI document describes the shapes the API sends and receives, while the database holds the tables and keys that persist them. The two are related but not identical, and a team that reads only the contract can miss the foreign keys, the link tables, and the indexes the storage needs.

The modeling layer reads the schemas and reconstructs the relational design so the contract and the database can be compared rather than maintained as separate guesses.

What the derivation produces

Output Role
Relational entities The tables behind the schemas
Foreign keys The relationships between tables
Link tables The many-to-many joins inferred from the shapes
DDL The table definitions for the target dialect
Indexes The access structures for the queries
Seed data Deterministic values for a fresh deployment
Deployment scripts Idempotent, forward-only change scripts

The dialects are the three supported databases, and the same source spec feeds each one rather than a separate hand-written design per engine.

Take an order schema that references a customer. The derivation resolves the customer entity, places a foreign key on the order table, and when the order also lists many products, it proposes the link table for the order-to-product relationship. The same source then renders the table and its keys in each dialect. A reviewer reads the proposed relationships against the business rules rather than reconstructing them, and anything the schemas do not pin down stays an open question rather than a forced column.

How the relationships are resolved

The derivation follows the structure rather than inventing it.

  1. Read the schemas and identify the entities.
  2. Resolve references and the foreign keys between them.
  3. Infer many-to-many link tables from the repeated relationships.
  4. Add indexes for the access paths the operations use.
  5. Mark anything ambiguous as an open question.

A many-to-many link table is a good example of inference. When two entities reference each other in a way that implies a join, the modeling layer proposes the link table rather than forcing the relationship into one side. The proposal stays reviewable, and it does not execute.

Where ambiguity is handled honestly

The tool does not guess when the business logic could be read more than one way. A relationship that could be a foreign key or a standalone value, or a cardinality that the schemas do not pin down, raises an open question rather than a confident table. That keeps the generated model honest and points the reviewer at the exact decision that needs a person.

This is the same boundary that keeps static signals from being written as guarantees. The derived model is a proposal grounded in the schemas, and it still needs reconciliation against the live database and a review before any change runs.

Powerduck keeps the data model as a supporting capability behind the core workflows, using it to connect the API contract to the storage rather than to become a general database tool.

Frequently asked questions

Does the model run the SQL it generates? No. SQL is generated for review and is never auto-executed, and the modeling package has no executing driver.

Which databases are supported? MySQL, SQL Server, and Oracle, with DDL, indexes, seed data, and deployment scripts generated from one spec.

What happens when a relationship is ambiguous? It raises an open question rather than a guessed table, so the decision stays with a reviewer.

The bottom line

Deriving a data model from OpenAPI reconstructs the relational entities, foreign keys, and link tables behind the contract, and generates the DDL, indexes, seed data, and deployment scripts for three databases. Ambiguous logic stays an open question rather than a guess, and the generated SQL is never executed by the tool. This closes the gap between the API and the storage while keeping the design reviewable, and it remains a supporting capability rather than the core. Read more in the API data model guide.

Security

AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Feature

You can now tune SQL queries using AI. Available starting with version 1.6.2 of the google_ml_integration extension, the ai.tune_sql function uses an LLM along with query execution plans, schemas, and runtime stats to recommend query optimizations. The function identifies performance bottlenecks and provides recommendations for query rewrites, indexes, statistics collection, Grand Unified Configuration (GUC) flags, and table analyze and vacuum operations. This feature is in Preview.

For more information, see Tune SQL queries using AI and Database advisor flags.

Apigee X

Announcement

On November 2, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee.

Note: Rollouts of this release began today and may take four or more business days to be completed across all Google Cloud zones. Your instances may not have the features and fixes available until the rollout is complete.

Feature

EKM health monitoring

You can now monitor EKM health and configure alerts for EKM-related issues using Cloud Logging. For more information, see EKM health monitoring.

App Engine flexible environment Python

Feature

Support for the Python 3.15 runtime is in Preview.

App Engine standard environment Python

Feature

Support for the Python 3.15 runtime is in Preview.

BigQuery

Feature

Lakehouse caching for cross-cloud data access is generally available (GA). Cross-cloud caching is disabled by default. You can opt in to caching on a Lakehouse federated catalog or a BigQuery cross-cloud connection to cache remote files in your Google Cloud region. This helps reduce cross-cloud egress costs and accelerate subsequent queries.

For more information, see About cross-cloud data access and Query remote data.

Feature

Lakehouse supports the following remote catalog providers for cross-cloud data access. This feature is generally available (GA).

  • Databricks Unity Catalog on Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud
  • AWS Glue Data Catalog on AWS
  • Snowflake Horizon Catalog on AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud
  • Workday Data Lake on AWS or Google Cloud

This feature lets you configure federated catalog endpoints to synchronize catalog metadata and query Apache Iceberg tables in remote catalogs directly from Google Cloud using BigQuery, Managed Service for Apache Spark, and Apache Spark without migrating data or building complex ETL pipelines. You can route background metadata refresh and queries over the public internet or privately over Cross-Cloud Interconnect, and protect cross-cloud data access with VPC Service Controls service perimeters. For Databricks Unity Catalog, you can also use user identity federation to propagate end-user identities on queries for permission enforcement and audit logging.

For more information, see About cross-cloud data access, Query remote data, and Use VPC Service Controls with federated catalog endpoints.

Feature

You can now monitor the performance, adoption, latency, and costs of your data agents and their conversations by using Google Cloud Observability in BigQuery. This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

You can use the AI.PARSE_DOCUMENT function to extract layout elements such as titles, headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, and images by using the Document AI layout parser to convert unstructured documents into structured JSON data.

This function is generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now use BigQuery change history and continuous queries for Apache Iceberg managed tables in Lakehouse.

You can use the APPENDS table-valued function (TVF) to track rows appended to Apache Iceberg managed tables over a specified time range, and use BigQuery continuous queries to read incoming data from and write output rows to Apache Iceberg managed tables.

This feature is generally available (GA).

For more information, see Work with change history and Introduction to continuous queries.

Feature

The SECURE_CONTEXT function is now available in Preview. SECURE_CONTEXT returns the value of a request-scoped secure context parameter provided at query runtime, allowing logical views to dynamically filter and evaluate data based on context variables such as user attributes, department IDs, or tenant identifiers.

Feature

The Data Engineering Agent now supports BigQuery AI, ML, and object functions and statements in generated Dataform SQLX pipelines and agent instruction files.

This feature is generally available (GA).

Cloud Asset Inventory

Feature

The following resource type is publicly available through the ExportAssets, ListAssets, BatchGetAssetsHistory, QueryAssets, Feed, SearchAllResources, and SearchAllIamPolicies APIs.

  • Cloud Scheduler
    • cloudscheduler.googleapis.com/Job

Cloud Load Balancing

Feature

Distributed tracing with Cloud Trace is available in Preview for Global external Application Load Balancers, Regional external Application Load Balancers, Regional internal Application Load Balancers, and Cross-region internal Application Load Balancers. Attach a telemetry policy to a load balancer's forwarding rule to generate trace spans that conform to W3C Trace Context and OpenTelemetry, and get end-to-end visibility into requests from clients through the load balancer to your backends. For more information, see Distributed tracing overview.

For mutual TLS (mTLS) on Application Load Balancers, frontend mTLS validation relaxations are generally available.

title: Vue Frontend File Upload Runbook: Direct Presigned URLs, Axios Progress, Node Control
description:
Use a short-lived upload capability, record an upload intent before issuing it, and make the browser report completion only after a separate finalize call succeeds. That is the operationally defensible way to let a Vue frontend send a file directly to private object storage while a Node backend retains authorization and application state.

The deciding constraint is not the progress bar. It is the boundary between bytes accepted by an object store and a file that the application is prepared to expose to a user. A browser can lose its final response, retry a request, or leave a tab halfway through an upload; a system that has no explicit state for those cases will eventually turn a harmless network interruption into an incorrect attachment record or an object nobody can account for.

Keep the data plane out of the API service. Keep the authority plane in it.

What should a Vue frontend, direct file upload, presigned URL, private object storage, and Node backend each own?

Treat a presigned URL as a narrow bearer capability, not as a login token. The Node backend authenticates the caller, decides whether that caller may create an object, allocates a server-controlled key, records an initiated upload, and returns a URL whose method, key, expiry, and required headers match that intent. The browser then sends the bytes directly to storage. It cannot choose another user's prefix merely by changing a form field.

The Vue component owns local interaction: selection, cancellation, display state, and the request lifecycle. Axios can update a progress value from its upload progress callback, but that value only represents bytes observed by the client transport. It is useful feedback, not proof of durability. Keep the UI in an uploading state until the browser has received a successful response from storage and the backend has accepted a finalization request. A short message such as “finishing upload” is more honest than a 100% indicator that has already implied availability.

This split changes capacity planning in a helpful way. Upload bytes do not consume API ingress, application memory, or long-lived Node request handlers, while authorization requests and finalization writes remain small control-plane operations with ordinary latency and availability objectives. Measure them separately: ticket latency, storage PUT completion, finalization latency, abandoned intents, and the age of every nonterminal upload state. A single “upload succeeded” counter hides the parts that page people later.

The control-plane contract should be idempotent. Have the client create one random upload token per user action and reuse it if it must request another capability; have the backend map that token and user identity to the same pending upload record. The object key stays server-generated. If a user retries after the URL expires, the backend can issue a fresh capability for the same intended object instead of silently creating another logical file.

Concern Browser Backend control plane Private object storage
Authorization Presents the user's session Authenticates and applies policy Accepts only the signed capability
Object identity Holds the upload token Allocates and persists the key Stores bytes at that key
Completion Shows transport and finalization states Verifies and records readiness Acknowledges the write

The failure signal is a false green progress bar

There are at least three completion events: the browser has handed bytes to its networking stack, the storage service has acknowledged the write, and the application has marked the object ready after checking the intended upload record. Collapsing them into one state is the common failure mode.

An Axios progress callback may have no computable total, and even a 100% value does not prove that the subsequent response and application finalization occurred. In Vue, represent this as a small state machine rather than a boolean: selected, authorizing, uploading, finalizing, ready, cancelled, and failed. The meter belongs only in uploading; finalizing has no percentage to invent.

Short state names help.

The browser also needs CORS permission for the direct storage request. The configured origin, upload method, and headers used by the signed request have to agree. Test this in a real browser before calling the endpoint done, because a browser-enforced CORS rejection can leave the API logs perfectly quiet. Do not loosen the rule to every origin and every header to get past a test; that trades a visible integration problem for an unnecessary write surface.

For private objects, access is a separate decision from upload. A successful PUT should not make the bucket generally readable. When an application later grants a download capability, use a response policy appropriate to the object and audience. Cache-Control: private prevents shared caches from storing a response, while no-store asks caches not to store it at all; the semantics and directives are defined in the HTTP specification and summarized by MDN. Pick deliberately, because cache behavior is part of the data-access policy, not a cosmetic header.

A safe Node control-plane shape

The following Go sketch represents the backend rules a Node implementation should preserve: authenticate before minting a capability, persist the intent before returning it, bind replay to an idempotency key, and transition to ready only through an explicit finalize operation. The actual signing mechanism depends on the storage protocol, so the interface keeps that provider-specific detail out of the application contract.

package uploads

import (
    "context"
    "time"
)

type Upload struct {
    ID        string
    UserID    string
    ObjectKey string
    State     string
}

type Store interface {
    Claim(ctx context.Context, userID, clientToken, contentType string, size int64) (Upload, error)
    MarkReady(ctx context.Context, userID, clientToken string) error
}

type Signer interface {
    PutURL(ctx context.Context, objectKey, contentType string, expiresAt time.Time) (string, error)
}

func IssueUpload(ctx context.Context, db Store, signer Signer, userID, clientToken, contentType string, size int64) (string, Upload, error) {
    // Claim returns the existing pending record for the same user and token.
    upload, err := db.Claim(ctx, userID, clientToken, contentType, size)
    if err != nil {
        return "", Upload{}, err
    }

    url, err := signer.PutURL(ctx, upload.ObjectKey, contentType, time.Now().Add(5*time.Minute))
    if err != nil {
        return "", Upload{}, err
    }
    return url, upload, nil
}

func FinalizeUpload(ctx context.Context, db Store, userID, clientToken string) error {
    // The implementation verifies the intended object before marking it ready.
    return db.MarkReady(ctx, userID, clientToken)
}

The details that deserve review are not framework details. Reject a missing or oversized file before signing, allow only content types the product is prepared to process, rate-limit capability issuance, and ensure finalization verifies the expected object identity and metadata. If malware scanning, content inspection, or transformation is mandatory before any byte reaches durable storage, direct browser upload may be the wrong architecture; route the content through a controlled processing path or quarantine it until the required checks complete.

There is a real trade-off here. Direct-to-storage upload is not suitable when files are tiny, upload volume is low, and the server must inspect every stream anyway. In that situation, proxying through the backend can be easier to operate because there is one request, one audit trail, and no reconciliation loop. Stick with the simpler path until API bandwidth, tail latency, or connection pressure gives you a measured reason to add the extra states.

How do you verify the path and roll it back?

Verification compares independent records, not two views of the same database. Regularly reconcile the set of ready upload rows, the set of object keys in private storage, and the set of objects referenced by the product. Make the reconciliation job produce counts for all three sets plus their differences, retain a bounded sample of keys for diagnosis, and tag the output with the storage namespace and application release so an operator can distinguish a policy error from a deployment change. An object with no completed record is an abandoned candidate subject to a retention rule; a ready record with no object is an availability defect that needs investigation before a user encounters it. Also track objects whose observed content type or size differs from the recorded intent, because a mismatch is evidence that the signing boundary or finalization check is too broad. Set an SLO for how long an upload may remain in finalizing, then alert on age and count rather than waiting for a support ticket; the useful alert identifies a growing backlog, while a one-off cancellation is expected behavior.

Exercise the browser flow with a throttled connection, a cancellation, an expired capability, a repeated authorization request using the same token, and a completed PUT followed by a failed or repeated finalization call. The expected outcome matters more than the HTTP client: repeated authorization resolves to the same pending upload, finalization is safe to repeat, and no object becomes visible merely because a percentage meter reached its end.

Rollback should remove the ability to issue new upload capabilities while leaving existing private objects under their normal read policy. A short expiration limits the time outstanding write URLs remain valid; document that interval in the runbook, observe its effect on long uploads, and choose it from the largest supported upload and expected network conditions rather than copying a number from a sample. Your mileage may vary with file size and user connectivity.

The design earns its complexity only when it improves a concrete operational limit. Otherwise, don't build a second workflow merely to make a diagram look modern.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs

title: Wie verkleinert man ein gescanntes PDF, indem man die Auflösung seiner Bilder in Python senkt?
description:
Ein PDF aus Handyfotos ist selten wegen des Texts groß. Es ist groß, weil jede Seite ein JPEG mit 3000 Pixeln ist, das auf ein Blatt Papier gezeichnet wird, das nur einen Bruchteil davon braucht. Zum Verkleinern muss man diese Bilder finden, ihre tatsächliche Pixeldichte bestimmen, sie auf einen sinnvollen Wert herunterrechnen und zurück in die Datei schreiben. Der PDF-Editor in der Desktop-App osFoundry macht das in zwei Klicks (All tools, Compress a PDF, Advanced optimization). Unten steht dieselbe Idee in rund 30 Zeilen Python mit PyMuPDF und Pillow, gemessen an einer Testdatei, dazu ein Vergleich mit dem, was die App aus derselben Eingabe gespeichert hat.

Die Testdatei ist ein Mietvertrag mit 6 Seiten, der für diesen Beitrag gebaut wurde: Jede Seite ist ein JPEG mit 3024×4032 Pixeln, mit Papierkorn und ungleichmäßiger Beleuchtung, platziert auf einer Seite von 612×816 pt. Die Datei hat 32,227,412 Bytes (30.7 MiB). Das Korn spielt eine Rolle: Rauschen macht ein JPEG groß, die absoluten Größen unten gelten also für diese Datei; ein saubererer Scan beginnt kleiner und schrumpft weniger.

Herausfinden, was den Platz belegt

Bevor man etwas ändert, addiert man die Datei nach Inhaltsart auf. Bei einem Scan genügt eine Zeile:

import os, pymupdf
doc = pymupdf.open("scan.pdf")
img = sum(len(doc.xref_stream_raw(i[0])) for p in doc for i in p.get_images(full=True))
print(img, "of", os.path.getsize("scan.pdf"))

32221241 of 32227412

Die Bilder machen 99.98% der Datei aus. Text, Seitenbaum und der gesamte übrige PDF-Verwaltungsaufwand zusammen sind 6,171 Bytes. Wäre die Zahl bei 20% herausgekommen, wäre das Herunterrechnen von Bildern das falsche Werkzeug gewesen, und keine Einstellung in irgendeinem Kompressor hätte viel gebracht. Die App hat diese Prüfung eingebaut (Audit space usage); ihre Tabelle für dieselbe Datei zeigt Images 32,225,071 Bytes (99.99%), Content Streams 714, Document Overhead 1,627. Sie zählt nicht genau wie die Einzeiler oben, deshalb weichen die beiden Zahlen um ein paar Kilobyte voneinander ab.

Ein Bild hat keine Auflösung, bis es gezeichnet wird

Ein JPEG in einem PDF ist nur ein Raster aus Pixeln. Seine Dichte in Pixeln pro Zoll bestimmt die Größe, in der die Seite es zeichnet. PyMuPDF liefert beide Hälften:

page = doc[0]
xref, w, h = page.get_images(full=True)[0][0], *page.get_images(full=True)[0][2:4]
rect = page.get_image_rects(xref)[0]          # where the page draws it, in points
ppi = w / (rect.width / 72)
print(w, h, round(rect.width / 72, 2), round(ppi))

3024 4032 8.5 356

Das Bild wird 8.5 Zoll breit gezeichnet, 3024 Pixel auf 8.5 Zoll ergeben also 356 ppi. Zum Lesen einer gedruckten Seite braucht man etwa 150, einem Bildschirm genügt weniger. Dasselbe Bild in halber Größe gezeichnet hätte 712 ppi. Deshalb muss man die ppi pro Bild und pro Platzierung berechnen und nicht aus einem Metadatenfeld lesen.

Was Auflösung und Qualität kosten

Um Zahlen auszuwählen, hier ein Durchlauf über die Bilder der ersten beiden Seiten: fünf Zieldichten mal vier JPEG-Qualitäten, mit der durchschnittlichen Größe eines Bilds und dem PSNR gegenüber einer Referenz. Die Referenz ist das Original, mit Lanczos auf 1275×1700 (150 ppi) verkleinert; jede Variante wird vor dem Vergleich auf dieses Raster skaliert, die Zeilen mit 100 und 72 ppi enthalten also die Unschärfe durch das erneute Vergrößern. Der PSNR ist ein grober Wert, und OCR habe ich hier nicht laufen lassen. Er soll nur zeigen, ab wo die Qualität schnell abfällt.

Ziel-ppi q90 q75 q60 q40
356 (Originalgröße) 3713 KiB / 44.0 dB 1392 KiB / 41.7 dB 941 KiB / 40.3 dB 590 KiB / 39.5 dB
225 985 KiB / 41.5 dB 491 KiB / 39.6 dB 333 KiB / 38.5 dB 244 KiB / 37.7 dB
150 431 KiB / 38.8 dB 225 KiB / 36.6 dB 167 KiB / 35.1 dB 135 KiB / 33.8 dB
100 210 KiB / 33.1 dB 119 KiB / 31.7 dB 94 KiB / 30.6 dB 76 KiB / 29.4 dB
72 118 KiB / 28.3 dB 72 KiB / 27.6 dB 57 KiB / 26.9 dB 45 KiB / 26.0 dB

Zwei Dinge fallen auf. Von 356 auf 150 ppi bei gleicher Qualität zu gehen, spart etwa 88% der Bytes (q75: von 1392 auf 225 KiB), während es allein durch Senken der JPEG-Qualität in voller Größe, von q90 auf q40, noch 590 KiB bleiben, mehr als das Doppelte der 225 KiB bei 150 ppi und q75. Und unter 150 fallen die Dezibel steil ab: 100 ppi bei q90 liegt unter 150 ppi bei q40. Für eine Seite mit gedrucktem Text ist 150 ppi bei mittlerer Qualität in diesen Daten der Knick der Kurve.

Das Skript

Die Regeln sind die, die die App in ihrem Dialog nennt: auf 150 ppi herunterrechnen, wenn ein Bild mit mehr als 225 ppi gezeichnet wird, JPEG in mittlerer Qualität, und ein Bild nur ersetzen, wenn das Ergebnis kleiner ist.

import io, os, sys, pymupdf
from PIL import Image

def shrink(src, dst, target=150, above=225, quality=60):
    doc = pymupdf.open(src)
    seen = set()
    for page in doc:
        for info in page.get_images(full=True):
            xref, w, h = info[0], info[2], info[3]
            if xref in seen:
                continue
            seen.add(xref)
            rect = page.get_image_rects(xref)[0]
            ppi = w / (rect.width / 72)
            if ppi <= above:
                continue
            raw = doc.xref_stream_raw(xref)
            im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(raw)).convert("RGB")
            im = im.resize((round(w * target / ppi), round(h * target / ppi)), Image.LANCZOS)
            out = io.BytesIO()
            im.save(out, "JPEG", quality=quality)
            if out.tell() >= len(raw):
                continue                      # not smaller: keep the original
            doc.update_stream(xref, out.getvalue(), compress=False)
            doc.xref_set_key(xref, "Width", str(im.width))
            doc.xref_set_key(xref, "Height", str(im.height))
            doc.xref_set_key(xref, "Filter", "/DCTDecode")
            doc.xref_set_key(xref, "ColorSpace", "/DeviceRGB")
    doc.save(dst, garbage=4, deflate=True)

shrink(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])
print(os.path.getsize(sys.argv[1]), "->", os.path.getsize(sys.argv[2]))

Auf der Testdatei, mit PyMuPDF und Pillow über uvx, dauerte es auf diesem Mac 2.8 Sekunden:

30.7 MiB -> 0.92 MiB (97% smaller), 6 images replaced

Eine Falle hat mich eine falsche erste Messung gekostet. Meine erste Version nutzte page.replace_image(xref, stream=...), was der naheliegende Aufruf zu sein schien, und die Ausgabe kam auf 1.83 MiB, doppelt so viel wie erwartet. Der Aufruf legte das neue Bild als neues Objekt an, und die alten Objekte blieben in der Datei, sie enthielt also beide Versionen jeder Seite: Ein Durchgang über die Streams der Datei zeigte 12 große, jeder neue mit einem gleich großen Zwilling. Schreibt man den Stream mit update_stream in das bestehende Objekt und korrigiert dessen Schlüssel Width, Height, Filter und ColorSpace, kommt man auf 0.92 MiB und sechs Streams von 107 bis 172 KB.

Wie nah die App herankommt

Die App hat dieselbe Eingabe als Kopie gespeichert, en (optimized).pdf, mit 1,097,087 Bytes (1.0 MiB), 97% kleiner, mit sechs optimierten Bildern. Liest man ihre Bilder mit PyMuPDF zurück, hat jedes 1275×1700 Pixel, 150 ppi auf der Seite, 130,834 bis 194,130 Bytes. Das Skript oben kommt auf 0.92 MiB, etwas weniger.

Der Unterschied liegt im Encoder. Pillow kann die Quantisierungstabelle eines JPEG ausgeben, und die erste Zeile der Tabelle der App ist [13, 9, 8, 13, 19, 32, 41, 49]. Pillow schreibt genau diese Zeile bei quality=60, "Medium" im Dialog der App entspricht hier also libjpeg-Qualität 60, genau wie der Standardwert im Skript. Die Bilder der App behalten außerdem die Farbe in voller Auflösung (Pillow liest ihr Chroma-Subsampling als 4:4:4, während Pillows Standard 4:2:0 ist). Für Seite 1 ergibt Pillow mit 4:4:4 und optimize=True 178,447 Bytes und mit dem Standard 171,678, gegenüber 194,130 bei der App, die vermutlich also auch auf optimierte Huffman-Tabellen verzichtet. Das sind ein paar Prozent Größe, und die volle Farbinformation ist bei einem Scan eines farbigen Formulars die Mühe wert.

Nur ersetzen, wenn es kleiner ist

Die Prüfung out.tell() >= len(raw) ist keine Zierde. Nimm die Ausgabe der App und kodiere das Bild von Seite 1 erneut mit Qualität 90: Es kommt auf 284,133 Bytes, gegenüber 194,130 für das Bild, das schon in der Datei liegt. Ein JPEG mit höherer Qualität neu zu kodieren, als die, mit der es entstand, macht es größer und nicht schärfer. Ohne die Prüfung kann die Datei wachsen, wenn man einen Kompressor zweimal oder auf einer bereits komprimierten Datei ausführt.

Den Rest erledigt die ppi-Prüfung. Das Skript auf seine eigene Ausgabe und auf die Ausgabe der App angewendet, ersetzte beide Male 0 Bilder: Jedes Bild hat schon 150 ppi, unter der Schwelle von 225, und die Datei wird nur erneut gespeichert (die 1.0-MiB-Kopie der App wurde 1.05 MiB groß, allein durch das Neuschreiben, ohne dass ein Bild angefasst wurde).

Wo es nicht mehr funktioniert

Das hilft nur, wenn die Prüfung zeigt, dass Bilder den Großteil der Datei ausmachen. Ein PDF, das aus einer Textverarbeitung exportiert wurde, hat keine Seitenbilder zum Herunterrechnen. Außerdem ist das Ergebnis verlustbehaftet: Der Qualitätsverlust in der Tabelle oben ist real, und das Original muss unverändert bleiben. Deshalb schreibt die App eine neue Kopie neben die Datei, und das Skript tut es auch, es braucht dafür ein dst, das sich von src unterscheidet.

Es gibt noch eine Zahl, die erklärt, warum das über die auf dem Bildschirm angezeigte Größe hinaus wichtig ist. E-Mail hängt Dateien als Base64 an, das sind 4 Bytes Text für je 3 Bytes Datei, plus Zeilenumbrüche. Kodiert man die Testdatei so mit Pythons base64.encodebytes, kommen für das 30.7-MiB-PDF 41.5 MiB heraus, ein Limit von 25 MB kann also stärker überschritten werden, als die Dateigröße vermuten lässt. Dieselbe Rechnung legt für eine Datei, die versendet werden soll, eine Grenze von etwa 18 MB nahe.

Der PDF-Editor ist Teil der osFoundry-Desktop-App, die auf deinem Computer läuft und auf der osFoundry-Downloadseite kostenlos erhältlich ist. Wie sie Dateien auf dem Gerät hält, beschreibt die Local-first-Seite.

title: Why Your WebSocket Users Go "Ghost Online" — A Real Production War Story
description:
First, a true story from our production environment.

Users reported that messages wouldn't send — the spinner just kept spinning. But the UI said "Connected", with a nice green dot. The server logs were even weirder: those users' connections were still alive on the server. The server thought they were online, and was faithfully pushing messages into dead sockets.

Restarting the app fixed it instantly. A few hours later, it came back.

Zombie connections — also known as half-open connections. Below is everything we learned, plus the four-part reliability kit we ended up shipping. Don't ask what version one looked like. Version one was the absence of everything below.

Why TCP Lies to You

WebSocket sits on top of TCP, and TCP has a property many people only learn about in production:

If the peer drops off the network abruptly — cable unplugged, laptop asleep, Wi-Fi to 4G — your socket fires no events at all. No close, no error, nothing.

In TCP's world, you only learn a connection is dead when you actively send data and the send fails. If neither side speaks, a "connection" can stay half-dead for hours: the routers in the middle dropped the session long ago, while both endpoints still believe the other is there.

So here's the iron rule: never rely on onclose to detect a dead connection. It will not come.

Part 1: Bidirectional Heartbeats

The fix is unglamorous: make both sides talk periodically, and declare death on silence.

// Client: ping every 30s; if no pong within 15s, kill the socket and reconnect
const HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL = 30_000;
const PONG_TIMEOUT = 15_000;

let pongTimer: number | undefined;

function startHeartbeat(ws: WebSocket) {
  setInterval(() => {
    if (ws.readyState !== WebSocket.OPEN) return;
    ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'ping' }));

    clearTimeout(pongTimer);
    pongTimer = window.setTimeout(() => {
      ws.close();
      reconnect();
    }, PONG_TIMEOUT);
  }, HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL);
}

// Server: reply to pings, track last-seen time
ws.on('message', (raw) => {
  const msg = JSON.parse(raw.toString());
  if (msg.type === 'ping') {
    ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'pong' }));
    markAlive(ws);
  }
});

// Reaper: clean up connections silent for 90+ seconds
setInterval(() => {
  for (const ws of clients) {
    if (Date.now() - lastActive(ws) > 90_000) {
      ws.terminate();
    }
  }
}, 30_000);

Two traps here, both of which we stepped on ourselves.

First: heartbeats must be bidirectional. Our first version only had client-side pings, so the server kept pushing into dead sockets — the client zombie problem was solved, the server-side zombie queue was not. The same logic applies in reverse.

Second: use terminate(), not close(), for server-side reaping. close() runs a graceful handshake and waits for the peer to respond. The peer is already dead. Stop waiting. terminate() destroys the socket immediately.

Part 2: Exponential Backoff Reconnect

Once you detect death, you reconnect. The laziest implementation is setTimeout(reconnect, 1000), which buys you two problems: when the server restarts, every client slams it at the same second (the reconnect storm), and during a long outage clients keep hammering retries every second for nothing.

The standard fix is exponential backoff with jitter:

let attempt = 0;

function reconnect() {
  const base = Math.min(1000 * 2 ** attempt, 30_000); // 1s → 2s → 4s … capped at 30s
  const delay = base * (0.7 + Math.random() * 0.6);   // ±30% jitter
  attempt += 1;
  setTimeout(connect, delay);
}

function connect() {
  const ws = new WebSocket(url);
  ws.onopen = () => {
    attempt = 0;
    resubscribe(); // don't skip this — next section
  };
}

The jitter line is what everyone skips. Don't. It exists precisely to prevent "all clients reconnecting in perfect unison", and it costs one line.

Part 3: State Recovery After Reconnect

The most commonly missed piece: a successful reconnect does not mean everything is fine.

While you were offline, other people sent messages, task states changed, and your subscriptions evaporated. Do nothing after reconnecting, and your users see a mysterious "time hole" in the conversation.

Our approach: reconcile after every reconnect.

ws.onopen = () => {
  attempt = 0;
  // Send the last message id we have; server replies with the delta.
  // If the gap is too large, fall back to a full refresh.
  ws.send(JSON.stringify({
    type: 'sync',
    lastMsgId: store.lastMsgId,
  }));
};

Delta catch-up with a full-refresh fallback — I haven't found a simpler scheme that actually holds up.

Part 4: Acks and Stale-Event Guards

Two smaller things, worth their own section.

Send acks. "The client sent it" and "the server received it" are different facts. For important collaborative operations, have the server acknowledge with a message id; only then does the client mark it as delivered, and unacked messages go into a retry queue. That gray-to-blue checkmark in your UI is local state — don't let it lie to you.

Stale events. Here's a nasty bug hiding in reconnect logic: after an old socket dies, it can still fire onmessage one last time — leftovers from the kernel buffer. Handle it normally, and a message from "the previous world" pollutes your current state. This one took us a full night to track down. The fix is a generation counter, three lines:

let generation = 0;

function connect() {
  const myGen = ++generation;
  const ws = new WebSocket(url);
  ws.onmessage = (e) => {
    if (myGen !== generation) return; // event from a stale socket — drop it
    handleMessage(e);
  };
}

This kit holds up well at a few thousand concurrent connections. Past tens of thousands, the heartbeat scan needs its own optimization pass — but that's a story for another post.

The Checklist

Audit your project against this:

  • [ ] Client pings and waits for pong; on timeout it declares death itself, never waiting for onclose
  • [ ] Server tracks last-active time and reaps zombies with terminate()
  • [ ] Reconnects use exponential backoff + jitter + a cap
  • [ ] After reconnecting: delta sync, or a full reconciliation fallback
  • [ ] Important messages have acks; unacked messages go to a retry queue
  • [ ] Events from stale sockets are dropped via a generation guard

Next post: reliable message delivery — how a server guarantees a message is delivered exactly once, and how out-of-order "paranormal events" actually happen. Follow me if that sounds like your kind of problem.

title: Building an AI agent chat UI with shadcn/ui components
description:
A basic chatbot can look like a list of messages and an input field. An agent interface needs to explain more: whether work is in progress, whether a tool failed, and whether an action is waiting for the user's approval.

Those are interaction and state-management problems, not just styling problems. This walkthrough outlines a component plan using Cuelark UI, an open-source library of 107 shadcn/ui components. I work on Cuelark. The aim here is to explain the interface structure, not promise that installing a component gives you a working agent backend.

Start with the conversation loop

Begin with three pieces from the catalog: Conversation, Message and Prompt Input. Use them as the starting points for the conversation area, individual entries and user input.

Before wiring a model, define your application states. At minimum, distinguish an empty conversation, a request in progress, a completed response and a failed request. Decide whether users can submit another prompt while work is running, and what cancelling actually does on the server.

Keep user input if submission fails. Avoid showing a confident-looking completed response when the backend has only delivered part of it. These decisions live in your application's logic; the visual components don't establish them for you.

Install source, then inspect it

Cuelark follows the shadcn model: its homepage says components install through the shadcn CLI into your codebase, rather than requiring a Cuelark runtime package. Start at the current Cuelark UI documentation and use the installation instructions for your chosen component.

Inspect the generated source and dependencies before integrating it. Check how its props, exports and styles fit your project. This article intentionally avoids an invented CLI command or undocumented component API: copy the current command from the component's own page.

Bring in the smallest useful slice first. A readable conversation with reliable input behavior is a better foundation than a screen full of agent activity that isn't connected to real state.

Give tool activity a clear state

Next, consider Tool for displaying tool activity. In your application model, distinguish requested, running, succeeded and failed operations. Use stable identifiers so that an update changes the correct activity rather than appending a duplicate.

Show a concise label that explains what is happening. When a tool fails, explain what the user can do next without dumping raw internal errors or credentials into the conversation.

Do not label an operation successful merely because the model described an intention. The UI should reflect the actual tool result. Where a result is uncertain or incomplete, say so.

Treat reasoning as a user-facing explanation

The catalog also includes Reasoning. Plan this area around useful, permitted progress summaries: what the agent is checking, what information is missing and why it needs a decision.

A component named Reasoning is not a reason to expose hidden model reasoning, raw prompts or private intermediate data. Send only information your application is allowed to show. Keep explanations short enough that users can tell whether anything requires their attention.

If no progress summary is available, a clear working state is better than fabricated step-by-step activity.

Make approvals real, not decorative

Use Confirmation as the visual starting point for an approval step when an operation needs consent. Explain the proposed action, destination and consequences before offering a choice.

The server must enforce that approval. A button in the interface is not a security boundary. Bind consent to the exact pending operation, reject stale approvals, and make repeated clicks safe. If the action changes after approval, require a new decision.

For external actions such as sending a message, show the recipient and content. Don't treat a general chat instruction as permission for every later operation.

Test transitions before adding polish

Exercise empty messages, long replies, interrupted streams, failed tools and expired approvals. Check keyboard navigation and visible focus in the integrated application, not just an isolated demo. Test narrow screens and reduced-motion preferences too.

Cuelark's homepage describes keyboard support, accessible primitives and reduced-motion handling, but your composition still needs testing. Custom wrappers and event handlers can introduce problems even when the starting pieces are sound.

The useful outcome is a UI where users know what they asked, what the agent actually did and what still needs their decision. Explore Cuelark UI for the components, then connect them to explicit application states and backend checks. That's the difference between an attractive chat mockup and an agent interface people can understand.

title: When a Code Review Says "No Issues" but Found Bugs
description:
Originally published on the DevReview blog.

DevReview caps every review at eight comments, ranked by severity. The point is to keep a pull request readable: a few findings that matter, not forty that don't. A cap like that only works if the reader can trust what is left out. This post is about a path where they couldn't.

We found it while checking our own claims against our own code, and we haven't measured whether it ever happened in production.

What the review did

After the model returns its findings, the review code does three things in this order:

  1. Sort the findings by severity and keep the top eight.
  2. Drop any finding whose file path is not in the pull request. The model sometimes cites a file that doesn't exist in the diff, and a comment on a file that isn't there can't be posted.
  3. If nothing is left to post, write "No issues worth your attention" with a green check.

The problem is the order of steps 1 and 2. Suppose the model returns ten findings, and the top eight all cite file paths that aren't in the PR. Step 1 keeps those eight. Step 2 drops all of them. Step 3 sees nothing left and posts the green check. The two real findings that were ranked ninth and tenth were already cut by the cap.

So the pull request shows "no issues" while the model has reported eight bugs it got the location wrong on, and two it got right. The reader gets a pass they shouldn't have.

Two separate things were wrong

A discarded finding looked the same as no finding. Step 2 removed findings without counting them anywhere the reader could see. A green check means "the reviewer looked and found nothing". It should not also mean "the reviewer found things and we threw them away".

Fake paths used up the budget. Even when the result wasn't a false all-clear, findings with invalid paths took slots from valid ones. A valid warning could be suppressed to make room for a comment that was never going to be posted.

What we changed

  • The path check now runs before the cap. Only findings that can actually be posted compete for the eight slots.
  • Discarded findings are counted and disclosed. If any findings were dropped because their file wasn't in the PR, or because they were malformed, the review says so: "N findings could not be posted because they did not match this PR's files or the expected format."
  • The green check is stricter. It appears only when the model reported zero findings. One discarded finding is enough to remove it.
  • Suppressed comments show a breakdown. When the cap cuts comments, the note now says what was cut, for example "2 remarks suppressed to keep this review focused: 1 NIT, 1 PRAISE." We also removed the word "lower-priority" from that note, because the cap can also cut a bug when there are more than eight.

We also weakened some of our own marketing copy. We had said nothing is hidden silently. That is true of comments cut by the cap, which are disclosed, but not of malformed comments, which were dropped without a count. The copy now says what is true.

What we checked, and what we didn't

We wrote the tests first and confirmed they failed on the old behaviour. The review function is now tested end to end with faked responses from the model and from GitHub, including the case above: eight invented paths plus two valid findings now posts the two valid ones and discloses the eight. Removing the counting of malformed findings makes a test fail, so that test does something.

What we have not done:

  • We haven't watched this on a real production review. The tests use faked responses. A real GitHub and Anthropic exchange is the next check.
  • The dashboard can still mislead. A review where every finding was discarded shows as "completed, 0 comments", which looks like a pass. The discarded count appears in the pull request comment and in our logs, but we don't store it in the database yet. Showing it on the dashboard needs a new column.
  • Related gaps exist. A green check can still appear when some files in a pull request were not reviewed at all, and a code fence inside a comment can make the whole review fail. Both are on our list as separate fixes.

The general rule

If a system filters, ranks and then reports, the order of those steps decides what the report means. Ask what the report says when the filter removes everything. For us, the answer was "all clear", which is the one thing it must never say after discarding findings.

DevReview is a GitHub App that reviews pull requests and caps every review at eight comments, ranked by severity. If you want to see how it works before trusting it with your repos, start with How DevReview Works.

title: I Built a Weather-Aware Truck Router with React and Django (and Why the Fastest Route Isn't Always the Right One)
description:
If you're driving a car, the fastest route is usually the best route. If you're driving a fully loaded 18-wheeler, 45 mph crosswinds or a band of heavy snow somewhere along the way can turn "fastest" into "dangerous" fast.

So I built Weather-Aware Truck Routing: a web app that takes a trip, gets three truck routes, checks the weather at every checkpoint for the hour the truck will actually be there, scores the risk, and recommends the safest route. Drive time is only used as the final tie-breaker.

It started as a time-boxed full-stack engineering challenge, and I ended up enjoying it way more than I expected.

  • 🚚 Live app: https://weather-aware-truck-routing-5h7c.onrender.com/ (free hosting, so the first load can take about a minute to wake up)
  • 💻 Source code: https://github.com/famousfishi/weather-aware-truck-routing

What the app does

  • Plan a trip: enter an origin and destination (with search-as-you-type), a departure time, the load weight, and how often you want weather checkpoints: every 10, 25 or 50 miles.
  • See 3 routes on a map: the selected route is colored by risk along its whole length. Each checkpoint shows its arrival time, wind, rain, snow, risk level and the reason for that level.
  • Get a recommendation that explains itself: not just "take Route B", but why, e.g. "Fewer Severe miles than Route A: 0 vs 42 mi", plus how much extra time it costs compared to the fastest route.
  • Scrub through the next 48 hours: a forecast slider (with a play button) animates a weather heatmap over the trip corridor, and a truck icon shows where you'd be at that hour.
  • Compare routes side by side: distance, drive time, arrival time, miles at each risk level and average risk.

The stack

Frontend

Tech What I used it for
React 19 UI
TypeScript Typed API client, typed responses, fewer surprises
Material UI (MUI 6) + Emotion Components, theming, layout
Leaflet + React-Leaflet 5 Interactive map, route lines, checkpoints, heatmap layer, truck marker
Vite Dev server and build (proxies /api to Django locally)
ESLint Linting

Backend

Tech What I used it for
Python 3.12 Language
Django 5.2 Web framework, settings, caching
Django REST Framework API views, request validation (serializers), consistent error handling
requests Calling TomTom and Open-Meteo
python-dotenv Loading config from .env
Redis (optional) Shared cache; falls back to in-memory caching if not set
Gunicorn Production WSGI server
WhiteNoise Serving the built React app straight from Django

External APIs and services

Service Role
TomTom Truck routing (with vehicle weight), route alternatives, geocoding and place suggestions
Open-Meteo Hourly forecasts: wind, rain, showers, snowfall
OpenStreetMap Map tiles

DevOps

Tech Role
Docker (multi-stage build) Builds the React app, then packages it with the Django API into one image
Render (Blueprint via render.yaml) Hosting on the free plan, one service, one URL
GitHub Actions Runs the backend tests and the frontend build on every push and PR

Fun fact: none of the services needs a payment card.

How a trip gets planned

When you hit "Plan trip", the backend runs this pipeline:

  1. Places – the typed text is geocoded with TomTom (skipped if you picked a suggestion that already has coordinates).
  2. Routes – TomTom's truck routing returns the best route plus up to 2 alternatives. I pass the gross vehicle weight (load + a 35,000 lb tractor-trailer, capped at 80,000 lb) so weight-restricted roads are avoided. If fewer than 3 distinct routes come back, the service asks for routes through points on either side of the trip's midpoint to force some variety.
  3. Checkpoints – placed at mile 0, every N miles, and at the destination.
  4. Weather – one batched Open-Meteo request fetches hourly wind, rain and snow for every checkpoint and every heatmap cell.
  5. Risk – each checkpoint uses the forecast hour closest to its arrival time and gets classified by the rules below.
  6. Ranking – routes are sorted and the deciding rule is explained in plain English.
  7. Heatmap – a grid of cells within about 30 miles of every route, with risk precomputed for all 49 hours (0–48).

The risk rules

Condition Low Moderate High Severe No Travel
Wind < 25 mph 25–34 35–44 45–54 ≥ 55 mph
Rain < 0.10 in/hr 0.10–0.25 0.25–0.50 0.50–1.00 > 1.00
Snow < 0.5 in/hr 0.5–1.0 1.0–2.0 2.0–3.0 > 3.0

Then there are load rules, because a heavy truck in strong wind is a different story:

  • ≥ 55 mph wind → No Travel for any load
  • 45–54 mph with more than 30,000 lb → No Travel
  • 35–44 mph with more than 40,000 lb → Severe

A checkpoint's final level is the worst of wind (after load rules), rain and snow. All of this lives in one small file, written to read exactly like the table:

def apply_load_rules(wind_level: RiskLevel, load_weight_lb: int) -> RiskLevel:
    """Heavy loads are riskier in strong wind (the wind level already covers the ≥55 mph rule)."""
    if wind_level == RiskLevel.SEVERE and load_weight_lb > NO_TRAVEL_IN_SEVERE_WIND_ABOVE_LB:
        return RiskLevel.NO_TRAVEL
    if wind_level == RiskLevel.HIGH and load_weight_lb > SEVERE_IN_HIGH_WIND_ABOVE_LB:
        return RiskLevel.SEVERE
    return wind_level


def assess(weather: WeatherReading, load_weight_lb: int) -> RiskAssessment:
    wind_level = classify_wind(weather.wind_mph)
    loaded_wind_level = apply_load_rules(wind_level, load_weight_lb)
    rain_level = classify_rain(weather.rain_in_hr)
    snow_level = classify_snow(weather.snow_in_hr)
    # ...build human-readable reasons...
    return RiskAssessment(level=max(loaded_wind_level, rain_level, snow_level), reasons=reasons)

Every checkpoint also carries a list of reasons like "Wind 47 mph → Severe" and "42,000 lb load in that wind → No Travel", so the driver never has to guess why something is red.

Picking the winner

Routes are ranked by, in order:

  1. Fewest No-Travel miles (I added this one so a route you shouldn't drive can never win on other numbers)
  2. Fewest Severe miles
  3. Fewest High miles
  4. Lowest average risk (weighted by miles, 0 = Low to 4 = No Travel)
  5. Shortest travel time

In Python this turned out to be a one-liner, because tuples compare element by element:

def rank_key(route: RouteDto) -> tuple:
    s = route.summary
    return (s.no_travel_miles, s.severe_miles, s.high_miles, s.average_risk, route.duration_seconds)

ranked = sorted(routes, key=rank_key)

To explain the result, the service walks the same criteria in order and finds the first one where the winner beats the runner-up. That becomes the headline reason shown in the UI.

The parts I found most interesting

1. Weather is checked for when you'll be there, not now

A storm that's over Nebraska right now might be gone by the time you get there, or one might roll in. So every checkpoint gets an estimated arrival time, and the risk uses the forecast for that hour.

I don't just divide distance by average speed either. TomTom returns a distance/time profile along the route, and I interpolate on that, so slow city stretches and fast interstates are timed correctly:

def estimate_arrival(route, fraction_of_route, departure_time):
    """Uses the provider's (distance, time) profile, so slow city stretches and fast highways are respected."""
    meters = fraction_of_route * route.distance_meters
    distances = [m for m, _ in route.time_profile]
    seconds = [s for _, s in route.time_profile]
    return departure_time + timedelta(seconds=interpolate(meters, distances, seconds))

2. Checkpoints that "cover" road, so the miles always add up

To say "Route A has 42 Severe miles", each checkpoint needs to stand for a stretch of road. Each one covers the road halfway back to the previous checkpoint and halfway forward to the next. That way the miles per risk level always add up to the full route length, whether you chose 10, 25 or 50 mile spacing.

3. Fewer weather calls with grid snapping + caching

Three routes between the same cities overlap a lot. So before fetching weather, every point is snapped to a 0.1° grid (roughly 7 miles). Points in the same cell share one forecast, all missing cells go out in one batched request, and results are cached for 30 minutes (in memory, or Redis if REDIS_URL is set).

4. Getting around shared-IP rate limits on free hosting

This one surprised me. Open-Meteo's free tier is limited per IP address, and on free hosting, lots of apps share the same outbound IP. So the server could hit the limit without me doing anything wrong.

The fix: on the live site, the visitor's browser downloads the forecasts, while the server still does all the risk work.

  • The browser asks the server to plan a trip.
  • The server works out exactly which forecasts it needs and responds with the exact Open-Meteo request URLs.
  • The browser fetches them (Open-Meteo allows calls from any website) and sends the raw responses back.
  • The server parses them and finishes the plan.

Each visitor uses their own free allowance, and browser-supplied data is only used for that one request, never cached for other visitors. It's controlled by one flag, WEATHER_FROM_BROWSER.

5. A slider that needs zero network calls

The 0–48 hour heatmap is computed up front for all 49 hours in the same response. So scrubbing or hitting play on the slider is instant: React just swaps which hour it's drawing.

6. Demo mode without touching service code

A tiny container.py builds each service once and wires its dependencies. Flip USE_FAKE_PROVIDERS=true and it swaps the real TomTom and Open-Meteo clients for fake ones with built-in data. No API key, no internet, and the same fakes power the tests.

@lru_cache(maxsize=1)
def tomtom_client():
    if settings.USE_FAKE_PROVIDERS:
        return FakeTomTomClient()
    return TomTomClient(settings.TOMTOM_API_KEY, settings.GEOCODE_COUNTRY_SET)

7. Thin views, logic in services

The DRF views do three things: validate, call one service, return. All the actual logic lives in small services (places, routes, checkpoints, weather, risk, assessment, recommendation, heatmap, and a planner that ties them together). Errors always come back in one shape, { "detail": "..." }: 400 for bad input, 422 when a place or route can't be found, 502 when an upstream API fails.

class TripPlanView(APIView):
    def post(self, request):
        trip = TripPlanRequestSerializer(data=request.data)
        trip.is_valid(raise_exception=True)
        return Response(to_json(container.trip_planner().plan_trip(trip.to_trip_request())))

Testing and CI

There are 44 backend tests covering the risk rules (including the tricky boundaries like exactly 0.25 in/hr), ranking, arrival times, the heatmap, the API client parsers, the API endpoints and the browser-weather flow.

GitHub Actions runs two jobs on every push and pull request:

  • backend: install requirements, run python manage.py test
  • frontend: npm ci and npm run build (which also type-checks with tsc)

Deployment

I wanted one service and one URL, so the Dockerfile is a two-stage build:

  1. A Node 22 image builds the React app into static files.
  2. A Python 3.12 image installs the Django API and copies the built frontend in. WhiteNoise serves it at /, and Gunicorn runs the app.

On Render it's a Blueprint: point it at the repo, it reads render.yaml, generates the Django secret key, and you only add your TomTom API key. There's a health check at /api/health.

API at a glance

Method Path Purpose
POST /api/trips/plan Plan a trip (routes, checkpoints, risk, recommendation, heatmap)
GET /api/places/suggest?q=denv Place suggestions for the search box
GET /api/health Health check (also reports demo mode)

What I'd add next

  • Hours-of-Service rest breaks. Right now arrival times assume continuous driving. Real drivers have legally required breaks, and those shift when they hit each stretch of weather.
  • Suggesting a better departure time when every route has No-Travel conditions, instead of just warning about it.

Run it yourself 

# Backend (Python 3.12)
cd backend
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate        # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env             # add TOMTOM_API_KEY, or set USE_FAKE_PROVIDERS=true
python manage.py runserver

# Frontend (Node 22)
cd frontend
npm install
npm run dev                      # http://localhost:5173

No TomTom key yet? Set USE_FAKE_PROVIDERS=true and try Denver to Chicago on the demo data.

Wrapping up

The biggest lesson for me: the hard part wasn't calling the APIs, it was making the answer trustworthy. Timing weather to the actual arrival hour, making sure the miles add up, and explaining every decision in plain words is what turns "a map with some colors" into something a driver could actually rely on.

If you've built anything with routing or weather data, or you have ideas for what a driver would want next, I'd love to hear about it in the comments. And if you check out the repo, a ⭐ is always appreciated.

  • Live app: https://weather-aware-truck-routing-5h7c.onrender.com/
  • GitHub: https://github.com/famousfishi/weather-aware-truck-routing

Routing and geocoding by TomTom. Weather by Open-Meteo. Map tiles © OpenStreetMap contributors.
