title: I made a free, open source alternative to Brilliant (140+ interactive math and science courses)
description:
What a Free, Open-Source Brilliant Clone Teaches Us About Lazy Eye Training

Someone on Lemmy posted a free, open-source alternative to Brilliant this week: 140+ interactive courses, 1000+ lessons in math, physics, and chemistry, no account, no ads — because the paid version costs up to $160 a year depending on region. It hit 128 upvotes and 70 comments, and the author was upfront that only about a third of pages have been human-reviewed, inviting people to flag what's wrong and fix it in public.

The part worth stealing isn't the price tag. It's the pedagogy: try the thing first, get the explanation after. Interactive practice over passive consumption. That's why it got traction.

I've been thinking about this as an engineering pattern, not just a content pattern. The OpenAha project treats learning like a feedback loop: present a challenge, capture the response, adjust difficulty. That's the same control structure you'd want in any skill-training system — and it's the structure most home vision routines simply don't have.

Where the same gap shows up in vision training

Amblyopia — lazy eye — has a classic home routine: patching. Cover the stronger eye, make the weaker one work, often for an hour a day while a child sits still. It has real clinical history behind it. It also has a real engagement problem, and engagement is what determines whether any routine actually gets done.

Dichoptic training takes a different angle: instead of isolating one eye, you give each eye its own view and force them to cooperate. That's the idea behind AmblyoPunch, a Meta Quest vision-training game.

What you actually do in it

You're in VR. Gabor-pattern coins — oriented, soft-edged striped targets — fly toward you and you punch them with controllers or hand tracking for points. Red spikes come at you; you dodge or duck. You have three hearts, and losing all of them restarts the run. Worlds progress from village to city to space, moon, Mars, Venus, with objects getting faster and smaller while spikes get larger.

If you're a builder reading this, the interesting part is the stimulus design. Gabor patches aren't decoration — they're the classic stimulus in vision science for driving contrast, orientation, and fine-detail processing in the visual cortex. Wrapping them in a punching game is essentially a way to get many trials per session without the user noticing they're doing trials.

It's also a nice systems problem: the game loop and the training loop are two different clocks. The player sees score, combos, and hearts; the training engine underneath sees trial-level accuracy and drives stage transitions. Keeping those decoupled means the difficulty controller can do its job without the player ever staring at a progress bar.

Under the game layer sits a four-stage dichoptic plan, run automatically:

  1. Monocular warm-up — targets go only to the lazy eye, building tracking and attention without dominant-eye competition.
  2. Breaking suppression — the dominant eye is heavily dimmed and washed out so the weak eye has to contribute.
  3. Rebalancing — clarity is gradually restored to the dominant eye across sub-steps while the lazy eye stays active.
  4. Fusion training — a slight misalignment within Panum's fusion area asks the brain to merge the two views into one 3D percept.

Progression is performance-gated rather than time-gated — typically around 70% accuracy across a rolling 10 outcomes, with demotion possible below 40%, and around 80% required for strabismus profiles before the final fusion stage. That's an adaptive-difficulty system with a hysteresis band, and it's the kind of thing that makes or breaks adherence: too easy and people disengage, too hard and they quit.

Tuned to your eyes

Setup matters. In the wall and wrist menus you choose:

  • Lazy eye: Left or Right (picking wrong reverses the intended effect)
  • Severity: Mild / Moderate / Severe — changes target size, speed, and stage length; severe profiles get larger, slower targets and longer monocular work, while mild may start closer to binocular training
  • Strabismus: Esotropia or Exotropia — shifts Stage 4 disparity and vergence

Automatic mode is the recommended path. Custom mode is there for people who know what they want, with manual monocular/binocular and fusion toggles.

Why the news item matters here

The OpenAha thread is a reminder that people stick with things they can interact with — and that shipping something honest and imperfect in public beats shipping nothing. AmblyoPunch is built on that bet: that daily coordination practice is easier to sustain when it's content someone actually wants to return to, and that real-world confidence (catching a ball, navigating stairs, reading depth) is the point.

Important

AmblyoPunch is a training and assistive game. It is not a medical device, treatment, or cure. It complements — and never replaces — professional eye-care guidance. Consult an eye-care professional for clinical advice about your or your child's vision.

Try it on Meta Quest: https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyopunch/1239507485902689/

title: Why Generated SQL Is Never Auto-Executed
description:
Quick answer: The modeling package has no executing driver. Every DDL, index, and deployment script is generated for review, and the software cannot run it against the database itself. The deployment script is idempotent and forward-only, so a person confirms each change before it is applied. This keeps a proposed migration from reaching the storage without a review.

Why auto-execution is the wrong default

A generated migration can look complete while carrying an assumption the reviewer should catch. An inferred link table, an open question, or a field diff that touches a shared table all need a decision, and running the SQL the moment it is generated would remove the pause where that decision happens.

The blast radius of a schema change is large and hard to reverse, so the default should favor review rather than speed. Keeping the executing driver out of the package enforces that boundary in the tooling rather than relying on discipline alone.

What the package can and cannot do

Capability Available?
Generate DDL and indexes Yes
Generate deterministic seed data Yes
Write deployment scripts Yes
Execute writes or DDL No
Execute a driver against the database No

The same package that produces the SQL deliberately lacks the ability to run it, so there is no hidden path where a generated change reaches the storage unconfirmed.

How a change actually reaches the database

  1. Review the four-layer reconciliation and the table status.
  2. Read the field diffs and the impacted operations.
  3. Resolve the open questions and confirm the inferred items.
  4. Review the generated SQL and the forward-only deployment script.
  5. Apply the change through your own controlled process.

The script is idempotent, so running it more than once does not produce duplicate changes, and forward-only means it moves the schema ahead rather than reversing earlier migrations. Those properties make the reviewed script safe to run, but the decision to run it stays with the team.

Picture a migration that adds a link table and a foreign key. The generated SQL is complete and internally consistent, but the link table is inferred from a relationship the business rules actually treat as one-to-many, and the open question is still attached. If the package could execute the script, the wrong join table would be created before anyone reads the note. With the executing driver absent, the reviewer opens the inference, resolves the cardinality, and only then runs the corrected script. The same protection catches a field diff that touches a shared table, because the pause is where the impacted operations get checked. This does not slow the happy path much, since a fully reviewed script still runs in one controlled step, but it removes the path where a confident-looking migration reaches the storage unconfirmed.

How this fits the safety model

This is the same boundary that keeps read-only access and static signals honest. The tool can read a live database through a saved profile and generate precise SQL, but it does not write, and a read-only SELECT is the only query the data layer runs. Writes and DDL are blocked at the connection layer.

Treat the generated SQL as a detailed proposal, not a pending action, and keep the execution step separate and deliberate. A script that cannot be triggered automatically cannot be triggered by accident.

Powerduck keeps the review and the execution separate by design, so every schema change is confirmed before it touches the storage.

Frequently asked questions

Can the tool run the migration for me? No. The modeling package has no executing driver, and SQL is generated for review.

What makes the deployment script safe to run? It is idempotent and forward-only, so it avoids duplicate changes and does not reverse earlier migrations.

Are writes blocked entirely? The data layer runs only a read-only SELECT, and writes and DDL are blocked.

The bottom line

The generated SQL is a reviewed artifact, not an executed action. With no executing driver in the package, every DDL and migration waits for a person to confirm it, and the idempotent, forward-only script makes the eventual run safe without making it automatic. This keeps a hard-to-reverse schema change from reaching the storage by accident. The line between generating and executing is the core safety control. Read more in the API data model guide.

title: TCP Provider: The Wait Operation Timed Out - It Was the Firewall, Not SQL Server
description:
We moved this site's database to a new SQL Server, and the first time I tried to connect from my own PC, sqlcmd sat for a few seconds and then printed this:

Sqlcmd: Error: Microsoft ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server : TCP Provider: The wait operation timed out.
Sqlcmd: Error: Microsoft ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server : Login timeout expired.
Sqlcmd: Error: Microsoft ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server : A network-related or instance-specific error
has occurred while establishing a connection to SQL Server. Server is not found or not accessible.

The connection string was right, the password was right and the server was running - the website was using it at that very moment. The problem was one layer below SQL Server: the new host's firewall was silently dropping connections from my IP address. The next day the same error came back, because my home internet connection had been given a new IP. Here is how to tell which layer is failing, and how to fix each one.

The short version: "TCP Provider: The wait operation timed out" (SQL Server error 258) means your computer sent a connection request and never got an answer. Something in the network path - usually a firewall - is dropping it. Run Test-NetConnection -Port 1433. If TcpTestSucceeded is False, fix the firewall (the server's, the host's or the cloud provider's) before touching SQL Server settings.

What the error actually means

A timeout is different from a refusal. When a port is closed but the machine is reachable, the server answers straight away with "no" and you get an error quickly, such as No connection could be made because the target machine actively refused it (error 10061). A timeout means there was no answer at all. Your packets went out and nothing came back, which is exactly what a firewall does when it drops traffic instead of rejecting it. The Login timeout expired line is just the client giving up after waiting. And error 258 is the Windows code for a wait that timed out, which is why it appears in SQL Server Management Studio and .NET versions of the same failure.

So the error tells you something useful: SQL Server probably never saw your attempt. Changing the password, the database name or the SQL login will not help.

Step 1: test the port, not SQL Server

PowerShell has a built-in test that tries a plain TCP connection to a port:

# Can this machine open a TCP connection to the SQL Server port at all?
Test-NetConnection -ComputerName 203.0.113.10 -Port 1433

# The line that matters:
# TcpTestSucceeded : False   -> blocked or nothing reachable; SQL Server never saw the attempt
# TcpTestSucceeded : True    -> the network path is open; look at SQL Server itself

This takes SQL Server, drivers, logins and connection strings out of the picture. When I ran it against both servers from the same PC, the answer was immediate:

PS> (Test-NetConnection 203.0.113.10 -Port 1433).TcpTestSucceeded   # new server
False
PS> (Test-NetConnection 198.51.100.20 -Port 1433).TcpTestSucceeded  # old server, same PC
True

Same computer, same network, same moment: one server reachable and one not. That rules out my PC, my router and my ISP blocking 1433, and points straight at the new server's side. (On macOS or Linux, nc -vz 203.0.113.10 1433 does the same job.)

Step 2: what to check when TcpTestSucceeded is False

Work from the outside in. Each of these drops traffic silently, which is what produces the timeout:

  1. The hosting or cloud firewall. Shared hosting panels, VPS providers and cloud platforms (Azure network security groups, AWS security groups) usually block 1433 from the internet by default and let you allow specific IP addresses. This was my case: the host only accepted SQL connections from listed addresses, and mine was not on the list. Once it was added, TcpTestSucceeded turned True and sqlcmd connected first time.
  2. Windows Firewall on the SQL Server machine. Even with the host's firewall open, Windows Defender Firewall on the server needs an inbound rule for TCP 1433.
  3. A different port. Named instances such as SQLEXPRESS use a dynamic port by default, not 1433. If the instance is not set to a fixed port, testing 1433 will fail even though SQL Server is fine. Check the port in SQL Server Configuration Manager, or connect with server\instance and let the SQL Server Browser service (UDP 1434) tell the client the port.
  4. TCP/IP disabled. SQL Server Express installs with TCP/IP turned off. In SQL Server Configuration Manager, enable it under SQL Server Network Configuration, set the port under IP Addresses → IPAll, and restart the SQL Server service. Strictly, this one usually gives a refusal rather than a timeout, but it is on every "allow remote connections" checklist for a reason.

For the Windows Firewall rule, allow your address rather than the whole internet:

# On the SQL Server machine (elevated PowerShell): allow 1433 only from your address
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "SQL Server 1433 from office" `
  -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 1433 `
  -RemoteAddress 203.0.113.45 -Action Allow

Step 3: when it worked yesterday - your IP changed

The day after everything worked, the same timeout came back. Nothing had changed on the server. Running Test-NetConnection again gave False, and checking my public IP explained it:

# Your public IP - the address the server's firewall sees, not your 192.168.x.x LAN address
(Invoke-RestMethod https://api.ipify.org)

Home and many office broadband connections get a dynamic IP from the ISP, which changes after a router restart or simply every few days. An allow-list with a single address breaks the moment it does. The options, from quickest to most robust:

  • Update the allowed address each time it changes - fine if it is rare.
  • Allow a small range from your ISP if the host supports CIDR ranges. This trades some security for fewer surprises; keep the range as tight as you can.
  • Use a static IP from your ISP, or a VPN with a fixed exit address, and allow only that.
  • Do not expose SQL Server at all: connect through an SSH tunnel or a VPN into the server's network, or run your scripts on the server itself. This is what I would recommend for anything beyond a small site.

Whatever you choose, do not solve this by opening 1433 to everyone. A SQL Server listening on the public internet gets password-guessing attempts within hours.

Step 4: when TcpTestSucceeded is True but it still fails

If the port test passes, the network is fine and the error will usually be different:

Error What it means
Login failed for user (18456) You reached SQL Server; the login, password or authentication mode is wrong
Cannot open database requested by the login Login is fine; the database name is wrong or the user has no access to it
The certificate chain was issued by an authority that is not trusted Encryption is on by default in newer drivers; install a trusted certificate or set TrustServerCertificate=true for testing
Still "wait operation timed out", only on large queries A query or command timeout rather than a connection timeout; look at the query, not the network

Two connection-string details are worth checking while you are there: put the port after a comma (Server=host,1433), not a colon, and give slow networks a longer connect timeout:

Server=203.0.113.10,1433;Database=MyDb;User Id=app_user;Password=<from config>;
TrustServerCertificate=true;Connect Timeout=30;

If you work with sqlcmd a lot, two other errors that cost me time on the same database are 'Scripting variable not defined' and Msg 1934 about QUOTED_IDENTIFIER. And if the connection works locally but the deployed app gets a 500 instead, see ASP.NET Core on Plesk: every error I hit.

FAQ

What does 'TCP Provider: The wait operation timed out' mean?

Your computer sent a connection request to SQL Server and got no answer at all. Something in the network path, usually a firewall, dropped it. SQL Server most likely never saw the attempt, so changing the password or database name will not help.

What is SQL Server error 258?

Error 258 is the Windows code for a wait that timed out. In SQL Server connection errors it appears with 'The wait operation timed out' and means the client gave up waiting for a reply from the server.

How do I test if SQL Server port 1433 is open?

In PowerShell run Test-NetConnection <server> -Port 1433 and look at TcpTestSucceeded. True means the network path is open; False means a firewall or routing problem, or SQL Server is not listening on that port. On macOS or Linux use nc -vz <server> 1433.

Why did my SQL Server connection stop working when nothing changed?

If the server only accepts connections from allowed IP addresses, your public IP may have changed. Home and many office connections get a dynamic IP from the ISP. Check your current public IP and update the allow-list, or use a static IP, a VPN or an SSH tunnel.

How do I allow remote connections to SQL Server Express?

Enable TCP/IP in SQL Server Configuration Manager, set a fixed port under IPAll (usually 1433), restart the SQL Server service, add a Windows Firewall inbound rule for that port, and allow your IP in any hosting or cloud firewall in front of the server.

Is it safe to open port 1433 to the internet?

No. A SQL Server reachable from anywhere attracts automated password-guessing quickly. Allow only the IP addresses that need access, or reach the server through a VPN or SSH tunnel instead.

What is the difference between a connection timeout and a refused connection?

A refused connection gets an immediate answer: the machine is reachable but nothing is listening on the port. A timeout gets no answer at all, which usually means a firewall is silently dropping the traffic. The fix for each is in a different place.

Originally published on knowledgemarkg.com.

title: Building a Browser-Based Excel Editor with Next.js and Univer
description:
Opening a spreadsheet, fixing a few cells, and downloading the result sounds like a small task. Building a browser application that handles that workflow involves more than putting an editable grid on a page.

An Excel workbook carries formulas, formatting, merged cells, multiple sheets, and sometimes charts or pivot tables. Those details need to survive the trip through the editor.

I'm building Workbook Editor, a browser-based spreadsheet editor built with Next.js, React, and Univer. This article covers three parts of its implementation: file conversion, loading the editor, and recovering local work.

The architecture: separate the grid from the file format

The project gives different libraries different jobs:

Layer Responsibility
Next.js and React Pages, navigation, and application UI
Univer The spreadsheet editing experience
ExcelJS The main XLSX import and export path
SheetJS The XLS, CSV, and TSV conversion path
IndexedDB Local recovery snapshots and version history

Univer provides the interactive workbook: cells, selection, formatting controls, and spreadsheet operations. The application registers presets for features such as sorting, filtering, data validation, and find and replace.

The file conversion layer connects that editing model to the files people bring with them.

For XLSX files, the basic flow is:

Local file
    ↓
ExcelJS workbook
    ↓
Application adapter
    ↓
Univer workbook
    ↓
User edits
    ↓
Application adapter + export preservation steps
    ↓
Downloaded XLSX file

Keeping conversion in a separate module makes the boundary explicit. UI code can work with the editor model, while the adapter handles differences in how workbook features are represented.

Importing values is only the beginning

A useful adapter has to translate more than cell contents.

The XLSX adapter handles values and formulas alongside fonts, fills, borders, number formats, alignment, merged cells, row heights, column widths, and sheet metadata.

Even dimensions require conversion. The implementation translates column widths into pixel dimensions for the editor and converts them back during export. Those calculations are approximations: a workbook's appearance also depends on font metrics and rendering behavior.

This is why “the file opened” is a narrow measure of compatibility. The more useful question is what happens after someone opens a workbook, edits it, exports it, and opens the result again.

The project also uses a separate adapter for XLS, CSV, and TSV. These formats have different capabilities, so the conversion paths have different expectations. CSV, for example, cannot carry a workbook's styling or multiple worksheets.

Preserve workbook parts outside the main conversion path

Some Excel features need handling beyond the main ExcelJS conversion path.

The project includes a preservation layer for native chart, pivot, and shape parts. During import, it captures relevant parts from the original XLSX package and stores serialized information with the workbook's resources. During export, it attempts to restore those parts into the generated package.

That adds a second path alongside normal cell conversion:

Original XLSX parts → captured resources → export restoration

Preserving a feature and editing it are separate capabilities. Keeping an original workbook part does not automatically give the browser editor complete control over that feature.

Restoration also has conditions. Sheet changes and drawing conflicts can affect whether an original part can be restored. This approach extends compatibility, but it does not establish complete Excel fidelity.

Load the spreadsheet engine when it is needed

The application includes both content pages and an interactive editor. They have different loading needs.

The editor component uses a client-side dynamic import with server rendering disabled. Its loading state displays a message and navigation links while the interactive component loads.

There is another asynchronous boundary inside the editor: Univer setup lives in a dedicated factory module, which the editor imports dynamically.

That module centralizes the engine's presets, styles, and locale configuration. The separation is intended to keep the engine's dependencies apart from frequently changed application code and improve opportunities for browser caching.

It is a loading strategy, not a performance measurement. Bundle output and cache behavior still need inspection to establish what a particular release actually delivers.

Keep recovery data in the browser

For the local-file editing path, the application reads file bytes in the browser and converts them into the editor's workbook model.

Recovery storage follows the same local approach. The application stores a current snapshot and a separate version history in IndexedDB.

Versions include metadata such as their timestamp, source, and affected sheets. The code distinguishes automatic versions, manual versions, and versions captured before importing content or restoring an earlier state.

History also needs limits. The retention policy keeps recent versions, thins older entries into time buckets, and applies count and storage caps. Users can pin a limited number of versions.

These snapshots help recover work in the same browser. Exporting a file remains useful for keeping a separate copy, since browser storage can be cleared.

Small tools alongside the full editor

The project also includes focused spreadsheet utilities: removing duplicate rows, trimming whitespace, comparing files, and converting between formats such as XLSX, JSON, and Markdown.

Those tools provide shorter paths for tasks that do not require a full editing session. Someone who only needs a format conversion can start with that operation directly.

What this project has taught me

The visible grid is one part of a spreadsheet application. Much of the implementation lives at its boundaries: converting workbook models, preserving file parts, loading large dependencies, and retaining enough local history to recover from mistakes.

Separating those responsibilities makes the application easier to reason about. It also makes compatibility limits easier to describe precisely.

You can try the project at workbookeditor.com.

If you've built spreadsheet tooling, which workbook feature has been the hardest to preserve through an import-and-export cycle?

title: Gemini 4 Argon now available on AI Gateway
description:
Gemini 4 Argon from Google is now available on AI Gateway.

Gemini 4 Argon is built for coding, agentic work, and complex reasoning. It has a 1M token context window, accepts text, image, PDF, and video input, and supports tool calling.

On coding tasks, Gemini 4 Argon builds features, fixes bugs, and researches unfamiliar codebases, carrying longer tasks through multiple steps. The model also reads dense diagrams, spreadsheets, layout-heavy documents, and video, which suits tasks like a financial analysis spread across several spreadsheet tabs. Beyond code, it handles work in finance, health, and law, and hard problems in math and science. Gemini 4 Argon uses thinking levels (low, medium, and high) instead of thinking budgets.

title: Introducing Vercel Schedules
description:
Cron jobs are useful for work that needs to happen regularly. You can use them to do things such as back up your database on a schedule, or keep data in sync between two systems.

You define them once in code and then can update them by editing their config and redeploying. But today, agents interact with users as work evolves, and schedules need to be updated in real time.

We built Vercel Schedules to allow agents and applications to create, change, or cancel one-time and recurring schedules through code, without redeploying.

What are Vercel Schedules?

Schedules builds on the static approach used by Vercel Cron Jobs, but are designed to let users and agents decide when work should happen while your application is still running. A schedule tells Vercel when to trigger a task and where to send it. Your application provides the code that carries out the work.

You can use schedules for both static and dynamic jobs:

  • Static schedules keep the timing in vercel.json or Build Output API configuration and sync when you deploy. You can use them to call private functions or HTTP paths, or send messages to Queue topics.

  • Dynamic schedules let your app create and manage schedules through the JS SDK, CLI, or API as it runs. They support one-time and recurring work through Queue topics.

You can also test scheduled work on Preview deployments and in custom environments before running it in Production.

How Schedules works

Take this example: A user could ask an agent with web access, “Tomorrow morning, summarize the top five stories on Hacker News.” The traditional solution would be storing the request and its schedule time in a database, then using a cron job to check for work that is due.

With Schedules, an agent can create a schedule that records the request and when to run it, without a separate database and polling job. The example below defines an AI SDK tool that gives an agent this capability.

When the task is due, Vercel uses Queues to deliver the saved request to your app. Your app provides code to read that request, check the user’s current permissions, and start the agent. The agent fetches the top five Hacker News posts with a web tool, then returns a summary for your app to save for the user.

If you already build agents with fx’s JavaScript library, libfx or Pi’s agent library, you can add a similar scheduling tool. The eve agent framework uses Vercel Schedules to provide dynamic scheduling tools for production agents hosted on Vercel.

Run recurring application jobs

You can schedule recurring work with Vercel Schedules. Schedules can be created dynamically via the JS SDK, API, and CLI, or set up in your project’s configuration.

For example, to create a job that cleans up expired records every day, you could define a schedule that invokes a private function in your chosen time zone:

Vercel calls this cleanup code directly, without exposing it at a public URL. It checks that each call comes from the scheduling service, so you don’t have to add that check yourself.

If your app already uses the Nitro 3 server framework, its experimental integration lets you run the recurring jobs in your existing scheduledTasks configuration as private functions.

You can also try the agent task and cleanup locally with vercel dev, then test them on a Preview branch or in a custom environment before production. Use Run Schedule in your project’s Schedules tab to try either task without waiting, and see when past runs happened.

Get started

Vercel Schedules is now in Public Beta, and you can use it for the recurring tasks your application already runs. When a user or agent chooses when work should happen, your code can create and manage a schedule for that task.

To get started, check out the Vercel Schedules skill and read the documentation.

title: What a Successful Code Scan Does Not Prove
description:
Quick answer: A successful scan proves the document was rebuilt from routes the scan could resolve, and nothing more. It does not prove the implementation conforms to the spec, behaves correctly at runtime, or is free of defects. Treat unresolved findings as unknown rather than inferred facts, and verify runtime behavior separately through tests and scenario runs. The scan does not run the app.

What the scan actually establishes

The output of a scan is a validated OpenAPI 3.2 document with routes proven through framework tracing and AST analysis, and contracts classified by the completeness gate. That is a real result, but it is a statement about the document and its provenance, not a statement about runtime behavior.

Confusing the two leads to over-trust. A route that was detected and emitted is a route the code mounts, not a behavior that was verified.

Consider a handler that returns 200 on the happy path but throws on an input the scanner never exercises. The scan resolves the route, reads the declared response, and emits the document with a clean status, because every step it performed succeeded. The defect is still there, waiting for the input that triggers it. The scan cannot distinguish a handler that always returns the declared shape from one that only does so for the common inputs, since it never sends a request. That difference only shows up when a test or a scenario actually calls the route and asserts the response.

Claims a scan does not make

Claim Why a scan cannot support it
The implementation conforms Conformance needs runtime and contract verification, not just detection
The code is correct The scan does not run the app or assert behavior
Every route was found Dynamic loading and framework entry points can be missed
The response values are valid Detected shapes are not executed results
There are no defects Model-only and unresolved elements remain unknown

Read the gate labels alongside the green status, because a document can be internally valid while carrying gaps that name unresolved behavior.

A successful scan can sit alongside real defects, because none of its checks require the system to run.

How to treat unresolved findings

The honest move is to keep unknowns visible rather than rounding them into facts.

  • A gap stays an unknown, not an inferred value.
  • A route reached through dynamic loading may be missed and should be checked another way.
  • A model-only note remains a hypothesis until verified.
  • An empty result is inconclusive, not a pass.

When you meet an unresolved finding, mark it for a dynamic test or a scenario run rather than assuming the scan's silence means the path is safe.

What actually closes the gap

The scan is a starting point that feeds reliable later verification.

  1. Review the detected routes and the open gaps.
  2. Run tests and smoke checks to cover runtime behavior.
  3. Build scenario tests from the scanned spec to verify connected flows.
  4. Confirm contract evidence against the declared spec version.
  5. Keep the scan result separate from the runtime verdict.

This is the same boundary that keeps static signals from being written as guarantees. A deterministic verdict from real evidence can fail or pass behavior, but the scan itself does not produce that verdict.

Powerduck states the limit rather than hiding it, keeping the scan's provenance and the later runtime evidence as distinct things.

Frequently asked questions

Does a green scan mean the API conforms to its spec? No. It means the document was rebuilt from resolved routes. Conformance needs runtime and contract checks.

Can a successful scan still miss routes? Yes. Dynamic loading and framework entry points can be outside the static view, so verify those separately.

Should I treat gaps as harmless? No. A gap is an unknown, not a confirmed empty. Keep it open until a test or a reviewed fill resolves it.

The bottom line

A successful scan is a rebuilt, provenance-backed document, not a proof of conformance or correctness. It cannot certify runtime behavior it never executes, and it can miss routes reached through dynamic loading. Keep gaps and model-only notes as explicit unknowns, and close the real verification with tests and scenario runs. Over-reading a green scan is how unverified behavior gets mistaken for confirmed behavior. Continue in the code-to-OpenAPI guide.

title: I Rewrote the Same Function 3 Ways. The Fastest One Wasn't Worth It
description:
Sum the squares of the even numbers in a list. That is the whole job. I wrote it three ways this morning, ran all three 200 times each on a list of 10,000 numbers, and the result embarrassed the version I was rooting for.

The three versions

Shortest first, the one-liner I would have written in a hurry:

def shortest(nums):
    return sum(x * x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0)

Clearest second, the plain loop I would hand to a junior dev:

def clearest(nums):
    total = 0
    for x in nums:
        if x % 2 == 0:
            total += x * x
    return total

Fastest third, the one with the bit trick. x & 1 instead of x % 2, because everyone knows modulo is slow and bitwise is fast:

def fastest(nums):
    total = 0
    for x in nums:
        if not x & 1:
            total += x * x
    return total

Same input, same answer. I asserted that before timing anything, because a fast wrong answer is just a fast bug.

The real numbers

Here is the actual output from my machine, timeit, 200 runs each:

shortest  result=166616670000  200 runs in 0.103s  (0.514 ms/run)
clearest  result=166616670000  200 runs in 0.100s  (0.499 ms/run)
fastest   result=166616670000  200 runs in 0.099s  (0.497 ms/run)
all three agree: True

Read those timings again. The "fastest" version beat the clearest one by 0.002 milliseconds per run. Two microseconds. On a list of 10,000 numbers. If this function ran a million times a day, the bit trick would save you two seconds, and you would spend far longer than that explaining x & 1 to the next person who reads it.

I ran the timing twice to be sure, and the ordering wobbled. Some runs the one-liner won. The differences are noise. At this scale there is no fastest version. There are three versions of the same speed, and one of them is harder to read for nothing.

Which one I would keep

The clearest one. Not because loops are morally better, and not because I have anything against one-liners. Because of what happens six months from now, when someone opens this file at 11 p.m. because a billing total is wrong.

They will read the loop version in one pass. total starts at zero, evens get squared and added, done. The one-liner takes two passes: first you parse the generator, then you check the filter. It is not hard. It is just slower to read, and reading is what code spends most of its life doing.

The bit-trick version is the worst of the three. It saves nothing measurable and it makes the reader stop and think about binary. Every reader who stops is a reader who might misread it. if not x & 1 is the kind of line that looks clever in a pull request and confusing in a production incident.

I know the counterargument. Someone will say the bit trick matters in a hot loop, on big data. Fine. That is a different function in a different program, and you would measure it there. In this function, on this data, the trick bought two microseconds and cost a reader's attention. Bad trade.

The habit this broke

I used to reach for the clever version first. It felt like the job. What I actually shipped was code that only I could read quickly, and even I slowed down on it a month later.

Now I write the boring version first and only get clever when a measurement tells me to. The measurement has to be real, on real data, with a real difference. "Everyone knows modulo is slow" is not a measurement. It is a rumour with a long career.

Try it on your own code. Pick a function you think is slow, write the plain version next to the clever one, and time both. Half the time you will find what I found: the clever version wins by an amount nobody will ever feel, and the plain version wins every time someone has to read it.

title: Drizzle ORM: Your Database Schema, Written in TypeScript
description:
A small ceramics shop renamed one column. The orders table had a column called customer, and someone renamed it to customer_id. The shop's code built its queries by joining strings together, so nothing complained. The first sign of trouble came from a customer, whose order page showed a blank where her name should have been. The query had failed quietly, and nobody noticed until she did. That is the problem an ORM is supposed to solve: the database and the code should agree about the shape of the data, and a rename should break loudly at build time instead of quietly in production. Drizzle ORM takes an angle on that promise, and this post tests whether it holds up.

What I would check before using it

My judgement, from years of building small web apps, is that Drizzle is the right call when you like SQL and want the compiler to watch your back, and the wrong call when you want the database to disappear entirely. Drizzle does not hide SQL the way some ORMs do. You write queries that look a lot like SQL, with select, eq, and innerJoin, and the result is typed. That suits a team that already reads SQL, and frustrates one that wants to think in objects and never see a JOIN.

I would check four things before committing. First, the database and the driver. Drizzle supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite, but each one needs its own driver package, and the driver decides what works. In this post I used better-sqlite3, because the node-sqlite driver is not exported by drizzle-orm 0.45.4. Check the driver for your database before you write any schema code. Second, migrations. Drizzle Kit generates SQL migration files from your schema; read them before applying. Third, relations. The relational query API, db.query, only works when you define relations between your tables. Without them, the call fails, as the mistakes section shows. Fourth, the ecosystem. Drizzle is younger and smaller than Prisma, so there are fewer tutorials and fewer answers to odd questions.

The verdict: choose Drizzle when your project is TypeScript, your team is comfortable with SQL, and you want type safety without giving up control of your queries. That recommendation flips if the team wants the database abstracted away, if you need the biggest possible ecosystem, or if your database driver is not well supported. Then a heavier ORM, or plain SQL with a thin query builder, is the better bet.

A small shop's orders, end to end

The worked example is the ceramics shop from the opening: customers, products, orders, and the items on each order. The schema is written in TypeScript, so the tables, columns, and foreign keys sit in one file, and the compiler knows about every column. Here is the schema:

// schema.js
const { sqliteTable, integer, text, real } = require('drizzle-orm/sqlite-core');

const customers = sqliteTable('customers', {
  id: integer('id').primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  name: text('name').notNull(),
  email: text('email').notNull().unique(),
});

const products = sqliteTable('products', {
  id: integer('id').primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  name: text('name').notNull(),
  price: real('price').notNull(),
  stock: integer('stock').notNull(),
});

const orders = sqliteTable('orders', {
  id: integer('id').primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  customerId: integer('customer_id')
    .notNull()
    .references(() => customers.id),
  status: text('status').notNull(),
});

const orderItems = sqliteTable('order_items', {
  id: integer('id').primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  orderId: integer('order_id')
    .notNull()
    .references(() => orders.id),
  productId: integer('product_id')
    .notNull()
    .references(() => products.id),
  quantity: integer('quantity').notNull(),
});

module.exports = { customers, products, orders, orderItems };

The references calls are the foreign keys: an order belongs to a customer, and each order item points at one order and one product, so the database refuses rows that point nowhere. The demo script creates the tables with plain SQL, inserts real rows, and totals each order with a join across all four tables:

// demo.js (inserts and the totals query; table creation uses plain SQL)
db.insert(customers).values([
  { name: 'Ayesha', email: 'ayesha@example.com' },
  { name: 'Bilal', email: 'bilal@example.com' },
]).run();

db.insert(products).values([
  { name: 'Ceramic mug', price: 18.0, stock: 40 },
  { name: 'Linen tote', price: 24.5, stock: 25 },
  { name: 'Desk lamp', price: 42.0, stock: 12 },
]).run();

db.insert(orders).values([
  { customerId: 1, status: 'ready to ship' },
  { customerId: 2, status: 'awaiting payment' },
]).run();

db.insert(orderItems).values([
  { orderId: 1, productId: 1, quantity: 2 },
  { orderId: 1, productId: 3, quantity: 1 },
  { orderId: 2, productId: 2, quantity: 3 },
]).run();

const totals = db
  .select({
    orderId: orders.id,
    customer: customers.name,
    status: orders.status,
    total: sql`round(sum(${products.price} * ${orderItems.quantity}), 2)`,
  })
  .from(orders)
  .innerJoin(customers, eq(orders.customerId, customers.id))
  .innerJoin(orderItems, eq(orderItems.orderId, orders.id))
  .innerJoin(products, eq(orderItems.productId, products.id))
  .groupBy(orders.id, customers.name, orders.status)
  .orderBy(orders.id)
  .all();

for (const row of totals) {
  console.log(
    'Order ' + row.orderId + ' (' + row.customer + ', ' + row.status + '): $' + row.total
  );
}

Running it against a fresh SQLite file gave this real output:

Order totals:
Order 1 (Ayesha, ready to ship): $78
Order 2 (Bilal, awaiting payment): $73.5

Both totals check out by hand: order 1 is two mugs at $18 plus one lamp at $42, which is $78, and order 2 is three totes at $24.50, which is $73.50. The query reads almost like the SQL it produces, and the rows are typed from the schema, so row.total is a number and row.customer a string, with no extra declarations.

Now the part the tidy tutorials skip: something goes wrong. A line of code adds an item to order 999, an order that does not exist, because the id came from a form field that was typed wrong:

db.insert(orderItems)
  .values({ orderId: 999, productId: 1, quantity: 1 })
  .run();

The real error from running this is short and to the point:

Insert failed: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed

The database refused the row because order 999 does not exist, and the foreign key on order_id caught it. That is the schema doing its job: the bad data never reaches the table. The fix is to use an order id that exists, which here means order 1:

db.insert(orderItems)
  .values({ orderId: 1, productId: 2, quantity: 1 })
  .run();

That insert worked at once, adding one linen tote to Ayesha's order. The habit to take away is to let the database enforce the relationships and to treat a constraint error as useful news. Without the foreign key, the orphan row would have sat there quietly until a report or a customer found it.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

1. Forgetting .all() or .run(). A select without .all() returns a query builder, not rows, and nothing complains: logging it shows an object, and .length is undefined. End every select with .all() or .get(), and every insert, update, or delete with .run().

2. Inserting a duplicate value in a unique column. A second customer with the email ayesha@example.com fails with UNIQUE constraint failed: customers.email. Check for the existing customer first, or catch the error and say the email is already registered.

3. Selecting a column that is not in the schema. Writing orders.total when the orders table has no total column gives Cannot convert undefined or null to object in plain JavaScript, while TypeScript catches it before the code runs. The fix is to compute the total in the query, as the worked example does.

4. Using db.query without defining relations. Calling db.query.customers.findMany() with no relations defined fails with Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'findMany'). The fix is to define relations in the schema, or to use the select query builder above, which needs none.

Where this leaves you

Drizzle earns its place when you want the compiler to know your database and want to see the SQL you are running. The schema is a file you can read, the queries look like the SQL they become, and the database catches bad rows. Its costs are real: you pick a driver per database, define relations before the query API works, and the ecosystem is smaller than the older ORMs. The next step: take one table from your own project, write its schema in Drizzle, and run one insert and one join against a local database. When a renamed column breaks the build instead of a customer's page, you have your answer.

Further reading

  • Drizzle ORM, Overview
  • Drizzle ORM, Get Started with SQLite
  • Drizzle ORM, Relations
  • SQLite, Foreign Key Support

Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/drizzle-orm-your-database-schema.html

title: Inferring Many-to-Many Link Tables
description:
Quick answer: When two schemas reference each other in a way that implies a repeated relationship, the modeling layer infers a many-to-many link table that holds the two foreign keys. It stays in the Inferred layer rather than being treated as a confirmed table, and when the cardinality is ambiguous it raises an open question instead of guessing.

Why a link table is needed

A one-to-many relationship fits naturally on one side, with a foreign key pointing back. A many-to-many relationship does not, because each side can relate to many rows on the other, and forcing the relationship into either table would require storing a list of keys rather than a clean relational design.

A link table resolves that. It carries one foreign key to each side, and each pair becomes a row, which keeps the design relational and easy to query.

What the inference looks like

Element Role
Left foreign key Points to the first entity
Right foreign key Points to the second entity
Composite key Enforces the unique pair
Indexes Support the queries from both sides

The link table is proposed from the repeated references in the schemas rather than a hand-named table, and it is kept separate from the observed tables.

How the inference is made

  1. Read the schemas and identify the entities that reference each other.
  2. Check whether the relationship repeats on both sides.
  3. Propose a link table with the two foreign keys.
  4. Add the composite key and the indexes.
  5. Keep it labeled as inferred and raise an open question if the cardinality is unclear.

The composite key matters because it stops the same pair from being recorded twice, and the indexes keep the lookups from either entity efficient.

The classic example is students and courses. A student enrolls in many courses, and a course has many students, so neither table can hold a single foreign key to the other. The inferred link table carries one key to the student and one to the course, and the composite key keeps the same enrollment from appearing twice. A query from either side stays simple: follow the link to read the related rows. If the real rule is closer to one-to-many, such as a course that belongs to only one department, the open question catches it before the join table is built, and the reviewer can confirm the cardinality rather than inherit a wrong join.

Why the inference stays labeled

An inferred link table is lower confidence than a table observed in the live database. The schemas may imply a join that the real design handles differently, or the cardinality may be closer to one-to-many than many-to-many, and promoting the inference would hide that uncertainty.

Keeping it in the Inferred layer is the honest move. The reviewer can confirm the relationship against the business logic, resolve the open question, and only then move the table into the proposed plan. This is the same boundary that keeps a static signal from being written as a guarantee.

The ER diagram reflects the node state, and the generated DDL for the link table is still never executed by the modeling package. The deployment script stays idempotent and forward-only.

Powerduck keeps the inferred link tables and their open questions visible rather than quietly emitting them as confirmed facts.

Frequently asked questions

How is a link table different from a foreign key? A foreign key fits a one-to-many relationship on one side, while a link table carries two foreign keys to model many-to-many.

What stops a duplicate pair? A composite key on the two foreign keys enforces the unique pair.

Is an inferred link table ready to deploy? Not by itself. It stays inferred until the relationship is confirmed and the open question is resolved.

The bottom line

A many-to-many relationship is best modeled by a join table with two foreign keys and a composite key, inferred from the repeated references rather than forced into one entity. It stays in the Inferred layer, and ambiguous cardinality raises an open question rather than a guess. Confirm the relationship before the table enters the plan, and remember the generated DDL is never executed for you. The inference is a proposal, not a confirmed table. Read more in the API data model guide.

title: S3 Alternative Storage Providers with a Free Tier for User Files — Tenant Isolation
description:
Short answer: For storing user files in a fintech report service, start with a private shared bucket and tenant-derived keys; test Backblaze B2 first if a free tier matters, and choose a separate bucket boundary only for tenants that need independent retention or administration.

The least complex implementation is a private, S3-compatible object store with tenant identity kept outside the object namespace. Keep reports private, make the tenant part of every key, and calculate storage, bandwidth, and request costs before choosing a provider. For a fintech product, that boundary matters more than whether a dashboard happens to call itself an S3 alternative.

Backblaze B2 is the strongest first experiment when a free tier matters. Wasabi is a credible alternative when a low flat-rate storage model fits the workload, although it does not offer a free tier for experimentation. Both expose S3-compatible APIs, so a migration can preserve much of the application-facing contract. Infrai is another candidate for teams that want a plain REST surface and one backend key, but its storage limitations make it a conditional fit rather than a default answer.

What does the bill actually contain?

The bill is not “number of files times storage price.” A report service pays for retained bytes, bytes downloaded when a customer opens or shares a report, and object operations. File-sharing applications often discover the second term late: a popular report can be downloaded many times while its stored size remains unchanged.

Start with three monthly estimates:

  • retained data, including unfinished or superseded files;
  • outbound bandwidth, including repeated downloads and previews;
  • operations, including uploads, reads, listings, and lifecycle transitions.

Then make the product decision that changes the dominant term. If customers repeatedly download the same generated PDF, a retention rule alone will not fix bandwidth. If reports are private and rarely revisited, retaining fewer intermediate artifacts may matter more than shaving a request charge.

Measure it.

This is where Backblaze B2 and Wasabi separate. B2 has a free tier and competitive pricing for additional storage and access requests, which makes a small proof of concept easier to measure. Wasabi offers a low flat-rate storage cost, but the absence of a free tier changes the experiment: you need a real usage estimate before treating it as the simpler financial choice. Neither statement replaces a current calculation.

The thing I deliberately stop keeping is every generated intermediate. That reduces retention, but it also removes an easy recovery path when a report is regenerated incorrectly. Keep the source inputs or a durable job record where the compliance policy requires it; do not pretend that lifecycle deletion is a backup strategy.

Two viable architectures for tenant isolation

There are two sensible shapes for this system.

The first uses a shared bucket with a tenant-prefixed key such as tenant_42/reports/2026/10/statement.pdf. The application authorizes the tenant before it constructs the key, and object reads happen through a server-issued signed URL or a backend stream. The invariant is simple: an authenticated request can address only keys derived from its authorized tenant identity. A prefix is an index, not an authorization decision. The database or authorization layer still has to make that decision.

The second uses separate buckets or storage accounts per isolation boundary. Its invariant is stronger at the storage boundary: a credential or policy associated with one tenant cannot address another tenant's container. The trade-off is operational weight. Provisioning, lifecycle changes, monitoring, and migrations now multiply with the number of boundaries. For a small number of regulated tenants, that burden can be justified. For thousands of ordinary customer tenants, it can become the system you spend more time operating than the report service itself.

I prefer the shared-bucket shape for most customer report workloads, with separate buckets for tenants whose contractual or regulatory requirements demand a hard storage boundary. It keeps the application model understandable and lets the authorization layer remain the source of truth. The decision is conditional, though: if a tenant must be independently recoverable, independently administered, or independently retained, use the stronger boundary.

Which S3 alternative storage providers have a free tier for user files?

The comparison should be about the invariants you can preserve during a migration, not a table of volatile prices.

Option Useful fit Boundary to verify
Backblaze B2 A cost-conscious evaluation that benefits from a free tier, S3 compatibility, and competitive storage and access pricing Confirm retention, lifecycle, compliance, and bandwidth assumptions with the current service terms
Wasabi A workload that suits a low flat-rate storage model and can start without a free trial tier Model actual retention and downloads before committing to the storage shape
Amazon S3 A direct S3 reference point when the existing application already speaks the protocol Compare lifecycle, retention, compliance, bandwidth, and operations for the exact workload
Cloudflare R2 An S3-compatible option worth including when the migration plan already covers R2-style providers Verify the required retention, lifecycle, and compliance behavior rather than assuming protocol compatibility means feature parity

S3 compatibility helps with migration, but it does not make providers interchangeable. Check retention policies, lifecycle rules, compliance support, and the behavior of signed reads. Also check the ugly cases: a partially uploaded object, a deleted tenant, a customer who downloads the same file 200 times, and an authorization record that disappears before the object does.

Infrai belongs in the comparison when the backend team values a plain REST API over installing and versioning a storage SDK. Anything that can send an HTTP request can use that surface, and the public discovery surface documents the available capabilities and runnable examples. The discovery surface is public with no key required, which is useful when a team wants to inspect request schemas before wiring a tenant path into production.

The second advantage is operational rather than storage-specific: Infrai's one-key / one-bill model covers 295 routes in 20 modules. The API is self-describing, so a report workflow can inspect a request schema before wiring it into a worker. That keeps one integration boundary as the job service adds adjacent backend work, instead of teaching every worker a new client-library lifecycle.

Here is the shape of a private object write. The application still authorizes the tenant and serves a signed read URL; the write key is never exposed to the browser.

import os
import time
import uuid

import requests


def put_private_report(report_bytes):
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
        "Idempotency-Key": str(uuid.uuid4()),
        "Content-Type": "application/pdf",
        "X-Object-Access": "signed-only",
    }

    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.put(
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/reports/tenant_42%2Freports%2Fstatement.pdf",
            headers=headers,
            data=report_bytes,
            timeout=30,
        )
        if response.status_code != 429:
            response.raise_for_status()
            return response
        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = int(retry_after) if retry_after and retry_after.isdigit() else 2**attempt
        time.sleep(delay)

    raise RuntimeError("storage write remained rate-limited after retries")

The idempotency key makes a retry safe for the write operation, while the signed-only access setting keeps the object out of a public-link pattern. A production caller should also log the response request ID and preserve the error body for a 4xx response.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for a private report-store path when your team wants HTTP-level integration and can enforce authorization in its own application layer, then keep provider-specific retention and recovery policy explicit. This angle matters because it reduces integration surface without pretending that the storage service supplies every durability control a regulated archive needs.

The limits are material. The storage path is not suitable for static website hosting, permanently public links, or an image-hosting pattern because public or public-read ACLs are unavailable and public_url is always null. There is no object versioning or object lock, so an accidental overwrite is not recoverable through the storage layer. Strict If-Match concurrency needs coordination in a queue or database. Browser-direct uploads cannot rely on a self-service CORS route. There is no automatic cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool.

Lifecycle rules have a one-day minimum, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and metadata cannot be searched server-side beyond prefix filtering in list operations. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes. Those constraints put a specialist or direct provider ahead of Infrai for immutable financial archives, browser-heavy direct upload, or a system that needs a built-in disaster-recovery copy.

How should retention and access be tested?

Treat the object key as an address, never as proof of permission. A report request should authenticate the customer, resolve the tenant from the application identity, check that the report belongs to that tenant, and only then issue a short-lived signed read. The storage credential should stay on the server. Do not send the backend authorization header to a returned signed URL.

Retention needs a written rule for each class of artifact. Generated reports, source documents, failed-job leftovers, and multipart fragments do not have the same value. A one-day minimum lifecycle can be fine for temporary reports, but it is not an hourly cleanup mechanism. If an object must be immutable, put that requirement in the architecture decision before choosing a provider; an overwrite that succeeds is not repaired by a later audit log.

The test matrix should include tenant A attempting tenant B's key, a report that has been deleted from the database, an expired signed URL, a repeated download, an overwrite race, and a failed multipart upload. Record storage, bandwidth, and operation counts for the same test data. Five minutes spent on those cases is more useful than another generic S3 compatibility claim.

The decision rule

Choose the shared-bucket architecture when tenant isolation is primarily an application authorization problem and your customers share retention policy. Choose separate buckets when the storage boundary itself must express customer independence. Start the provider comparison with B2 if a free tier makes experimentation important; evaluate Wasabi when its flat-rate storage model matches measured retention and download behavior; include S3 and R2 as real migration references rather than assuming one API means one operational model.

Choose Infrai only when its plain REST integration and consolidated backend surface are valuable enough to accept the missing public access, versioning, object lock, self-service CORS, and replication features. That is a useful fit for private authenticated reports. It is not a universal storage answer.

Further reading

  • Infrai storage discovery
  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet
  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Backblaze B2 documentation
  • Wasabi documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation

If this boundary fits your system, start by inspecting the storage discovery documentation and verify the retention and access rules against your own tenant policy.

title: PNG vs WebP vs AVIF: Which Image Format Should You Use?
description:
PNG vs WebP vs AVIF: Which Image Format Should You Use?

Images account for over 50% of the total byte weight of the average web page. For web developers and digital designers, selecting the proper image format is one of the most effective levers for optimizing Core Web Vitals, reducing Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) latency, and conserving user data.

For decades, the web relied on two legacy formats: JPEG for continuous-tone photography and PNG for graphics requiring crisp lines or alpha transparency. Today, modern codecs like WebP and AVIF offer dramatically superior compression ratios and versatile feature sets. Browser-based platforms like PixKilo allow developers to take advantage of these modern formats immediately by converting assets locally with zero server latency.

However, each format comes with distinct architectural trade-offs regarding encoding performance, decoding latency, fidelity preservation, and legacy browser support. In this guide, we will break down the underlying mechanics of PNG, WebP, and AVIF, compare their strengths and weaknesses, and provide an actionable decision framework for modern web development.

1. Portable Network Graphics (PNG)

Introduced in 1996 as a patent-free successor to GIF, PNG is a raster graphics container built strictly on lossless compression.

The Underlying Mechanics

PNG uses a two-stage compression pipeline:

  1. Filtering: Predictive filters (None, Sub, Up, Average, Paeth) convert absolute pixel values into relative differences between neighbors, increasing data redundancy.
  2. Deflate Algorithm: The filtered deltas are compressed using Deflate, combining LZ77 dictionary substitution with Huffman coding.

Key Strengths

  • True Lossless Quality: Zero mathematical degradation of pixel data. Every single RGB color value and alpha transparency level is preserved bit-for-bit.
  • Flawless Text & Line Art: Highly effective for UI mockups, icons, technical diagrams, and typography where lossy compression artifacts would create noticeable edge fuzziness.
  • Universal Compatibility: Supported by every web browser, operating system, and image editing application in existence.

Where PNG Falls Short

PNG is structurally inefficient for photographic content. Continuous real-world color variations produce low repetitive entropy for the Deflate algorithm, resulting in file sizes that are frequently 5x to 10x larger than modern lossy alternatives.

2. WebP: Google's Modern Web Workhorse

Released by Google in 2010 and now universally supported across all major evergreen browsers, WebP was explicitly engineered to accelerate web page loading speeds.

The Underlying Mechanics

WebP is based on the intra-frame encoding technology of the VP8 video codec:

  • Spatial Block Prediction: Rather than encoding pixels in isolation, WebP analyzes sub-blocks, predicting neighboring pixel values based on adjacent blocks already decoded, storing only the residual difference.
  • Dual Personality: WebP supports both lossy compression (VP8 based, with 4:2:0 chroma subsampling) and lossless compression (VP8L).
  • Alpha Channel Support: Unlike JPEG, lossy WebP natively supports 8-bit alpha transparency. You can have a high-compression photographic element seamlessly blend into a colored background.

Real-World Performance

Lossy WebP files are on average 25% to 34% smaller than comparable JPEGs at equivalent visual quality, while lossless WebP is approximately 26% smaller than standard PNGs.

3. AV1 Image File Format (AVIF)

Standardized in 2019 by the Alliance for Open Media (AOMedia)—including Google, Apple, Mozilla, and Microsoft—AVIF is an image container derived from AV1 video keyframes.

The Underlying Mechanics

AVIF utilizes directional prediction filters, variable block partitioning (from 4x4 up to 128x128 superblocks), and Chroma-from-Luma prediction:

  • Extreme High-Compression Fidelity: Where JPEG and WebP break down into blocks at low bitrates, AVIF retains structural coherence.
  • Wide Color Gamut & HDR: Supports 10-bit and 12-bit color depths, HDR, and the BT.2020 color space.

The Trade-offs of AVIF

While AVIF delivers up to 50% smaller files than JPEG and roughly 20% smaller than WebP, it demands higher computational power during encoding. Encoding high-resolution images to AVIF can take 5x to 10x longer than WebP, occasionally introducing CPU bottlenecks on dynamic media servers.

Comparison Matrix

Feature PNG WebP AVIF
Compression Mode Lossless Only Lossy & Lossless Lossy & Lossless
Transparency (Alpha) Yes (Full 8-bit) Yes (In both modes) Yes (In both modes)
Animation Support APNG (Limited) Yes (Animated WebP) Yes (AVIS / Image Sequence)
Color Bit Depth 8 / 16-bit 8-bit 8 / 10 / 12-bit (HDR)
Encoding Speed Very Fast Fast Moderate to Slow
Decoding Speed Instant Extremely Fast Fast on modern hardware
Browser Support 100% >97% Global >93% Global

Actionable Decision Matrix: What Should You Use?

  1. Use PNG when:
    • You need pixel-perfect precision for digital illustrations, logo vectors, screenshots with micro-text, or graphics requiring mathematical fidelity.
    • The graphic is being exported as a master source asset for printing or design software.
  2. Use WebP when:
    • You want an optimal balance between exceptional compression, fast encoding speed, and near-universal browser compatibility.
    • You are replacing standard product photos, blog hero banners, and social avatars across an existing web property.
  3. Use AVIF when:
    • You are optimizing performance-critical hero images or mobile landing pages where every kilobyte directly impacts revenue and SEO rankings.
    • You are utilizing modern responsive <picture> tags with progressive fallback mechanisms.

Implementing Progressive Fallbacks in HTML

To harness the bandwidth savings of AVIF and WebP without breaking older devices or specialized web view clients, implement the modern <picture> element:

<picture>
  <!-- Modern browsers supporting AVIF will load the smallest file -->
  <source srcset="/images/hero.avif" type="image/avif" />

  <!-- Fallback for browsers supporting WebP -->
  <source srcset="/images/hero.webp" type="image/webp" />

  <!-- Universal baseline fallback -->
  <img 
    src="/images/hero.png" 
    alt="Detailed application analytics dashboard preview"
    width="1200" 
    height="630" 
    loading="lazy" 
    decoding="async" 
  />
</picture>

Programmatic Browser Conversion

You can easily convert images between these formats right in your web app using canvas:

async function convertImageFormat(sourceFile, targetMimeType = 'image/webp', quality = 0.85) {
  const bitmap = await createImageBitmap(sourceFile);
  const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
  canvas.width = bitmap.width;
  canvas.height = bitmap.height;

  const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
  ctx.drawImage(bitmap, 0, 0);

  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    canvas.toBlob(
      (blob) => resolve(blob),
      targetMimeType,
      quality
    );
  });
}

If you need to batch convert images on your computer without uploading them to remote servers, explore PixKilo's Image Converter. It lets you drop up to 10 images at once and convert between PNG, JPG, and WebP instantly using local browser memory. You can also pair it with PixKilo's Image Compressor to achieve maximum byte savings for your web projects.

Conclusion

The web has moved past the era of one-size-fits-all image formatting. PNG remains essential for crisp, lossless digital assets, while WebP provides the most reliable workhorse for everyday web media. AVIF represents the future of cutting-edge web compression. By combining smart format selection with modern <picture> element fallbacks, you can deliver visually stunning web experiences while keeping your asset payload minimal.

To convert and optimize your web graphics for free with 100% privacy, visit PixKilo and explore their complete suite of browser-based image utilities.

title: Skip sending request bodies to Routing Middleware
description:
You can now skip sending client request bodies to Routing Middleware with skipMiddlewareRequestBody. This reduces incoming Fast Origin Transfer usage for middleware invocations and can improve time to first byte, especially for requests with large bodies.

Enable this option only if your Routing Middleware doesn’t read request bodies. Vercel Functions and rewrite targets still receive the body, so you can read and process it there.

Set skipMiddlewareRequestBody to true in your project’s JSON configuration file, vercel.json:

If you use a TypeScript configuration file, add the same setting to vercel.ts instead. This example assumes @vercel/config is installed:

Redeploy your project for the change to take effect. The option defaults to false, so existing projects are unchanged unless you enable it.

title: Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available on Vercel
description:
Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available for builds and Vercel Functions.

This release includes:

  • HTTP/2 by default for built-in fetch (Undici 8) lets multiple requests share a connection with servers that support it. This can reduce latency when your functions call APIs or databases over HTTP.

  • Temporal API offers an alternative to Date with immutable values and built-in time zone and calendar support.

  • V8 version 14.6, the updated JavaScript engine, adds features such as Map.prototype.getOrInsert() to retrieve an existing value or insert a default when a key is missing.

Using Node.js 26

Node.js 26 is the default for all new projects.

  • Automatic upgrades: If engines.node in your existing project’s package.json allows 26, such as >=20, your Node.js builds on Vercel will use 26 on the next deployment.

  • Manual upgrades: Set engines.node to 26.x in your project's package.json and redeploy.

  • Prebuilt deployments: Use Vercel CLI version 65.8.0 or later to deploy Node.js 26 Functions.

  • HTTP/1.1 in Functions: To keep HTTP/1.1, set the VERCEL_FETCH_DISABLE_H2 environment variable to 1 and redeploy.

Minor and patch updates to Node.js 26 roll out automatically for builds and Vercel Functions.

Read the Node.js version documentation to learn more.
