title: What are the best Hyperstack alternatives for AI training?
description:
Nodus is the Hyperstack alternative to pick for AI training if you want a lower H100 price and no bill for idle machines: it lists the NVIDIA H100 SXM at $2.60 per GPU-hour on the Nodus pricing page, against $3.20 on demand at Hyperstack. It runs training as a job that stops billing when it ends and restores your latest checkpoint if a machine is lost. Pick RunPod for pods at a fixed price, Lambda for whole 8-GPU machines, Modal for short Python functions, and stay on Hyperstack for VMs with free data transfer.

We build Nodus, so read this with that in mind. Every fact about another company links to its own pricing page or docs, and the arithmetic is written out so you can redo it with the prices you see today.

What does Hyperstack do well, and why do teams look elsewhere?

Hyperstack sells GPU virtual machines with per-minute prepaid billing and no bandwidth charges. Its pricing page lists everything from an NVIDIA RTX A4000 at $0.15 per hour to an NVIDIA B300 at $7.40, plus reservations, spot VMs and free ingress and egress.

If you are comparing alternatives, the reason is usually one of these. You want a lower H100 SXM rate without signing a reservation. You are tired of paying for machines that sit idle between runs. Or you want spot prices without writing your own recovery logic, because Hyperstack spot VMs come with no termination notice.

None of these is a flaw in the product. They come with running your own VM, and some alternatives move them onto the platform.

How much does the same training run cost on each platform?

We priced one run, GPU compute only: 8 x NVIDIA H100 SXM for 10 hours, which is 80 GPU-hours. Storage, CPU-only machines and taxes are left out on every platform.

Platform H100 SXM per GPU-hour 80 GPU-hours How billing works
Nodus $2.60 $208.00 Prepaid credits; a Job is charged only for the time it used
RunPod Community Cloud $2.69 $215.20 Per second, pods
Hyperstack on demand $3.20 $256.00 Per minute, prepaid, VMs
Modal $3.95 $315.94 Per second, functions
RunPod Secure Cloud $3.99 $319.20 Per second, pods
Lambda (8-GPU instance) $4.59 $367.20 Per GPU-hour, instances

Prices checked November 7, 2026: Nodus pricing, Hyperstack pricing, RunPod pricing, Modal pricing and Lambda pricing. Modal's $0.001097 per second is multiplied by 288,000 seconds for the Modal row.


Nodus lists the H100 SXM below Hyperstack's on-demand rate and below its reservation starting price.

Hyperstack's reservation pricing narrows the gap. Its pricing page shows H100 SXM reservations starting from $2.72 per hour, which would make the same run $217.60, but that rate needs a reservation and Hyperstack invoices reservations monthly.

Do you pay for a Hyperstack VM after you stop it?

Yes, and it is the easiest cost to miss. Hyperstack's VM states and billing page says a stopped VM enters the SHUTOFF state and billing continues for all its resources, because they stay reserved for that VM. To stop GPU charges you have to hibernate it or delete it.

Here is what that means for our example. Say the 10-hour run ends at 6 pm and the VM is shut off until 8 am, a 14-hour gap.

  • Shut off: 8 GPUs x $3.20 x 14 hours = $358.40, more than the run itself.
  • Hibernated: GPU, CPU and RAM are not billed, but the root disk is saved at $0.000096774 per GB-hour. For a 500 GB root disk, that is 500 x $0.000096774 x 14 = $0.68.
  • Deleted: $0.00.

On Nodus there is no VM to forget. A Job that has finished shows Succeeded, Failed or Cancelled, and the Jobs guide says nothing is running or billed in those states. The overnight cost of a finished Job is $0.00.


A shut-off VM keeps billing at the full GPU rate; hibernating or deleting it fixes that, and a finished Job never starts.

The rule we take from this: if your team runs training in bursts, the platform that bills only while work runs often beats a lower hourly rate. If you keep one machine busy all day, the hourly rate is what matters.

Can you train on Hyperstack spot VMs safely?

You can, but recovery is your job. Hyperstack's spot VM docs say spot VMs carry a non-zero risk of termination without prior notice, with no email or in-platform alert. Its spot VMs page adds that they cannot be paused or saved as custom images, and that spot prices are a fixed 20% below on demand.

That 20% is real money. Hyperstack's spot NVIDIA H100 PCIe was $2.00 per hour when we checked, against $2.50 on demand. But a run that is not checkpointing off the machine gives the savings back fast. If an 8-GPU spot run is lost at hour 6 of 10 and restarts from zero, you pay again for 48 GPU-hours, which is $96.00 at $2.00.

Nodus handles interruptible capacity differently. Its attempts and recovery docs say that on a reclaim notice Nodus asks your job for an urgent checkpoint and prepares a replacement machine at the same time. A machine that goes silent gets a replacement prepared after 20 seconds and is declared lost after 60.

A Checkpointed run restarts from its latest committed checkpoint, so it loses only the work since that checkpoint. Our spot vs on-demand guide covers when interruptible capacity is worth it.

Which Hyperstack alternative fits your training job?

Start from the problem you want gone.

  • You want to stop babysitting machines and paying for idle ones: Nodus. Jobs bill only while they run, a --max-cost cap stops a run at a dollar limit, and checkpoints are restored on a new machine.
  • You want a fixed hourly price and a pod you can SSH into: RunPod. Its Community Cloud H100 SXM was $2.69 per hour; our RunPod alternatives guide compares it in more depth.
  • You want a whole 8-GPU machine or a reserved cluster: Lambda, at $4.59 per GPU-hour for an 8 x H100 instance, with 2-week to 1-year cluster terms on its pricing page. See Nodus vs Lambda for the trade-offs.
  • Your work is short Python functions next to web endpoints: Modal, billed per second.
  • You want a VM with root access, free egress and a reservation: stay on Hyperstack.

Hyperstack is not a cloud account you can connect to Nodus today. The supported clouds are listed in the cloud accounts guide.

Where is Hyperstack the better choice?

Hyperstack wins when data movement and control matter more than the hourly rate. Ingress and egress are free on its pricing page, which matters if you move large datasets or checkpoints in and out every day. You get a full VM, hibernation that keeps your root disk while GPU billing stops, and an On-Demand Kubernetes service with a free master node.

It also has the cheapest H100 in our research. Its spot H100 PCIe at $2.00 per hour is below every H100 SXM rate in the table above, if your job checkpoints and tolerates sudden loss.

Location can decide it too. Hyperstack's regions page lists data centers in Norway, Canada and Texas, and marks the Norway and Canada regions as sustainably powered. It quotes up to 350 Gbps of inter-VM bandwidth in SR-IOV environments in Canada and Texas. If you need those regions or that networking, the switch may not be worth it.

How do you move a Hyperstack training job to Nodus?

Point your checkpoint writes at /nodus/state and run your existing command with the Nodus CLI. Install it and sign in:

pip install nodus-compute
nodus login

Then dry-run the job to see the estimate. Every flag below is in the nodus run CLI reference; the torchrun part is your own command:

nodus run --name ft-h100 --gpu H100:8 --image nodus/pytorch \
  --checkpoint /nodus/state --continuity Checkpointed --interruptible \
  --max-cost 250 --dry-run -- torchrun --nproc_per_node 8 train.py

Remove --dry-run to submit. The --max-cost 250 cap sits above the $208.00 list-price estimate for 80 GPU-hours. If the run would spend more, it saves its state and suspends instead of billing past the cap.

FAQ

Is Hyperstack cheaper than Nodus?

For the NVIDIA H100 SXM, no: Hyperstack listed $3.20 per hour on demand and reservations from $2.72, against $2.60 on Nodus when we checked. Hyperstack's spot H100 PCIe at $2.00 is cheaper per hour, for jobs that can handle termination without notice.

Does Hyperstack charge for data transfer?

No. Its pricing page lists ingress and egress traffic as free. A retained public IP costs $0.00672 per hour.

What happens when a Hyperstack prepaid balance runs out?

Hyperstack's pricing FAQ says resources are scheduled for termination after a short grace period, and may be permanently deleted if the account is not recharged within a week. On Nodus, a Job that runs out of credits saves its state, suspends and resumes on its own once funded, per the Jobs guide.

Does Hyperstack bill per second?

No. Hyperstack bills on-demand usage per minute. Nodus, RunPod and Modal all list per-second or exact usage billing, so short runs cost slightly less on them.

Can I keep using Hyperstack and Nodus together?

Yes. You can keep a VM for interactive work and send long or interruptible training runs to Nodus as Jobs. Nodus does not run on your Hyperstack account, so the two bill separately.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: Game Replay Files: Browser Direct Object Storage Uploads via Presigned PUT
description:
Short answer: for a gaming app moving large media, let the browser send bytes to private object storage with a short-lived presigned PUT, and make Node.js or Express sign and confirm the handoff. Keep signed download URLs on the read path. The decision is about access control versus delivery simplicity: the API should authorize the object, while storage carries the file.

That boundary is a capacity decision. A proxy makes every slow player connection consume an API worker, socket, and egress path. A direct upload makes the control plane handle short requests while the storage service handles the long transfer. I put separate SLOs on those paths: signing and confirmation latency belong to the API SLO; upload completion and download time belong to the data path. They fail differently.

Keep the bucket private. No public shortcut.

What should a Node.js Express signer and React client agree on for a private bucket upload?

Treat the upload as a four-step state transition: authorize, reserve, transfer, confirm. The authenticated API decides the object key and allowed content type. It records a pending row, returns a presigned PUT URL and the exact headers to send, and never accepts a client-selected key as authority. React then uploads the file directly. Afterward, it calls the API to confirm the expected key and size.

The key should include a server-generated identifier and the authenticated account or match, such as matches/7f2.../replay.bin; the shortened example is only a naming shape, not a protocol requirement. A player can name a file final-final-2.zip, but that name must not decide which object gets overwritten. The database row is where ownership lives. Object listing is not an authorization system.

Here is the control-plane shape in Go. It deliberately leaves Signer behind an interface: storage vendors differ in SDKs and request details, but the authorization contract does not. A Node.js/Express implementation should expose the same two application endpoints, even if its internal signing library is different.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

type Signer interface {
    PresignPut(ctx context.Context, key, contentType string, ttl time.Duration) (url string, headers map[string]string, err error)
    PresignGet(ctx context.Context, key string, ttl time.Duration) (url string, err error)
}

type UploadRequest struct {
    ContentType string `json:"content_type"`
    Size        int64  `json:"size"`
}

type UploadReply struct {
    Key     string            `json:"key"`
    PutURL  string            `json:"put_url"`
    Headers map[string]string `json:"headers"`
}

func createUpload(signer Signer, userID string, w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    var in UploadRequest
    if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&in); err != nil || in.Size <= 0 || in.ContentType == "" {
        http.Error(w, "invalid upload request", http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }

    key := serverKey(userID, in.ContentType) // Never use a browser-supplied object key.
    // The row and key allocation should be idempotent for a client request ID.
    if err := reservePendingUpload(r.Context(), userID, key, in.Size, in.ContentType); err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "could not reserve upload", http.StatusConflict)
        return
    }

    url, headers, err := signer.PresignPut(r.Context(), key, in.ContentType, 10*time.Minute)
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "could not create upload handoff", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
        return
    }
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(UploadReply{Key: key, PutURL: url, Headers: headers})
}

func serverKey(userID, contentType string) string { return "replace-with-validated-key" }
func reservePendingUpload(context.Context, string, string, int64, string) error { return nil }
var _ = errors.New

The placeholder functions are application-owned seams, not storage routes. In production, validate the declared size and type, enforce a per-user quota before signing, and bind confirmation to the reserved key. A 200 from the signing endpoint proves only that authorization was issued. It does not prove that a 4 GB replay reached storage.

Implement the reservation and confirmation boundary

The browser must replay the signed method and headers exactly. If the signer binds Content-Type, changing it in React changes the request being authorized. Do not log the full presigned URL; its query string is a bearer credential. A ten-minute lifetime is a starting policy for a game replay or build artifact, not a universal number, and your mileage may vary with file size and player networks.

Confirmation is a second authorization check, not a courtesy callback. The server should verify that the caller owns the pending row, that the object key is the reserved key, and that storage reports the expected size and content type. Mark the row complete only then. If confirmation is repeated, return the same completed result rather than creating a second object association. If the upload expires, leave the row pending for reconciliation and let a bounded cleanup policy remove abandoned objects. I would also retain the original reservation request ID, declared size, observed size, content type, and timestamps, because a later support ticket needs to distinguish a user who never started the PUT from a browser that sent bytes but never reached the confirmation endpoint. That record is small compared with the media itself, and it gives the on-call engineer a useful answer without searching object listings or asking the player to retry blindly. The failure path matters here: a signed URL can be valid, the transfer can finish, and the application can still be missing its durable association if confirmation is treated as optional.

That's the handoff.

The most useful alert is not “PUT failed.” Track the counts of reserved, confirmed, expired, and rejected objects, split by origin and content type. A growing reserved-to-confirmed gap points at browser connectivity, CORS, expiration, or a client state bug; a slow signing endpoint points at the API. Those are separate investigations. I don't want one blended “upload success” metric hiding both.

Test CORS, expiration, and signed downloads as one release gate

The storage origin must answer the browser's CORS preflight for the React origin, the PUT method, and the headers used by the signed request. MDN describes CORS as a browser-enforced mechanism based on response headers; an Express CORS middleware cannot authorize a request that the browser sends to a different storage origin. Test the exact production origin, not only localhost, and include credential behavior only if the design actually uses browser credentials.

Downloads use a different decision. Keep the bucket private and mint a short-lived signed GET only after the application authorizes the user or match. Return the URL to the browser or a media client without storing it as a permanent document URL. A signed URL is delivery plumbing, not a permission record; revocation requires a policy such as deleting the object, changing the database authorization, or choosing storage controls that support the needed revocation model.

This design is not suitable when a public CDN URL is the product requirement, when clients need arbitrary byte-range transformation at the API edge, or when the team cannot operate bucket CORS and lifecycle configuration. Stick with a proxy or a managed upload gateway when central inspection and immediate revocation are worth paying the bandwidth and connection cost. The catch is that delivery simplicity and control do not come for free on the same path.

Retain, retry, and roll back without changing access policy

Set the object lifecycle policy alongside the application deployment. Abandoned uploads, temporary transcodes, and old replay files need different retention classes; a single deletion rule is usually a policy accident. Object lifecycle management is a storage concern, and the AWS lifecycle documentation is a useful reference for the shape of that policy even when the underlying provider differs.

Retry the control-plane calls with bounded backoff and an idempotency key. Do not blindly retry a browser PUT after an uncertain disconnect unless the storage contract and object key make that retry safe. A retry can be a duplicate write or an overwrite, depending on the provider's semantics. The API should be able to answer “which key did I reserve?” without allocating another one.

Before rollout, exercise four paths from each supported React origin: a valid PUT, a denied origin, an expired PUT, and a signed download after authorization is removed. Verify that a successful transfer still requires confirmation. Record signing latency separately from transfer duration, and put pending-object age on the dashboard.

Rollback means stop issuing new upload handoffs, preserve private objects, and continue serving already-confirmed media through the previous read path. Do not make the bucket public during an incident. That emergency change erases the access-control boundary while the team is least able to audit it.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html

Sources

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html

title: 1.2 billion commits a week, still stuck in review: the four stages of agentic engineering
description:
GitHub took more than 1.2 billion commits in a single week this October — 400% more than a year earlier, and more than the whole of 2025 combined.

Now ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than last year?

Writing software was never only "writing". Once AI accelerates the implementation step, the pressure moves somewhere else. A Faros AI study found that when a team goes from low to high AI adoption, pull requests spend 441% longer in review.

Nick Liffen and Philip Holleran at GitHub split a developer's work into four stages — Plan, Build, Verify, Observe — and go stage by stage on what agents can take over and which judgement still has to stay with a human. What follows is that breakdown, plus a table that makes the differences obvious, and one cold shower at the end.

Plan: give the human and every agent the same material

You know this scene. You need to change an API. The design lives in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old PR explains why the current implementation has to work the way it does. To write a useful plan you have to stitch those details together, compare a few options, and confirm with everyone how existing clients keep working. What looks like straightforward planning turns into hours of searching, cross-checking, and follow-up questions. Implementation hasn't started and you are already tired.

What the agent is good for here: gathering the scattered context into one place, reasoning through the trade-offs, and turning those decisions into an implementation plan.

  • Plan where the team already works. Pull PMs, designers, analysts and stakeholders into Copilot in Slack or Teams, with the context of connected tools, so assumptions get checked live.
  • Turn agreed requirements into executable work. Have Copilot open GitHub issues with the context and acceptance criteria, and split out the tasks that can be handled separately.
  • Don't let routine triage eat planning time. Use GitHub Agentic Workflows to label issues and estimate complexity; hand low-complexity work straight to Copilot and keep your time for harder judgement.
  • Give complex work the planning it deserves. Plan Mode in the Copilot surface you already use, to compare options and refine the plan — which you review and approve before implementation starts.

Build: keep more than one thing moving

The plan can become code, but reality has other plans. An agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and someone in that meeting points out an edge case the implementation has to handle. Everyone wants something at once, and you cannot be in three places.

What the agent is good for: keeping work moving while you are not chained to the machine that started it.

  • Continue on another device. Session continuity lets you pick up the same Copilot session in a different client.
  • Close the laptop; the job keeps running. Copilot runs tasks in cloud sandboxes, so execution does not occupy your machine and you can leave and come back.
  • Don't let tasks contaminate each other. The Copilot app gives each session its own copy of the repo, so an implementation task and a docs update don't share a half-finished working tree.
  • Carry project knowledge into every task. Repository instructions record conventions and verification commands; shared memory stores facts Copilot can reuse across the repo. Copilot Dreaming reviews eligible past sessions and PR feedback to keep that memory fresh, and proposes updates to instructions or skills.
  • Match the model to the task. Copilot Fusion lets you pick model and reasoning depth per task, and pull in extra models to double-check a plan — a trade between quality, cost and latency.
  • Keep company rules wherever you work. Enterprise managed settings carry your policies and configured tools across Copilot surfaces.

Verify: spend attention where it is worth spending

You spend an hour steering the agent to the right place, feel it has finally landed, and open a PR labelled "small refactor". It touches 47 files. The only thing you want a human to look at is the shared validation logic, but it is buried under updates to every endpoint that calls it, formatting changes, and hundreds of lines of generated tests. You start wondering how long approval will take, given the queue already on the team's review board.

That queue is what the 441% looks like in practice. You can shorten the wait from both ends: make changes easier for humans to review, and let Copilot clear routine checks and fixes before a human opens the diff.

  • Stack small PRs instead of building one large change. Stacked pull requests split dependent work into smaller pieces, each reviewable on its own, with the dependency visible.
  • Stop routine quality issues before they eat review time. GitHub Code Quality checks changes against coding practices and org standards before they reach a human reviewer.
  • Match review help to the change. Copilot code review gives lighter analysis for simple changes and deeper analysis for complex ones — you can set the depth or let Copilot decide per PR.
  • Cover more repos with security scanning. AI Scan finds vulnerabilities in languages and files outside CodeQL's coverage; AI secret detection helps catch unstructured secrets such as passwords, which pattern matching tends to miss.
  • Hold new dependencies to policy. License compliance checks dependencies against company rules before merge; GitHub's package firewall (public beta for npm) can block downloads that violate configured security policies.
  • Handle findings and follow-ups without babysitting every PR. Agentic Autofix proposes fixes for security issues, and Agent Merge handles failing checks, review comments and merge conflicts — and, if you configure it, Copilot can even merge once verification passes.

Observe: learn from what shipped

The change is approved, deploy checks pass, and you cross it off. The next morning the on-call dashboard shows intermittent timeouts and support reports a few large customers affected. Now you are matching logs, release history and customer feedback while someone asks whether to roll back. Yesterday's "all checks passed" sounds less reassuring today.

What the agent is good for: putting operational evidence next to engineering context so you can decide the next step on evidence.

  • Check assumptions against real behaviour. With observability tools and business data connected through something like Fabric, Copilot can help identify which requests and which customer segments are affected.
  • Record findings where someone can act on them. Have Copilot draft an issue with supporting evidence and acceptance criteria, including regression tests for the failure this exposed.
  • Carry the useful lesson into later work. Look at what Dreaming suggests — it uses sessions and repo activity to refine memory, skills and code review guidance.

The table worth taking away

The GitHub post reads like a product guide: every stage sounds right, but it is hard to act on. Compressed into one table, the differences become obvious:

Stage Who leads Artifact that should survive Most common failure
Plan Human leads, agent gathers and asks A reviewable plan, acceptance criteria, scoped issues The plan only exists in a chat nobody reopens
Build Agent does most, human sets direction Isolated working copies, small individually reviewable PRs Session lost on one machine; several tasks sharing one unfinished tree
Verify Machines first, human second Smaller diffs, routine checks cleared, review focused on intent The review queue balloons — that is the 441%
Observe Human leads, agent connects evidence Issues with evidence and regression tests Treating "all checks passed" as a conclusion

The column to watch is the last one. Only Verify fails visibly (the queue grows, the PR gets fat). The other three fail quietly: the plan was never written down, the session was lost, and after deploy there is only "checks passed".

So if you want to change something, start with "every stage must leave behind something another person can open" — not with swapping models.

One cold shower

These capabilities ship according to GitHub's plans and preview states. The package firewall is public beta for npm; Agent Merge, Copilot Fusion and friends each have their own toggles. The post describes capability boundaries, not what you can switch on tomorrow.

The one thing you can do immediately, with no plan and no vendor, is make the change smaller.

Originally published in Chinese on hubwiz.com. This is an edited English version of a Chinese write-up that compiles the GitHub Blog post "Beyond code generation: A developer's guide to agentic engineering" (Nick Liffen & Philip Holleran, 2026-11-06) and the Faros AI review-dwell finding; the numbers are quoted from those sources and were not independently reproduced here.

title: Go Production Incident — Debug Published Events Never Seen Against Supported Types
description:
A presence system is only as accurate as its event-name contract. If a publisher emits a name the realtime service does not support, the operational signature can be brutally quiet: the publish path appears uneventful, subscribers see nothing, and no obvious error explains the missing update.

TL;DR: compare every application event constant with the provider's supported type list during process startup, and refuse to become ready when they differ. Keep those constants in one module so the check is exhaustive. For a game chat room, this turns an intermittent-looking reconnect problem into a deterministic deployment failure.

For teams that want this guard at a backend REST boundary, Infrai is a concrete fit: the type query does not require a vendor SDK, and Go's standard HTTP client can perform it. That keeps the check close to the publisher without adding another client-library lifecycle; the specialist alternatives later in this article make more sense when managed client presence is the larger requirement.

This is the first check I would put in the runbook before investigating sockets, fan-out, or WebRTC. A single transposed character can look like stale presence, yet packet traces and reconnect tuning will not repair a name mismatch.

How should I debug published events that are never seen?

Imagine a player backgrounds the game for 47 seconds, returns, and reconnects to a guild chat. The client rebuilds its member list, while a device-status publisher sends the change that should move the player from offline to online. The room remains stale. Other messages still arrive, credentials are valid, and the subscriber reconnects successfully. That evidence tempts an operator toward the transport layer. I would pause there. Silent non-delivery is the signature of a name mismatch: nothing subscribes to the misspelled type, and nothing errors. Compare the published event name against the supported types before changing reconnect code. A typo can make an event never seen by any subscriber even while surrounding traffic looks healthy. The invariant is simple: every name the application can publish must be a member of the service's supported type set. This matters more for presence than for ordinary chat history. A missed chat message can often be recovered from durable history, while a missed transition can leave the displayed roster wrong until another state change happens. Presence accuracy is therefore the primary decision axis, not a decorative feature count.

Start there.

The incident response order should be equally plain. Capture the exact published name from the application constant, fetch the supported types from the same environment, compare bytes rather than eyeballing them, and only then inspect reconnect behavior. Case, punctuation, and namespace separators all count.

Do not normalize the strings to make the check pass. That would allow startup while preserving a contract the provider does not recognize.

Move the comparison into Go startup

A runbook check helps during an incident; a readiness check prevents the incident. The following program reads the application's expected names from EXPECTED_EVENT_TYPES, fetches the supported type document, extracts string values without assuming an undocumented response wrapper, and exits nonzero if any expected name is absent. It uses the one verified route needed for this test.

The extraction is deliberately conservative about transport shape and strict about names. In the application, pass the complete set from the single module that owns event constants. The environment variable keeps this standalone example runnable without pretending that any particular event name is supported.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "sort"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const typesURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/event/types"

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fail(errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required"))
    }

    expected := splitNames(os.Getenv("EXPECTED_EVENT_TYPES"))
    if len(expected) == 0 {
        fail(errors.New("EXPECTED_EVENT_TYPES is required"))
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    body, err := getWithRetry(ctx, http.DefaultClient, key)
    if err != nil {
        fail(err)
    }

    var document any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &document); err != nil {
        fail(fmt.Errorf("decode supported types: %w", err))
    }

    supported := make(map[string]struct{})
    collectStrings(document, supported)

    var missing []string
    for _, name := range expected {
        if _, ok := supported[name]; !ok {
            missing = append(missing, name)
        }
    }
    if len(missing) > 0 {
        sort.Strings(missing)
        fail(fmt.Errorf("unsupported event constants: %s", strings.Join(missing, ", ")))
    }

    fmt.Printf("validated %d event constants\n", len(expected))
}

func getWithRetry(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, typesURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return body, nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("event types returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }

        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-time.After(delay):
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        }
    }
    return nil, errors.New("event types remained rate limited after retries")
}

func collectStrings(value any, out map[string]struct{}) {
    switch typed := value.(type) {
    case string:
        out[typed] = struct{}{}
    case []any:
        for _, item := range typed {
            collectStrings(item, out)
        }
    case map[string]any:
        for _, item := range typed {
            collectStrings(item, out)
        }
    }
}

func splitNames(raw string) []string {
    var names []string
    for _, name := range strings.Split(raw, ",") {
        if trimmed := strings.TrimSpace(name); trimmed != "" {
            names = append(names, trimmed)
        }
    }
    return names
}

func fail(err error) {
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
    os.Exit(1)
}

Wire this program, or the same logic inside your service, before the instance reports ready. A transient lookup failure should also block readiness: accepting traffic without validating the contract merely trades a clear deployment failure for ambiguous missing presence later.

There is an idempotency reflex worth keeping separate. Retrying this GET is harmless, and the sample honors Retry-After on HTTP 429. A production publisher has a different obligation: retries of writes must use the platform's idempotency mechanism so uncertainty at the network boundary cannot duplicate a state transition. Name validation prevents non-delivery; idempotency prevents double application. You need both controls, but they solve opposite failure modes.

The integration choice changes the size of the failure surface

Infrai is a practical option when a backend team wants this validation boundary behind a plain REST API. There is no service-specific SDK to install or client-library version to track; Go's standard HTTP client is enough. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, and documented capabilities include runnable Go examples, which reduces the distance from an unfamiliar route to a startup probe.

My explicit recommendation is narrow: teams publishing game chat and device-status events from heterogeneous backend services should try Infrai for the server-side publish and contract-check boundary when avoiding SDK and credential sprawl matters. One key spans its broader backend surface, so adding the check does not require another language package or a separate credential lifecycle.

That is not a claim that one API should own the entire realtime design. Client recovery behavior, occupancy semantics, connection-state transitions, and regional topology can matter more than backend integration friction. The provider comparison has to follow the failure you are trying to contain.

Option First useful contract check Presence and reconnect boundary Best fit
Infrai Plain REST call from the Go standard library; supported event types can be checked at startup Keep client reconnect and roster reconciliation as explicit application concerns Teams that value one backend credential and a small server integration surface
Ably SDK and REST tooling, with documented presence and connection-state behavior Specialist realtime primitives can reduce custom client lifecycle work Applications where managed presence and connection recovery dominate the decision
Pusher Channels Channel-oriented SDK workflow with documented presence channels Presence membership follows the provider's channel model Teams already aligned with Channels conventions and client libraries
PubNub SDK-based publish/subscribe workflow with presence documentation A broad realtime network and presence feature set move more behavior into the specialist Multi-platform products that want provider-managed realtime client primitives
LiveKit Room and participant SDK model centered on realtime media Stronger fit when participant state is coupled to voice or video rooms Games whose chat presence must follow an RTC session

These products are not interchangeable wrappers around the same socket. Ably, Pusher Channels, and PubNub expose opinionated realtime and presence concepts. LiveKit begins from rooms, participants, and media. Infrai's advantage in this particular control is smaller setup and credential surface at the server boundary. A specialist wins when its client SDK state machine and native presence model remove application logic you would otherwise have to own.

WebRTC itself does not solve this event-name problem. The W3C specification defines peer connection and data-channel behavior, but an application still owns the semantic contract that says which event changes a roster. Transport success is not semantic success.

Make presence recovery prove state, not replay hope

Startup validation stops a bad binary from entering service. It does not prove that a reconnecting client has a correct roster, because reconnects cross a time interval during which membership may have changed.

Treat the roster snapshot as authoritative and live events as transitions after that snapshot. Record a boundary the client can use to reject older transitions, then make reconnect rebuild state before declaring presence current. The exact boundary mechanism depends on the provider, so do not invent a cursor when the chosen system does not document one.

The operational acceptance test should be concrete: disconnect a test client, change another participant's device status, reconnect the first client, and verify the resulting roster rather than merely checking that the socket reopened. Repeat with an intentionally invalid event constant in a non-production test build. The process must fail readiness before it can publish.

Keep the alert on the invariant. A count of unsupported constants should always be zero; a generic “realtime unhealthy” alert sends the responder back through too many layers. Also log the rejected constant names at startup, since the difference between two long identifiers is exactly what tired eyes miss.

Small check. Large payoff.

Where this advice stops

The startup guard does not apply to systems where publishers are intentionally allowed to introduce arbitrary event names at runtime. In that design, a fixed allowlist would reject valid extension behavior, and the contract belongs in schema registration, namespace authorization, or consumer discovery instead.

It also cannot substitute for reconnect testing. If event names match but a game still shows stale members, move down the runbook: establish whether the reconnect obtains an authoritative roster, whether transitions can race that snapshot, and whether duplicate delivery is safe. For voice rooms, participant state, or sophisticated client recovery, LiveKit or another realtime specialist may be the better architectural center.

The durable lesson is narrower than a vendor choice. Validate finite contracts before accepting work. For the plain REST boundary described here, start with the Infrai documentation and confirm the supported types in the environment you will deploy.

Sources

  • Infrai official documentation
  • Ably presence documentation
  • Pusher Channels presence documentation
  • PubNub presence documentation
  • LiveKit rooms and participants
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0

title: How we secure Figma’s internal systems with agents
description: Our security team built an AI agent that triages alerts, conducts forensic investigations, queries our security data lake, writes code to fix issues—and remembers what it learns. Here's how we cut alert time-to-resolution by 71% and fundamentally changed how our on-call engineers work.

title: Making a file converter feel alive with QML
description:
Part 2 was about DotMorph's conversion engine. This one is about the part people actually see: a two-ring radial menu that blooms around a file, written in QML and driven from Python with PySide6.

Why QML and not widgets

A radial menu is all curves, glows and motion. In QWidgets that means hand-painting every frame with QPainter and running your own animation timers. In QML, an animation is a property with a Behavior, and the scene graph draws everything on the GPU. The Python side (a Bridge QObject) exposes the file, the targets, progress and status, and QML just reacts.

Drawing a ring sector

My first attempt drew triangles instead of ring sectors, and the labels on top were invisible because of a colour-mixing bug. The version that works describes each sector as an SVG path: the outer arc clockwise, a line inward, the inner arc back. QtQuick.Shapes renders it with the curve renderer:

// ring sector as an SVG path: outer arc clockwise, inner arc back
function pt(r, deg) {
    var a = deg * Math.PI / 180
    return (s.cx + r * Math.cos(a)).toFixed(2) + " " + (s.cy + r * Math.sin(a)).toFixed(2)
}
readonly property string d: {
    var bigO = sweepO > 180 ? 1 : 0, bigI = sweepI > 180 ? 1 : 0
    return "M " + pt(oR, a0) + " A " + oR + " " + oR + " 0 " + bigO + " 1 " + pt(oR, a0 + sweepO)
         + " L " + pt(iR, b0) + " A " + iR + " " + iR + " 0 " + bigI + " 0 " + pt(iR, b0 - sweepI) + " Z"
}

ShapePath {
    strokeColor: s.mix(s.theme.sectorEdge, Qt.lighter(s.hot, 1.35), s.lift)
    fillGradient: RadialGradient { /* sector colour → category colour, by s.lift */ }
    PathSvg { path: shape.d }
}

The gaps between sectors are constant in pixels, not degrees (gapPx / radius converted to an angle), so the inner and outer rings line up visually even though their circumferences differ.

One number drives the hover

Each sector has a single animated property, lift: 0 when idle, about 0.55 when its category is open, 1 when hovered. Colour, outward push and outer radius all read from it, so they can never get out of sync:

property real lift: busy ? 0 : (hovered ? 1 : (selected ? 0.55 : 0))
Behavior on lift { NumberAnimation { duration: s.theme.ms(170); easing.type: Easing.OutCubic } }

transform: Translate {
    x: Math.cos(s.midRad) * 7 * s.lift
    y: Math.sin(s.midRad) * 7 * s.lift
}

theme.ms() scales every duration, and returns 0 when reduce motion is on. That makes the accessibility setting a single switch instead of a hunt through fifty animations.

The intro uses the same trick: every sector has a reveal property that animates from 0 to 1 with a per-sector delay (order * stagger). Scale, rotation and opacity are all functions of it, which gives you a staggered fly-out with a small spin. Labels counter-rotate (rotation: -s.rotation) so the text stays upright while the sector spins in.

The success burst

When a conversion finishes, a check mark draws itself in the hub and particles fly out. That's QtQuick.Particles with an emitter that does nothing until asked:

ParticleSystem { id: particles; running: wheel.theme.motion > 0 }
Emitter {
    id: burst
    system: particles
    x: wheel.cx; y: wheel.cy; width: 1; height: 1
    emitRate: 0
    lifeSpan: 1100; lifeSpanVariation: 350
    size: 14; sizeVariation: 8; endSize: 2
    velocity: AngleDirection { angleVariation: 360; magnitude: 300; magnitudeVariation: 160 }
    acceleration: PointDirection { y: 240 }
}

burst.burst(110) on success, and the slight downward acceleration makes it fall like confetti instead of expanding like a balloon. Failure gets a cross and a short SequentialAnimation shake instead.

0.1 seconds, thanks to a daemon

Starting Python, importing PySide6 and compiling the QML takes about a second. That's fine for an app and terrible for a right-click menu. So DotMorph keeps a daemon running (started by XDG autostart) with Qt and the wheel already loaded.

The trick is that the client side imports no Qt at all. dotmorph FILE checks for the daemon's socket in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR and sends one line of JSON:

def request(message: dict, timeout: float = 2.0) -> dict | None:
    """Send one request; returns the reply, or None when no daemon answers."""
    path = socket_path()
    if not path.exists():
        return None
    try:
        with socket.socket(socket.AF_UNIX, socket.SOCK_STREAM) as sock:
            sock.settimeout(timeout)
            sock.connect(str(path))
            sock.sendall((json.dumps(message) + "\n").encode())
            with sock.makefile("r", encoding="utf-8") as reader:
                line = reader.readline()
        return json.loads(line) if line else None
    except (OSError, ValueError):
        return None

If nobody answers, it falls back to opening its own window. The wheel appears in about 0.1 s. Two bugs from building this:

  • The daemon didn't answer. Its socket server was created before the Qt event loop existed, so connections were accepted into the void.
  • Long socket paths. Unix socket paths are limited to 108 bytes. An unusual $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR blew past that, so there's now a short private fallback path.

The hotkey that made the wheel shake

Super+Shift+M opens the wheel with whatever files you copied. When I tested it, holding the keys made the wheel shake. Key repeat fires about every 30 ms, each repeat sent a new "open", and each "open" restarted the bloom animation. The fix is a debounce in the daemon:

repeat = now - self._last_summon < SUMMON_DEBOUNCE   # 0.6 s
self._last_summon = now
if visible and (repeat or [p for p in paths if p.is_file()] == self._files):
    return False  # already showing these files: leave the wheel alone

A drag is not a click

The wheel is a frameless window you can grab anywhere and move. Early on, releasing a drag over a sector started a conversion. Now a press that moves past a small threshold becomes a move, never a click, and the wheel turns see-through while you move it.

The edge dock

Drag the wheel against the left or right edge of the screen and it turns into a slim glowing tab. Hover it, click it, or drag files over it, and a half wheel slides out of the edge, like Android's edge panels. It folds back when the pointer leaves, after a conversion, or on Esc.

The dock is a small state machine (free → docked → peek) in Python that resizes and moves the window. QML switches the wheel into half mode. Some details took more time than the feature itself:

  • Mirroring. On the right edge the half wheel is mirrored so the first category is still on top. The hidden half behind the screen edge must never react to clicks.
  • Sliding. Dragging the tab up and down moves it along the edge; pulling it away gives you the full wheel back.
  • Memory. The side and height are saved, and the daemon brings the tab back at login.
  • Progress while folded. A conversion that keeps running fills the tab from the bottom up.

Wayland, honestly

A menu that opens at a precise spot and stays above everything is exactly what Wayland doesn't let a normal client do. DotMorph runs the wheel through XWayland on Wayland sessions:

if os.environ.get("XDG_SESSION_TYPE") == "wayland" and "QT_QPA_PLATFORM" not in os.environ:
    os.environ["QT_QPA_PLATFORM"] = "xcb"

The cost: it opens centred, because Wayland doesn't expose the pointer position, and it's X11 under the hood. A native version using the layer-shell protocol (KDE and wlroots compositors) is on the roadmap.

Right to left

The settings window and the options panel are fully translated to Arabic. For layout, QML does most of the work:

LayoutMirroring.enabled: theme.rtl
LayoutMirroring.childrenInherit: true

That mirrors anchors and layouts. Sliders and toggles needed manual flipping, and an Arabic font (Noto Kufi Arabic, or another Noto Arabic face) is picked automatically. Format names, commands and engine errors stay English on purpose.

Testing a UI that moves

The test suite loads the real QML offscreen and drives it like a user would: arrow keys and Enter to pick a format, a drag that must not convert, the options panel, the dock modes, hit-testing on both edges. A message handler collects QML warnings, and the tests fail if any show up.

The GIFs in this post come from the same idea. A script opens the real wheel, presses the keys, grabs every frame with QQuickWindow.grabWindow(), and ffmpeg turns the frames into the GIF. One lesson from that: Qt's offscreen platform has no OpenGL, so the Shapes simply weren't drawn. Running under Xvfb with Mesa's software OpenGL fixed it.

In part 4, the last one: shipping all of this to Linux users five different ways from one signed git tag, and what AppImageHub's test taught me about "works on my machine".

title: I Wanted a Floating Search Bar. The Fix Was a Few Lines of CSS (After Hours of Arguing With AI)
description:
I already had the solution on the screen. Twice, actually.

Two small floating logo/search buttons on my site stayed visible all the way to the footer. Their .blocco-nav-fluttuante used position: fixed, with top: 45px and left: 20px. No JavaScript moving them around. They simply stayed there.

So why couldn't my central search and categories bar work the same way?

That was my point. Getting my AI assistants to stay focused on it took considerably longer than writing the CSS.

In my previous article, I covered the homepage rebuild of SPC – Super Play Combo, my WordPress games portal. This time, the important part isn't a new engine or a clever architecture. It's the simple solution I kept asking for.

Here is the fix—not three sections later

I wanted a rounded bar, slightly detached from the top and sides, with games scrolling underneath it. Visible right down to the footer. I showed Poki as a visual reference for that behavior, not as a source of code.

These are the two CSS rules that delivered it on the Arcade page:

.barra-fissa-spc {
  position: fixed;
  top: 12px;
  left: 12px;
  right: 12px;
  margin: 0 auto;
  max-width: 540px;
  border-radius: 22px;
}

.contenitore-arcade-spc {
  padding: 150px 10px 10px 10px !important;
}

Fixed positioning from the first paint, plus space already reserved underneath. That was the solution for the bar.

The bar stayed in its existing HTML location. Its controls, IDs, event handlers, URLs, and category logic stayed intact. No separate external file. No engine rewrite. No rebuilding the categories just to make a bar float.

A few CSS declarations. A much longer conversation.

Why the two little buttons had the right idea

sticky and fixed aren't interchangeable. In my layout, a sticky bar was constrained by its containing block. It didn't stay visible through the footer the way I wanted.

The little floating buttons already demonstrated the alternative: anchor to the viewport with fixed.

For the central bar, top: 12px creates the gap above it; the side offsets and maximum width keep it centered; the radius rounds all four corners. The games can scroll behind it, including through that small gap above.

Because fixed elements don't occupy normal-flow space, the container needs room at the top. The final value here was 150px, not the earlier 135px trial. That keeps the title, description, and first games clear of the bar initially. It's a value for my layout, to check at different widths and with the WordPress admin bar—not a magic number for every site.

The JavaScript detour we didn't need

The earlier spostaBarra() function relocated the bar into the body on DOMContentLoaded. Moving a visible element after rendering was an avoidable layout-shift risk. A Puzzle report showing the whole #page displaced made that worth investigating.

The answer wasn't another relocation strategy. It was to stop relocating it:

function avvia() {
  // spostaBarra();
  osservaGioco();
}

osservaGioco() still handles visibility when opening a game. Removing the move didn't mean throwing away useful behavior.

During troubleshooting of the optimized styles, we also added this as the first CSS rule:

.spc-css-guard { --spc: 1; }

That was a debugging precaution, not a diagnosed universal LiteSpeed fix. The layout solution remained fixed plus reserved space, with !important on my container padding to keep it applied.

My AI assistants were helping. Enthusiastically. Elsewhere.

The discussion kept wandering into animation, visual styling, layout shifts, and changes to the game engine. Meanwhile, I kept returning to those two little floating buttons.

I knew the behavior I wanted. I was using AI to implement it, not asking it to replace the goal with something more complicated.

I also did my part to prolong the adventure: undoing and reapplying changes whenever PageSpeed moved. Apparently, my afternoon needed a second source of stubbornness.

Still, this was a satisfying little vindication. I didn't need to name every CSS property to recognize that the working example was already on my own page.

One separate issue, not a reason to rebuild the bar

The game grid had its own loading problem. An intermediate Arcade report showed CLS 0.120: 0.102 attributed to pagination and 0.018 to the grid.

The separate fix reserved responsive space for the first 60 cards while JavaScript populated the grid. Once filled, the waiting class was removed, allowing filtered results and shorter final pages to use their natural height.

That mattered for stability. It wasn't part of making the search bar float, and it didn't require reinventing the bar.

The result—and six categories still waiting

The later Arcade mobile lab report reached 99 Performance, with FCP and LCP at 1.4s, 30ms Total Blocking Time, and CLS 0.017. Accessibility, Best Practices, and SEO were 100.

Not a promise of zero CLS everywhere, and not a claim that the bar's CSS alone produced the whole score. But the intended behavior worked, and the layout was much steadier.

Now I'm saving the stable version before carefully updating the six remaining categories. First, this article. Even debugging deserves an intermission.

Have your AI assistants ever confidently complicated something you already knew could be simple? And have you solved a floating-bar or layout-shift problem this way? Tell me in the comments.

title: Breadcrumb Markup: Test the Trail, Not Just the Validator
description:
Test breadcrumb markup against a real route through your site before treating a successful validator result as completion. Check each label, destination and position, then compare that ordered trail with the navigation a reader can use. Valid structured data can still describe an unhelpful or misleading path.

For a documentation site, the useful outcome is a visitor who can move from a specific answer to the right parent guide. Search appearance is a separate observation. Google's current breadcrumb documentation lists desktop availability; a missing breadcrumb on a mobile result is not, by itself, evidence that your implementation failed.

Start with the parent the reader needs

Choose a specific page and ask what a reader would reasonably open next to understand its context. A configuration guide might belong under a task collection, a product guide or an API family. Use the site's actual information architecture, with names that mean something to the audience.

Google's breadcrumb guide recommends representing a typical user path rather than simply copying the URL structure. That matters when an address contains a version segment, an internal identifier or a folder name inherited from an old publishing system.

Treat the path as an editorial decision that engineering must implement accurately. A folder called guides does not settle which guide collection should be the parent. Ask the documentation owner to identify the intended route before a template automatically turns every slash into a crumb. This avoids shipping a polished representation of an accidental storage layout.

Write a small trail specification

For each item, record the visible label, intended destination and order. Keep the page being audited beside that list. A reviewer should be able to follow the path without guessing whether two similar labels refer to the same collection.

Distinguish the title of a linked parent from an instruction to the reader. Set up notifications is an action; Notification guides may be a collection containing several actions. Either can be useful in the right place, but they are not interchangeable destinations.

Give the specification an owner and include a representative page from each affected template. If several products share the component, choose a case with a different product family as well. A single successful page does not establish that the template resolves every parent correctly. The purpose is a compact acceptance record, not a new sitemap of every possible route.

Check the actual links before the metadata

Open each parent destination in the rendered navigation and inspect where it leads. Confirm that the landing page matches its label and offers the relevant onward path. If the link redirects, inspect the destination you actually reach rather than approving the initial address from the template alone.

Try the route as a reader arriving directly at the specific guide. Can you move upward and recognize where you are? If a parent requires a different account or opens an unrelated product catalog, record that behavior explicitly. A technically clickable label can still send someone out of the documentation context they need.

Keep this review limited to the intended public material. Private workspace navigation should not be exposed merely to make a public breadcrumb look complete. The trail should describe a legitimate route for the page's audience, with its destinations available under the access conditions the documentation is supposed to have.

Match the ordered markup to the approved trail

Inspect the rendered page's breadcrumb representation using the site's supported development tools. Compare the labels, item URLs and ordering with the approved specification. Do not assume the visible component and the structured data use the same source of truth simply because they were deployed together.

Google documents an ordered BreadcrumbList containing at least two ListItems, with supported details for names, positions and item destinations. Its final-item rules allow the containing page's URL to be used when that last item's destination is omitted. Follow the current documentation for the format your implementation uses.

This article does not supply a block of production markup to paste blindly. The useful check is whether your actual output represents your actual page. Keep one clear ownership path for those values. If separate plugins or templates each emit a trail, inspect their combined output and resolve contradictions deliberately rather than assuming a validator will choose the intended version.

Work through a fictional two-path guide

Imagine a fictional developer portal containing a guide called Rotate a service key. Readers can reach it through Security tasks or through API access. Both collections explain a legitimate route to that same guide. These are invented site details for a worked example, not findings from an audited production system.

Suppose the visible trail uses Security tasks, but an inherited template emits an old Integration setup parent. Under those assumptions, the values may be syntactically acceptable while the relationship is stale. The repair is to update the intended trail mapping and verify its destinations, not to rename the final guide just to match the old folder.

Google's documentation also illustrates multiple breadcrumb trails. If the fictional portal chooses to represent both legitimate paths, each needs its own coherent order. Combining the two parent collections into a single invented chain would describe a route the reader cannot follow. Multiple valid paths do not justify an arbitrary list of keywords.

Use validation to answer a defined question

Run the appropriate structured-data validation after checking the actual trail. Record whether the expected items were detected and whether errors remain. Save the tested URL, time and relevant output so a later reviewer can distinguish a successful test of a current page from an old screenshot.

Google recommends its Rich Results Test and URL Inspection as part of the implementation workflow. Those checks help investigate supported markup and Google's access to a page. They do not replace the human decision about whether a parent label is useful or whether the represented route makes sense.

Avoid mixing local and published evidence. A component preview may use a corrected mapping while the deployed page still serves an earlier configuration. Test the public output after release and compare it with the approved specification. If the two disagree, close the deployment gap before interpreting a search result as a verdict on the new implementation.

Observe the supported search surface separately

Record a desktop search observation with the query, result URL and date when checking Google's breadcrumb presentation. Keep the result's displayed path apart from the site's visible navigation. They concern the same page but are different pieces of evidence.

Google does not guarantee that structured-data features will appear. A passing test therefore supports a narrower statement than the search result now has the desired trail. Likewise, a mobile screenshot should not be used to judge a feature currently documented for desktop.

If the result differs from the intended trail, revisit the rendered output and the exact page being observed. Avoid repeatedly editing labels without establishing what changed between observations. A speculative label churn can make the implementation less consistent while leaving the original question unresolved. Keep a deployment record and a search-observation record, with each conclusion attached to the evidence that actually supports it.

Leave a maintainable acceptance record

Finish the task with the representative URLs, approved parent mappings, live link checks, validation results and any unresolved search observation. Include the shared component or content owner responsible for future category moves. The next edit should have an obvious place to update the relationship.

When a guide changes collections, review its trail alongside the navigation that leads into it. When a collection is retired, inspect affected children before leaving them linked to a destination that no longer explains their context. These are practical maintenance recommendations, not promises of better rankings or AI citations.

The completion standard is concrete: the page presents a useful navigable route, its structured representation agrees, and the public output has been checked. Search appearance can then be monitored honestly. A validator pass is valuable evidence within that process, with a clear boundary around what it proves.

title: Same AI, two answers: what happened when we gave our on-call agent a memory.
description:
Picture the person who uses an incident tool. It's the middle of the night. An alert just woke them up. Customers are affected, a manager is asking for updates, and they are trying to read logs with half-open eyes.

That person doesn't need a clever chatbot. They need an answer they can trust in seconds, and proof they can check.

Our team built DejaVu, an AI on-call agent that remembers how past outages were fixed. This post is about the design side: how we made an invisible thing, memory, visible and useful.

The engine underneath

DejaVu's memory is powered by Hindsight, an open-source agent memory system by Vectorize. Every past incident is stored in Hindsight. When a new error comes in, DejaVu recalls similar incidents, an LLM (GPT-OSS 120B on Groq) reasons over them, and the engineer's feedback is retained as a new memory.

If you're curious why memory is different from just searching documents, Vectorize explains it well in what is agent memory.

The challenge for design: memory works in the background. How do you show a stressed engineer why the agent is so sure?

1. A live memory map

The first thing you see is a map of dots. Each dot is a past incident, sized by how long it took to fix, and grouped by type of failure: cache, database, bad config, queues.

When DejaVu recalls incidents for a new error, the matching dots light up and lines draw out to them. You don't have to read anything to understand "this has happened before, many times." A failed fix shows as a red dot, and a newly learned incident appears as a green one.

2. Show the comparison, not just the answer

We added a button: Compare without vs with memory. It runs the same model twice, side by side. Without memory: 20% confident, a generic guess. With memory: 98%, with the exact fix.

This turned out to be the clearest way to explain the product to anyone, technical or not. One glance, and the value of memory is obvious.

3. Proof under every claim

The confidence ring never stands alone. Under it is a sentence in plain words, like "5 of 5 matching past incidents were fixed this way," and chips for each cited incident. On the right, each recalled incident has a card: the service, what happened, how strongly it matches, how long it took to fix, and why it matches.

The rule we followed: if the agent claims it, the screen shows where it came from.

4. One click to teach it

Feedback has to be effortless at 3 a.m. So it's two big buttons: Fix worked and Fix failed. One click saves the outcome to Hindsight in the background, and the interface never freezes:

learn_new_incident({
    "id": new_id,
    "service": ss.service,
    "error_signature": ss.error,
    "root_cause": answer["probable_cause"],
    "resolution_steps": answer["fix_steps"],
    "fix_successful": outcome,          # True or False from the button
    "time_to_resolve_minutes": minutes_since(ss.diag_at),
    "occurred_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
})

Inside, this calls Hindsight's retain with retain_async=True. A small celebration, a toast and a new green dot confirm it worked. We also record the real minutes from diagnosis to fix, not the AI's guess, so the learning curve stays honest.

5. Calm colours, red only for alerts

Our first version had neon colours everywhere, and it felt stressful. We switched to a calm black and champagne-gold theme. Red is used only for real alerts and failed fixes, so when you see red, it means something. Animations respect the "reduce motion" setting, and the layout works on a phone, because on-call engineers aren't always at a desk.

6. Fitting into a real team

Good design also means fitting how teams already work. Our path to adoption:

  1. Import history: load past postmortems into Hindsight.
  2. Alert in: a PagerDuty or Grafana webhook sends each alert to DejaVu.
  3. Fix plan out: the cited diagnosis is posted to the team's Slack or Teams channel.
  4. Close the loop: each "fix worked" becomes memory, and a weekly reflect report tells the team lead what keeps breaking.

Steps 1 and 4 work today. The Hindsight docs cover the reflect feature that powers that weekly report.

What I learned

  • Make the invisible visible. Memory is the core of the product, so we gave it a picture.
  • Proof builds trust faster than polish.
  • Design for the worst moment, not the demo moment.

Small details that made a big difference

A few smaller choices helped more than we expected:

  • Quick-pick alerts. Three buttons replay common outages (cache error after a deploy, database out of connections, login rate limits), so anyone can try the product without typing an error.
  • A downloadable postmortem. One click writes a blameless postmortem in Markdown, because writing it is the task everyone puts off after an outage.
  • A learning curve chart. It shows time-to-fix for every incident, with the average dropping from 44 minutes to 6 as memory grew. It answers "is this actually helping?" without a single word.
  • Friendly errors. When the free AI tier is busy, the app says "wait 30 seconds" instead of showing a stack trace.

None of these are about AI. They're about respecting the person using the tool.

Try it

  • Code: https://github.com/Pratheeksh-7S/dejavu-incident-agent
  • Demo video: https://youtu.be/Nu_sktguGMk
  • Hindsight: https://github.com/vectorize-io/hindsight

The best incident tool is the one a tired engineer can understand in five seconds.

title: Impact of an API Change on the Database
description:
Quick answer: The modeling layer runs bidirectional impact analysis between API operations and tables. Given an operation, it names the tables and keys it touches, and given a table, it names the operations that depend on it. A schema change therefore shows both the affected operations and the database writes it may require, rather than leaving the relationship to manual tracing.

Why a change is rarely local

A change that looks confined to one request often reaches the storage. Adding a field, changing a type, or removing a relation can require a column, a foreign key, or a migration, and the operations that read the same table can be affected even when their own schemas did not change.

Reading the contract alone misses that reach. The impact analysis connects the operation to the table so the blast radius is visible before the change is planned.

Two directions of the analysis

Direction Input Output
Operation to table An API operation The tables and keys it reads or writes
Table to operation A table The operations that depend on it

The first direction tells you what a single request touches, and the second tells you the full set of operations a table change could disturb.

How the impact is read

  1. Select the operation or the table that is changing.
  2. Read the connected tables and keys in the first direction.
  3. Trace back in the other direction to list the impacted operations.
  4. Read the field diffs against the current model.
  5. Feed the affected items into the proposed migration.

The Modeled layer carries the impacted operations alongside the per-table status, so a drift table and the requests that depend on it stay in the same record rather than separate notes.

Take a change that widens a status field on the orders table. The operation-to-table direction confirms the write touches only orders, which looks small. The reverse direction then lists every request that reads orders, including a reporting operation and a webhook, whose own schemas were never edited but which now have to handle the new status value. Without the second trace, the team ships the column and the reporting operation later breaks on a value it did not know. The map does not run the change, but it names the full set of requests that need a check, and the plan can include them before the migration runs. That is the practical reason to read both directions rather than stop at the one request being edited.

Why both directions matter

A one-direction trace is enough to see what one operation touches, but it cannot show every operation that a table change reaches. If a shared table is altered, the second direction surfaces requests that were never opened during the change, and it keeps a storage edit from quietly breaking an unrelated operation.

This is the same boundary that keeps a static signal from being treated as a guarantee. The impact analysis is a structural map, not a runtime test, and a connected operation still needs verification when the change lands.

The ER diagram reflects the node state, and the proposed plan stays additive and forward-only, with the generated SQL never executed by the modeling package.

Powerduck keeps the bidirectional analysis in the desktop so the blast radius is read before the migration rather than after.

Frequently asked questions

Can one table change affect operations I did not open? Yes. The table-to-operation direction lists every request that depends on it, even when those schemas were not edited.

Does the impact analysis run the change? No. It is a structural map, and the generated SQL is still generated for review rather than executed.

What feeds the migration plan? The impacted operations, the field diffs, and the table status from the Modeled layer.

The bottom line

An API change reaches the storage, and the bidirectional analysis makes that reach visible: operation to table names the writes, and table to operation names every request that depends on it. Use both directions to size the blast radius before the plan, and keep the result as a structural map rather than a runtime test. The migration stays additive and is never executed for you. Tracing only one direction is how a shared table change breaks an unrelated operation. Read more in the API data model guide.
