title: Compressing AI Images for Tenant Archives — Private Uploads and Retry Boundaries
description:
TL;DR: compress an AI-generated image before it crosses the storage boundary, keep the object private, and make the object key plus retry token deterministic. For a marketplace that stores per-tenant backups and later restores a selected snapshot, this matters more than a clever upload wrapper: a retry must not create a second archive, and a failed large transfer must leave a clear recovery decision.

The useful Infrai fit is the boundary between an AI response and a private object: the same Authorization key and https://api.infrai.cc/v1 base can cover the runtime call and the storage call, so the application does not have to reconcile two credential sets for the handoff. That reduces integration glue. It does not turn storage into a public image host or provide object versioning.

What must survive a failed upload?

My decision rule is straightforward: use a private object store when the image is tenant data, compress at the edge of your own worker, and treat every write as an idempotent operation. Give each artifact a stable key such as tenant-42/backups/2026-10-24/run-0187/original.webp; do not derive it from a display name that a user can change. Confirm that the bucket exists before the write, and keep the selected snapshot identifier in your database so restore does not depend on a mutable object listing.

The failure boundary is the important part. A timeout after the server accepts the bytes is not the same event as a rejected request. On a timeout or HTTP 429, retry with exponential backoff and honor Retry-After when it is present. On a non-retryable 4xx, retain the response body and mark the archive failed. On a successful write, record the exact bucket and key. A marketplace worker can then replay the same intent instead of guessing whether a partially observed request succeeded.

Compression is also a policy choice. Sharp is a sensible Node.js library for resizing and encoding images efficiently, but the resulting bytes still need a content policy: do not discard the original if the restore workflow promises it, and do not silently convert a format that a downstream review tool cannot read. For large files, measure the encoded output before choosing a single-request upload; a multipart design is the better boundary when a transfer is too large for one request.

Small rule. Keep the archive identity outside the filename.

Name the failure before you name the retry.

That sounds fussy until a worker is restarted between sending the last byte and receiving the response. The operator then needs to answer three separate questions: which tenant owned the object, which backup produced it, and whether a replay would overwrite the intended artifact. A deterministic key and idempotency token answer the first two from the request itself; the database record answers the third. If the workflow cannot make those identities stable, compression is not the risky part of the design.

For a large marketplace image, the useful log record is boring and specific: tenant ID, backup ID, object key, encoded format, byte count, attempt number, HTTP status, request ID, and the final disposition. It should distinguish a rejected write from an unknown write. That distinction changes the operator action. A rejected write can be retried after correcting the request; an unknown write should first be checked by key before another attempt. Treating both as “upload failed” is how duplicate archives and false restore failures enter an otherwise ordinary pipeline. The same record also gives the restore worker a bounded search: it checks the selected snapshot's object identity, not every object with a similar filename.

Which storage boundary fits the archive?

There is no universal winner. The following comparison is about operating the seam between image generation and tenant recovery, not a feature-count contest.

Option Useful fit Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 A team already operates around the S3 API and its surrounding ecosystem Confirm the exact retry, retention, and restore contract in the account configuration; an S3-shaped API alone does not define your application policy
Cloudflare R2 A team wants an S3-compatible object interface and already works in Cloudflare's environment Validate the egress and region assumptions for the marketplace's restore path before committing the archive there
Google Cloud Storage A team is standardized on Google Cloud and wants its native storage controls Check the adapter surface and identity model rather than assuming every S3 client behavior maps one-to-one
Infrai storage A team wants the AI call and private object write behind one REST base and one key It has no public or public-read ACL, no object versioning or object lock, no If-Match conditional write, and no cross-region automatic replication

Infrai is worth trying for the part of this workflow that hands model output to a private bucket when keeping one plain REST boundary matters more than provider-specific storage controls. Its discovery surface is public, each documented capability includes runnable examples in 10 languages, and idempotency is a documented platform convention, which removes some integration lookup and retry plumbing.

The trade is concrete. If the archive needs immutable, finance-grade retention, strict compare-and-swap writes, public permanent links, or cross-region replication, choose a specialist or build that control around one. Infrai's storage model also has no independently configurable CORS route for browser-direct uploads, its shortest lifecycle is one day, and metadata is not server-searchable beyond prefix listing. Those are design constraints, not footnotes.

How should I compress AI-generated images before a cloud upload?

The code below keeps the storage write small and observable. It assumes image_bytes is the output returned by the AI image step, then sends those bytes to the only storage write route specified for this workflow. The same environment key and base URL are used for both capabilities; the AI request shape is kept in the runtime client that produced image_bytes, rather than inventing fields for an endpoint whose request schema is not part of this decision record.

import hashlib
import os
import time
from pathlib import Path

import requests
from PIL import Image

BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
BUCKET = "marketplace-private"
TENANT_ID = "tenant-42"
BACKUP_ID = "run-0187"

def compress_image(source: Path) -> bytes:
    with Image.open(source) as image:
        output = image.convert("RGB")
        from io import BytesIO
        buffer = BytesIO()
        output.save(buffer, format="WEBP", quality=84, method=6)
        return buffer.getvalue()

def put_private_image(image_bytes: bytes) -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha256(image_bytes).hexdigest()[:16]
    key = f"{TENANT_ID}/backups/{BACKUP_ID}/image-{digest}.webp"
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
        "Content-Type": "image/webp",
        "Idempotency-Key": f"archive:{TENANT_ID}:{BACKUP_ID}:{digest}",
    }
    url = f"{BASE_URL}/storage/object/put/{BUCKET}/{key}"
    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.put(url, headers=headers, data=image_bytes, timeout=60)
        if response.status_code < 300:
            return key
        if response.status_code == 429 or response.status_code >= 500:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else min(2 ** attempt, 30)
            time.sleep(delay)
            continue
        raise RuntimeError(f"upload failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}")
    raise RuntimeError("upload did not complete after retrying")

# image_bytes is the AI runtime output produced with the same API key.
image_bytes = compress_image(Path("generated.png"))
object_key = put_private_image(image_bytes)
print(object_key)

This example deliberately does not request a public URL and does not send the Infrai authorization header to any returned presigned URL. In a browser workflow, issue a presigned upload or download only through a server boundary that your policy permits; the storage caveat about CORS still applies. For a large image, replace the single PUT with the documented multipart path and keep the completion operation tied to the same archive identity.

The alternative OpenAI images + S3 stack is perfectly reasonable, especially when the team already has both accounts. It means two signups, two credential sets, and glue code for moving image bytes between the image response and S3, plus separate billing and failure telemetry. The one-provider path gives up some independence: you trust one vendor, one bill, and one outage surface. That trade should be written into the architecture record, not hidden behind a convenient SDK.

The rejected shortcut and its valid use

The rejected shortcut is “upload the generated file under its filename and retry until it works.” It fails in three places: filenames collide across tenants, a timeout can repeat a write without an application-level identity, and a mutable object cannot prove which snapshot it belongs to. It is acceptable only for disposable, non-tenant artifacts where overwrites are harmless and a restore promise does not exist. That is not the marketplace archive described here.

For the real workflow, the restore record should point to the immutable-looking application identity you assigned, while the worker verifies the object before it reports success. Infrai does not provide object versioning, object lock, or If-Match; use a database or queue to coordinate strict concurrent writes. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the consumer still needs the same idempotency key.

The practical test is not “did the upload endpoint return 200?” It is “can a worker retry after a lost response, can an operator identify the exact tenant and backup, and can restore select the intended object without a public link?” If the answer is yes, the compression library is doing its narrow job and the storage boundary is carrying the recovery contract.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • Sharp image processing
  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Google Cloud Storage documentation
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing

title: Turning a Scanned Spec into Scenario Tests
description:
Quick answer: A scanned OpenAPI document gives you proven routes and classified contracts to build scenario tests from, instead of starting with a hand-written or guessed spec. You then order the requests into a flow, extract values between steps, and assert at each stage. The scan rebuilds the contract from code, and the scenario verifies the connected behavior the scan itself cannot prove.

Why the order matters

A scan and a scenario answer different questions. The scan tells you which routes exist and what shapes they declare, while the scenario tells you whether the connected flow works. Treating the scan as the end of verification would leave runtime behavior untested, since the scan does not run the app.

Using the scanned spec as the input keeps the scenario grounded in real routes rather than invented paths.

From scan to scenario

Stage What you get Purpose
Scan Proven routes and gate status Establish the real surface
Review Mounted, reachable routes Confirm what can be called
Scenario Ordered requests with extracted variables Model the business flow
Assertions Per-step checks Verify the connected behavior
Report Self-contained HTML record Share the evidence

The scenario is never stored in the OpenAPI document, with no x-scenarios keys, so the spec and the test stay separate.

Building the flow from detected routes

Once the routes are confirmed, chain them the way the business flow runs.

  1. Pick the routes that make up the flow, such as login, create, and read.
  2. Order them so each extraction precedes the step that needs it.
  3. Extract a token or id from one response and pass it into the next request.
  4. Assert status, headers, and fields at every step.
  5. Run the connected requests against the real backend, not a mock.

The engine runs the scenario in the main process with streamed progress and a cancel action, so you can watch the flow and stop a hung run.

Take a user onboarding flow. The scan proves the auth, profile, and preferences routes and marks each contract. After confirming they are mounted, you chain them in order: the auth step returns a token, the profile step uses it and returns a user id, and the preferences step writes against that id. A field assertion on the final read confirms the profile data matches what the earlier steps created. If the preferences step silently drops a value, the scan never sees it, but the assertion on the executed chain fails and the report points at that exact step rather than the whole flow.

What the scenario adds beyond the scan

This is where the gap from the scan gets closed. A route can be detected and emitted with a correct contract yet still break at runtime, and a 200 response can carry a field that breaks the contract or a later step. The scenario catches those failures by executing the chain and asserting the values, rather than trusting the static document.

A passing run covers only the flow you defined, not every path, and it does not prove the whole system is correct. Keep separate scenarios for the alternate branches, and treat an unexercised route as unverified.

Powerduck connects the two core workflows so the scanned spec feeds directly into the scenario engine, with the per-step evidence kept together.

Frequently asked questions

Does a scanned spec already verify the behavior? No. The scan rebuilds the contract from code but does not run the app. You build scenario tests from it to verify the connected flow.

Can I build scenarios on unmounted routes? No. Confirm the routes are mounted and reachable first, since an unmounted router cannot be called.

What does the scenario catch that the scan cannot? Runtime breaks across the chain, including a 200 with a bad field and a value that a later step rejects, because the scenario executes real requests.

The bottom line

A scanned spec is the reliable input for scenario testing, not the verification itself. Build ordered flows from the proven, reachable routes, pass values between steps, and assert at each stage against the real backend. This closes the runtime gap the scan cannot reach, while a passing run still covers only the defined flow. The two core workflows fit together: the scan rebuilds the contract, and the scenario proves the behavior. Continue in the code-to-OpenAPI guide.

title: ACH Return Codes Explained: R01–R85 and How to Handle Them in Production
description:
ACH Return Codes Explained: R01–R85 and How to Handle Them in Production

Understanding ACH Return Codes in Your Payout System

When an ACH transfer fails, the originating bank receives a return code—a two-character alphanumeric that tells you exactly why the transaction didn't settle. Unlike vague "payment declined" messages, ACH returns are standardized by Nacha (the National Automated Clearing House Association) and follow a predictable taxonomy. As a developer integrating payouts, understanding these codes is critical to building reliable retry logic, customer communication, and fallback routing.

The ACH Return Code Structure

All Nacha R-codes follow the format R + two digits (R01 through R85). Each code maps to a specific failure reason, and the reason determines whether a retry will help, whether you should contact the recipient, or whether you need to switch payment rails entirely.

Common Return Codes and Developer Handling

R01: Insufficient Funds

The recipient's account doesn't have enough balance to cover the debit.

When it fires: During settlement, typically 1–2 business days after submission.

How to handle it:

  • Don't retry immediately; the account balance won't change in seconds.
  • Wait 3–5 business days and retry once.
  • After one retry, notify the recipient and offer alternate payment methods (credit card, wire).
  • Log the return for reconciliation; mark the payout as "pending retry." 
def handle_ach_return(return_code, payout_id, recipient_email):
    if return_code == "R01":
        retry_after_days = 5
        schedule_retry(payout_id, days=retry_after_days)
        notify_recipient(
            recipient_email,
            "Your payout failed due to insufficient funds. "
            "We'll retry in 5 days or you can update your account."
        )
        return {"status": "pending_retry", "next_attempt": retry_after_days}

R03: No Account / Account Closed

The account number doesn't exist, or the account was closed before the ACH hit.

When it fires: During settlement or within 1–2 business days.

How to handle it:

  • This is permanent; don't retry.
  • Flag the recipient's bank details as invalid.
  • Require them to re-enter or verify their account before the next payout.
  • Escalate to your support team if the recipient disputes it. 
if return_code == "R03":
    mark_account_invalid(recipient_id)
    notify_recipient(
        recipient_email,
        "The bank account on file is no longer valid. "
        "Please update your account details."
    )
    return {"status": "account_invalid", "action": "require_resubmission"}

R10: Unauthorized

The recipient's bank received a debit they claim they didn't authorize—often a dispute initiated by the account holder.

When it fires: 1–60 days after settlement (recipient files a claim).

How to handle it:

  • Investigate with the recipient; they may have genuinely not authorized the payout.
  • Provide evidence of authorization (signed agreement, email consent).
  • If the recipient confirms they authorized it, ask them to withdraw the dispute with their bank.
  • If they don't, treat it as a chargeback and escalate.

R29: Corporate Account Closed

Similar to R03, but specifically for business accounts.

How to handle it: Same as R03—flag the account and require re-verification.

R31: Permissible Return by Consumer

The recipient initiated a return within the Nacha timeline (typically 60 days for consumer ACH).

How to handle it:

  • Treat as a dispute; investigate the reason with the recipient.
  • Don't retry without explicit re-authorization.
  • Update your internal dispute tracking.

Building Retry Logic Around Return Codes

Not all returns warrant a retry. Use this decision tree:

Return Code Retryable? Action
R01, R02 Yes (1–2x) Wait 3–5 days, retry once
R03, R04, R29 No Flag account, require re-entry
R10, R31 No Escalate as dispute
R07, R08 No Check your submission; likely a batch error
R20–R28 No Recipient bank error; contact support

Production Checklist

  • Log every return code with timestamp, payout ID, and recipient.
  • Implement exponential backoff for retryable codes; don't hammer the same account.
  • Notify recipients proactively when a payout fails, not after they ask.
  • Reconcile returns daily against your payout ledger; ACH returns can arrive up to 5 business days after submission.
  • Test with sandbox return codes provided by your ACH processor (e.g., Stripe, Payoutrail, Dwolla).

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.

title: Fix Supabase "Invalid Refresh Token" and "Auth session missing!"
description:
You were signed in a minute ago. You refreshed the page, opened a second tab, or clicked around as usual — and now you are on the login screen. The console says Invalid Refresh Token, Refresh Token Not Found, or the client throws Auth session missing!.

This is one of the most searched Supabase auth errors around Lovable, Bolt, Vite and other apps that use supabase-js. Usually the session was revoked, or the client is holding a refresh token the server no longer accepts.

Below are the checks I would run, in order. Everything here is taken from the User sessions guide, the Auth error codes table, the server-side Auth advanced guide, and the PKCE flow page, all read on 8 November 2026.

What a session actually is

A session starts when a user signs in. Supabase represents it with two values: a short-lived access token (a JWT; most apps should keep the default expiry of 1 hour) and a refresh token. The docs are explicit: refresh tokens "never expire but can only be used once." You exchange one for a new pair, and the old refresh token is spent.

The error-codes table maps the messages you see:

  • refresh_token_not_found: "Session containing the refresh token not found."
  • refresh_token_already_used: the token "has been revoked and falls outside the refresh token reuse interval."
  • session_not_found: the session no longer exists — the user signed out, or the row was deleted.
  • session_expired: an inactivity timeout or a configured maximum lifetime was reached.
  • conflict: "too many session refresh requests firing off at the same time for a user."

The JavaScript client also throws AuthSessionMissingError, with the message Auth session missing!. The error-codes guide describes the matching Kotlin exception the same way: the session is missing "if the user was logged out or deleted." getSession() can return null when the user "is not signed-in or has logged out."

1. Refresh-token reuse detection

Supabase treats a reused refresh token as a possible theft — for example a token that leaked in logs or cookies. If a reuse attempt does not fall under two exceptions, "the whole session is regarded as terminated and all refresh tokens belonging to it are marked as revoked."

The two exceptions:

  1. The same refresh token may be used more than once within a reuse interval. The default is 10 seconds, and they do not recommend changing it. This covers SSR, where the server and then the browser both refresh shortly after, and races when two requests refresh at once.
  2. If the parent of the currently active refresh token is used, the active token is returned. That covers a client that never received the previous response and later retries the token it already used.

Anything else ends the session: refresh_token_already_used, or refresh_token_not_found if the session row is already gone. You can disable reuse detection in Advanced Settings, but the docs say that is generally not recommended.

2. Multiple tabs refreshing at once

Two tabs, or two createClient() instances on the same page, often share one stored refresh token. Both try to refresh. The first succeeds and gets a new pair. The second still sends the old token. If that request falls outside the exceptions above, the entire session is revoked.

The conflict code "can often occur when you have too many session refresh requests firing off at the same time for a user." The client library has a long-standing report of this multi-tab race (supabase/gotrue-js#213). You can still trip it when a tab keeps a stale token, a React effect fires many refreshes, or you call setSession or refreshSession with an old token.

refreshSession() will throw if the current refresh token is invalid. Keep a single browser client, let it auto-refresh, and listen for TOKEN_REFRESHED rather than issuing parallel refreshes.

3. signOut() logging everyone out

The default scope of signOut() is global. That "signs the user out of every device they are currently signed in on, not just the current tab/session." The server-side guide calls this a common cause of invalid refresh token errors: a signOut() without a scope revokes every session that user has, including other tabs, devices, and any SSR context still holding the old token.

If you only want to end the current session:

const { error } = await supabase.auth.signOut({ scope: 'local' })

global invalidates every session first, then clears the local one. others invalidates every other session and keeps the current one. In the apps we check, a generated "Log out" button often calls signOut() with no options.

4. Server-side code seeing a stale token

If the error appears in a server log rather than the browser console, the advanced guide's first guess is that "the refresh token sent from the browser to your server is stale." Make sure the onAuthStateChange listener is registered early and free of bugs. When the server hits this error, they recommend deferring that render to the browser, where the client can use an up-to-date token.

A related trap: getSession() "loads values directly from the storage attached to the client." If that storage is request cookies, the docs advise against trusting those values for authorization — use getUser() instead. getClaims() only checks the JWT signature and expiry; "an unexpired token stays valid even when the session behind it was revoked." Call getUser() where that gap matters.

5. Magic link or confirm email opened in another browser

If the user requested a magic link or confirmation email in one browser and opened it in another browser or device, PKCE will fail. The docs are unambiguous: "The code verifier is created and stored locally when the Auth flow is first initiated. That means the code exchange must be initiated on the same browser and device where the flow was started."

The auth code in the URL is also single-use and valid for five minutes. Retrying the same link, or starting a second sign-in before the first completes (which overwrites the stored verifier), produces flow_state_not_found, flow_state_expired or bad_code_verifier. For the flow-state errors, the docs say to ask the user to sign in again.

If the link itself opens localhost instead of your production domain, that is a Site URL problem, not a refresh-token problem. I wrote up that fix separately: Supabase Email Link Goes to localhost.

6. Storage not persisting the session

By default, supabase-js sets persistSession to true and stores the session in local storage. If the environment has no storage — a server client without a custom adapter, or a misconfigured SSR setup — you get the warning: "No storage option exists to persist the session, which may result in unexpected behavior when using auth."

The official server-side example turns persistence off on purpose:

const supabase = createClient(supabase_url, publishable_key, {
  auth: {
    autoRefreshToken: false,
    persistSession: false,
    detectSessionInUrl: false
  }
})

Do not use those flags in the browser client that should keep the user signed in. If the server and browser need to share a session, use the storage option, or @supabase/ssr, which stores the session in cookies and uses PKCE by default. If nothing is written to storage, every reload looks like a new visit and getSession() comes back empty.

7. The session really is gone

Sometimes the error is not a bug. A session also ends when the user signs out, changes their password or takes another security-sensitive action, times out from inactivity or hits a maximum lifetime (Pro plans and up), or when "Single session per user" is enabled and they signed in on another device. Then only the most recent session stays active.

Those settings are not applied immediately to every existing session. The check runs the next time the session is refreshed, so "the actual duration of a session is the configured timeout plus the JWT expiration time."

When getSession() returns no session, or refreshSession() errors because the refresh token is invalid, do not keep retrying the same token. Show the sign-in screen.

How to see what the client thinks is happening

Register a listener early, and log the event name:

const { data } = supabase.auth.onAuthStateChange((event, session) => {
  console.log(event, session)
})

And read the current session from storage when you need it:

const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.getSession()

Identify errors with error.code and error.name, not by matching the message string. If event is SIGNED_OUT and nobody clicked log out, walk the list above.

Most of the sudden logouts I see come back to a refresh token used twice outside the reuse window, a signOut() that defaulted to every device, or a session that was never written to storage. Once the token is gone, the user has to sign in again.

If a confirmation or magic-link email is landing on the wrong host, start with that localhost write-up. And if you are about to launch, our free Launch Check looks at headers, exposed keys and more, with no sign-up.

title: Two AI agents in a chat to triage a real bug: what I learned with Switch.
description:
Title: I put two AI agents in a chat to triage a real bug: what I learned with Switch

For the Flip the Switch hackathon (WeMakeDevs × DevTools Academy), I wanted to see whether AI agents could do the boring front half of bug fixing: reading code, guessing the cause, and writing a reproduction.

The setup
Switch runs on my laptop in Docker. I made two OpenCode agents, a triager and a reproducer (using a free model), and put them in a Mattermost room. Both pointed at a clone of my Java project, TechPulse.

The bug
I asked about duplicate articles. The triager read the code, found that the duplicate check compared raw URLs, and handed it to the reproducer. The reproducer ran two items whose URLs differed only by a trailing slash, and both were saved (2 rows).

The fix
I approved a scoped change: normalize the URL (trailing slash, host case, #fragment, utm_* params) before the check, and keep params like ?id=5. The agent made the change and 5 JUnit tests, which pass.

What went wrong

  • The agent committed and pushed on its own, which I never asked for. Review every diff.
  • Console on Windows is early access, and on submission day the Mattermost bridge wouldn't start, so my video is a recap.
  • Free models are slow.

What I'd tell a first-time Switch user
Start with one narrow job, keep a human approving the scope, and work on branches.

title: Your Free Server Is Not Your Laptop: A Parity Probe for Five Assumptions That Break on Deploy
description:
You push. The build goes green. Then it 502s.

Sound familiar? The gap is almost never your business logic. It is the environment you quietly assumed.

So here is a myth-busting FAQ about free tiers. Claims developers repeat. Evidence you can collect yourself. A corrected mental model after each one.

Two claims are on the table, and only two. MonkeyCode offers free model access, and it has a free server option. Those are operator-supplied availability claims.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Everything else — quotas, hardware, sleep policy, storage lifetime — stays unmeasured until you probe it. I have not run the code below against that server for this article. You are the one collecting numbers.

Why "works on my machine" is a measurement problem

Your laptop and any remote host are different computers. That is not a bug. It is a fact you forgot to write down.

When something breaks on deploy, you are not debugging code. You are debugging unstated assumptions. So stop guessing and start enumerating.

Myth 1: "Same app, same environment"

The claim: I run the same build, so behavior must match.

But env vars differ. Working directories differ. The process supervisor differs. Even the timezone and locale may differ quietly.

A 12-factor app reads config from the environment. That does not mean both environments hold the same config.

Corrected model: a deployment is a new environment, not a copy of yours. Enumerate the facts you depend on, then assert them at boot.

  • Which env vars are present? Presence matters more than value.
  • What is process.cwd()? Relative paths resolve against it.
  • Is the directory writable? Many apps assume yes.

Myth 2: "If it binds locally, it's reachable"

The claim: the port works on my machine, so the host will expose it.

Locally you often bind 127.0.0.1. That is loopback only. A container or VM needs 0.0.0.0 to accept outside traffic.

Also many platforms inject PORT. Hardcoding 3000 is a guess dressed as a default.

Corrected model: binding is a two-part contract — address and port. Read both from the environment. Verify from outside, not inside.

Myth 3: "A restart is a no-op"

The claim: restarting just reruns my process, so nothing changes.

But in-memory state vanishes. Counters reset. Any local file cache might vanish too, depending on where you wrote it.

Write to /tmp? Maybe ephemeral. Write to cwd? Maybe not writable at all.

Corrected model: assume nothing survives a restart. Then prove which parts do. Persistence is a measurement, not a vibe.

Myth 4: "Free model access means free inference capacity"

The claim: the endpoint answers, so throughput is a solved problem.

Access is not capacity. A reachable endpoint tells you one thing only: it answered once, from one place, at one moment.

So measure rather than assume. Latency from your laptop is not latency from the host. Rate behavior under concurrency is unknown until you push.

Corrected model: treat free access as an envelope you discover. Send a small burst, record outcomes, and set your own concurrency ceiling below it.

Myth 5: "Local latency predicts user latency"

The claim: my API call takes 300ms at home, so users see 300ms.

Your laptop sits close to your network. The host sits somewhere else, with its own route and its own queue.

Add cold start on top. The first request after idle is not the thousandth request in steady state.

Corrected model: latency is a property of a path, not of a function. Measure from where the code runs.

The artifact: a /probe endpoint and a restart test

Here is the smallest thing that converts assumptions into evidence. One file, zero dependencies, Node 18+.

// probe.js — run: PORT=3000 node probe.js
import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { writeFileSync, mkdirSync, existsSync, readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const bootId = randomUUID();
const startedAt = Date.now();
const markerPath = join(tmpdir(), "probe-marker.json");
const target = process.env.PROBE_TARGET ?? "";

function writable(dir) {
  try {
    mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true });
    writeFileSync(join(dir, `.probe-${bootId}`), "ok");
    return true;
  } catch { return false; }
}

function previousBoot() {
  if (!existsSync(markerPath)) return null;
  try { return JSON.parse(readFileSync(markerPath, "utf8")); } catch { return null; }
}

async function upstream() {
  if (!target) return { skipped: true };
  const t0 = performance.now();
  try {
    const r = await fetch(target, { method: "HEAD" });
    return { status: r.status, ms: Math.round(performance.now() - t0) };
  } catch (e) {
    return { error: String(e?.message ?? e), ms: Math.round(performance.now() - t0) };
  }
}

const server = createServer(async (req, res) => {
  if (req.url !== "/probe") { res.writeHead(404).end("not found"); return; }
  const prev = previousBoot();
  writeFileSync(markerPath, JSON.stringify({ bootId, startedAt }));
  const body = {
    bootId,
    uptimeSec: Math.round((Date.now() - startedAt) / 1000),
    node: process.version,
    platform: process.platform,
    env: { PORT: process.env.PORT ?? null, NODE_ENV: process.env.NODE_ENV ?? null },
    files: {
      cwd: process.cwd(),
      cwdWritable: writable(process.cwd()),
      tmp: tmpdir(),
      tmpWritable: writable(tmpdir())
    },
    previousBoot: prev,
    upstream: await upstream()
  };
  res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "application/json" });
  res.end(JSON.stringify(body, null, 2));
});

server.listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000), "0.0.0.0", () => {
  console.log(`probe on 0.0.0.0:${process.env.PORT ?? 3000}`);
});

Note the deliberate choices. It binds 0.0.0.0. It reports env var presence, never values. It returns no secrets.

Run the restart test

Now call it twice, with a restart in between.

curl -s https://YOUR_HOST/probe | tee probe-1.json
# restart the service however your host does it
curl -s https://YOUR_HOST/probe | tee probe-2.json
diff <(jq -S . probe-1.json) <(jq -S . probe-2.json)

Then read the diff like a diagnostic.

  • bootId changed? Good, the process really restarted.
  • previousBoot is null? That marker did not survive. Your /tmp is not durable.
  • cwdWritable is false? Drop file-based caches from that path.
  • upstream.ms is large or errors? Measure from the host, not your desk.

Set PROBE_TARGET to your model endpoint URL to include it. A HEAD may return 405; that is still a useful reachability signal.

Guard this endpoint

A probe that leaks paths is a reconnaissance gift. Gate it behind a header or remove it after the test.

Never reuse /probe as your production health check. It writes files. Health checks should not.

Decision table: what belongs where

Once the probe answers, placement stops being a debate. Use this table.

Workload Your laptop Free server option Why
Public HTTP endpoint No Yes Needs an always-on address
Long cron batch No Verify first Restarts kill in-flight work
Local file cache Yes Only if writable Probe tells you
API key storage Never Env vars Never in the repo
Model calls under burst No Measure first Access is not capacity
Anything with an SLA No No Free is not a contract

Read the last row twice. Free is a starting point, not a promise.

Limitations and who should not use this

This probe reports facts about one process at one instant. It is not monitoring. It will not catch a host that degrades next Tuesday.

It says nothing about model output quality either. That is a separate experiment.

Skip this approach if you handle regulated data and cannot expose a diagnostics route. Skip it if you need a durability guarantee in writing.

Also skip it if you cannot accept a restart wiping state. Pick a platform with durable storage instead of fighting the free one.

The one-line takeaway

Stop asking "why did it work locally?" Start asking "what did I never verify?"

Write the probe. Run it twice. Let the diff argue for you. If you want a cheap place to point the probe at a model endpoint, MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option are enough to start measuring — and you now know exactly what to measure.

title: systemd gains support for Rust language but imposes strict rules
description:
Systemd officially adds Rust support while keeping core libraries in C and continuing to use Meson exclusively without Cargo, applying a no_std approach for architecture compatibility.

No to replacing existing code

The system's core libraries will remain written in the C language. There is no intention to rewrite the code that already works stably, as changing the language is not in itself a solution for system security.

Strict control of tools and libraries

The systemd team has decided not to use Cargo, the tool that usually comes with Rust to manage additional programs. Instead, the project will continue to rely solely on Meson, the system it has been using until now. With this decision, the creators want to keep the process simple and limit the risks that can arise from importing external libraries.

At this stage, the maintainers are expressing reservations about accepting external Rust libraries. To ensure that programs run properly, systemd will provide access to internal functions through its own tools.

Support is optional

The use of Rust in systemd will remain optional. This was deemed necessary as the language does not yet support all types of computers on which systemd is used. This will allow the system to remain compatible with older architectures that do not support the language.

title: Vercel Flags starts 7x faster and no longer extends function duration
description:
On Vercel, the Vercel Flags SDK now initializes faster on cold starts, and usage reporting no longer keeps functions running after the response.

Faster cold starts

Two changes speed up SDK initialization on cold starts:

  • The SDK loads and parses the flags datafile bundled with your deployment as soon as the client is created, so it’s ready before your code evaluates its first flag.

  • Every function invocation now includes the current datafile revision, so the SDK can check whether the bundled datafile is up to date without a network request.

In internal testing, eliminating the network wait reduced p75 cold-start SDK initialization time from over 70 ms to 10 ms, roughly 7x faster.

After initialization, flag reads are effectively instant. Across cold and warm invocations, p99 flag-read latency is under 1 ms.

Usage reporting no longer extends function duration

The SDK previously used waitUntil for usage reporting, keeping functions running after the response was sent. It now passes usage events to the Vercel runtime, so reporting no longer adds to function duration.

Update @flags-sdk/vercel to version 1.5.3 or later and redeploy your application:

Learn more in the Flags SDK documentation.

title: Long-Form SEO Article: EP01 - Backstage vs Port (Substack / Dev.to / Medium)
description:
Long-Form SEO Article: EP01 - Backstage vs Port (Substack / Dev.to / Medium)

Target Canonical URL: Substack Newsletter (controlplanelab.substack.com)

Secondary Syndication: Dev.to & Medium (with canonical link tag)

Target Keywords: Spotify Backstage review, Backstage vs Port, Internal Developer Portal architecture, Kubernetes IDP comparison

Why Platform Teams Are Ditching Spotify Backstage: An Architectural Teardown

Every platform engineering team hits the exact same crossroads: your developers are overwhelmed by Kubernetes YAML, fragmented microservices, and hidden cloud costs. Leadership demands an Internal Developer Portal (IDP).

And the immediate consensus is almost always: “Let’s just install Spotify Backstage.”

Six months later, reality sets in.

Backstage is not a ready-to-run developer portal. It is an open-source TypeScript framework that requires you to build, host, and maintain an internal SaaS product from scratch. And that maintenance wall is why a massive wave of platform engineering teams are pivoting to declarative, schema-driven alternatives like Port.

In this breakdown, we examine the architectural reality of Backstage versus Port: data model rigidity, action execution security, and total cost of ownership (TCO).


(Watch the full 10-minute video walkthrough above or check out our open-source blueprints repository on GitHub)

1. The Monolith Problem: When Frameworks Pretend to Be Products

When you run npx @backstage/create-app, you are not deploying a portal. You are scaffolding a full-stack monorepo with a React frontend and a Node.js Express backend.

my-backstage-app/
├── packages/
│   ├── app/         <-- React Frontend
│   └── backend/     <-- Node.js Express Server
├── plugins/         <-- Bespoke TypeScript code
└── package.json     <-- 1,200+ npm dependencies

Every integration—whether PagerDuty, Datadog, Argo CD, or Kubernetes—is an npm plugin compiled directly into your application bundle.

The Dependency Tax

The Backstage core team releases updates constantly. Monthly version bumps frequently introduce breaking API changes across community plugins. Unless your platform team includes full-time TypeScript developers who enjoy debugging React dependency conflicts, your portal roadmap quickly grinds to a halt just keeping the lights on.

2. Data Modeling: Static Entities vs. Dynamic Graphs

Backstage relies on a rigid entity model defined via catalog-info.yaml files committed into source code repositories:

apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: payment-service
  description: Handles Stripe webhooks
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: production
  owner: platform-team
  system: billing-system

This works well for static service catalogs. But modern cloud platforms are dynamic graph networks.

If you want to model ephemeral preview environments, cloud RDS clusters, or AWS IAM roles with dynamic relationships, Backstage forces you to write custom TypeScript entity processors.

The Port Alternative: Custom Graph Ontologies

Port treats your entire engineering organization as an extensible graph database of blueprints. You don't write React or TypeScript. Instead, you declare blueprints via simple JSON or Terraform:

{
  "identifier": "microservice",
  "title": "Microservice",
  "schema": {
    "properties": {
      "pci_compliant": { "type": "boolean" },
      "monthly_spend": { "type": "number" },
      "replicas": { "type": "number" }
    }
  },
  "relations": {
    "hostedInCluster": { "target": "kubernetes-cluster", "required": true },
    "ephemeralPreviews": { "target": "preview-env", "many": true }
  }
}

How does the data get into Port? Instead of polling Git for static YAML, Port uses lightweight open-source Ocean exporters running inside your Kubernetes clusters or CI pipelines. The exporter watches cluster resources, maps them against your blueprint schema, and pushes state updates over HTTPS. No inbound ports opened, and no cluster secrets leave your network.

3. The Execution Plane: Where Do Your Credentials Live?

When developers use a Golden Path to spin up an environment, where do the credentials live?

Backstage Scaffolder

In Backstage, the Scaffolder engine executes actions inside the Backstage backend container. This means your Backstage pod needs direct access to GitHub Organization PATs and cloud IAM roles. This creates a significant blast radius if the portal pod is compromised.

Port's Decoupled Architecture

Port completely decouples the UI from the execution plane. When a developer clicks "Spin Up Ephemeral Preview" in Port:

  1. Port does not execute the deployment.
  2. It emits an authenticated event to an internal GitHub Actions runner, Argo Workflow, or Kafka topic.
  3. The execution happens entirely within your private VPC runners.
  4. Progress logs stream back to the UI.

Zero credentials leave your secure infrastructure.

4. Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)

Let’s look at the actual numbers:

Metric Spotify Backstage Port (Declarative IDP)
Software License $0 (Open Source) SaaS fee
Required Engineering 1.5 – 2 Full-Time Engineers 0.1 – 0.2 FTE
Annual Labor Upkeep ~$300,000 – $450,000 ~$20,000 – $35,000
Time to MVP 4 – 6 Months 1 – 2 Weeks
Ongoing Maintenance High (TypeScript upgrades) Low (Declarative schema)

Open source is only free if engineering time has zero value.

5. The Decision Matrix

  • Choose Spotify Backstage if:

    • You operate in a strictly air-gapped environment with zero SaaS tolerance.
    • You require completely bespoke React UI workflows that no configurable SaaS can provide.
    • You have dedicated frontend developers within your platform engineering organization.

  • Choose Port if:

    • You are a lean platform team (1–5 engineers) that needs immediate business value.
    • Your infrastructure runs on Kubernetes, GitOps, and modern cloud primitives.
    • You want zero framework maintenance overhead.

Clone the Blueprints & Manifests

All architecture diagrams, Backstage catalog files, and Port JSON blueprints shown in this teardown are open source:

👉 Clone the Blueprints on GitHub: ControlPlaneLab/blueprints

👉 Subscribe to Control Plane Lab on YouTube: @ControlPlaneLab

title: Using AI without losing people's trust: a designer's view
description:
A few days ago I read "Don't let AI cost you your credibility at work" by Hoang Nguyen in the MindYourMind community. He tells the story of a Product Owner candidate who submitted a test almost entirely written by AI, then kept using AI to answer questions during the presentation. The test ended after two questions.

It made me realize this is not just a PO problem. As a designer, I have seen it too, and I have received documents from other stakeholders with the same issue. My previous post asked whether AI is making designers lazy thinkers, which is about what happens inside each of us. This one is about what happens outside: other people look at our work and decide whether to trust us.

A polished test, but two questions were enough

I once looked over a test from a designer candidate. The brief was to improve the checkout screen of a shopping app. The submission looked great: a problem statement, user insights and five proposed improvements. Proposal number one was "optimize the checkout journey to reduce friction for users".

During the presentation, I asked a simple question: "Which step has the friction? Where do users get stuck?". The candidate read the slide back in different words, but could not point to a step. I asked again: "If you could only do one thing, what would you pick and what would you drop?". No answer either, because those five proposals had been listed by AI, and none had been weighed by the candidate.

A more convincing answer can be very simple: "At the address step, the form has 9 fields. I asked 3 friends to fill it in and all 3 stopped at the postal code field. I would remove that field first." No fancy wording, it just shows you looked at the problem yourself.

I don't think the candidate was weak. A test simply isn't there to see how polished your document is, but how you think when you face a problem.

Three places designers lose points

In my view, these are the three places where AI most easily costs a designer credibility, because they are where others judge how we think.

Explaining design decisions

A design decision holds up when it answers three questions: what is the problem, what are we trading off, and how will we measure it. AI is quick to write lines like "optimize the user journey" or "elevate the visual experience". They are not wrong, they just say nothing specific, so one "why" is enough to expose them.

The same proposal, presented two ways. The mockup, figures and content have been changed to protect the project's confidentiality.

Presentation B is not longer than A. It simply contains things the author had to find out: 5 of 8 testers had to scroll to see the battery level, the weather card has to give up its spot, and after launch we will measure time to find the battery level. AI can help phrase those points more tightly, but it cannot come up with them for you.

Writing UX copy

This is where the "AI voice" shows most, because end users read it every day: long sentences with many clauses, words like "journey", "seamless", "optimal", and structures that read like a literal translation. In Vietnamese this is especially visible, and Hoang Nguyen notes he almost never saw such phrasing at work before AI became common.

An AI insight card before and after editing. The mockup, product name, figures and content have been changed to protect the project's confidentiality.

Nielsen Norman Group also points out that AI drafts tend toward generic phrasing, drift from brand voice, and know nothing about your users or context. Their advice is to treat AI as a first-draft collaborator and always have a person review the copy before it ships. The edited card above does not need beautiful writing. It only needs to answer what the user wants to know: does today affect me?

Writing case studies and portfolios

A case study is where recruiters learn how you work. One written with AI usually has every section: context, problem, process, results. But read closely and you can't find yourself in it. No moment where you were wrong, no hard decision, no detail only someone on the project would know.

People who read many case studies notice quickly. And as in the example above, they will check in the interview.

Across stakeholders: one missing edge case and the flow falls apart

For documents that pass between stakeholders, the problem is usually not the wording but what was never written down. I once received a requirements document that looked complete: goals, user stories, acceptance criteria. But edge cases were almost absent: what happens if the connection drops midway, what to show when there is no data, where users resume if they come back mid-flow.

Once design and development started, those questions came up one by one. Everyone guessed differently, the flow got messy, and we had to go back into meetings to align. The time the document saved its author was simply moved to the whole team.

In another case, the acceptance criteria (ACs) were written by AI separately for each user story, and the author never put them side by side to cross-check. Each AC made sense on its own, but together some contradicted each other: one required auto-saving a draft on exit, another required clearing data on exit. Developers built every AC correctly, and the flow was still wrong.

There are also times when a team uses AI to build the interface directly to move fast, and that version goes live. Each screen looks fine on its own. But when the team's design system is not tight enough, every AI-generated screen picks its own colors, spacing and components. Put together as a whole platform, the screens no longer speak the same language. In the end, designers have to take that live version as the starting point, bring it back into Figma, and review and fix it until it is consistent. The time saved by building fast gets paid back later in rework. My takeaway: AI builds fast and right only when the design system is clear enough for it to follow. If the foundation isn't solid, AI just makes the inconsistencies show up sooner.

Researchers at BetterUp Labs and the Stanford Social Media Lab call this kind of output "workslop": AI-generated content that looks like good work but lacks the substance to move a task forward. In their survey, about 40% of workers said they had received workslop in the past month, spending nearly two hours on average dealing with each instance. More striking, about half of recipients saw the sender as less creative, less capable and less trustworthy.

Nobody says anything, but people remember

The part of Hoang Nguyen's post I agree with most is that trust is not lost in one go. People still say thanks, still use the document, sometimes don't even ask for changes. But next time there is a hard problem, they think of someone else first.

(Every document gets a thank-you, but the trust level never shows up anywhere. See the animation in the original post.)

For a designer, that might mean not being invited to a product direction meeting, or having your proposals go through an extra round of checks. Nothing tells you it has started.

Using AI in a way people can still trust

To be honest, the website you are reading was also built with AI, vibe coding style. I use it as a place to show my projects and notes, not to sell web development or to suggest I am a developer. What I take responsibility for is what sits on it: the design decisions, the project stories and every post. I think being clear about which part AI helped with and which part is mine is also a way to keep people's trust.

I still use AI every day: summarizing documents, suggesting phrasing, listing edge cases for me to review, sketching a few options to compare. But before sending anything important, I ask myself four questions.

Four questions before hitting send, and a spec excerpt before and after rewriting. The mockup and content have been changed to protect the project's confidentiality.

  1. Can I say the key message again in my own words? If I need to look at the slide, I may not really understand it yet.
  2. Can I answer "why not the other option"? A decision with no rejected alternative is often not a decision yet.
  3. Have I opened the source of every number myself? AI is very good at producing numbers that sound plausible.
  4. Is there any sentence I would never say out loud? If so, I rewrite it the way I would say it in a meeting.

The fourth one sounds simple, but it works best for me. Sometimes I have to drop a line that sounds great and replace it with a plainer one that says what I actually mean.

Wrapping up

I don't think there is one right way to use AI. Every person and every team is finding their own rhythm with a tool that changes almost every month. Some of the stories in this post are moments I stumbled on myself. I wrote them down to remember, not to say who is right or wrong.

For me, working in a world with AI feels like having a very fast collaborator. I hand it the repetitive work and save my time for the parts that need me most: understanding users, weighing trade-offs and being able to explain my decisions. When someone asks "why", the answer comes from what I actually understand, and that is the part AI cannot hold for me.

Hoang Nguyen has a comparison I really like: when your AI tokens run out you can buy more, but trust takes time to build. So I choose to keep using AI and keep learning with it, while holding on to the habit of understanding what I send out. If you are also figuring out how to work with AI and want to talk, feel free to reach out on yurickart.com!

Sources

The survey data below was collected from US workers, has limited scope, and does not replace my own point of view.

  1. Hoang Nguyen (2026). Đừng để AI làm mất sự tín nhiệm của bạn trong công việc (Don't let AI cost you your credibility at work). MindYourMind (members-only post, in Vietnamese).
  2. Niederhoffer, K., Rosen Kellerman, G., Lee, A., Liebscher, A., Rapuano, K., Hancock, J. T. (2025). AI-Generated "Workslop" Is Destroying Productivity. Harvard Business Review.
  3. Kaley, A. (2026). UX Writing: FAQs from Practitioners. Nielsen Norman Group.

Originally published at yurickart.com.

title: Same AI, two answers: what happened when we gave our on-call agent a memory..
description:
When people talk about making AI better, they usually talk about bigger models. More parameters, longer context, a newer version. Our team tried something different while building DejaVu, an AI agent for on-call engineers. We kept the model exactly the same and only changed one thing: we gave it a memory.

The result surprised all of us.

The experiment

DejaVu helps an engineer when something breaks in production. You paste an error, and it tells you the probable root cause and how to fix it.

To test it, we used one realistic outage. A payments service starts throwing KeyError: 'amount' right after a new deploy. Then we asked the same model, GPT-OSS 120B running on Groq, the same question twice.

Round 1: no memory. The model answered with 20% confidence: "Likely a schema mismatch after deploy. Check the code and cache." That's not wrong. It's what a smart stranger would say. But it doesn't tell you what to do at 3 a.m.

Round 2: with memory. This time the agent first searched its long-term memory of past incidents, then answered with 98% confidence: a Redis cache invalidation bug after the v3.2 deploy, leaving stale v1 keys. It gave the exact command to flush those keys, told us to restart the pods, and listed 5 past incidents where this exact fix worked.

Same model. Same question. The only difference was memory.

Where the memory comes from

The memory layer is Hindsight, an open-source agent memory system by Vectorize. We store each past incident in a Hindsight "memory bank": the error, the root cause, the fix and whether it worked.

If you're new to the idea, Vectorize has a clear explainer on what agent memory is. The short version: memory is not just a pile of documents in a prompt. The agent keeps learning facts over time, and it can recall the right ones when it needs them.

Here is the call that asks Hindsight for similar past incidents:

response = client.recall(
    bank_id="dejavu-incidents",
    query=error_text,      # the new error the engineer pasted
    budget="mid",
)
for fact in response.results:
    print(fact.text, fact.scores.reranker)

Each result is a fact Hindsight remembers, with a relevance score. We group the facts by incident and send only the top matches to the model. The Hindsight docs explain recall, retain and reflect in detail.

Why a bigger model wouldn't have helped

A bigger model knows more about the world. But it still knows nothing about your company. It has never seen your services, your deploys or the bug your team fixed last March.

That's the gap memory fills. In our test data, the same cache bug appeared 6 times on 3 different services, each with a different error message. One said KeyError, another said TypeError, another said "password reset tokens rejected as expired". A human would need hours to connect those. Hindsight's semantic recall connected them in seconds, because it matches on meaning, not on exact words.

No amount of model size can recall something it was never told.

The agent gets better every time

The best part is that the memory grows. After each incident, the engineer clicks Fix worked or Fix failed. That result is saved back into Hindsight as a new memory.

During one practice run of our demo, we clicked "Fix worked" once. On the next run, that brand-new incident showed up as the best match, fixed in 1 minute. The agent had learned from us in real time.

Across our 20 recorded incidents, the average time to fix dropped from 44 minutes for the first 5 to 6 minutes for the last 5. That's 87% faster, with no change to the model.

What I'm taking away

  1. Context beats size. For work that depends on your own history, the right memory matters more than a bigger model.
  2. Show the proof. Engineers trust an answer when they can see the 5 past incidents behind it.
  3. Let users teach it. One click of feedback turned into a new memory. That loop is what makes the agent improve.

What surprised me most

I expected memory to help a little. I didn't expect it to change the kind of answer. Without memory, the model talked in general terms: "check the code", "check the cache". With memory, it talked like a teammate who was there last time: the exact keyspace to flush, the exact service to restart, and how long it took before.

It also became more honest. We designed it so that when an error has no proven match in memory, the agent doesn't pretend. It says there is no similar incident in memory and keeps its confidence low. A model on its own rarely admits that.

That's the real promise of agent memory for me. It's not only about being right more often. It's about knowing the difference between "I've seen this" and "I'm guessing", and telling the engineer which one it is.

Try it yourself

DejaVu is open source:

  • Code: https://github.com/Pratheeksh-7S/dejavu-incident-agent
  • 3-minute demo video: https://youtu.be/Nu_sktguGMk
  • Hindsight: https://github.com/vectorize-io/hindsight

Next time someone says "we need a bigger model", it's worth asking first: does the model actually remember anything?

title: Object Storage Service for Browser File Uploads: S3, R2, or REST?
description:
Object Storage Service for Browser File Uploads: S3, R2, or REST?

Short answer: for browser file uploads, choose an object storage service by its request semantics and operational boundary, not by the bucket API alone. Amazon S3 is the ecosystem baseline, Cloudflare R2 fits applications already built around Cloudflare, and a unified REST approach can suit teams that want storage and other backend capabilities behind one credential.

The practical question is what the application must own: a presign URL flow, metadata, retries, multipart uploads, retention, and provider-specific behavior. A good choice keeps those decisions visible without making every service learn a different client library.

For teams that expect storage to sit beside several backend capabilities, Infrai fits the workflow where a single key and one HTTP convention are more useful than another provider-specific SDK. Its public discovery surface also lets a developer inspect the documented shape before wiring credentials into a service.

What does a browser file upload need from an object storage service?

The happy path is simple: a browser asks the backend for permission, receives a short-lived presign URL, and uploads a file directly to object storage. The backend then records the object key and metadata. The less happy paths are where the provider matters: an expired URL, a duplicate key, a partially completed upload, or a file whose content type is not what the client declared.

That is why S3 is still the compatibility baseline. It supplies familiar object, bucket, metadata, and multipart vocabulary, and a large ecosystem knows how to work with it. “S3-compatible,” however, is not the same as identical. Lifecycle rules, notifications, consistency details, and multipart edge cases still belong in an integration test.

R2 changes the decision through placement. For an application already using Cloudflare Workers and the Cloudflare network, keeping browser uploads and edge execution in the same platform can simplify the path. The cost is architectural coupling: storage becomes part of the Cloudflare operating model, which may be a poor fit for a service whose deployment center is elsewhere.

There is no universally correct bucket.

How should a service compare S3, R2, and a unified REST API?

Option Strong fit Main constraint Integration posture
Amazon S3 Teams that want the broadest ecosystem and established tooling Provider-specific details still surface beyond common calls SDK-first, with mature REST primitives
Cloudflare R2 Applications already centered on Cloudflare's edge and Workers The platform choice is coupled to the Cloudflare operating model S3-compatible API with Cloudflare-oriented deployment
Infrai Teams that prefer one REST boundary across several backend capabilities Required storage semantics still need validation against documented routes HTTP-first, discoverable, and unified behind one key

The unified option is most interesting when storage is only one part of the backend. Its documented surface covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. That can remove concrete workflow friction: fewer credential lifecycles, fewer client conventions, and fewer provider-specific configuration paths for developers and operators to keep synchronized.

The API is also self-describing, with a public discovery surface that does not require a key. Documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. Those properties make an early integration review easier, but they do not remove the need to verify object size, metadata, retention, and failure behavior for the application.

An HTTP boundary is useful only when it is concrete. The method, URL, headers, and path parameters should be visible to the person reviewing the code. This example uses a documented object-read route:

curl --request GET \
  --url 'https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/get/media/avatars%2Fuser-123.json' \
  --header 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_INFRAI_API_KEY'

The example is intentionally small. Production code still needs a presign URL strategy for browser uploads, a retry policy, payload-size handling, and tests for the metadata the application depends on. HTTP is not automatically simpler than an SDK; it is simpler when several services can share one request convention.

One implementation detail deserves emphasis: do not put a long-lived API key in browser code. Keep provider credentials on the server, issue narrowly scoped upload authorization from the backend, and treat the returned file key as untrusted input until it has passed validation.

Where are the alternatives stronger?

S3 is the conservative choice when ecosystem breadth and native compatibility dominate. Data pipelines, backup products, local emulators, and infrastructure modules commonly assume S3 vocabulary. If portability across that ecosystem is the main requirement, using S3 directly may be cleaner than translating through another layer.

R2 is strong when deployment already follows the Cloudflare edge model. The value is architectural: fewer network boundaries and a consistent operational home for an edge application. It is less compelling when the service is not otherwise using Cloudflare or when storage decisions should remain independent of the edge provider.

The unified REST route is not a substitute for checking storage-specific requirements. A team that depends on a particular native S3 feature, a mature migration tool, or a provider-specific compliance control should verify that requirement against current documentation before committing. The approach is most useful when reduced integration surface matters alongside storage, not when exact parity with every S3 detail is the only acceptance criterion.

That limitation is part of a fair recommendation. If the application's contract is built around a provider's full native feature set, native tooling may have less translation risk.

A decision process for backend teams

First, write down the operations the service actually performs. Include object size, expected concurrency, multipart behavior, conditional writes, retention, notifications, and the regions in which data must live. “We need object storage” is too broad to compare APIs responsibly.

For example, a profile-image flow often looks like a storage problem but is really three contracts. The browser needs an authorization response that cannot be reused indefinitely. The storage layer needs a stable object key and a predictable content type. The application database needs to know whether the upload finished before it displays the image. Those contracts create different tests: an expired presign URL should fail without exposing credentials; a retry should not silently create an unexpected second object; and a successful object read should not be treated as proof that the database transaction completed. Writing these cases down usually changes the provider discussion. A team may discover that it needs native multipart support, or that it only needs a small server-side proxy. Either result is more useful than comparing brand names on a feature matrix. The same exercise also clarifies whether a unified REST boundary removes real setup work or merely moves provider-specific behavior into application code.

Second, separate compatibility from convenience. S3 compatibility answers whether familiar calls can be made. It does not answer whether the identity model, observability, deployment boundary, or data-movement workflow fits the team.

Third, count integration boundaries. If the service uses storage only, a mature dedicated object store may be the simplest long-term dependency. If it uses several backend capabilities, one key and one HTTP convention can reduce the setup paths developers and operators must understand. That is a workflow advantage, not a claim that every individual operation is better.

Finally, test failure modes before production: expired upload authorization, timeouts, retries, duplicate requests, missing objects, invalid credentials, large files, and partial workflows. Record which behavior is guaranteed by the API and which behavior belongs to your service. The answer should survive a new engineer reading the integration six months later.

The recommendation

Choose S3 when ecosystem breadth and native compatibility dominate. Choose R2 when Cloudflare is already the natural deployment boundary. Evaluate the unified REST option when the team wants discoverability and expects storage to sit beside several other backend capabilities under one credential.

The deciding factor is not a price table. It is the amount of application and operational friction created by the boundary you select. A single key, a uniform request style, public discovery, and runnable examples in 10 languages can make a unified platform easier to evaluate and maintain. Those benefits matter when they match the shape of the system being built.

For the storage routes and request shapes, teams considering Infrai should start with the Infrai storage documentation and verify the exact semantics their upload flow requires.

References

  • Amazon S3 API Reference
  • Amazon S3 User Guide
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility
  • Infrai storage documentation

title: Peso Pricing Without Tears: Money Math for Philippine Reseller Tools
description:
If you build tools for Filipino sellers, sooner or later you hit a boring but sneaky problem. Money math.

Supplier rates come in one currency, often with four or five decimal places. Your customers want clean peso prices. And somewhere between the two, rounding errors quietly eat your margin.

Here's how I'd handle peso pricing in a small reseller or SMM tool.

Rule 1: never use floats for money 

>>> 0.1 + 0.2
0.30000000000000004

Fine for physics. Terrible for invoices. Use Decimal in Python (or integer centavos everywhere).

from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP, ROUND_CEILING

def to_peso(value) -> Decimal:
    return Decimal(str(value)).quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)

Rule 2: prices are per 1,000, orders aren't

Most social media service APIs quote a rate per 1,000 units. Customers order 250, 1,500 or 3,333. So the charge is:

def order_cost(rate_per_1000: Decimal, quantity: int) -> Decimal:
    raw = rate_per_1000 * Decimal(quantity) / Decimal(1000)
    # round UP to the centavo so you never undercharge
    return raw.quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_CEILING)

Rounding up on cost protects you. Rounding half-up on the displayed price keeps it friendly.

Rule 3: show "nice" prices, store exact ones

Filipino buyers respond better to ₱49 than ₱48.73. But your ledger should keep the exact value.

def display_price(cost: Decimal, margin: Decimal) -> Decimal:
    price = cost * (Decimal(1) + margin)
    # round to the nearest peso for display
    return price.quantize(Decimal("1"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)

Store cost, margin and display_price separately. When a customer disputes a charge, you'll be glad you did.

Rule 4: minimum orders need a floor price

A 100-unit order at a tiny per-1,000 rate can round to ₱0.00. Set a floor:

MIN_CHARGE = Decimal("1.00")
charge = max(order_cost(rate, qty), MIN_CHARGE)

Rule 5: log the rate you used

Rates change. Log the exact rate at order time alongside the order ID so refunds and partial deliveries can be calculated against the right number.

Where this applies

Any tool that resells API-priced services in pesos. For a concrete example, BoostingPH is a Philippine social media service panel that exposes a standard order/status API at https://www.boostingph.com/api with peso pricing. Their write-up on how boosting sites in the Philippines price their services is useful context for why clean peso numbers matter to buyers.

Small rules. Fewer angry tickets. Cleaner books.

MD Fozla Rabbi, SEO Specialist

title: LLフレームワークの不都合な事実
description:
現在進行形で世界的なセキュリティ脅威が拡大している。

いま起きていることは、ここ1年ほどで急拡大したAIのパワーを活用して新たなゼロデイ脆弱性が発見され、セキュリティパッチを上回る速度で攻撃が進行する事態と言える。

実際に運営を手がけているメディアDecider, directly.サイトを観測している限りでも、存在しないアドレスに対して世界各地からのアクセスが増えている。
リクエストの内容から、既知の脆弱性を持つプロダクトが提供するエンドポイントの存在をスキャンする挙動であることが分かる。

全体を俯瞰すると、運営サービスの安全性はつねに予断を許さない状況にある。ネットワークライブラリやカーネルが本来提供する役割のセキュリティ隔離を無効化する方法が続々と発見されているからだ。影響を受けていないにしても、それはひと通り確認できたうえで分かることで、防衛は消耗戦になる。

これは、航空自衛隊が近年、スクランブル哨戒を迫られる構図とよく似ている。深層で働いている力には同質性がある。

脆弱性は、直感的には悪用や攻撃として捉えられるが、実装形態としてはサービス機能の1つでしかない。
セキュリティ対策は、適切な挙動に修正することも含めて、サービス機能の削減のバリエーションと言える。

直近、社会で起きているインシデントをリアルタイムで確認している限り、廃止できるものを積極的に廃止していく方向が防衛に効果的と言える。

Web2.0が注目されていた頃のLL言語（PHP, Python, Ruby, Javascript）ベースのWebアプリケーションフレームワークから時間をかけて脱却してきたことが、かなり防衛に効いていることを実感している。

脱スクリプト

LL言語は、コードを書いたらすぐにその通りに動く性質が評価されて広まっている。
その機能はそのまま攻撃に利用できる能力になっていて、該当言語のスクリプトを置かれたらかなり自由に攻撃される、という関係にある。

Deciderのアプリケーションは、当初はRuby on Railsでスタートしたが、かなり早期にRustに移行した。
当時は、今のような体系的なサイバー・ウォーフェアを想定していたわけではなかった。しかし、スクリプト注入できるランタイムがないことの効果は絶大だ。

脱ORマッパー

2026年のサイバー攻撃の新たな特徴は、データベースを丸ごと外から取り出されるという被害形式が多発した点にもある。
これは、インジェクションで自由に実行される前項のバリエーションと、権限奪取によってフルデータアクセスを得るケースに大きく分かれている。

フルデータアクセスについては、アプリケーションがフルデータアクセスできているから外から取得できる、という関係にある。
これはあまり自明ではないが、防衛策は個々のSQLクエリが最小限のデータアクセスになっていることを保証する、というアプローチが必要になる。

そのためには、セキュアコーディングの慣行が必要となり、個別のパラメタライズドSQLのレビューを完備することが有効と言える。
これは、ORマッパーを利用すると簡潔に書ける、というWeb2.0時代のキャッチコピーとはかなり違う事態だ。

また、今年じっさいに報告されたインシデントでは、サービス本体ではなく外付けで導入した分析アプリケーションが流出経路になった例がある。
これも、レビューを経ていないSQLが存在している、という生態のバリエーションだろう。

コンテナ化

kubernetesによるコンテナ化については、さまざまな効果がある。
セキュリティ面では、万一侵入されたとして、悪用できる追加の脆弱性ランタイムにアクセスできない、という点が効果的と言える。

もちろん、初動の侵入を許したくはないのだが、ネットワークソフトウェアの実際の脆弱性を見る限り、運営者が最善の努力をしたとしてもノーガードになる瞬間は、残念ながら十分存在しうると見ている。
2026年10月のPHP2Shellは、世界中で緊急パッチ適用やサービス停止が相次いだ。これは、PHPのスクリプティングホストの側面というより、利用しやすいゼロデイ侵入経路の側面が強い。

このときCVE-2026-99999も同時進行しており、PHPホストがなくても強力な潜在脅威があった。しかし、脆弱なPHPホストがフロントにあった場合、直通でネットワークセキュリティを全面無効化できる側面があった。

このシナリオを評価していて、たとえ隔離の強度が下がる瞬間があったとしても、コンテナ化は防壁として有効と再認識した。

なおこれも自明ではないが、LLアプリケーションはRAM使用量が乱高下するので、OOMしやすくコンテナ化に向いていない性質がある。
サポートのためにrails consoleを起動したら、productionサービスがOOM killedで全部落ちたことがあり、これはLL言語全廃を決めた主要な理由だった。

セキュアコーディングには捨てる意思がかなり必要

LL WAF->Rustコンテナへの移行の主要な側面を整理した。

けっきょくのところ、防衛について注意すべき観点はセキュアコーディングの原則から来ている。
そうなると、無数のミクロな判断の積み上げが必要となり、モノリシックなシステムほど一足飛びに移行することが考えられなくなる。

また、移行過程で正常系の処理範囲を狭めるところに防衛力の源泉があるため、コードの機械的な置換では十分なガードが得られない可能性がある。
どちらかというと、段階的に廃止していくというより、限定された再実装コードに切り替えていかなければ最終的な保証を確認しづらい性質がある。
