title: It won on the steady sellers and lost on the rest
description:
On one Walmart store, a machine-learning forecast was 3.9 percent worse than a 28-day moving average on absolute error, and the worse forecast for 58 percent of the 823 items. Split by demand class, the result is two opposite ones: it wins on the steady sellers and loses by about 10 percent on the intermittent and lumpy items, which are most of the store.

The usual way to choose a forecast is to compare one error number per model and pick the smallest. This note shows, on real retail data, why that number alone can point the wrong way for most of the catalogue. Everything below was measured with forelint, the open-source library I wrote for auditing forecast backtests, and the script that produces every figure is in its repository.

The setup

The data is the public M5 competition set: daily unit sales from Walmart. I took one store, CA_1, and one department, FOODS_3: 823 items. Each forecast covers the next 28 days, and the backtest repeats it at ten forecast origins 28 days apart, so the ten forecasts do not overlap and every comparison rests on ten separate results.

Two forecasts compete. One is a gradient-boosting model from scikit-learn, trained on all items together, with six features: the item, the day of the week, sales 28 and 35 days earlier, and 7- and 28-day averages of those. It is deliberately plain. The other is a 28-day moving average: each item's mean daily sales over its last four weeks, repeated forward.

Overall

On absolute error the model is worse. Its MAE was 1.742 against 1.676 for the moving average, a forecast value added of −3.9 percent, and it was the worse of the two on 58 percent of items.

On squared error it looks slightly better: RMSE 3.44 against 3.51. But a Diebold-Mariano test across the ten origins gives p = 0.20, so that difference is not established. Squared error weights big misses heavily, and big misses happen on the items that sell a lot; the RMSE versus MAE note works through why the two can disagree.

By demand class

The Syntetos-Boylan classification sorts each item by how often it sells and how much the sale sizes vary, using its history before the first forecast: smooth, erratic, intermittent or lumpy. Breaking the same backtest down by class, on absolute error:

Demand class Items Value added vs moving average Items where the model is worse
Smooth 152 +5.0% 23%
Erratic 33 +1.4% 33%
Intermittent 463 −10.5% 68%
Lumpy 171 −9.2% 69%


The model earns its keep on the steady sellers and loses about a tenth of its accuracy on everything that sells in bursts.

The model wins on the 152 smooth items and loses on the 463 intermittent and 171 lumpy ones, which together are 77 percent of the store. On about two thirds of the intermittent and lumpy items, the moving average was the better forecast.

That changes the decision. The overall number says the moving average is a little better. The breakdown says use the model for the steady sellers, where it is better, and a simpler forecast or a method built for intermittent demand for the rest. One model for every item is the choice the overall number hides.

Two more things worth knowing

Bias, item by item. Across the store the model's bias was small, −0.6 percent of sales. But its mean error was significantly different from zero on 24 percent of items, against under 1 percent for the moving average: too high on some items and too low on others, cancelling out in the total. Item-level bias is what turns into empty shelves and overstock, as the forecast bias note works through.

Concentration. The 82 items with the largest error, a tenth of the store, held 74 percent of the model's squared error. Improving the squared-error score mostly means fixing that list, and the audit names the items.

What I would check on any forecast

  • Value added against a simple baseline, on the error measure that matches the cost of a miss.
  • The same comparison per demand class. Steady items and intermittent items reward different methods, and one average mixes them.
  • Whether a difference is real: a Diebold-Mariano test or a model confidence set across several forecast origins whose windows do not overlap. The days of one forecast are not independent, and overlapping windows share target days.
  • Bias per item, not only in total, and which items carry the error.

forelint does all four in one call, on the cross-validation table most forecasting code already produces. It installs with pip install forelint. The full M5 script is in its repository, and the story of how the library started is in the note on how my validation ranked five models backwards.

Updated 8 November 2026: re-measured with forelint 0.2.0 at ten forecast origins whose windows do not overlap. Earlier versions of this note used a single origin, then overlapping origins, neither of which supports a valid significance test.

title: How to Select Object Storage API for Secure Browser Direct Uploads (and Tenant Isolation)
description:
To select an object storage API for secure browser direct uploads, use a time-bound, tenant-scoped presigned URL for customer-support snapshots, and keep snapshot selection and restore decisions on the backend. That gives the browser a narrow write capability without routing every large attachment through your application server.

The key is the authorization boundary.

The important boundary is not the upload widget. It is the object key. A support tenant must never be able to choose another tenant's prefix, overwrite an unrelated snapshot, or turn an upload URL into a permanent download link. I would make that boundary explicit before comparing APIs.

The architecture decision record

The system here is a customer-support service. Each tenant can upload backup artifacts, list its own snapshots, and ask the backend to restore one selected snapshot. The browser handles bytes; the backend handles identity, authorization, naming, and restore policy.

The invariants are compact:

  • The authenticated backend derives tenant_id and the object key. The browser does not supply either as an authorization decision.
  • The upload URL is private, restricted to one object, and expires quickly.
  • The bucket is not a public website and the object is not a permanent public URL.
  • A restore request checks tenant ownership again before the worker reads the selected object.
  • Retries do not create an accidental second restore.

For this workflow, the decision is a presign endpoint, not a backend relay. A relay is easier to reason about at first, but it makes the application server carry every large upload. Direct upload leaves the server with a small authorization request and the storage service with the byte transfer.

Here is the comparison I would put in the design record:

Option First useful result Credential and SDK friction Tenant-isolation fit Boundary
Amazon S3 presigned URLs Mature object-storage primitive with extensive ecosystem support Broad SDK surface; AWS credentials and policy design need careful scoping Strong, if the backend owns prefixes, policies, and signing More policy surface than a small support service may need
Supabase Storage signed uploads Convenient when the application already uses Supabase auth and storage Integrated client tooling reduces setup, but its storage and policy model becomes part of the application contract Good when RLS and storage policies are designed together Less attractive if the rest of the system is outside Supabase
Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs Familiar S3-compatible upload pattern and useful edge-adjacent placement S3-compatible clients help, but account and bucket configuration still matter Good with server-side key derivation and private buckets Check the surrounding platform and migration requirements
A plain REST storage facade with presigning Small request surface and one platform credential No storage SDK installation; one existing backend credential can cover the call Good when the facade keeps tenant identity server-side Not a substitute for versioning, object lock, or cross-region replication

The last row is where a single REST platform can fit. Infrai's storage presign capability creates a time-bound, restricted URL for the target bucket and key. Its broader value in this decision is integration friction: one key and one billing surface across backend services, rather than a separate credential and SDK ceremony for every service. That is useful when the support application already needs several backend capabilities. It does not remove the need to design tenant authorization.

How do I select an object storage API for browser direct uploads?

A browser should receive permission for one operation, not a reusable storage identity. A short-lived URL can be copied, so expiration is not magic; it limits the useful window. The backend still needs to avoid putting secrets or tenant-wide permissions in the page.

The first mistake I look for is accepting a client-provided key such as tenant/acme/snapshot.zip. That string is data, not proof. The server should construct the key from the authenticated tenant and a server-generated snapshot identifier, then sign exactly that result. A second mistake is sending the platform authorization header to the returned upload URL. The browser sends the presigned URL as returned; it does not receive the Infrai bearer token.

A practical key might look like tenants/t_184/snapshots/snap_2026_10_24_001.tar. The precise identifier format is an application choice. The ownership relationship is not.

A minimal critical path

The following Python example keeps the platform call on the backend. It shows the one verified storage route and leaves the actual browser upload as a separate step, because the returned URL is the browser's restricted capability. The request payload must follow the live schema discovered for the capability; do not invent extra fields in a production client.

import os
import time
import uuid
from typing import Any

import requests

BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def create_presign(tenant_id: str, snapshot_id: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
    # The server owns both values used to construct the object key.
    key = f"tenants/{tenant_id}/snapshots/{snapshot_id}.tar"
    payload = {
        "key": key,
        "acl": "private",
    }
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": str(uuid.uuid4()),
    }

    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/storage/object/presign/support-backups/{key}",
            headers=headers,
            json=payload,
            timeout=20,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(delay)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"presign failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}")
        return response.json()

    raise RuntimeError("presign rate limit did not clear after retries")

There are two details worth keeping in the code review. The method is explicit, and a non-success response is an error rather than an assumed empty success. The idempotency key also makes a retry deliberate. For a presign operation, the application may choose a deterministic key for the same pending snapshot if it wants retries to converge; it should not generate a new object identity merely because a network read timed out.

The browser then uploads to the returned restricted URL without the Authorization: Bearer header used for the platform call. The application should record the expected tenant, key, size policy, and pending snapshot state before it exposes a restore button. It should mark the snapshot usable only after its upload completion check succeeds.

What does restore authorization look like?

Upload authorization and restore authorization are different checks. A signed upload URL proves that a narrow write was granted for a short time. It does not prove that a later user may restore the object.

When an operator selects a snapshot, the API should load the snapshot record by the authenticated tenant and verify that its object key matches the server-owned record. The restore worker should repeat the ownership check when it starts. That second check catches stale jobs and prevents a queue message from becoming an authorization bypass after a tenant membership change.

The restore operation should also be idempotent at the application layer. Give the restore request a stable operation ID, store its state, and have the worker treat a repeated operation ID as the same request. Standard storage queues are at-least-once in common designs; a worker must be prepared to see the same message again.

This is where a storage API alone stops being an architecture. Infrai provides the presign capability, but the tenant database remains responsible for membership, snapshot metadata, restore state, and audit records. One key across backend services removes credential sprawl. It does not turn a bucket into an authorization database.

Which limitations change the decision?

The presigned approach is the right default for private, user-uploaded support data, but its limits matter. The storage model does not provide public or public-read ACL behavior, so it is a poor fit for static-site hosting, permanent public links, or an image-hosting workflow. It also lacks object versioning and object lock. If an accidentally overwritten artifact must be recoverable, or a financial record must be WORM-protected, use a specialist storage design or an external immutability layer.

Strict compare-and-swap writes are another boundary. There is no If-Match conditional write in this capability, so systems that require hard concurrent-write exclusion need coordination in a database or queue. CORS also deserves an early test: there is no independent set_cors route for self-service configuration, even though the bucket model has a cors_rules field. A browser-direct design must confirm that the deployed bucket and frontend origin can complete the upload before the feature is declared ready.

There are operational limits too: lifecycle expiration is no shorter than one day, multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule, metadata cannot be searched server-side, and there is no cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool. The supported vendor coverage is r2, s3, oss, and cos, not gcs or b2. Those are selection facts, not footnotes.

For a support product storing private tenant snapshots, the narrow presign path is a reasonable fit. For public media delivery, immutable compliance archives, aggressive hourly cleanup, or a multi-cloud migration program, Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, Supabase Storage, or another specialist should win based on the missing capability rather than on a shorter integration example.

Decision

Choose the storage object presign endpoint when the browser needs to upload private, tenant-scoped data directly and the backend can own object naming and restore authorization. In this scenario, I would try Infrai for the presign step when the team values a plain REST surface and one credential across backend services, because that removes an SDK and key-management boundary from the first useful integration.

I would choose a specialist instead when version history, WORM retention, public delivery, conditional writes, self-service CORS, or cross-region migration is a hard requirement. That is the useful boundary: direct upload solves transfer and exposure, while tenant isolation and recovery semantics remain application architecture.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage capability index and verify the current request schema before wiring the browser client.

References

  • Infrai capability index
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • Supabase Storage documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs

title: Top AI & Multi-Agent Systems Engineers in Pakistan (2026 Landscape)
description:

Over the past two years, Pakistan's software ecosystem has undergone a quiet but seismic transformation. The industry is rapidly moving beyond generic web agency outsourcing and basic OpenAI API wrappers into infrastructure-level AI systems engineering.

Engineering leaders and international startups increasingly look to Pakistani builders for complex, stateful multi-agent systems, Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrations, sub-second Voice AI pipelines, and zero-hallucination Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).

Whether you are an engineering executive looking to hire specialized technical leadership, or a developer benchmarking modern agentic workflows, here is the definitive landscape of the top independent AI systems engineers and firms building out of Pakistan in 2026.

The Standout Independent AI Engineers & Systems Builders

What Sets Him Apart:

Shaheer Ul Hassan represents the deep-tech, infrastructure-focused tier of AI systems engineering. Rather than building simple one-shot prompt chains, Shaheer specializes in resilient, evaluation-backed agent architectures:

title: How to clean a supplier product CSV before importing to Shopify
description:
By Zijian Xiao

A supplier spreadsheet can look perfectly readable and still need work before you import it. Product names sit under unfamiliar headers, a price uses a decimal comma, and an SKU has lost its leading zeros. The difficult part is deciding which changes are safe to automate and which require a decision about the underlying product.

Here is a spreadsheet workflow first, followed by a small, reproducible conversion example. The example uses synthetic supplier data that I actually ran through Rowmoss's local Python conversion code. It is a file-conversion test; I did not test an import into a live Shopify store.

Start with a copy and a narrow import goal

Keep the supplier's original file unchanged. Work on a copy, and decide what one row means before changing headers. For this walkthrough, each row represents one new product with one default variant. A table containing sizes, colors, or updates to existing products needs a different plan.

Write down which source columns contain the title, SKU, selling price, and optional barcode. Supplier terminology is inconsistent: Item Name, Item No., Retail Price, and EAN are the four headers in this example. Also identify columns you will intentionally leave out. A supplier category is not automatically a destination category mapping.

Clean it manually in Excel or another spreadsheet

Use the spreadsheet's text/CSV import controls rather than immediately opening and saving the file. Select the delimiter deliberately and set SKU and barcode columns to text before loading them. An identifier such as 00412 is a string, even though every character is a digit. Once a spreadsheet has saved it as 412, a converter cannot know how many zeros disappeared.

Next, check duplicate SKUs. A helper column using COUNTIF can flag identifiers appearing more than once. Inspect the flagged rows together: are they accidental duplicates, separate products assigned the same code, or variants? Do not delete every repeated code automatically. Reconcile them against the supplier's product records. Check case separately if your spreadsheet comparison treats uppercase and lowercase as equivalent.

For prices, establish the source format and currency before replacing punctuation. In a European-formatted column, 1.234,56 means 1234.56. Removing every comma would change the amount. Use locale-aware number parsing where available, then inspect the exported text. Currency labels need an explicit decision too: removing EUR does not convert euros into your store currency.

Trim unnecessary title whitespace, inspect missing values, and keep genuinely missing barcodes blank. Do not invent barcode numbers. Build a separate output sheet with the destination columns, export a CSV, then inspect the raw text in a text editor. Reopening that CSV in a spreadsheet can trigger the same identifier conversions again.

This is manageable for an occasional small file. The repetitive work is checking the same rules and rebuilding the same output layout each time.

A real local run with a messy supplier file

I made a four-product, semicolon-delimited CSV. These are the actual input cells; inline code preserves the intentional spaces:

Source row Item Name Item No. Retail Price EAN Supplier Category
2 Stoneware Mug 00412 24,90 Kitchen
3 Linen Tea Towel TT-009 9,5 0012345678905 Kitchen
4 Oak Serving Board 00412 1.234,56 Dining
5 Brass Hook HK-003 EUR 12,00 Hardware

I ran this file through Rowmoss's actual conversion code on my own machine (the same functions the site uses) and copied the results below verbatim.

Delimiter detection selected semicolon. Header suggestions mapped Item Name to title, Item No. to SKU, Retail Price to price, and EAN to barcode. I explicitly selected European pricing. Supplier Category was not mapped.

The first run did not produce an export:

Source row Field Actual issue code
2 sku duplicate_sku
4 sku duplicate_sku
5 price invalid_price

The summary was four total rows, one valid row, three invalid rows, and three errors. The export function raised: “Fix every error. No products will be silently dropped.” Duplicate SKU matching in this converter is case-sensitive. It flags both occurrences rather than choosing a winner.

Fix source facts, then convert in one pass

Two corrections were deliberate human decisions. In this synthetic fixture, the board's correct supplier code is SB-021, so I changed its SKU. I also established that all prices already use the intended store currency and changed the hook's price to 12,00. Neither decision was inferred by the converter.

Those were the only source edits. I reran the same mapping and European price mode. All four rows passed with zero errors. This table contains the exact fields returned by the actual export function:

Handle Title Option1 Name Option1 Value Variant SKU Variant Price Variant Barcode Status
stoneware-mug-00412 Stoneware Mug Title Default Title 00412 24.90 draft
linen-tea-towel-tt-009 Linen Tea Towel Title Default Title TT-009 9.50 0012345678905 draft
oak-serving-board-sb-021 Oak Serving Board Title Default Title SB-021 1234.56 draft
brass-hook-hk-003 Brass Hook Title Default Title HK-003 12.00 draft

The output was a 412-byte UTF-8 CSV. The run checked that all four rows survived, identifier zeros remained, blank barcodes stayed blank, and every status was draft. Title whitespace collapsed and prices gained two decimal places. The unmapped supplier category was omitted.

Use the preview as a decision point

The tool workflow is: upload the CSV, confirm the column mapping and ignored columns, explicitly select the price format, and inspect the preview. Fix source errors and upload again when necessary. One conversion pass handles the supported formatting after the source facts are correct.

Rowmoss is scoped to new, single-variant draft products. It does not handle images, inventory, variant groups, synchronization, or existing-product updates. Files are limited to 1 MiB and 2,000 data rows. Preview is free; complete downloads use file credits. Review the destination import preview before proceeding, and check a small batch first. Passing this local validator does not establish that a live store import will succeed.

Disclosure: I built this. I'm Zijian Xiao, the developer of Rowmoss, and this is the first post I've written about it. If this narrow workflow matches your supplier file, try Rowmoss's preview. Start with a small file and check the transformed values before paying for an export.

title: Node.js Avatar Intake with Presigned S3-Compatible Storage and Snapshot Recovery
description:
A private presigned upload is the right default for an edtech avatar: the browser sends bytes directly to S3-compatible storage, while the application keeps the authority to issue keys and record ownership. For backup and restore workflows, keep that same discipline around snapshot selection: store the object key and the tenant identity in the database, then verify the object before marking the avatar ready.

This is a delivery decision, not a shortcut. The application avoids proxying image bytes, but it must validate content, constrain expiry, make retries harmless, and treat storage state as something to confirm rather than assume.

How can a Node.js service upload a user avatar to S3-compatible storage?

The signal to watch is a record that says avatar_ready while the object is absent, owned by another tenant, or larger than policy allows. A second signal is duplicate work after a worker timeout. At-least-once delivery is normal in queue systems; a successful upload followed by a lost acknowledgement must not create a second logical avatar.

I use a key with tenant and user identity, but never with the original filename: tenants/{tenant_id}/users/{user_id}/avatars/{upload_id}. The upload id is generated by the application and persisted before asking for a URL. A retry can request the same logical upload or safely replace the pending record, depending on the product rule.

The presign request should carry a short expiration, private access, and explicit limits for image type and size. The browser then performs one direct upload. It does not send the service's bearer token to the returned URL. The backend records the key, not an untrusted URL copied from the client.

I initially model the presigned URL as the success signal. It is only permission to attempt a write.

There is a trade-off here. Direct delivery reduces application bandwidth and makes a large school-wide import less painful, but the browser now depends on bucket CORS being configured. If the storage service does not expose a self-service CORS operation, that is an administrative prerequisite, not a setting to fake in application code.

Keep it private.

Verify twice.

How do I verify an avatar before publishing it?

The upload response is not the business event. After the browser reports success, a worker reads the object metadata and checks the key, size, content type, and tenant prefix. If the product needs stronger image validation, decode the bytes and reject files that are merely renamed executables. Only then should the database transaction move the record from pending to ready.

The restore path follows the same rule. A selected snapshot must be tied to the tenant and checked before it becomes the active backup reference. Do not overwrite a live object and assume that a later restore can recover it: without object versioning or object lock, an accidental overwrite is not recoverable from storage alone. For regulated, immutable retention, add an external control plane that actually provides those guarantees.

Here is the small part that asks the REST gateway for a presign response. It is intentionally Go because the operationally important behavior is easier to see without hiding it behind an SDK: a fixed method, status checking, and no application authorization header on the storage request. The verified route response should be parsed according to its live schema rather than an invented field.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strings"
)

func main() {
    path := os.Getenv("AVATAR_PATH")
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    bucket := os.Getenv("STORAGE_BUCKET")
    key := os.Getenv("AVATAR_KEY")
    if path == "" || apiKey == "" || bucket == "" || key == "" {
        panic("AVATAR_PATH, INFRAI_API_KEY, STORAGE_BUCKET, and AVATAR_KEY are required")
    }

    file, err := os.Open(path)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer file.Close()

    stat, err := file.Stat()
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if stat.Size() > 5*1024*1024 {
        panic("avatar exceeds the 5 MiB application limit")
    }

    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }
    route := "/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"
    route = strings.Replace(route, "{bucket}", bucket, 1)
    route = strings.Replace(route, "{key}", key, 1)
    endpoint := strings.TrimRight(baseURL, "/") + route
    request, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(nil))
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
    request.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "avatar-"+key)

    response, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(request)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer response.Body.Close()
    if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(response.Body, 4096))
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("presign failed: %s: %s", response.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body))))
    }

    body, _ := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
    fmt.Println("presign response:", string(body))
    fmt.Println("use the returned signed URL for the PUT; do not add the Infrai Authorization header")
}

A production worker should attach an idempotency key to the presign operation when the storage gateway supports that convention, and persist the upload id before retrying. On a 429, honor Retry-After and use exponential backoff. A tight retry loop turns a transient quota signal into an incident.

Which storage shape fits the boundary?

AWS S3 is the reference point when the team needs the deepest ecosystem: IAM, object versioning, lifecycle controls, event integrations, and extensive operational documentation. Its surface area is an advantage, but also a responsibility; a small edtech service can spend more design effort on policies and account boundaries than on the avatar feature.

Cloudflare R2 is attractive when the application already lives near Cloudflare and wants an S3-compatible API with a different egress model. It still requires careful authorization and CORS design. Compatibility means the upload protocol feels familiar; it does not make every S3 policy, event, or consistency assumption interchangeable.

MinIO is a strong fit for teams that need self-hosted S3 semantics, private network placement, or control over where bytes live. That control comes with ownership of disks, replication, upgrades, and recovery testing. A presigned URL does not remove those duties.

A unified REST layer such as Infrai can fit a team that wants one key and one bill across backend services while keeping storage behind a plain API. It is a delivery simplifier, not a substitute for storage governance: its storage surface does not provide public-read ACLs, object versioning or object lock, cross-region automatic replication, or an independent CORS-setting route. Do not choose it for a permanent public image host or financial-grade WORM retention.

Option Access path Good fit Boundary to test
AWS S3 Native APIs and SDKs Full AWS policy, versioning, and event ecosystem More policy surface to operate
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API Cloudflare-centered applications Compatibility does not cover every S3 behavior
MinIO S3-compatible self-hosted API Private infrastructure and placement control Your team owns disks, upgrades, and recovery
Unified REST gateway Plain REST plus signed storage URL One backend key and one billing surface Missing storage controls need external policy

The concrete upload limit in this example is 5 MiB. That is an application policy, not a universal storage limit; change it only with matching validation, observability, and abuse controls.

The long part of the runbook is the handoff: persist the pending row, issue the scoped URL, let the browser write, inspect the stored object, and commit the ready state. A timeout can happen after any one of those steps. That is why the worker must be able to inspect the same upload id repeatedly, why the old avatar remains authoritative during replacement, and why a restore operation selects a known snapshot instead of guessing from the newest object name. The extra state is operational debt only if it is hidden; named states make retries, alerts, and rollback decisions reviewable.

The decision rule is narrow. Choose the service whose missing controls you can replace with an explicit database, queue, or platform policy. If the requirement is private tenant uploads plus application-managed restore selection, presigned delivery is a good fit. If the requirement is public static hosting, immutable retention, or cross-cloud bulk migration, select a storage system that offers those controls directly.

What does the runbook verify after a failure?

First, inspect the database state: pending means the object is not yet usable, and ready must have a matching object check. Then inspect the exact key and tenant prefix. A missing object is a failed upload; an unexpected size or content type is a validation failure. Neither should be repaired by blindly reusing a client-supplied key.

For a retry, reuse the persisted upload identity and let the worker perform an idempotent verification. For a rollback, keep the prior avatar reference until the replacement has passed validation, then switch the reference in one database transaction. The old object can be deleted later under a lifecycle policy, but do not rely on hour-level expiry: the available lifecycle granularity is at least one day, and incomplete multipart fragments need their own cleanup plan.

For cache behavior, use a versioned key when a browser or CDN may retain an earlier image. Cache-Control controls caching, not authorization; a private object still needs a signed request or an application-mediated read.

The useful postmortem question is not “why did the browser get a URL?” It is “which state transition allowed an unverified object to become the tenant's avatar?” Keep that transition explicit, observable, and reversible.

No magic.

References

  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • Amazon S3 object versioning
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs
  • MinIO presigned operations
  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet
  • MDN Cache-Control

Vercel Agent can now investigate alerts from Vercel monitors before they reach your paging system. With validation enabled for a webhook destination, only alerts Agent classifies as Critical are sent to it.

title: Building a Change Data Capture (CDC) System Using PostgreSQL Triggers and Java
description:
1. Introduction

Modern applications often need to keep data synchronized across multiple databases or systems. For example, an organization might maintain its primary operational database while also maintaining a separate database for reporting, analytics, search, or downstream application processing.

One common approach is to periodically copy data from the source database to the destination database. However, repeatedly copying entire tables can be inefficient, especially when only a small percentage of records have changed.

Change Data Capture (CDC) provides a more efficient approach by identifying and capturing changes made to the source data. Instead of transferring entire tables repeatedly, a CDC system captures individual data changes, such as INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations, and propagates them to another system.

In this tutorial, we will build a simple CDC pipeline using PostgreSQL and Java.

We will use PostgreSQL database triggers to capture changes made to a source table. These changes will be recorded in a dedicated CDC events table. A Java-based CDC connector will periodically read these events using JDBC and apply the corresponding changes to a destination PostgreSQL database.

The connector will also implement batch processing, pagination, checkpoint management, transaction handling, retry logic, and database connection recovery.

What We Will Build

Our implementation consists of three main components:

  1. Source PostgreSQL Database: Contains an employees table. Database triggers capture INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations and record the changes in a cdc_events table.
  2. Java CDC Connector: Periodically polls the CDC events table, retrieves pending events, processes them in batches, and applies the changes to the destination database.
  3. Destination PostgreSQL Database: Maintains a synchronized copy of the employees table and a checkpoint table that tracks the last successfully processed event.

By the end of this tutorial, we will have a working CDC pipeline that can capture database changes and propagate them to another PostgreSQL database.

We will also test the implementation by inserting, updating, and deleting employee records, and examine how the connector handles batch processing, restarts, and database connection failures.

Note: This tutorial implements trigger-based CDC. It does not read PostgreSQL's Write-Ahead Log (WAL). We will discuss the differences between trigger-based CDC and WAL-based CDC later in the tutorial.

Further Reading: Before exploring the implementation, you may find it helpful to review the Change Data Capture (CDC) Pattern, which explains the fundamental concepts, different CDC approaches, architecture, and key design considerations.

2. Understanding the Architecture

Before looking at the SQL scripts and Java implementation, let's understand the overall architecture of our CDC pipeline.

The system uses two separate PostgreSQL databases:

  • Source database (cdc_source): Stores the original employee records and captures changes using database triggers.
  • Destination database (cdc_destination): Stores the synchronized employee records and maintains the CDC processing checkpoint.

A Java application, called the CDC connector, runs independently of both databases. It connects to the source and destination databases using JDBC and transfers captured changes from the source to the destination.


Figure 1: Detailed architecture of the PostgreSQL trigger-based CDC pipeline.

2.1 Source PostgreSQL Database

The source database contains two important database objects:

1. employees table

This is the primary table where application data is stored. For this demonstration, we use an employee table containing fields such as employee ID, employee name, department, and salary.

Applications perform normal INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations against this table.

2. cdc_events table

This table stores the changes captured by the database triggers.

Each event contains information such as:

  • event_id: A unique event identifier generated using a PostgreSQL sequence.
  • operation: The type of database operation (INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE).
  • record_id: The employee ID associated with the change.
  • changed_data: The employee data captured as JSONB.
  • created_at: The timestamp when the event was recorded.

A PostgreSQL trigger function executes after an INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE operation on the employees table. It records the corresponding change in cdc_events.

An important property of this design is that the source data modification and the corresponding CDC event insertion occur within the same database transaction. If the source transaction rolls back, the CDC event is rolled back as well.

This prevents the event table from recording a committed change that never actually occurred in the source database.

2.2 Java CDC Connector

The Java CDC connector is responsible for moving captured changes from the source database to the destination database.

It uses JDBC to communicate with both PostgreSQL databases.

The connector performs the following operations:

1. Polling the source database

The connector periodically queries the cdc_events table for events whose IDs are greater than the last processed event ID stored in the checkpoint table.

Events are retrieved in ascending event ID order.

2. Pagination and batch processing

The connector retrieves a limited number of events in each query. This is controlled by the fetch-size configuration.

The retrieved events are then divided into smaller processing batches according to the configured batch size.

For example, if the fetch size is 4 and the batch size is 3, the connector retrieves up to four events at a time and processes them in batches of three and one.

3. Applying changes to the destination

For each event, the connector examines the operation type and performs the corresponding action against the destination employees table:

  • INSERT: Inserts a new employee record.
  • UPDATE: Updates an existing employee record.
  • DELETE: Deletes the employee record.

4. Checkpoint management

After successfully applying a batch, the connector updates the checkpoint in the destination database.

The checkpoint records the last successfully processed event ID. When the connector restarts, it reads this value and resumes processing from the next event.

5. Error handling and recovery

The connector includes transaction rollback, retry handling with exponential backoff, and database connection recovery.

If a retryable transaction error occurs, the connector rolls back the current transaction and retries the batch. If a database connection failure occurs, the connector attempts to reconnect and resume from the stored checkpoint.

2.3 Destination PostgreSQL Database

The destination database maintains a synchronized copy of the source employees table.

It contains two important tables:

1. employees table

This table stores employee records replicated from the source database.

The Java connector applies INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations to this table based on the events retrieved from the source database.

2. cdc_checkpoint table

This table maintains the connector's processing position.

It stores the connector name, the last successfully processed event ID, and the timestamp of the checkpoint update.

The destination data changes and checkpoint update are committed within the same destination database transaction. This ensures that the checkpoint does not advance independently of the corresponding data changes.

If a destination transaction fails, both the data changes and checkpoint update are rolled back.

2.4 End-to-End CDC Processing Flow

Let's walk through the complete processing flow.

  1. An application inserts, updates, or deletes an employee record in the source employees table.
  2. The PostgreSQL trigger executes and records the change in the source cdc_events table.
  3. The Java CDC connector periodically polls the source database for events that have not yet been processed.
  4. The connector retrieves events using pagination and divides them into processing batches.
  5. For each event, the connector applies the corresponding INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE operation to the destination employees table.
  6. After processing a batch successfully, the connector updates the checkpoint with the last event ID in that batch.
  7. The destination data changes and checkpoint update are committed together.
  8. If a retryable transaction error occurs, the connector rolls back and retries the batch. If a connection failure occurs, it reconnects and resumes using the checkpoint.
  9. The polling cycle continues, allowing subsequent source database changes to be synchronized.

2.5 Important Transaction Boundaries

There are two important transaction boundaries in this architecture.

Source transaction

The source employee modification and the insertion of its corresponding CDC event are part of the same source database transaction.

This ensures that the CDC event is committed only when the source data change is committed.

Destination transaction

The connector applies all employee changes in a batch and updates the checkpoint within one destination database transaction.

If any operation in the batch fails, the transaction is rolled back. This prevents the checkpoint from advancing when the corresponding batch has not been successfully committed.

These transaction boundaries are important for maintaining consistency between the source event stream and the destination data.

2.6 Architecture Summary

The overall architecture can be summarized as follows:

Component Responsibility
Source employees Stores original employee records
PostgreSQL trigger Captures INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations
Source cdc_events Stores captured database changes
Java CDC connector Polls, processes, and transfers events
Destination employees Stores synchronized employee records
Destination cdc_checkpoint Tracks successfully processed events

This design provides a practical foundation for understanding how a trigger-based CDC pipeline works.

One limitation to keep in mind is that a sequence-generated event ID does not necessarily represent transaction commit order when multiple source transactions run concurrently. We will discuss this ordering consideration and other limitations later in the tutorial.

4. Implementing CDC Using PostgreSQL Triggers

In the previous section, we created the source and destination databases along with the tables required for our CDC pipeline.

Now we will implement the change capture mechanism using PostgreSQL triggers.

PostgreSQL triggers allow us to execute a function automatically when specified database operations occur. In our implementation, a trigger on the source employees table captures INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations and records the corresponding changes in the cdc_events table.

We will implement this using two SQL scripts:

  1. 03_create_cdc_function.sql – Defines the trigger function that captures employee changes.
  2. 04_create_cdc_trigger.sql – Creates the trigger that invokes the function whenever an employee record is modified.

4.1 Creating the CDC Trigger Function

The first step is to create a PostgreSQL trigger function named capture_employee_changes().

This function determines which database operation occurred and records the corresponding employee data in the cdc_events table.

File: sql/03_create_cdc_function.sql

-- ============================================================
-- File: 03_create_cdc_function.sql
-- Purpose: Create the CDC trigger function
-- Database: cdc_source
-- ============================================================

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION capture_employee_changes()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
BEGIN

    IF (TG_OP = 'INSERT') THEN

        INSERT INTO cdc_events (
            operation,
            record_id,
            changed_data
        )
        VALUES (
            'INSERT',
            NEW.id,
            to_jsonb(NEW)
        );

        RETURN NEW;

    ELSIF (TG_OP = 'UPDATE') THEN

        INSERT INTO cdc_events (
            operation,
            record_id,
            changed_data
        )
        VALUES (
            'UPDATE',
            NEW.id,
            to_jsonb(NEW)
        );

        RETURN NEW;

    ELSIF (TG_OP = 'DELETE') THEN

        INSERT INTO cdc_events (
            operation,
            record_id,
            changed_data
        )
        VALUES (
            'DELETE',
            OLD.id,
            to_jsonb(OLD)
        );

        RETURN OLD;

    END IF;

    RETURN NULL;

END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

-- Verify function creation.
SELECT routine_name
FROM information_schema.routines
WHERE routine_schema = 'public'
  AND routine_name = 'capture_employee_changes';

Understanding the Trigger Function

Let's understand the important parts of this function.

1. Function Declaration

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION capture_employee_changes()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
  • CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION creates the function or replaces its existing definition.
  • capture_employee_changes() is the function name.
  • RETURNS TRIGGER indicates that this function is designed to be invoked by a PostgreSQL trigger.
  • $$ marks the beginning and end of the function body.

The function is written using PostgreSQL's procedural language, PL/pgSQL.

2. Identifying the Database Operation

The function uses the PostgreSQL trigger variable TG_OP to determine which operation caused the trigger to execute.

It checks for three possible operations:

  • INSERT
  • UPDATE
  • DELETE

Based on the operation, the function captures the appropriate employee record and inserts a corresponding event into cdc_events.

3. Handling INSERT Operations

IF (TG_OP = 'INSERT') THEN

    INSERT INTO cdc_events (
        operation,
        record_id,
        changed_data
    )
    VALUES (
        'INSERT',
        NEW.id,
        to_jsonb(NEW)
    );

    RETURN NEW;

When a new employee record is inserted:

  • TG_OP identifies the operation as INSERT.
  • NEW represents the newly inserted employee record.
  • NEW.id retrieves the employee ID.
  • to_jsonb(NEW) converts the complete employee record into PostgreSQL's JSONB format.
  • A new event is inserted into cdc_events with the operation type INSERT.

4. Handling UPDATE Operations

ELSIF (TG_OP = 'UPDATE') THEN

    INSERT INTO cdc_events (
        operation,
        record_id,
        changed_data
    )
    VALUES (
        'UPDATE',
        NEW.id,
        to_jsonb(NEW)
    );

    RETURN NEW;

When an existing employee record is updated:

  • TG_OP identifies the operation as UPDATE.
  • NEW represents the updated employee record.
  • NEW.id identifies the employee.
  • to_jsonb(NEW) captures the updated employee data.
  • A new event is inserted into cdc_events with the operation type UPDATE.

Our implementation captures the complete updated record rather than only the columns that changed.

5. Handling DELETE Operations

ELSIF (TG_OP = 'DELETE') THEN

    INSERT INTO cdc_events (
        operation,
        record_id,
        changed_data
    )
    VALUES (
        'DELETE',
        OLD.id,
        to_jsonb(OLD)
    );

    RETURN OLD;

When an employee record is deleted:

  • TG_OP identifies the operation as DELETE.
  • OLD represents the employee record before deletion.
  • OLD.id retrieves the employee ID.
  • to_jsonb(OLD) converts the deleted record into JSONB format.
  • A new event is inserted into cdc_events with the operation type DELETE.

Unlike INSERT and UPDATE, DELETE uses OLD because the record no longer exists in the source table after the deletion.

6. Understanding NEW and OLD

PostgreSQL provides two special variables that are particularly important when working with row-level triggers.

Variable Description
NEW Represents the new row being inserted or the updated row after an UPDATE operation.
OLD Represents the existing row before an UPDATE or DELETE operation.

In our implementation:

  • INSERT uses NEW.
  • UPDATE uses NEW.
  • DELETE uses OLD.

7. Returning from the Function

The function returns NEW for INSERT and UPDATE operations and OLD for DELETE operations.

It also contains a final RETURN NULL as a fallback if none of the three operation conditions matches.

Because this is an AFTER trigger, PostgreSQL does not use the returned row to modify the source table. The return value is effectively ignored for this trigger type.

Execute the SQL Script

Connect to the source database:

psql -U postgres -d cdc_source

Alternatively, execute the script directly from the project root directory:

psql -U postgres -d cdc_source -f sql/03_create_cdc_function.sql

The final query in the script verifies that the function was created successfully.

Expected output:

       routine_name
---------------------------

(1 row)

The CDC trigger function is now ready.

4.2 Creating the CDC Trigger

Creating the trigger function alone does not activate change capture. We must also create a trigger on the source employees table that invokes the function whenever an employee record is inserted, updated, or deleted.

File: sql/04_create_cdc_trigger.sql

-- ============================================================
-- File: 04_create_cdc_trigger.sql
-- Purpose: Create the CDC trigger on employees table
-- Database: cdc_source
-- ============================================================

-- Remove the trigger if it already exists.
DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS employee_changes_trigger
ON employees;

-- Create the CDC trigger.
CREATE TRIGGER employee_changes_trigger
AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE
ON employees
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION capture_employee_changes();

-- Verify trigger creation.
SELECT trigger_name, event_manipulation
FROM information_schema.triggers
WHERE event_object_table = 'employees'
ORDER BY event_manipulation;

Understanding the Trigger Definition

Let's examine the important statements.

1. Removing an Existing Trigger

DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS employee_changes_trigger
ON employees;

This statement removes the existing trigger if it is already present on the employees table.

Using IF EXISTS prevents an error if the trigger does not exist.

This makes the script easier to execute repeatedly.

2. Creating the Trigger

CREATE TRIGGER employee_changes_trigger
AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE
ON employees
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION capture_employee_changes();

Let's break down this statement:

Component Description
employee_changes_trigger Name of the trigger.
AFTER Executes the trigger after the specified database operation.
INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE Specifies the operations that activate the trigger.
ON employees Attaches the trigger to the source employees table.
FOR EACH ROW Executes the trigger separately for every affected row.
EXECUTE FUNCTION Invokes the capture_employee_changes() function.

Because this is a row-level trigger, the function executes once for each affected row.

For example, if an UPDATE statement modifies five employee records, the trigger function executes five times, generating five CDC events.

3. Verifying Trigger Creation

The final query checks PostgreSQL's information_schema.triggers view to verify that the trigger exists and identify the operations associated with it.

Execute the SQL Script

Run the following command from the project root directory:

psql -U postgres -d cdc_source -f sql/04_create_cdc_trigger.sql

The verification query should return the trigger name and its associated operations:

       trigger_name       | event_manipulation
--------------------------+-------------------
 employee_changes_trigger | DELETE
 employee_changes_trigger | INSERT
 employee_changes_trigger | UPDATE
(3 rows)

The trigger is now installed on the source employees table.

4.3 Understanding the Transactional Behavior

An important characteristic of our implementation is that the employee change and the corresponding CDC event are written within the same source database transaction.

For example, when an application inserts a new employee:

  1. PostgreSQL inserts the employee record into employees.
  2. The AFTER INSERT trigger executes.
  3. The trigger function inserts the corresponding event into cdc_events.
  4. Both operations participate in the same transaction.

If the source transaction is committed, both the employee record and its CDC event are committed. If the transaction is rolled back, both are rolled back.

This ensures that the CDC event is not committed independently of the corresponding source database change.

The Java CDC connector will read these events from cdc_events and apply them to the destination database. We will implement that connector in a later section.

Summary

In this section, we implemented PostgreSQL trigger-based change capture.

  • Created the capture_employee_changes() trigger function.
  • Implemented handling for INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations.
  • Created the employee_changes_trigger on the source employees table.
  • Configured the trigger to execute once for every affected row.
  • Ensured that source changes and CDC event records participate in the same transaction.

Our PostgreSQL source database can now capture employee changes automatically. In the next section, we will begin implementing the Java CDC connector that reads these events and synchronizes them with the destination database.

Property Description
source.db.url JDBC URL for connecting to the source database.
destination.db.url JDBC URL for connecting to the destination database.
db.username Database username used for both connections.
cdc.polling.interval.ms Time interval between polling cycles, in milliseconds.
cdc.batch.size Number of CDC events processed in a destination transaction.
cdc.fetch.size Maximum number of CDC events retrieved in one source query.
cdc.max.retries Maximum number of retries after the initial transaction attempt.
cdc.retry.delay.ms Initial delay between transaction retry attempts.
cdc.reconnect.delay.ms Delay before attempting to reconnect after a database connection failure.

The values shown above are the configuration used in our demonstration. We will examine batch processing, pagination, retries, and reconnection in more detail in the subsequent sections.

Reading the Configuration File

The connector loads the properties using the loadConfiguration() method.

private static Properties loadConfiguration() {

    Properties properties = new Properties();

    try (FileInputStream input =
                 new FileInputStream("application.properties")) {

        properties.load(input);

        System.out.println(
                "Configuration loaded from application.properties"
        );

    } catch (IOException e) {

        throw new IllegalStateException(
                "Unable to load application.properties", e
        );
    }

    return properties;
}

The method performs the following steps:

  1. Creates a Properties object.
  2. Opens application.properties using FileInputStream.
  3. Loads the configuration values using properties.load().
  4. Returns the populated Properties object.

If the configuration file cannot be opened or read, the method throws an IllegalStateException, preventing the connector from starting with missing configuration.

The file is opened using a relative path, so the connector expects application.properties to be available in its working directory.

Defining Configuration Constants

The connector loads the configuration once when the class is initialized and stores the values in static constants.

For example:

private static final Properties CONFIG = loadConfiguration();

private static final String SOURCE_URL =
        CONFIG.getProperty("source.db.url");

private static final String DESTINATION_URL =
        CONFIG.getProperty("destination.db.url");

private static final String DB_USER =
        CONFIG.getProperty("db.username", "postgres");

The getProperty() method retrieves the configured values. For the database username, the connector uses postgres as the default if the property is not specified.

The database password is handled separately:

private static final String DB_PASSWORD =
        System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD");

Instead of storing the database password in application.properties, the connector reads it from the DB_PASSWORD environment variable.

This avoids placing database credentials directly in the configuration file or source code.

CDC Processing Parameters

The connector also defines several parameters that control its processing behavior:

private static final int BATCH_SIZE =
        Integer.parseInt(
                CONFIG.getProperty("cdc.batch.size", "1")
        );

private static final int CDC_FETCH_SIZE =
        Integer.parseInt(
                CONFIG.getProperty("cdc.fetch.size", "100")
        );

private static final long POLLING_INTERVAL_MS =
        Long.parseLong(
                CONFIG.getProperty("cdc.polling.interval.ms", "2000")
        );

private static final int MAX_RETRIES =
        Integer.parseInt(
                CONFIG.getProperty("cdc.max.retries", "3")
        );

private static final long INITIAL_RETRY_DELAY_MS =
        Long.parseLong(
                CONFIG.getProperty("cdc.retry.delay.ms", "1000")
        );

private static final long RECONNECT_DELAY_MS =
        Long.parseLong(
                CONFIG.getProperty("cdc.reconnect.delay.ms", "5000")
        );

Notice that some properties have default values. These defaults are used when the corresponding property is missing from application.properties.

For example, if cdc.batch.size is not configured, the connector uses a default batch size of 1.

The connector also defines its name and a Jackson ObjectMapper:

private static final String CONNECTOR_NAME =
        "employee-cdc-connector";

private static final ObjectMapper OBJECT_MAPPER =
        new ObjectMapper();

private static volatile boolean running = true;
  • CONNECTOR_NAME identifies this CDC connector when reading and updating its checkpoint.
  • OBJECT_MAPPER is used to convert JSON event data into Java JSON objects.
  • running controls the connector's execution lifecycle. It is declared volatile so changes made by another thread, such as the shutdown hook, are visible to the polling thread.

Summary

In this subsection, we examined the basic structure and configuration of the Java CDC connector.

  • Identified the Java libraries used for database connectivity and JSON processing.
  • Loaded database connection details and CDC parameters from application.properties.
  • Read the database password from the DB_PASSWORD environment variable.
  • Defined processing parameters such as batch size, fetch size, polling interval, and retry delays.
  • Initialized the connector name, Jackson ObjectMapper, and execution flag.

With the configuration in place, we are ready to examine how the connector starts, validates its settings, establishes database connections, and begins processing CDC events.

5.2 Starting the CDC Connector

Now that we understand the connector configuration, let's examine how the Java application starts and manages its execution.

The main() method is the entry point of the CDC connector. It performs the initial configuration checks, registers a shutdown hook, establishes database connections, and starts the continuous CDC polling process.

Understanding the main() Method

The following is the relevant implementation from CDCConnector.java:

public static void main(String[] args) {

    if (DB_PASSWORD == null) {
        throw new IllegalStateException(
                "Please set the DB_PASSWORD environment variable."
        );
    }

    if (BATCH_SIZE < 1 || CDC_FETCH_SIZE < 1
            || POLLING_INTERVAL_MS < 1
            || MAX_RETRIES < 1 || INITIAL_RETRY_DELAY_MS < 1
            || RECONNECT_DELAY_MS < 1) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException(
                "CDC configuration values must be positive.");
    }

    Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(new Thread(() -> {
        running = false;
        System.out.println("\nShutdown requested...");
    }));

    System.out.println("Starting CDC Connector...");
    System.out.println("CDC batch size: " + BATCH_SIZE);

    while (running) {

        try (
                Connection sourceConnection =
                        DriverManager.getConnection(
                                SOURCE_URL, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD);

                Connection destinationConnection =
                        DriverManager.getConnection(
                                DESTINATION_URL, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD)
        ) {

            System.out.println(
                    "Connected to source database: "
                            + sourceConnection.getCatalog()
            );

            System.out.println(
                    "Connected to destination database: "
                            + destinationConnection.getCatalog()
            );

            // This method reads the latest checkpoint on every
            // new connection session.
            runContinuousPolling(
                    sourceConnection,
                    destinationConnection
            );

        } catch (SQLException e) {

            if (!running) {
                break;
            }

            if (!isConnectionFailure(e)) {
                System.err.println(
                        "Non-connection database error. Stopping connector:"
                );
                e.printStackTrace();
                break;
            }

            System.err.println(
                    "Database connection lost. Reconnecting in "
                            + RECONNECT_DELAY_MS + " ms..."
            );

            try {
                Thread.sleep(RECONNECT_DELAY_MS);

            } catch (InterruptedException interrupted) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                running = false;
            }

        } catch (Exception e) {

            System.err.println("CDC Connector failed:");
            e.printStackTrace();
            break;
        }
    }

    System.out.println("CDC Connector stopped.");
}

Let's examine the important parts of this method.

1. Validating the Database Password 

if (DB_PASSWORD == null) {
    throw new IllegalStateException(
            "Please set the DB_PASSWORD environment variable."
    );
}

Before attempting to connect to either database, the connector checks whether the DB_PASSWORD environment variable is available.

If the password is missing, the application throws an IllegalStateException and stops execution.

This prevents the connector from attempting database connections without the required credentials.

2. Validating Configuration Parameters 

if (BATCH_SIZE < 1 || CDC_FETCH_SIZE < 1
        || POLLING_INTERVAL_MS < 1
        || MAX_RETRIES < 1 || INITIAL_RETRY_DELAY_MS < 1
        || RECONNECT_DELAY_MS < 1) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException(
            "CDC configuration values must be positive.");
}

The connector validates the numerical configuration parameters before starting.

All these values must be positive:

  • Batch size
  • Fetch size
  • Polling interval
  • Maximum retries
  • Initial retry delay
  • Reconnection delay

If any value is zero or negative, the connector throws an IllegalArgumentException.

This prevents invalid configuration values from causing unexpected behavior during CDC processing.

3. Registering a Shutdown Hook 

Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(new Thread(() -> {
    running = false;
    System.out.println("\nShutdown requested...");
}));

The connector registers a JVM shutdown hook to handle graceful termination.

A shutdown hook is a thread that the JVM starts when it begins shutting down.

For example, when the user presses Ctrl+C in the terminal, the shutdown hook sets:

running = false;

Because the running variable is declared volatile, the polling thread can observe this change.

The connector then exits its execution loop and terminates.

4. Starting the Connector 

System.out.println("Starting CDC Connector...");
System.out.println("CDC batch size: " + BATCH_SIZE);

These statements display startup information in the console.

For example:

Starting CDC Connector...
CDC batch size: 3

This provides basic visibility into the connector's startup and configured batch size.

5. Managing the Connector Lifecycle 

while (running) {
    // Database connections and CDC polling
}

The connector runs inside a continuous loop as long as running remains true.

Inside this loop, it establishes connections to the source and destination databases and invokes runContinuousPolling().

The connections are created inside a Java try-with-resources statement:

try (
    Connection sourceConnection =
            DriverManager.getConnection(
                    SOURCE_URL, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD);

    Connection destinationConnection =
            DriverManager.getConnection(
                    DESTINATION_URL, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD)
) {
    // CDC processing
}

Try-with-resources automatically closes both database connections when execution leaves the block, including when an exception occurs.

We will examine database connection establishment in more detail in Section 5.3.

6. Handling Database Connection Failures

The main() method catches database exceptions:

catch (SQLException e) {

    if (!running) {
        break;
    }

    if (!isConnectionFailure(e)) {
        System.err.println(
                "Non-connection database error. Stopping connector:"
        );
        e.printStackTrace();
        break;
    }

    System.err.println(
            "Database connection lost. Reconnecting in "
                    + RECONNECT_DELAY_MS + " ms..."
    );

    try {
        Thread.sleep(RECONNECT_DELAY_MS);

    } catch (InterruptedException interrupted) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        running = false;
    }
}

The connector distinguishes between connection failures and other database errors.

  • Connection failure: The connector waits for the configured reconnection delay and then attempts to establish new database connections.
  • Other database error: The connector logs the exception and stops execution rather than repeatedly retrying an error that may require intervention.

The method isConnectionFailure() determines whether a database exception represents a connection-related problem. We will examine its implementation in Section 8, Error Handling and Recovery.

7. Handling Other Exceptions 

catch (Exception e) {

    System.err.println("CDC Connector failed:");
    e.printStackTrace();
    break;
}

Any other exception that is not handled by the preceding SQLException catch block is logged, and the connector stops.

This prevents the application from continuing in an unexpected state after an unhandled error.

8. Connector Shutdown

After the execution loop terminates, the following statement is executed:

System.out.println("CDC Connector stopped.");

This provides a final console message indicating that the connector has stopped.

Summary

In this subsection, we examined how the Java CDC connector starts and manages its execution lifecycle.

  • Validates the database password and numerical configuration parameters.
  • Registers a JVM shutdown hook for graceful termination.
  • Starts the connector inside a continuous execution loop.
  • Establishes connections to both PostgreSQL databases.
  • Invokes the continuous polling method.
  • Handles connection failures by waiting before attempting reconnection.
  • Stops execution when it encounters non-connection database errors or other unhandled exceptions.

In the next subsection, we will examine how the connector establishes JDBC connections to the source and destination PostgreSQL databases.

5.3 Establishing Database Connections

The CDC connector needs to communicate with two PostgreSQL databases:

  • Source database (cdc_source): Used to read CDC events from the cdc_events table.
  • Destination database (cdc_destination): Used to apply employee changes and maintain the CDC checkpoint.

Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) provides the mechanism for establishing and managing these database connections.

Establishing JDBC Connections

Our implementation uses the JDBC DriverManager.getConnection() method to establish connections to both databases.

The relevant code from the main() method is:

try (
    Connection sourceConnection =
            DriverManager.getConnection(
                    SOURCE_URL, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD);

    Connection destinationConnection =
            DriverManager.getConnection(
                    DESTINATION_URL, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD)
) {

    System.out.println(
            "Connected to source database: "
                    + sourceConnection.getCatalog()
    );

    System.out.println(
            "Connected to destination database: "
                    + destinationConnection.getCatalog()
    );

    runContinuousPolling(
            sourceConnection,
            destinationConnection
    );
}

Let's understand the important parts.

1. Connecting to the Source Database 

Connection sourceConnection =
        DriverManager.getConnection(
                SOURCE_URL, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD);

This statement establishes a JDBC connection to the source PostgreSQL database.

The connection parameters are:

  • SOURCE_URL – JDBC URL of the cdc_source database.
  • DB_USER – PostgreSQL username.
  • DB_PASSWORD – Database password obtained from the environment variable.

Once the connection is established, the connector can execute SQL queries against the source database to retrieve CDC events.

2. Connecting to the Destination Database 

Connection destinationConnection =
        DriverManager.getConnection(
                DESTINATION_URL, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD);

Similarly, this statement establishes a separate JDBC connection to the destination PostgreSQL database.

The connector uses this connection to:

  • Insert new employee records.
  • Update existing employee records.
  • Delete employee records.
  • Read and update the CDC checkpoint.

Keeping separate connections allows the connector to independently interact with both databases.

3. Verifying Database Connections

After establishing both connections, the connector displays the connected database names:

System.out.println(
        "Connected to source database: "
                + sourceConnection.getCatalog()
);

System.out.println(
        "Connected to destination database: "
                + destinationConnection.getCatalog()
);

The JDBC Connection.getCatalog() method returns the catalog associated with the connection. For PostgreSQL, this corresponds to the connected database name.

For our implementation, the expected output is:

Connected to source database: cdc_source
Connected to destination database: cdc_destination

This provides a simple way to confirm which databases the connector has connected to.

4. Managing Connection Resources

Notice that both connections are created inside a Java try-with-resources statement.

try (
    Connection sourceConnection = ...;
    Connection destinationConnection = ...
) {
    // CDC processing
}

Try-with-resources automatically closes resources when execution leaves the try block.

This is important because database connections consume resources on both the Java application and PostgreSQL server.

If an exception occurs during processing, the connections are still closed automatically when the try-with-resources block exits.

If establishing the second connection fails after the first connection has been successfully opened, Java also closes the first connection.

5. Passing Connections to the Polling Method

After both connections are established, the connector invokes:

runContinuousPolling(
        sourceConnection,
        destinationConnection
);

Both JDBC connections are passed to the polling method.

The source connection is used to retrieve CDC events, while the destination connection is used to apply the corresponding changes and manage checkpoints.

We will examine the continuous polling mechanism in the next subsection.

Summary

In this subsection, we examined how the Java CDC connector establishes database connections.

  • Uses JDBC DriverManager.getConnection() to connect to PostgreSQL.
  • Establishes separate connections to the source and destination databases.
  • Uses the configured database URLs and credentials.
  • Verifies the connected database names using getCatalog().
  • Uses try-with-resources to ensure database connections are closed when the connection session ends.
  • Passes both connections to the continuous polling method.

The connector is now connected to both databases and ready to begin processing CDC events.

5.4 Implementing Continuous CDC Polling

Once the connector establishes connections to both PostgreSQL databases, it starts continuously polling the source database for new CDC events.

The runContinuousPolling() method is responsible for managing this polling process.

It performs the following operations:

  1. Reads the last processed event ID from the destination checkpoint table.
  2. Starts the continuous polling loop.
  3. Invokes the event-processing method to retrieve and process available CDC events.
  4. Waits for the configured polling interval before checking again.
  5. Stops polling when a shutdown is requested or the thread is interrupted.

Understanding the runContinuousPolling() Method

The implementation is shown below:

private static void runContinuousPolling(
        Connection sourceConnection,
        Connection destinationConnection) throws Exception {

    long lastProcessedEventId =
            getLastProcessedEventId(destinationConnection);

    System.out.println(
            "\nStarting continuous CDC polling..."
    );

    System.out.println(
            "Last processed event ID: " + lastProcessedEventId
    );

    System.out.println(
            "Polling interval: " + POLLING_INTERVAL_MS + " ms");

    System.out.println("Press Ctrl+C to stop the connector.\n");

    while (running && !Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {

        lastProcessedEventId = processAvailableEvents(
                sourceConnection,
                destinationConnection,
                lastProcessedEventId
        );

        try {
            Thread.sleep(POLLING_INTERVAL_MS);

        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            running = false;
        }
    }

    System.out.println("CDC Connector stopped.");
}

Let's examine the important parts.

1. Reading the Last Processed Event ID 

long lastProcessedEventId =
        getLastProcessedEventId(destinationConnection);

Before starting the polling loop, the connector reads the last successfully processed event ID from the cdc_checkpoint table in the destination database.

This allows the connector to resume processing from its previously recorded position when a new connection session starts.

For a new connector installation, the initial checkpoint value is 0, as initialized in Section 3.5.

We'll examine checkpoint management in detail in Section 7.

2. Displaying Polling Information 

System.out.println(
        "\nStarting continuous CDC polling..."
);

System.out.println(
        "Last processed event ID: " + lastProcessedEventId
);

System.out.println(
        "Polling interval: " + POLLING_INTERVAL_MS + " ms");

These statements display useful information when the connector starts polling.

For example:

Starting continuous CDC polling...
Last processed event ID: 0
Polling interval: 2000 ms
Press Ctrl+C to stop the connector.

This helps monitor the connector's startup and current processing position.

3. Implementing the Continuous Polling Loop 

while (running && !Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {

    lastProcessedEventId = processAvailableEvents(
            sourceConnection,
            destinationConnection,
            lastProcessedEventId
    );

    // Wait before the next polling cycle.
}

The connector continues polling as long as both conditions are satisfied:

  • running is true.
  • The current thread has not been interrupted.

During each iteration, the connector invokes processAvailableEvents().

This method retrieves available CDC events from the source database, processes them, and returns the updated last processed event ID.

The returned value is used in the next polling iteration.

We'll examine the event retrieval and processing logic in Section 5.5.

4. Controlling the Polling Interval 

Thread.sleep(POLLING_INTERVAL_MS);

After processing the currently available events, the connector waits for the configured polling interval before starting another polling cycle.

In our demonstration:

cdc.polling.interval.ms=2000

This means the connector waits for two seconds between polling cycles.

The polling interval controls how frequently the connector checks for newly available events when the current batch of available events has been processed.

5. Handling Thread Interruption 

catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    running = false;
}

If the polling thread is interrupted while sleeping, the connector handles the interruption by:
