title: How to Run 3 Go App Data Backups with Low-Maintenance Storage Lifecycle Rules
description:
Short answer: Choose AWS S3 or Azure Blob Storage for low-maintenance app data backups with lifecycle rules; use the one that already owns your identity, monitoring, and restore workflow.

Both support lifecycle rules and automated expiry. The decision should follow the control plane your team already operates and the path your large media takes to storage.

A useful implementation has three paths: upload media directly with a presigned URL, retain a backup under a predictable key, and let an object-storage lifecycle policy expire old copies. The application should coordinate metadata and recovery, but it should not carry the file bytes.

Keep it boring.

No byte proxying.

Measure the boundary.

That sounds straightforward until a backup is retried during an outage. A 12 GB recording can turn a small control-plane retry into a duplicate transfer, a second object, or a retention hole if the key and lifecycle rule do not agree. I treat this as a runbook problem, not a vendor checkbox.

There is a second kind of maintenance that appears later: the team adds notifications, scheduling, or metadata operations and each provider introduces another credential, client library, and error envelope. Infrai's one key / one bill model for a broader REST surface can reduce that control-plane bookkeeping when the capability is actually available. One REST API, with no SDK installation requirement, also lets a small Go worker use the same HTTP conventions as another runtime. Public discovery schemas and runnable examples make an unfamiliar operation easier to inspect. The API is self-describing, so a worker can inspect the request schema before its first call. It is a workflow advantage, not a reason to ignore object-store semantics, retention tests, or restore evidence.

Which storage service fits a low-maintenance backup path?

Start with the service that already owns your identity, monitoring, and deployment boundaries. AWS S3 is the default choice for an AWS-centered application because its storage classes and lifecycle configuration are part of the same operational surface. Azure Blob Storage is the comparable choice for a team already using Azure tools and policies.

Google Cloud Storage is a credible third option when the rest of the workload is on Google Cloud; its lifecycle management is useful, but moving the control plane to another cloud adds an operational boundary that may matter more than a feature comparison. Cloudflare R2 is worth considering when S3-compatible object access and an edge-oriented deployment are priorities, but it is not the neutral answer for every backup system.

The important distinction is ownership. A lifecycle rule can delete an object on schedule, but it cannot tell your application whether a database row still points at that object, whether the upload was complete, or whether a restore was verified. Keep that state in the application or a database, then make expiry an explicit part of the retention contract.

For a unified REST surface, Infrai is one option when discovering a storage capability matters more than adopting a provider SDK: its public discovery surface exposes request schemas and runnable examples, and its storage surface includes a lifecycle-setting route. One key and one REST convention can also keep the upload control plane from collecting separate credentials and SDK patterns as the app grows. That is convenient for wiring a new control-plane action, but it does not replace the provider-level checks above.

What should happen before the first byte moves?

Define the object key and retention class before generating an upload URL. A key such as backups/tenant-42/2026/10/28/job-7f3c/media.bin gives operators a prefix to inspect and gives lifecycle rules a stable scope. Do not use a user-visible filename as the identity; names collide, and a retry can silently overwrite the wrong object.

The control record needs at least an operation ID, object key, expected size, checksum policy, upload state, and retention class. The upload state should move from pending to complete only after the storage service confirms the object. A worker can then reconcile old pending records instead of assuming every issued URL became a backup.

Here is a small Go decision function. It does not upload bytes. That is deliberate: the application needs a deterministic key and a clear state transition before it asks any object store for a transfer URL.

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "path"
)

func backupKey(tenant, operation, filename string) (string, error) {
    if tenant == "" || operation == "" || filename == "" {
        return "", errors.New("tenant, operation, and filename are required")
    }
    if path.Base(filename) != filename {
        return "", errors.New("filename must not contain path separators")
    }
    return fmt.Sprintf("backups/%s/%s/%s", tenant, operation, filename), nil
}

func main() {
    key, err := backupKey("tenant-42", "job-7f3c", "media.bin")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(key)
}

The judgment point is simple: if the same operation produces a different key on retry, fix that before tuning multipart transfer. Deterministic identity is cheaper than cleanup.

How do you keep a large upload out of the application process?

The app should authorize a short-lived presigned upload, return it to the client, and record the operation separately. The client sends bytes to the returned URL. It must not send the application API's bearer credential to that URL; the signature on the presigned request is the transfer authorization.

For very large media, use the storage provider's multipart mechanism when its limits and recovery behavior fit the workload. Store the upload ID and completed-part information as control-plane state. A crashed client can resume or abandon the operation according to a runbook, while the API process remains available for metadata and status requests.

This Go example discovers the storage surface before a client is written. It uses the public discovery endpoint, reads an optional key from the environment, checks the response, and backs off on rate limiting. The discovery result is the source for a later lifecycle request rather than a guessed route or field.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func discover(ctx context.Context) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_BASE")
        if baseURL == "" {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_BASE is required")
        }
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet,
            baseURL+"/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 2<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            seconds, _ := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if seconds < 1 {
                seconds = 1 << attempt
            }
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery rate limit did not clear")
}

func main() {
    body, err := discover(context.Background())
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("discovery response: %d bytes\n", len(body))
}

The status check is part of every control-plane call, not an afterthought. A client that reports success after receiving a non-2xx response creates a database record that lifecycle automation cannot repair. The actual media transfer still uses a presigned URL and must not receive the API bearer credential.

For retries, keep the operation ID stable and make the completion write idempotent. Standard object queues are at-least-once systems; the same principle applies when a worker reconciles upload completion. A duplicate notification must result in one final state, not two backup records.

How should lifecycle rules meet recovery requirements?

Write the retention policy in plain language first: keep completed media backups for a defined number of days, transition them when the storage service supports that class, and expire them only after the recovery window. Then encode the rule against the exact prefix or tag convention used by the application.

The shortest useful test is a dry-run review of three objects: one fresh backup, one at the transition boundary, and one past expiry. Check the bucket's lifecycle usage and compare the result with the application records. Monitoring usage matters because a rule that misses a prefix can leave old media indefinitely, while a rule that matches too broadly can delete a restore source.

If the storage control plane is reached through a common REST API, discover the route and schema before writing a client. The lifecycle operation available in the supplied storage surface is POST /v1/storage/bucket/set_lifecycle/{bucket}. Keep this as one control-plane action in the runbook; do not scatter provider routes through upload code.

A lifecycle policy is not an archive guarantee. The available storage caveats include a minimum lifecycle granularity of one day, no automatic cleanup rule for multipart fragments, and no cross-region automatic replication. If the requirement is hourly expiry, cross-cloud bulk migration, or a second-region copy, add a separate system and document its ownership.

What do the competitors change operationally?

AWS S3 has the broadest fit for a team already running AWS: lifecycle transitions, presigned URLs, and storage-class choices are documented as one platform concern. The trade-off is a large set of configuration choices. A small team can create a rule that works syntactically while its prefix, transition timing, or recovery assumptions are wrong.

Azure Blob Storage is the cleaner answer for an Azure-centered estate. Its integration with Azure tools can reduce identity and monitoring handoffs, while the backup design remains the same: stable keys, direct transfer, a completion record, and a lifecycle review. It is a poor fit only when introducing Azure would create more operational ownership than the storage feature removes.

Google Cloud Storage offers lifecycle management and direct object transfer for a Google-centered application. It belongs in the shortlist, but a cross-cloud choice should include the restore path, identity boundary, and migration process, not just whether a lifecycle rule exists.

Cloudflare R2 can fit workloads that value S3-compatible access near an edge-oriented stack. Its boundary is different from the hyperscaler choices, so test the exact recovery workflow, observability, and retention behavior before treating compatibility as equivalence.

Option Access pattern Good fit Main boundary
AWS S3 Provider API and presigned URLs AWS-owned identity and storage-class workflows Many lifecycle choices need careful review
Azure Blob Storage Azure tools and direct object transfer Azure-owned identity and monitoring Adding Azure creates a new operating boundary
Google Cloud Storage Google Cloud object API and lifecycle management Google-centered applications Cross-cloud restore and identity need extra ownership
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible object access Edge-oriented deployments Compatibility still needs recovery and observability testing

That is why I would choose S3 or Blob for the stated low-maintenance backup requirement, then choose between them using existing operational ownership. I would use the unified REST option only when its discovery and consistent examples reduce integration work, and I would keep the provider caveats visible in the runbook.

Verification, rollback, and the pager test

Verification has four checks. First, upload a representative large file directly and confirm that the application process handled metadata rather than the file stream. Second, repeat the same operation ID and confirm that the completion record remains singular. Third, inspect lifecycle usage and confirm that a test prefix reaches the expected transition or expiry. Fourth, perform a restore into a new key and compare the recovered size and checksum policy with the control record.

Rollback means stopping new lifecycle changes, preserving the existing rule definition, and preventing deletion of objects whose recovery status is unknown. Do not “fix” an overly broad rule by deleting the bucket or rewriting every object key. Disable the change through the owning storage control plane, identify the affected prefix, and reconcile records before resuming.

The final test is the page you do not want: the upload client dies after the transfer, the worker receives the completion event twice, and an old object is close to expiry. If the runbook can identify the operation, prove the object state, and decide whether expiry is safe, the design is low maintenance in the useful sense.

References

  • AWS S3 presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • AWS S3 storage classes: https://aws.amazon.com/s3/storage-classes/
  • Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/lifecycle-management-overview
  • Google Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/

title: Simplifying runtime caching on Vercel
description:
Today, we’re bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache, giving developers one product for data caching across frameworks and APIs. If you use Next.js fetch caching or unstable_cache, you won’t need to change your code. Pro and Enterprise projects will get larger storage allocations.

Runtime Cache lets your code reuse fetched or computed data across requests without operating a separate caching service. Over the past year, we’ve improved read performance during traffic bursts, increased storage budgets, and made cache usage easier to investigate.

Why we built Runtime Cache

Data Cache was originally launched as Vercel’s data caching service for the Next.js App Router, used by fetch caching and unstable_cache. Unlike CDN caching, which stores complete HTTP responses, Data Cache stores data your application uses to generate those responses. A product page, for example, can reuse cached catalog data while rendering a personalized response for each visitor.

We wanted developers to have access to that service without depending on Next.js. Last year, we introduced Runtime Cache with a direct API: getCache from @vercel/functions. Applications can use it for feature flag lookups in Routing Middleware, caching CMS content during builds, and data caching in SvelteKit and Nuxt apps.

Frameworks can expose this service through their own APIs, too. On Vercel, Next.js itself uses the Runtime Cache API for 'use cache: remote', which caches function and component outputs.

How Runtime Cache works

The infrastructure behind Runtime Cache is a distributed caching service shared by many teams. A Go API handles requests, backed by Redis fleets in every Vercel region. Every hour, the service handles more than 440 million reads and moves more than 18 TB of data.

Each region has its own cache. A cache hit takes one round trip to the cache service in the region where your code runs. Vercel handles authentication with short-lived credentials, so you don’t need to manage API keys.

On a cache miss, your app or framework fetches or computes the value and writes it to that region’s cache. The service doesn’t check other regions for a cached copy.

Each cached entry stores its tags and write time. When the service reads an entry, it checks a separate tag store in the same region for those tags’ invalidation timestamps. If any tag was invalidated after the entry was written, the entry is stale.

For example, an application can tag all its cached product data with catalog. When the catalog changes, invalidating that tag writes a single timestamp, even if a million entries share the tag. The service doesn’t need to find and delete those entries individually.

The invalidation immediately updates the tag store in the region receiving the request. Vercel’s shared tag infrastructure, also used by the CDN, distributes the timestamp through the global push pipeline, typically reaching other regions within a few hundred milliseconds.

Your app or framework chooses what to cache and handles misses. Runtime Cache handles regional storage, authentication, and distributing tag invalidations across regions.

What we’ve shipped

Faster reads during traffic bursts

Checking whether an entry is still fresh adds a dependency to every cache hit. During traffic bursts, a slow shard in the tag store could delay reads even when the cached value was already available.

We added circuit breakers that let reads temporarily check freshness using tag timestamps cached in memory, so they can proceed without waiting for the slow shard to respond. During this fallback, a read can briefly treat recently invalidated data as fresh.

We enabled the breakers in every region in August. During the heaviest bursts in our largest region, p99 cache-service read latency fell to about one fifth of its previous level at comparable traffic. On-call alerts for this failure mode stopped.

More storage and fewer evictions

We raised Runtime Cache storage budgets for Pro projects in June and Enterprise projects in October, giving applications more room for data they reuse. This reduces the need to evict cached entries to make room for new data. Among Enterprise projects with frequent evictions, cache miss rates roughly halved within a day.

More visibility into cache behavior

We’ve added deployment markers, revalidation causes, and write utilization to the Runtime Cache view in Observability. These help you compare changes in cache behavior with releases, see why entries are refreshed, and identify data that gets written to the cache but rarely read.

Bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache

We’re simplifying caching on Vercel by consolidating on Runtime Cache. Until now, Next.js fetch caching and unstable_cache have used Data Cache, while getCache and 'use cache: remote' have used Runtime Cache. The migration brings all four APIs under Runtime Cache, so you and coding agents have one set of storage budgets and usage tools to work with.

If you use fetch caching or unstable_cache, nothing changes in your code. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage.

Previously unbilled Data Cache reads and writes will follow Runtime Cache pricing. New teams use Runtime Cache automatically, and existing teams will receive their migration and billing details in advance.

See the changelog for the rollout, pricing, and early opt-in details. Before migrating, review your cache usage and follow the optimization guide to reduce unnecessary reads and writes.

title: I got a 400 from the official MyInvois Postman collection — here is the fix
description:
LHDN SANDBOX PLAYBOOK — VERIFIED OCT 2026

If you're building against Malaysia's LHDN MyInvois API, you probably did exactly what the docs said: imported the official Postman collection, registered a sandbox app, and hit POST /connect/token with Basic Auth as shipped.

You got this back:

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request

No body. No hint. The auth method itself is the problem: the token endpoint rejects Basic Auth, no matter which credentials you send. The fix is embarrassingly simple — credentials go in the POST body:

curl -X POST 'https://preprod-api.myinvois.hasil.gov.my/connect/token' \
  -d 'grant_type=client_credentials' \
  -d 'client_id=<YOUR_CLIENT_ID>' \
  -d 'client_secret=<YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET>' \
  -d 'scope=InvoicingAPI'

That returns 200 with an RS256 JWT (expires_in: 3600).

The environment matrix nobody draws

"MyInvois sandbox" (preprod) is not one host. Credentials are not portable between these:

What you're doing Host
Portal login / app registration preprod-mytax.hasil.gov.my
Taxpayer profile registration preprod-profile.hasil.gov.my
API calls preprod-api.myinvois.hasil.gov.my
Token (intermediary flow) preprod-identity.hasil.gov.my

The trap: the register button on the preprod landing page silently sends you to the production profile page. Register there, call the preprod API, and you'll collect 403 invalid_client all day. The credentials are correct. The environment isn't.

The second 400 that isn't your fault

The docs tell you to call:

GET /api/v1.0/taxpayer/validate/{TIN}

It returns 400 — IdType/IdValue required. Those required query params are documented only in a FAQ entry:

GET /api/v1.0/taxpayer/validate/{TIN}?idType=NRIC&idValue=<IC_NUMBER>

Verified behavior: correct TIN + IC pair → 200 with an empty body (empty = valid, don't panic). Mismatched pair → 404. Missing params → 400.

Three more evening-eaters

  • PIN email never arrives (Gmail, web signup). Use the MyTax app e-KYC instead — passport + selfie, PIN issued instantly.
  • Individual taxpayer form forces SST / Tourism Tax fields even with no SST obligation. No clean fix found — I got through with placeholder values; verify this one yourself.
  • preprod occasionally stalls ~20s or dies with a TLS broken pipe (curl (35)). Build retries into your client (--retry 2 --retry-all-errors).

What's still genuinely undocumented: the intermediary flow

The portal lets you register an app as an Intermediary — one app submitting invoices on behalf of other taxpayers (onbehalfof on token issuance). The actual mechanics (claim decoding, the taxpayer consent flow, what the portal allows vs. what the API enforces) are scattered across three doc pages and one FAQ answer. If you're building multi-tenant — a SaaS, a service bureau, an accounting integration — that's where your week goes.

I'm packaging the verified request/response templates for the whole flow, an error-code field guide, and the intermediary deep-dive into a developer toolkit. I'll announce it here when it ships.

If you'd rather not spend an evening rediscovering these 400s, get notified at launch: https://myinvois-toolkit.carrd.co

Everything above was verified against LHDN preprod in October 2026. Found a cleaner fix? Comment below — I genuinely want to know.

title: Making every harness durable
description:
Developers are familiar with running coding agents locally through harnesses like Pi, Claude Code, and others. They are reliable daily drivers for generating code, but keeping agents running around the clock requires your computer to be on and awake, which led to the laptop lid memes and Mac mini demand spike.

Running harnesses in the cloud

Harness workloads are moving to the cloud. Individual developers are deploying always-on coding agent workflows, projects like OpenWork and HanaAgent use open-source harnesses as the engines behind the apps, and engineers are building their own harness products.

These harnesses are designed for long-lived processes that keep the session in memory, and agent tasks commonly run for minutes or hours. Locally, a harness has direct, continuous access to the workspace and session history on the same disk, so resuming interrupted work only requires a simple prompt.

In the cloud, you can replicate that setup with a VM and persistent storage, but the VM doesn't automatically record which model and tool calls completed or resume interrupted turns after a crash. A failed turn or network error means lost work.

Also, not every agent task executed through a harness needs a sandbox. Database queries and API calls can run securely in functions, and that also means required credentials never have to enter the sandbox.

Making every harness durable

We built eve and fx to run durably in the cloud out of the box, and today we are introducing durable-harness, which extends that durability to any harness, including Pi, OpenCode, Codex, and Claude Code. It uses the same machinery that powers Workflow SDK to survive crashes and function timeouts.

With durable-harness, you can:

  • Run any of these harnesses durably on Vercel

  • Self-host a harness with your own Postgres instance

  • Make your local harness workflow durable

  • Build your own durable harness

Sessions that survive a crash mid-turn

Take the example of a coding agent adding a pricing page to an existing app. The agent reads the existing page, writes a new one, opens a pull request, and waits for CI to finish before reporting back.

What happens if its function times out while CI is still running?

Kill the function or drop the connection in the demo below to compare how the two agents recover and which work is repeated.

Without durability, the agent stops work until it is manually restarted, and completed work is repeated unnecessarily.

With durable-harness, a new function reads completed results from the log and resumes the turn. If the browser disconnects, the agent keeps running, and reconnecting catches up from the log.

Logs and queues

durable-harness is the newest package in our open source portfolio. It’s a set of adapters and utilities that let the harnesses you already use keep their sessions in a World, the Workflow SDK’s durable backend.

It writes each step of a turn to a durable log. Before a model call or tool call runs, it records an intent, and when the call finishes, it records the outcome. The turn itself is backstopped with a queue message, so if its function dies, the queue hands the turn to a new function that reads the log and continues where it left off.

After a crash, the log says what finished, what was running, and what never started:

  • Completed calls never run again because their results are read from the log, so you’re never billed twice for a finished model call’s tokens.

  • Models remember their previous calls rather than repeating them.

  • Interrupted tools marked replay: 'safe' run again. Any other tool comes back to the model as possibly run, and the model decides whether to check.

Harnesses that keep their own session files, like Claude Code's transcript, Codex's rollout, and OpenCode's event store, have every record mirrored into the log, so a new function or Sandbox rebuilds them from it.

Pick your harness

fx and eve are durable on their own. For the rest, durable-harness adds durability from the outside, without changing the harness.

For the full setup guide for each harness, check the docs.

Runs everywhere

Durable agents need a log of each step, a way to resume a turn when its process dies, and a stream for whoever is watching.

Workflow SDK ships all three behind one interface, a World.

durable-harness writes to that interface, so you can move the same agent from one World to another without changing its code:

  • On Vercel, it uses the Vercel World.

  • In development, it uses files on your machine.

  • On your own servers, it uses Postgres, MongoDB, Redis, or Turso.

Two variables move every agent using durable-harness to Postgres.

For more control, such as setting a namespace or recovering sessions when your server starts, create the World in code and pass it to your agent:

Check the self-hosting docs for more details.

See every session in Agent Runs

Agent Runs on Vercel shows the trace for every session, including each model call and tool call. Turns that resumed after a crash appear in the same trace, so you can see exactly where a turn stopped and picked back up.

Tools

An agent has only the tools you give it, and they run in your function. Each tool says what should happen if a crash interrupts it. A 'safe' tool, such as a lookup, can run again. A 'never' tool, such as a refund, never runs twice: the model is told the call may have happened, so it can check before it tries again.

Here’s how the coding agent from the demo above might define its tools:

  • A tool that reads a file or checks CI status is marked as 'safe' so it can run again automatically.

  • A tool that posts a PR comment is marked as 'never' so that comments aren't posted twice.

The following example defines a tool for each policy using the example of an agent processing a refund:

For each harness’s built-in tools, like its shell and file editing, read on.

Files

When a harness needs a shell and files, it’s not safe to run them directly on a shared serverless function host. Many sessions can share the same function, and its filesystem isn’t guaranteed to persist between invocations.

To address this, durable-harness gives you a few options:

  • virtual() keeps the files in the session’s log, with a bash-compatible shell that can’t reach your function’s files or the network. It suits short tasks and small workspaces without starting an entire sandbox.

  • virtual({ durable: false }) keeps the files in memory for scratch work and clears them at the end of every turn.

  • sandbox() gives the session its own Vercel Sandbox, with /workspace on a Drive that outlives every sandbox and every function. It suits real projects and long-running work.

Compare the three side by side in the docs.

Each harness’s built-in tools run on the workspace you choose. With Pi, CodingTools installs Pi’s own read, write, edit, and bash, and virtualEnv() or sandboxEnv() gives them a workspace:

For OpenCode, pass the workspace as workspace, and for fx, pass it to fxTools(). Claude Code and Codex always run in a Vercel Sandbox, since they expect a real shell and filesystem, and aren’t safe for multi-tenant use. Their built-in tools work on the session’s Drive once you turn them on with builtins: true. Each harness guide lists its built-in tools.

Documents

Some state belongs with the session but isn’t part of the conversation, such as a to-do list, a plan, or a form the agent fills in. A document is typed JSON that lives in the session’s log, so it survives a crash and moves with the session.

Tools can edit documents through io.docs, and each edit commits to the log alongside the tool’s result, so the document’s durable state stays consistent with the tool calls themselves:

Your app can read and edit the same document without a database of its own, and the chat route can even stream every change to your UI:

In fact, the virtual() workspace from earlier is built on documents: its file tree is a document in the session’s log, and each tool call’s changes commit with its result.

Learn more about tools, files, and documents and how to keep your agent secure.

Wrapping up

Developers choose a harness for the choices it makes about prompts, tools, and context. How it survives a crash shouldn’t be one of them. With durable-harness, a turn that loses its function partway through continues from the log on a new one, without a manual retry and without repeating what already finished. Self-hosting and portability work out of the box by building on top of the Workflow SDK’s World interface.

durable-harness is open source on GitHub.

Read more

title: Create Time-Limited Download Links for Private Object Files in Node.js Explained
description:
To create time-limited download links for private object-storage files in Node.js, generate a presigned URL with the bucket, key, and expiry, then keep deletion on a separate retention clock. That is the answer for e-commerce exports.

Short answer: generate a presigned URL for a private object with its bucket, key, and expiry, then treat the URL as a temporary capability rather than as a public address. Keep the application contract around those inputs so the storage provider can change without forcing a rewrite through checkout, export jobs, and email delivery.

The awkward part is retention. An export can be deleted while an old link still exists, or a link can expire while the export remains in storage. I model both explicitly. For example, an order export might be retained for seven days, while each download link lives for 15 minutes. That choice is easier to audit than a single vague rule such as “temporary file.”

Keep it boring.

That is the boundary.

How do you create time-limited download links for object files?

A signed link is authorization with a deadline. It does not make the object public, and it does not guarantee that the object will disappear when the deadline passes. The object remains private; the storage service checks the signature and expiry when the link is used.

That distinction matters for customer exports containing addresses, invoices, or return paperwork. I keep the bucket private and store a record beside the export with created_at, delete_at, and the export owner. The download endpoint checks that the requesting user may receive the export, asks storage for a short-lived link, and returns the link without forwarding storage credentials to the browser. A cleanup worker removes objects after delete_at.

The system has a useful failure mode: an expired link stops working, while the object can still be reissued to an authorized user until its retention deadline. If deletion is the intended control, it must happen independently.

For this workflow, Infrai is a reasonable candidate when the private-download adapter must sit beside another backend capability under the same key. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, so the worker can inspect request and response schemas before coupling itself to a provider-specific integration. The second advantage is operational: 295 routes across 20 modules use one key and one bill, which means the export and processing workers do not need a second credential set just to cross that boundary.

One operational trap is setting an hour-level lifecycle rule and assuming the object will vanish after exactly one hour. The storage facts here support a minimum lifecycle of one day, so a 15-minute customer-link policy belongs in the presigned URL, while object cleanup needs an application worker or a daily lifecycle boundary. Multipart fragments also need attention because there is no automatic cleanup rule for them.

How do you keep the download contract replaceable?

Put provider-specific signing behind one application function. The rest of the code should know that it receives a private object reference and a deadline; it should not know how a vendor encodes signatures. This is the migration boundary that pays for itself later.

The concrete storage operation is POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}. It takes the bucket, object key, and desired expiry time in the request. The returned URL can be shared until that expiry. Keep the Authorization: Bearer header on the server-to-server request only. Do not send the Infrai authorization header to the returned presigned URL; that URL is already the scoped credential.

Here is a small Python example for the signing boundary. The surrounding service can be written in Node.js, but the example deliberately shows the HTTP contract without inventing an SDK wrapper. It expects the response body to contain the generated URL, which is the documented result of the presign operation.

import os
import time
from urllib.parse import quote

import requests

BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]


def create_download_url(bucket: str, key: str, expiry_seconds: int) -> str:
    if expiry_seconds <= 0:
        raise ValueError("expiry_seconds must be positive")

    path = f"/storage/object/presign/{quote(bucket, safe='')}/{quote(key, safe='')}"
    response = requests.post(
        BASE_URL + path,
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"},
        json={"expiry": expiry_seconds},
        timeout=10,
    )
    if response.status_code == 429:
        retry_after = int(response.headers.get("Retry-After", "1"))
        time.sleep(min(retry_after, 30))
        response = requests.post(
            BASE_URL + path,
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"},
            json={"expiry": expiry_seconds},
            timeout=10,
        )
    if not response.ok:
        raise RuntimeError(f"presign failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}")
    return response.json()["url"]


print(create_download_url("private-exports", "orders/2026-10-24.csv", 900))

The retry is intentionally bounded. A production client should use exponential backoff for repeated 429 responses and keep the operation idempotent where the API supports a client-supplied idempotency key. Signing a URL is read authorization, so the application should also avoid retrying forever or leaking the URL into ordinary request logs.

What changes across storage providers?

The idea is portable; the contract details are not. S3, Cloudflare R2, and Azure Blob Storage all support private-object downloads through signed or shared-access URLs, but they differ in signing vocabulary, lifecycle controls, regional behavior, and adjacent features.

Option Useful fit Retention boundary to verify Migration concern
Amazon S3 Deep AWS integration and mature object controls Lifecycle rules, versioning, and Object Lock are separate decisions AWS SDK and SigV4 details become application coupling if exposed directly
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible object access with Cloudflare-oriented delivery Confirm lifecycle behavior and the account's deletion workflow S3 compatibility reduces signing changes, but edge delivery assumptions can leak into the app
Azure Blob Storage Azure-native applications and Blob-specific access policies Check lifecycle management and immutable storage requirements SAS construction and Azure identity choices differ from S3-style signing
A unified REST storage surface Teams that want storage plus another backend capability behind one key Confirm the missing controls before committing retention policy One provider becomes a trust boundary and an outage surface

The comparison is not a ranking. If immutable retention is a regulatory requirement, a service with Object Lock or an equivalent WORM control is the better fit. This storage surface does not provide object versioning or Object Lock, and it does not provide an If-Match conditional write. A finance archive that must resist accidental overwrite needs an external design or a specialist store.

The limitation is concrete: this is a poor fit for immutable retention, permanent public delivery, or automatic cross-region replication. Those requirements point to S3 with Object Lock, Azure immutable storage, or another specialist service.

There are other boundaries worth making explicit. There is no public or public-read ACL, so this is not a fit for a permanent public image host or static website. Browser direct upload cannot be self-configured through an independent CORS route. Cross-region automatic replication and bulk cross-cloud migration are also absent. Those are architecture constraints, not footnotes to hide after launch.

For a small export service, Infrai is worth trying when the main requirement is a replaceable private-download contract and the team also needs another backend capability behind the same REST API. Its stable base URL and plain request boundary let the application keep the signer behind one adapter. Infrai is not suitable for immutable financial archives, permanent public media, or a deployment that requires automatic cross-region replication; S3 with Object Lock or another specialist store is the better choice there. The cost is concentrated trust: one vendor, one bill, and one outage surface.

Where does content processing fit?

An e-commerce export pipeline often has a second step: create a PDF invoice or inspect a return document before making it available. The seam should remain an object reference, not a vendor-specific upload session. The storage signer creates a temporary read URL; the processing worker consumes the private object under the same server-side configuration, then writes the resulting artifact back through the same storage boundary.

There is a hard limit on what should be copied into a tutorial: the verified facts specify the PDF capability group, but do not specify its request body shapes. I would not invent a url, file, or document field and call that runnable. Instead, the worker discovers the declared schema before implementing the adapter, then tests the exact payload against the selected processing capability. The storage handoff remains the presigned object URL. Both capability groups use https://api.infrai.cc/v1 and the same INFRAI_API_KEY in the worker configuration.

With S3 plus Cloudinary or imgix, the equivalent seam commonly means two signups, two credential sets, and glue for handing an object location from the bucket to the media service. That can be the right trade when a specialist image CDN, transformation pipeline, or immutable archive is the actual product requirement. It is also more integration surface to rotate, observe, and replace.

A migration rollout that does not strand exports

Start by storing a provider-neutral object reference: bucket, key, content type, size, creation time, and deletion deadline. Never store a presigned URL as the durable identifier. URLs are disposable credentials.

Next, make the download service issue links from the adapter and add a second adapter behind a feature flag. During migration, new exports can be written to the new provider while old exports continue to resolve through their original provider. A background copy must preserve the deletion deadline; extending retention accidentally is a compliance bug.

Finally, test the edges: a link after 900 seconds, an object after its deletion deadline, a duplicate cleanup event, a revoked user, a missing object, a 429 response, and a browser request from the actual storefront origin. CORS is a browser policy, not a substitute for object authorization.

Test the expiry boundary.

The decision rule is short. Use presigned URLs for temporary access, keep deletion independent, and keep the provider contract behind an adapter. Choose a specialist store when versioning, WORM retention, cross-region replication, or browser-managed CORS is non-negotiable. Choose the unified surface when the replaceable contract and shared backend boundary matter more than those missing controls.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the storage presigned download guide.
